about: Coach rewrites and verdicts from the coaching calls, for the engine to show a case the closest few. Student emails and rewrites are reconstructions of what was on screen and said: learn the move, never copy the words. Built by comms/example_bank.py; do not edit by hand.

entries.situation: Student reads a long follow-up email to a brand that pitches an additional creator in detail.
entries.student_email: We're also working with this guy whose review combined humor with real life situation. His audience can easily relate to name integration and written to flow naturally with the rest of video.
entries.points: Follow-ups must be short (maximum three short sentences, or about one-third the length of the initial email) and act as a low-friction reminder that directs the prospect back to your first email rather than pitching a whole new offer.
entries.rewrite: Hey, I know things might get busy. I'm just checking in case you missed my last email. We pitched a good creator, maybe you should check it.

quote.quote: I'm just checking in case you missed my last email. We'll pitch some good creator. Maybe you should check it. You know, something like that. Obviously, not exactly like that, but in that, Insha Allah, in that style.

entries.situation: Student reads five cold emails to 2M+ DIY creators that use statement subject lines ('the wind is at your back', 'Hey, careful with that cactus', 'Well done with Altium'), one-sentence personalizations, bridge lines placed inside the personalization paragraph, and offers promising specific brands ('good fit for eGizmo or Banggood', 'proposing you for our next campaign', 'about to reach out to brands').
entries.student_email:
Email 1: Subject: Hey, Dawud, the wind is at your back.
Recreate an actual wind is an original challenge. Speaking of challenges, mine is to find brands for DIY creators. You have no sponsors in your last video, but I think your content would be a good fit for eGizmo or Banggood. Are you interested?
Email 2: Subject: what did this red boat do to you?
Your red painted boat squishes in your video, makes me want to try my next sprint with TPU. What I also want to try is to find you a new sponsor. I think your channel will fit with brands this and this. Are you interested?
Email 3: Subject: Hey, careful with that cactus.
The cactus you bring makes me think about dusting off my 3D printer. What I'm also thinking about is proposing you for our next campaign. We are about to reach out to brands like X and Y.
Email 4: Subject: Well done with Altium.
I liked your smooth integration of Altium in your last video. For that reason, I'd like to propose you for our next campaign. I'm about to reach out to brands like PCBWay, DFRobot, and others for sponsorships. And I think you are a good fit. Are you interested?
Email 5: Subject: you just create a new YouTube category
That soldering ASMR in your last video is honey to my ears. And now hopefully, what's honey for you is looking for creators like yourself for our next sponsorship campaign.
entries.points: Turn statement subject lines into curiosity questions without giving away the video subject (e.g., 'What did it do to you?' instead of 'What did this red boat do to you?', or 'Did you really make it?'). Make the personalization longer than one sentence, place the bridge line as the first line of the offer paragraph rather than the end of the personalization, and never promise specific brands, say 'for our next campaign' (which triggers questions about budget, talking points, timeframe, and usage rights), or say 'we are about to reach out to brands' (which makes you look unready).
entries.rewrite:
Subject line 2 rewrite: What did it do to you?
Subject line 5 rewrite: Did you really do it? / Did you really make it?

quote.quote: What I'm also thinking about is proposing you for our next campaign. This is dangerous, because they will, this basically opens door to new questions. Let me draw doors real quick. Here are doors. Boom, boom. That is budget, talking points, time frame, usage rights

entries.situation: Student submits three outdoor brand initial outreach emails and two follow-ups, asking if 'Hey' is okay for brands, whether to add extra creator value in Follow-up 1, and showing Follow-up 2 pitching a different specific creator.
entries.student_email:
Initial 1: Subject: Wouldn't you agree, [Name]?
Hi [First Name], nice to see [Brand] getting global recognition for its influencer work. Congrats to the team behind this milestone. While we are on the topic of collaboration, I partner with this travel creator, whose cinematic hiking content turns the destination into stories. With up to 7% engagement, I can see [Brand] fitting naturally into his next journey. Should I send a proposal?
Follow-up 1: Curious how this landed with you. I also wanted to flag one more thing about this guy: his previous pre-workout collab sparked comments about putting the brand logo on his parachute because of how many people loved it.
Initial 2: Subject: Hey [Name], your take
I noticed [Brand] making a strong move into golf and outdoor sports... I'm working with this guy, a creator who tests products in real adventures. His last collab hit 146,000 views, 10% engagement and reached a 94% US audience.
Follow-up 2: I wanted to bring another creator to your attention. We teamed up with this guy... reaching viewers aged [X-Y].
entries.points: Saying 'Hey' to brands is fine, and the initial emails are strong because they use concrete case studies and tailored metrics (7% engagement, 146,000 views, 10% engagement, 94% US audience, viewer comments asking about gear). However, say 'we are working with' instead of 'I'm working with' to represent an agency, A/B test a hyper-short version against the current length, keep Follow-up 1 as a simple reminder without extra creator details, and in Follow-up 2 mention your broader creator roster in that sub-niche rather than pitching a single replacement creator that undermines your first offer.

quote.quote: I'm working with this guy, stick with, we are working, because we are agency, a creator who tests products in real adventures, his last collab hit 146,000 views, 10% and reach out 94% US audience, this is nice, bro, case studies

entries.situation: An Inner Circle student shares the unpersonalized outreach email he sent to a talent agency when he already had a brand campaign on hand, stating the brand name, deliverable, and month upfront.
entries.student_email: high team, hope you're doing well, we're currently working with X brand, and the onboarding for our campaign. Would you be interested in exploring a 60 to 92nd integration in December?
entries.points: When you have a real brand campaign on hand, stating the brand name, specific deliverable, and timeline upfront works well even without personalization. Although leading with curiosity might get a higher reply rate, laying everything out acts as an automatic filter so anyone who replies is already onboard with the brand, integration, and timeline.

quote.quote: once you do get a reply, you know the guy is down for the integration, know he's down for the timeline, and you know he's down for the brand, so it's like an automatic filter

entries.situation: A student pitches two UK home renovation creators to a heater brand, citing a 'combined US-UK audience share of 63% and 11% engagement rate' and asking 'Would you like me to send over their analytics?'
entries.student_email: Subject: Can drying walls get any easier? Something, something heater integration aligned well with the camper video, and the temperature test officially showcased the strength of something, something heaters. I'm reaching out regarding two UK home renovation creators with a combined US-UK audience share of 63% and 11% engagement rate. The heater lineup would suit their content perfectly, as they often need to quickly dry skimmed or freshly painted walls. Would you like me to send over their analytics?
entries.points: Do not combine US and UK audience percentages into one metric (either group US and Canada or say 'majority English-speaking audience'), actively explain the value of a 10%+ engagement rate by highlighting audience trust and comment activity, and do not ask to send analytics when you already shared metrics in the email.
entries.rewrite: Hey, we are working with these guys, majority of their audience is English-speaking audience, with the outstanding 11% engagement rate.

quote.quote: So, if you have 11%, talk about it, like, a lot of people in comments suggest this, suggest that, they talked about in their last video, they're asking about this, so use that, leverage that engagement rate, because that's a huge selling point

entries.situation: A student's brand email uses 'Influencer X Brand' in the opening line, suggests how the brand should improve its integrations, and vaguely offers creators 'across a range of audience size and engagement levels'.
entries.student_email: Subject: Here's one for you. Hi, first name. Came across [Influencer X Brand] integration. It was well structured, although I do think spending a little more time would show the true value of the insights in a better way. Anyway, we represent creators across a range of audience size and engagement levels. If you're planning upcoming campaigns, I'll be happy to learn more about your goals and suggest creators that align.
entries.points: Include the prospect's first name in the subject line, avoid putting 'Influencer X Brand' in the body opener, save integration suggestions for when you are reviewing a brief, and replace vague 'range of audience sizes' claims with two concrete options (e.g., Option A: high-engagement micro-influencer vs. Option B: larger 300K-view creator) so the brand can simply choose one.
entries.rewrite: Subject: Here's one for you, [First Name]. ... Hey, we have these two ends: Option A is a micro-influencer doing 50K with a crazy engagement rate, or Option B is a bit pricey, but he is averaging 300,000 views. Let me know which you would be interested in, and I can send you more details.

quote.quote: This one, across a range of audience, I would mention two ends, like there is micro-influencer who is doing, I don't know, 50K with crazy engagement rate, right, like option A or option B, he's a bit pricey, but he is averaging 300,000 views

entries.situation: A student reaches out to a construction/DIY creator starting with 'Hello, I love your tips and tricks videos, especially the one with the sawzall...'
entries.student_email: Hello, I love your tips and tricks videos, especially the one with the sawzall where you were using the shim to create some space between the two posts. I'm seeing a lot of potential in this type of content, and I have some brands in mind that are a good fit. Would you be open to it? Thank you.
entries.points: Never start an influencer cold email with 'I love your videos' (which sounds like a fanboy); instead, reference one specific moment from a video and transition immediately into having aligned sponsors ready.
entries.rewrite: I watched the videos, saw that, perfect stuff. By the way, speaking of this, we have sponsors in mind, aligned, ready. What do you think? Let me know.

quote.quote: Just pick one moment. Be like, I watched the videos, saw that, perfect stuff. By the way, we have, speaking of this, we have sponsors in mind, aligned, ready, anything you can. What do you think? Let me know.

entries.situation: A student starts an influencer cold email with 'Good morning', praises their pool house and wooden concrete bench, and ends with a vague offer about spring partnerships.
entries.student_email: Good morning. This pool house is coming together perfectly. And since spring is already here, the addition of that wooden concrete bench gave it so much more detail and color. Speaking of spring, many brands are starting to book creators for partnerships, would you be interested in joining?
entries.points: Never use time-of-day greetings like 'Good morning' or 'Good evening' in cold emails because recipients read emails asynchronously (reserve those for cold calls where latency is zero), and do not follow fan-like praise with a vague offer; tie the specific item (the concrete bench) directly to a sharp offer ('let's concrete a couple of deals').
entries.rewrite: Wooden/concrete, always a good combination, stood out good, you're gonna make me make another one at home. Speaking of concrete, let's concrete a couple of deals. Brands are ready, are you? Let me know.

quote.quote: Good morning, boom, with emails, we're not doing it, the only time when you can say good morning, good evening is cold call, you know, why? Because latency is zero, right?

entries.situation: A student emails a filmmaker named Jack with a good first sentence about Paris, followed by salesy fluff ('The ability to share a unique perspective is why we focus on filmmaking...').
entries.student_email: Subject: Jack, here's an idea. Hey, Jack, it's funny how beautiful Paris looks through the lens of filmmaking and business in the city. The ability to share a unique perspective is why we focus on the filmmaking niche... I believe your content could align well with several of them.
entries.points: Keep the punchy opening observation about Paris, cut the salesy filler explaining why your agency focuses on the niche, and transition straight into naming the brands you are in contact with.
entries.rewrite: Hey, Jack, it's funny how beautiful Paris looks through the lens of filmmaking and business in the city. If you can make Paris beautiful, what about these collaborations? We are in contact with these brands. They are looking for creators like you. Would you be open to partnerships? Best regards, Ammar.

quote.quote: So, be like, okay, if you can make Paris beautiful, what about these collaborations? We are in contact with these brands. They are looking for creators like you.

entries.situation: A student emails a filmmaker referencing their quote 'my lighting sucks, go black and white' and immediately pivots to pitching filmmaking gear brands they are working with.
entries.student_email: Subject: go black and white. 'My lighting sucks, go black and white' - besides being honest, it showcases problem solving during production, as you can't always control the lighting on a shot. Speaking of which, we are looking to help [Brand] and other filmmaking gear brands showcase their products in the hands of creators. I believe your content could fit nicely with them.
entries.points: This email is strong and straight to the point because it links a brief observation about lighting problem-solving directly to named filmmaking gear brands without extra layers of fluff.

quote.quote: go back to this, my brother, this is good email, this is where we spoke, right, this one, not on your offer, no, this one, perfect, this is all I'm looking for

entries.situation: A student opens a brand email by stating they also reached out to a teammate, followed by generic fluff ('their viewers are always interested in what their favorite influencer promotes').
entries.student_email: Subject: Let me know what you think? I reached out to [Name] on your team, but I also think this might be useful for you too. I have a roster of travel influencers ready to promote different travel gears, such as [Product]. Their viewers are always interested in what their favorite influencer promotes, and the majority of their audience watches from the United States.
entries.points: If you mention reaching out to a colleague, place that note at the bottom of the email rather than the opening line, and strip out all 'fairy tale' fluff so busy brand managers and AI inbox filters do not archive your message; if using a LinkedIn personalization (like a promotion), keep it brief, polite, and formal.
entries.rewrite: Subject: Jessica, what do you think of this? Hey Jessica, saw you got promoted. I wish you all the best—to help you get even better results, we have a couple of guys...

quote.quote: They are receiving a lot of emails. Let's assume they are getting 100 emails a day. They have no time to read your emails full of this stuff. Let's call it fluff for now.

entries.situation: A student wrote a cold email to a tech creator ('Jack') about leather vs. metal wrist straps, pitching 'We are onboarding influencers who are looking for sponsorship integrations and dedicated video.'
entries.student_email:
Subject: Jack, you've sold me.

When it comes to wrist straps and choosing between leather and metal, you did sell me on the leather, on leather being unique and molding to your own wrist. We are onboarding influencers who are looking for sponsorship integrations and dedicated video. And you seem to be a fit. Are you open to collaboration with brands like this and this? Cheers, Ahmed.
entries.points: Do not put a period in the subject line, fix punctuation in the personalization, and rephrase 'we are onboarding influencers' to focus on actively helping influencers get sponsorships with specific matching brands.
entries.rewrite: We are actively helping influencers to get more sponsorships. Based on your content, you might be a fit for these and these brands. What do you think?

quote.quote: We are onboarding influencers. Be like, we are actively helping influencers to get more sponsorships. Based on your content, you might be a fit for these and these brands.

entries.situation: A student wrote an outreach email to a creator with the statement subject line 'Jack, there are levels to this' and the closing offer 'These brands feel like a good fit for your content. Let me know your thoughts.'
entries.student_email:
Subject: Jack, there are levels to this

...with and how your sponsorships fit your style of content. We are onboarding influencers to collaborate with brands. These brands feel like a good fit for your content. Let me know your thoughts.
entries.points: Turn the subject line into a question, replace vague offers ('feel like a good fit') with firmer phrasing ('based on your content, these brands would align'), and use a direct question as the CTA.
entries.rewrite: Based on your content, these brands would align. What do you think? Would you be interested?

quote.quote: Let me know your thoughts. Put more pressure on it. You know, based on your content, these brands would align. What do you think? Would you be interested?

entries.situation: A student wrote an email to a creator about skincare and collagen ('Can collagen really help my skin?') using ChatGPT to summarize the video and transition with 'in that case, we have something that can be helpful too'.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Can collagen really help my skin?

I did not realize that skin care can affect your hormones as well until you gave insight into this and the fact that collagen helps skin 75 to 80%. In that case, we have something that can be helpful too... Would this interest [you]?
entries.points: Shorten the subject line to 'Does it really help?', stop using ChatGPT to write emails because it summarizes the entire video and creates nonsensical transitions, and make the transition to partnerships clear and direct.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Does it really help?

...You helped me with my skin, let me help you with partnerships.

quote.quote: in that case, which case, we have something that can be helpful too, so, like collagen, and then we have brands, if they're not collagen bro, don't mention it

entries.situation: A student showed four long follow-up emails to the Japan creator that added new personalization, pitched new brand categories (storybooks, stationery, meditation apps), and claimed 'Q2 starting from March'.
entries.student_email:
Follow-up 1: Hey [first name], following up in case you missed my email. Outside of language, since you use storytelling in your videos, it makes integrating brands like storybooks, stationery and self-growth services like meditation apps very easy...

Follow-up 2: Checking to see if you had time to read my email. We are enlisting creators for quarter two starting from March and want to know...

Follow-up 4: Sorry for the trouble... You end a phone call the Japanese way and we are only opening the doors. Let me know if you're in collaborations. This might not be the perfect time for you. This is my last email to you regarding partnerships.
entries.points: Never make follow-ups longer than the initial email; keep follow-ups as short reminders rather than writing a whole new pitch, keep the final breakup follow-up to one sentence asking to circle back next quarter, and make sure you get calendar quarters right (Q2 starts in April, not March).
entries.rewrite: Since you're not interested in my offer, should I circle back in Q2?

quote.quote: Guys, don't make your follow-up longer than your initial email. Because your initial email. Everything's there. The whole offer and everything, okay?

entries.situation: Omar Katoo shows a draft counteroffer email to a large YouTuber's talent agency (who asked for $60k while the brand offered $20k guaranteed up to 2M views plus a $10 CPM bonus at 40% ROAS capped at $30k).
entries.student_email: In reviewing past partnerships, they found that younger audiences don't tend to convert as effectively, and 40% of the YouTuber's viewership falls into that demographic, so they're unable to justify going up to 60k. Would you be open to coming down to around 35k?
entries.points: Do not pitch a flat $35k when the brand has only guaranteed $20k with a $30k performance cap—send the brand's actual structured offer instead. Keep the point that younger audiences convert less effectively, but replace the negative statement about 40% of the creator's audience being young with the exact age range and demographics the brand wants. Cut repetitive mentions of $60k and unnecessary jargon, and close with a takeaway line showing you are ready to walk away.
entries.rewrite: I understand the rate. In reviewing past partnerships, they found that younger audiences don't tend to convert as effectively. The brand is looking for [specific age range and demographics]. Therefore, after analysing the channel, we're willing to offer [the brand's actual offer]. Let me know if this is of interest to you. And if not, I completely understand.

quote.quote: Instead of saying that 40% of YouTuber viewership falls into that demographic, I say exactly what the brand is actually looking for, and the age range that they're looking for, and then demographics that they're looking for.

entries.situation: After an influencer ghosted on WhatsApp upon learning the student was an agency, the student sent a follow-up email and read it out for feedback.
entries.student_email: hi. just wanted to follow up on my last email. We are really excited about the potential of working together. And I think it would be a great fit. Let me know if you need any more info from me.
entries.points: The follow-up email is generic, invites too many questions, and still fails to give the influencer 'candy' (specific big brand names you plan to pitch for them); if they don't reply in a day, message their personal WhatsApp clarifying what you do and naming specific brands you plan to reach out to.
entries.rewrite: clarify to him what you are, what you're doing, planning on reaching out to brands like Apple, and more.

quote.quote: or clarify to him what you are, what you're doing, planning on reaching out to brands like Apple, and more. And then, you know, build it from there because asking him what brands he wants is not the way.

entries.situation: A student in the business niche submits an initial cold email to a brand.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Jack, notice you put this together

I could totally see a business owner wanting to build out receptionists who use one of these tools, this could help them save time and money while running the business.

I noticed your integration with [Creator] and liked how simply he explained what you offer.

We work with business creator and there's one who'd be great fit for you. He brings a 70% of U.S. audience, which aligns closely with brand, largely U.S. based customer base.

I have the details ready, want me to send them over?
entries.points: Make the subject line a curiosity question, remove customer-like praise of the brand's tool, avoid dragging out the email with two separate personalizations, give a specific reason why the creator's audience will buy rather than just stating US audience overlap, and use 'Should I send?' as the CTA.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Did you put this together?

I noticed your integration with [Creator] and liked how simply he explained what you offer.

We work with a business creator who'd be a great fit for you [with a specific reason why his audience will buy].

Should I send the details over?

quote.quote: Want me to send them over? It's better. It's better. It's yes and no. But I always go for a should. Should I send? Like, I'm ready. Should I go? Like, do you want me to go? It's different.

entries.situation: A student in the business niche shares a second follow-up email using a campaign case study while still pitching only one creator.
entries.student_email: We recently run a campaign with the same influencer, and we were able to achieve over 350,000 views. That worked out roughly 210,000 US-based eyeballs lending on the brand's integration.
entries.points: Name the specific brand in your case study, highlight the conversions generated from those views, and avoid pitching only one single creator repeatedly across three emails.
entries.rewrite: Just a quick heads up, in the last video we worked with NordVPN, and that video got 350,000 views. You can imagine how many conversions that was. If you want to get the same or better results, let me know. Want me to share more details about the influencer?

quote.quote: And the issue is, it's your third follow-up or third email, and you are pitching the same guy over and over again. Like, please, please, please, I have just him. If you cannot pitch the other guy, that's the issue.

entries.situation: A student in the business niche submits a final breakup follow-up email to a brand.
entries.student_email: Seems like right now isn't the best fit. Would next quarter work better? Either way, just let me know.
entries.points: Never say 'Seems like right now isn't the best fit' because you are calling your own offer a bad fit and giving the brand an easy excuse to walk away; instead frame it around their interest or timing and offer to share other influencers or circle back later.
entries.rewrite: Seems like you're not interested, or the timing is not the best. Should I get back with other influencers, or should I circle back in a couple of months? Either way, let me know.

quote.quote: So don't say it's not fit. Seems like you're not interested, or the timing is not the best. Should I get with another influencers, or should I circle back in a couple of months, a couple of days, a couple of weeks, whatever?

entries.situation: A student in the software development niche submits a third brand email that reuses the same template and says a creator brought back a sponsor 11 times.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Another one, Blake

The way [Creator] moved from reinforcement learning to [topic]...

We work with creators like [Creator 1, Creator 2, Creator 3] who have brought back sponsors such as CodeRabbit 11 times. Their audience are clearly used to evaluating and buying developer tools, which makes them a strong fit for Clerk.
entries.points: Vary your email templates and subject lines rather than sending identical structures, and instead of saying a creator brought back a sponsor '11 times', state more naturally that they have long-term partnerships with multiple brands.
entries.rewrite: They have long-term partnerships with multiple brands, including CodeRabbit. Their audience is clearly used to evaluating and buying developer tools, which makes them a strong fit for Clerk.

quote.quote: Who have brought back sponsors such as CodeRabbit 11 times. Super. Okay, I think you are putting the accent on this one way too much, okay? It's okay to be proud of those, but you can just say it will probably be easier.

entries.situation: A student in the travel vlog niche submits his initial cold email to an unsponsored influencer.
entries.student_email:
Hey,

Swimming with those seals must have been epic. They are like the puppies of the ocean.

I noticed your videos are not sponsored. We are reaching out to brands for influencer sponsorships, and want you on board. Are you open to the partnerships? Let me know.
entries.points: A short, lighthearted personalization ('swimming with those seals... puppies of the ocean') combined with pointing out that their videos are unsponsored works well for an initial influencer email; just drop 'Let me know' after the CTA question and sign off with 'Best regards'.
entries.rewrite:
Hey,

Swimming with those seals must have been epic. They are like the puppies of the ocean.

I noticed your videos are not sponsored. We are reaching out to brands for influencer sponsorships, and want you on board. Are you open to partnerships?

Best regards,
[Your Name]

quote.quote: Okay, this is nice. For the first email, I like it. I noticed your videos are not sponsored. We are reaching out to brands for influencers, sponsorships, and want you on board. Are you open to the partnerships? Let me know.

entries.situation: A student in the travel vlog niche submits five one-line follow-up emails asking if the creator read his first email.
entries.student_email:
Follow-up 1: Wanted to know if you got my email.
Follow-up 2: Curious to see if you read my email. Any thoughts? Questions?
Follow-up 3: Hey, just wondering if you had a chance to go through my email. Got any questions?
Follow-up 4: Sending through a reminder about my first email. What do you think?
Follow-up 5: I know this is like my fifth follow-up. LOL. Curious to know what you think.
entries.points: Never send rude, lazy one-line follow-ups demanding to know if they read your email. Limit follow-ups to 3–4 messages of 2–3 sentences each, starting soft by assuming they may have missed the previous email and reminding them of the value, then trying a different angle before closing.
entries.rewrite: Hey [Name], I'm just following up in case you missed my last email. There are a couple of brands that could be a good fit for your channel.

quote.quote: But let's say three, four follow-ups. Don't hurt your reputation. Five is when you know what you're doing. Soft, right? Soft. Uh, still could be strong sometimes, right? Doesn't have to be, uh, here is different approach, and this one is closing.

entries.situation: A student in the tech and AI niche submits a second brand email congratulating the brand on getting into Walmart and then describing the features of the brand's own power bank.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Take the power with you.

Congrats on getting into Walmart. Once you are used to 140 watts charging at home, being away from your setup can be a pain. That's where the 220 power bank could be a great fit for some of the techies we work with who carry multiple devices. We reach a mainly U.S. and U.K. audience with 69,000 average views.

Should I send over a few profiles we had in mind?
entries.points: Congratulating a brand on a business milestone like getting into Walmart is great B2B personalization, but remove the paragraph pitching the brand's own product specs back to them and instead bridge directly from the milestone into expanding their influencer marketing.
entries.rewrite: Congrats on getting into Walmart. Let's expand on influencer marketing as well. Here we have [Creator] who can do this for you. We have a couple of others who are good in this field, but it's up to you. Should I send their details?

quote.quote: Take the power with you. Congrats on getting into Walmart. Enough. Trust me. Good. B2B. That's it. Walmart is a huge stuff. It's a huge shopping mall, whatever. Nice. Okay. It's an achievement. And you, as someone who knows business, understand it.

entries.situation: A student in the tech and AI niche submits a third brand email starting with three lines about his own Monday coffee routine and detailed personal facts about a creator's family.
entries.student_email:
Subject: I can't be the only one.

I occasionally love Mondays too, but only with my Americano and a croissant in my right hand, and they are usually on top of my list.

That made me think of [Creator 1], a father and YouTube creator who combines tech reviews with humor, focusing on how products fit into everyday life. With two young children, a wife, and a demanding job, I could see how [Brand] would fit naturally into his routine.

We have others in mind as well, open to a chat?
entries.points: Make personalization one line about the prospect rather than three lines about yourself, cut unnecessary personal details about the creator's wife and children, and use an either/or CTA ('Should I send details of all of them or just one?') so the brand chooses between two options instead of saying no.
entries.rewrite: We work with [Creator 1], a YouTube creator who combines tech reviews with humor, focusing on how products fit into everyday life. We also have other guys from this sub-niche. Should I send details of all of them or just one?

quote.quote: We also have other guys from this sub-niche. They would be good because of this. Should I send details of all of them or just one? I'm not leaving you to say no. You have to pick one of those. That would be better.

entries.situation: An influencer replied saying they are open to sponsorship offers, only do integrations (no dedicated videos), and only work with reputable brands. The student reads out the reply they sent naming reputable brands and asking for a screenshot of recent analytics with reasons why.
entries.student_email: completely understand your view on brands and looking forward to or something along the lines and I named a couple of brands in the field that are generally have a good reputation just to give an idea in mind as to what I would reach out to at the start of the new year ... I'd love to know a bit more about your audience and and like is there any way you send the screenshot of recent analytics it would help facilitate like a sort of smoother process when i'm talking to them and it also helped me find brands that better align with your audience.
