entries.situation: A student (Abdullah) shares a cold outreach email he sent to Chantal at Headspace after getting zero replies across 180 emails.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Chantal, have something for Headspace

Hi Chantal,

I noticed your recent work with [Creator], great fit for Headspace. I'm working with a creator in the self-improvement space, and his content is focused on productivity/functionality. I think there's a great opportunity to feature Headspace in a video about [managing daily routines], as it'll fit very naturally with the content and audience. The videos usually get around 50 to 150k views with people who are actually trying to improve their mindset and overall well-being. I can share more details, let me know what you think.

Best,
Abdullah
entries.points: The email is too vague, robotic, and repetitive with 'I' statements: explain specifically why the past sponsorship was a good fit, specify what makes your creator unique in the self-improvement space, eliminate weak 'I think' phrasing, tie specific Headspace features to the creator's content, narrow the 50k–150k view range and define why the audience needs Headspace, use a confident CTA, and write a curiosity-driven subject line.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Chantal, could this be an idea for Headspace? / Chantal, how about we end stress once and for all?

There's a great opportunity for [specific feature] within Headspace...

quote.quote: you have to create curiosity with your subject lines, like Daner mentioned again, you know, instead of saying, Sanza, have something for Headspace, it's like, Santel, could this be, you know, something for Headspace, or could this be idea for Headspace

entries.situation: A student in the cooking niche submits a cold brand email for review with a 'Collaboration worth considering' subject line, mentioning working closely with interested creators averaging 200,000+ views in the US/UK, and asking to send a brief.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Collaboration worth considering
Hi [First Name], Collaboration [Brand] with [Creator 1] and [Creator 2] really stood to me because of their polished and natural integration style. Fish Friday is definitely my favorite day of the week as well. I wanted to reach out and see if you're open to exploring more partnership with similar creators in the cooking space. I work closely with a group of food influencers who would be interested in promoting [Brand]. Several of these creators consistently average 200,000+ views and majority of their audience is from the U.S. and the U.K. Shall I send over a brief?
entries.points: The email is too long and has major issues: avoid 'collaboration' in subject lines; start personalization with the specific detail ('Fish Friday'); cut filler phrases like 'I wanted to reach out and see if you're open to exploring'; never falsely claim you 'work closely' with creators or promise they 'would be interested' before asking them; give an exact average number rather than '200,000 plus'; and offer analytics or a media kit in a strong CTA rather than asking to send a 'brief' (which comes from the brand).
entries.rewrite: Fish Friday is definitely my favorite. Collaboration with this guy, prove that, blah, blah, blah, two sentences.

quote.quote: big no-no is when it comes to subject line, no-no, anything that has collaboration, anything that has partnership, anything that has paid, so all of those stuff are not good, why? Because inbox are full of those

entries.situation: A student in the health/fitness niche shows two initial brand outreach emails (one for Crusher Evo headphones and one for a walking pad) that use a fill-in-the-blank template stating the creators reach a fitness crowd and the product is aimed at that crowd.
entries.student_email:
Email 1: Hey Kaelin, partnering up with [Creator] on Instagram was a strong move. Well done on connecting the Crusher Evo with the fitness crowd as the main target audience for it. I was curious to see if you'd be interested in working with some influencers like [Creators]. They reach a US/UK fitness oriented crowd, and those headphones are of course aimed at that crowd, which is why it looks like a natural match on the outside. Let me know what you think.

Email 2: Partnering up with [Creator] was a smart choice. The connection between her fitness driven audience and the walking pad seemed authentic. I was wondering if you'd be open to working with influencers like [Creators]. They all reach a fitness oriented following and the walking pad is aimed at such a following, so it'd be a natural fit.
entries.points: The emails sound like ChatGPT and use a lazy, repetitive fill-in-the-blank offer where only the product name and creator name are swapped. Stating that fitness creators match a fitness product is stating the obvious and doesn't explain why these specific creators will drive sales better than 700 other fitness creators. Focus on unique video styles, upcoming videos, or comment section demand.
entries.rewrite: Since headphones are must-have in any gym or anything, it would be a good chance for him to do this and this... Influencers [X] and [Y] are going to make these type of videos in the next couple of months.

quote.quote: It's vague, bro. It's vague, like, okay, fitness-oriented crowd, and those headphones are, of course, aimed to that crowd. Yeah, Faris, but it's not something that I'll be like, yo, that's a great idea.

entries.situation: The same health/fitness student shows their first follow-up email to a brand, asking if they have any questions or if anything seems unclear, and asking if they prefer to discuss over a Zoom meeting with the team.
entries.student_email: Just following up with my previous email to see if you got any questions or things that seem unclear. We are looking forward to hearing from you and potentially moving things forward. Would you prefer for us to discuss this over Zoom meeting with a team or such? If so, let me know and I'll send over my availability.
entries.points: The follow-up is way too soft and reads like an email you send after an offer has already been discussed, not after getting ignored on cold outreach. Also, asking if they prefer a Zoom meeting with their team when they haven't even replied is creepy; if you use a call CTA, keep it casual and direct in the initial outreach ('Let's hop on a call and we can discuss more').
entries.rewrite: Let's hop on a call and we can discuss more. Let me know when you're free and we can book a call.

quote.quote: Just following up with my previous email to see if you got any questions or things that seem unclear. We are looking forward to hearing from you and potentially moving things forward. This is after-offer email in my opinion.

entries.situation: An automotive niche student submits a set of 4 short brand emails where he shortened his personalization and repeatedly used words like 'repairs' and 'audience' along with US audience percentages (67%, 81%, 75%).
entries.student_email:
1) Hey [First name], [Brand] naturally fit into [Creator]'s recent videos as their content focuses on repairs. Speaking of car repairs, we work with creators such as [Creators] who repair cars, and their content reaches over 67% of US audience. We believe they would be an excellent fit to promote your product.
2) Subject: Worth checking
Hey [First name], the way [Creator] used [Brand] while tracking down that fault works well with their usual repair content. Speaking of repairs, we work with [Creator] whose repair content reaches an audience of 81% US, and we believe his audience would align well with the product.
3) Hey [First name], [Brand] was presented during an integration with [Creator] regarding a move into tech, the transition theme was clear. Speaking of moving, we work with a creator whose content focuses on car repair and reaches a strong US audience (75% US audience), and we believe his audience would align...
4) Hey [First name], [Brand] featured during a segment about exploring insurance companies, the comparison angle stood out. We work with creators whose content focuses on repairs and reaching out to 75% US audience, mostly workers who lack time to shop for groceries. Should I share more details?
entries.points: While keeping brand personalization short is good, the emails repeat the same words ('repairs', 'audience') too many times in a couple of sentences. Use varied vocabulary ('restoring', 'car parts', 'wrenching'). Put the strongest hook—like an 81% US audience stat—at the end of the offer sentence so it sticks in the reader's mind, or say 'strong US audience' without the number to build curiosity, and add a compelling reason why the creator's audience trusts their recommendations (or reference comments showing audience pain points).
entries.rewrite: Speaking of car repairs, we have these guys. Their content is all about restoring them, it's all about car parts, they are only known for wrenching... We believe his audience would align well with the product, his content is [X], and also 81% US audience.

quote.quote: If you switch these two things, we believe his audience would align well with the product, obviously not word by word, I would change this, his content is blah, blah, blah. And also, 81%, be like, oh, wow, nice.

entries.situation: To close the deal, the student sent an email accepting the offer and summarizing the exact per-video base pay, view milestones, and maximum total payout for both videos.
entries.student_email: hey, thanks for the offer, this works on our end. For two videos, per video, 600 base pay, $500 if it hits 5k views, another 500 if it hits 15k, max total, $1,600 per video, $3,200 for both. If we're on the same page regarding the pricing, we're happy to kick things off as quickly as possible. Feel free to share all the required info to get started on production.
entries.points: Recapping and confirming all pricing terms and milestones in writing before kicking off production is a great practice that ensures clear alignment on both sides.

quote.quote: Note, I always like to confirm we align on terms, goes a long way. I agree. This is good. Just a recap, make sure all language is clear, everything is understood on both sides.

entries.situation: A student emails a DIY creator duo who had the same brand sponsor 3 of their last 5 videos, telling them they are 'leaving money on the table.'
entries.student_email:
Subject: Don't leave it on the table

Lads, I work with my younger brother too, so I get the dynamic, ha ha, and the quality you're putting out is a cut above. Three of your last five videos had integrated sponsors, all from the same brand. There's really money sitting on the table here, open to hearing what else is out there?
entries.points: Replace the overly casual greeting 'Lads' with 'Hi', 'Hey', 'Hello', or 'Hi there' (for multiple people). Do not start the first sentence with 'I', which puts the spotlight on yourself instead of the creator. Most importantly, having the same sponsor on 3 of the last 5 videos (60%) is a massive green flag showing they have a repeat retainer deal and can deliver for brands—never frame it as a mistake. Flip the script and ask if they are ready for more brands (e.g., 5 out of 5), and replace the weak CTA ('Open to hearing what else is out there?').
entries.rewrite:
Subject: ready for more

Hi there, working with younger brother for sure is painful. Don't ask me how I know... if you saw three out of five, why not five out of five?

quote.quote: Starting with I, kind of selfish. It's not the best. You know, you're putting attention to yourself, like spotlight, to me, just me. I'm talking about me. No, they are born of it. You should rephrase it

entries.situation: A student pitches a fitness creator to a fitness brand by listing his 2.5M followers, 51% US audience, named past brand sponsors, and 500,000+ guaranteed views.
entries.student_email:
Subject: The collab

Hey, the collab you did with [Creator] was clean with a strong message behind the campaign. Our influencers constantly make viral videos in the fitness industry with 2.5M followers and with 51% of his audience being in the U.S. He's working with brands like [Brand A] and [Brand B]. His sponsored videos are guaranteed to make over 500,000 views, resulting in a massive increase in the brand's revenue. Are you open to explore partnerships with this guy? Best
entries.points: Make the opening compliment about their past collaboration shorter and explain why it was good. Never mention follower count to brands—focus on views. Do not name specific brands the creator is currently working with in the first email, because if those brands are competitors and the creator has exclusivity or usage rights (like Nike), it can kill the deal; instead say 'he has long partnership with brands in this space.' Finally, turn strong view counts into a bold risk-reversal offer: guarantee a minimum view threshold (e.g., 300,000 views) and offer to redo the ad for free if it falls short.
entries.rewrite: He has long partnership with brands in this space... we can guarantee you 300,000 views minimum — if your video gets lower than 300,000 views, we do the ad again.

quote.quote: holding a lot of views, we can guarantee you, I don't know, 300,000 views minimum, something like that, guys, if he is, if he has strong views, use it, use it, be like, if we get less than this, we do this again

entries.situation: A student writes a cold email to a supplement brand praising their new flavor release and promising 'ROI through the roof' and a 'nonstop stream of buyers.'
entries.student_email:
Subject: The campaign

The campaign you have showcasing the release of new flavors was innovative, super clean and short, can go a long way. Well, having fitness influencers like ours generates millions of views a month, brings an audience that can massively impact your brand... recover everything you spend, ROI through the roof, viewers can bring nonstop stream of buyers...
entries.points: Avoid sounding like a fan of the product; comment on their marketing or point out a recent influencer collab that flopped and offer to fix it. Cut hyper-salesy fluff like 'recover everything you spend, ROI through the roof, nonstop stream of buyers.' Remember that the first email is only meant to get a reply, not close the deal—stay reserved and ask if you should send over details on a couple of high-performing creators in their niche.
entries.rewrite: We have a couple of guys in this space crushing it with views, high engagement rate, stuff like that. Are you interested? Should I send more details?

quote.quote: Recover everything you spend, blah, blah, blah, ROI through the roof, stuff like that, nonstop streamers of buyers. What was this? Viewers can bring nonstop stream of buyers. Too fluffy, okay? Too salesy, I would say.

entries.situation: A student sends a cold email and follow-up to a men's fashion creator referencing a video where staff members were given the power to choose items.
entries.student_email:
Subject: The power of options

Hey [Name], giving staff members the power to choose items was a cool concept, as it added in... Something that might interest you is that we have brands in mind we can potentially align you with for upcoming campaigns. Is this something you're open to?

Follow-up 1: Hello [Name], following up on the potential opportunities mentioned in my earlier emails, just wondering if you had a chance to go over it, let me know if this sounds like a fit.
entries.points: The offer, CTA, and first follow-up are solid. To improve the initial email, turn the subject line 'The power of options' into a curiosity question about the video ('Are you sure?', 'Is this the right decision?', 'Was it a safe?') so the creator opens to see what you mean. For the second follow-up, pivot the offer slightly by suggesting alternative brands ('Maybe this opportunity wasn't the best for you, what do you think about these brands instead?').
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Are you sure? / Is this the right decision? / Was it a safe?

Second follow-up: Maybe this opportunity wasn't the best for you, what do you think about these brands instead?

quote.quote: Hello, someone. Following up on the potential opportunities mentioned in my earlier emails, just wondering if you had a chance to go over it, let me know if this sounds like a fit. Good, that's all we have to look for.

entries.situation: A student emails a men's fashion creator about going from hating Paraboot shoes to wearing them and joking about playing basketball in them.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Hater to lover

Going from hating on the Paraboot to wearing them is a classic example of how fashion can come full circle. It will be funny to see if you actually try to go hooping in them. Speaking of basketball, another thing I may have for you is brands and sponsorship. We have companies in mind like [Brand A] and [Brand B] and others in that space that we think your channel could be a fit for. Let me know if you're interested.
entries.points: Good overall structure, offer, and CTA. Tighten up the subject line and personalization, and replace 'another thing I may have for you is brands and sponsorship' with 'brands that you will be interested in working with.'
entries.rewrite: Speaking of basketball, another thing I may have for you is brands that you will be interested in working with. We have companies in mind like [Brand A] and [Brand B] and others in that space that we think your channel could be a fit for. Let me know if you're interested.

quote.quote: We have companies in mind like this and this and others in that space that we think your channel could be a fit for. Let me know if you're interested. Good. This brother is watching.

entries.situation: A creator or talent representative replied to the student's outreach declining collaboration at the moment ('Thanks so much for reaching out. This is not something we are looking for at the moment. But I wish you all the best moving forward.'), and the student reads out his polite reply aimed at keeping the door open.
entries.student_email: Thanks for getting back to me. I appreciate Totally understood. If it makes sense, I can reach out again later when things change. In the meantime, if there is any sponsor categories when the creator's name is open to in the future, feel free to let me know.
entries.points: Always act cool when rejected on the first response and make one last attempt to keep the door open. The student's reply is good, or he can make it even punchier by asking them to let him know when they have available sponsorship spots in the future because he wants to book something.
entries.rewrite: okay, no problem, just let me know if you have any available spots in the future, because I would love to book something.

quote.quote: Always act cool, which is what you did, but always try your last attempt to keep the doors open. So, what you did is good, or you can say something like, okay, no problem, just let me know if you have any available spots

entries.situation: After pitching seven creators to a brand and receiving counter-offers (some reasonable and several at half price/below the influencers' own rates), the student sent a reply countering the close ones with specific go-live dates and walking away from the severe lowballs.
entries.student_email: We're willing to meet in the middle for this, [Creator 1] and [Creator 2], the earliest we can go live is [date], and [Creator] will be in January. I'll confirm shortly if we can proceed with the remaining creators, we're a bit too far apart for now.
entries.points: Giving exact go-live months/dates while offering to meet in the middle on reasonable offers shows the brand you have already confirmed details with your creators and are in full control, while saying 'we're a bit too far apart for now' on the lowballed creators establishes strong power dynamics (which led the brand to lock in the two creators at $1.25k each).

quote.quote: we're willing to meet in the middle for this, full line of full line, the earliest we can go live is, so I'd like to say, he's given a timeline, right, you what mean, this is not as human or close, but it's close

entries.situation: A European brand replied to outreach requesting creators with specific age demographics (audience over age 35), and the student pitched a matching creator with attached demographics and a price in Euros.
entries.student_email: Check out [Creator], over 50% of his audience is age 35+ as requested. I've attached demos for your reference. We can do an integration for 4,000 euros.
entries.points: Keep creator pitches ultra-lean with zero wasted words: state only the exact metric the brand requested ('over 50% of his audience is age 35 as requested') without over-explaining extra stats like US audience or engagement (which they can see in the attached demographics), and quote the price in the brand's local currency (Euros). Over-explaining exposes neediness.

quote.quote: So the brother said, I've attached demos for your reference. I like this, right? Look at, look at, look at this, this, the way the brother's speaking. There's no wasted words. Every word in this email, it serves a purpose.

entries.situation: After a brand countered a €4,000 pitch with €2,700 + 20% affiliate commission citing a strict 0.04 CPV policy and tight Q4 budget, the student countered at €3,200 + 20% commission.
entries.student_email: Amazing, glad to hear the team likes the channel. Just to clarify, the original rate I shared already falls within your CPV policy of 0.04, as the channel averages just over 100k views per video based on the last 12 uploads. That said, we'd love to kick things off and build a long-term partnership, so we're happy to accept 3.2k including the 20% commission for our first collaboration. Let me know if you can make this work and I'll send over the shipping details.
entries.points: This counter-offer works well because: (1) saying 'Glad to hear the team likes the channel' (rather than 'happy to hear') maintains high status; (2) using the brand's own 0.04 CPV metric and the channel's 100k+ average views over the last 12 uploads proves the original €4,000 rate was already fair; (3) mirroring their 'build a long-term partnership' phrasing gives a clear reason ('for our first collaboration') for dropping the price to €3,200 while keeping the 20% commission; and (4) ending with 'I'll send over the shipping details' assumes the close.

quote.quote: my first collaboration, let me know if you can make this work and I'll send over the shipping details. So, this CTA brothers, look at it, look very closely now, what is the brother doing? He's, yeah, assuming the clothes

entries.situation: A high-engagement creator who rarely does sponsorships asked Samer 'What are you getting out of this?', then after Samer's replies and a 1-week follow-up, wrote back: 'I'm confused. What is your offer? You just want me to send my stats for nothing. What do you advertise?'
entries.student_email: That's between us and the brands, if you feel uncomfortable proceeding further, just let me know. ... Yes, we will provide a contract once a deal is finalized. Just a reminder, I still need you to send me your demographics and rates. ... I can't help you further if you don't send what's required. PS: For our partnership, we prefer quick communication, so if you aren't active on email, tell us which method suits you.
entries.points: Saying 'that's between us and the brands' and demanding demographics without context left the creator confused and defensive. Instead: (1) explain clearly that you typically take your cut from the brand side for running their campaigns and sourcing creators, or offer an alternative structure where you represent him exclusively for a percentage (and offer a call); and (2) act like the buyer and explain that his rate and his audience demographics depend on each other (e.g., whether he has an 80% tier-1 audience) so you need his analytics to price him properly, while adding a non-needy takeaway ('if you're not comfortable with this, that's fine').
entries.rewrite: We typically take our cut from the brand side, as we're running these campaigns for them and finding influencers like you for them. Alternatively, we can discuss exclusivity under our agency or a percentage based on your pay if you want to jump on a call. Also, your analytics and your rate are dependent on each other—if I don't have your analytics, I don't know what your audience is to get you paid accordingly. If you're not comfortable with this, that's fine.

quote.quote: let them know, look, we typically take our car from the brand side, as we're running these campaigns for them, and finding influencers like you for them, right? However, if you want a different structure, we could, yeah, and discuss exclusivity

entries.situation: A student shares his cold outreach email to an influencer in the chat containing food personalization ('the chicken on the grill, the steak, and all the other food looked delicious'), a vague pitch ('I have a clear vision for partnerships with several brands' that works 'in your favor' and 'drives significant results'), and a request for a call.
entries.student_email: the chicken on the grill, the steak, and all the other food looked delicious ... I have a clear vision for partnerships with several brands ... in your favor ... drives significant results
entries.points: Avoid generic personalization that could apply to any creator, fanboyish multi-item compliments that hurt power dynamics, and AI-sounding phrases like 'in your favor' or 'drives significant results' (creators care about business, not brand results). Make the offer more concrete by stating you are currently doing outreach for specific potential campaigns and how they integrate into their content, keep any compliment to a few words or omit it altogether, and offer the choice between a quick call or continuing over email.
entries.rewrite: We're currently doing outreach for these potential campaigns ... by the way, that chicken from last video looked delicious. ... by the way, we can jump on a quick call or keep things moving over email.

quote.quote: when you just say like clear vision for partnerships with several brands, it's like we can utilize the ambiguity in more beneficial ways. Right. So we could say we are. We're currently doing outreach for, you know. These potential campaigns

entries.situation: Initial cold outreach email to a brand tying a recent feature release and Black Friday momentum to a potential November YouTube partnership.
entries.student_email: With the recent release of the feature, and the year wrapping up, I wanted to check if you're planning any YouTube partnerships. This would be like a great time to capture momentum with Black Friday around the corner. Can I send over a few creators we worked with who could showcase naturally in a November video?
entries.points: Referencing a recent product feature and seasonal momentum like Black Friday before asking to send over a few creators for an upcoming video is a solid initial outreach approach.

quote.quote: Can I send over a few creators we worked with who could showcase naturally, naturally, in a November video? Okay. Um, not too bad. Not too bad.

entries.situation: After the brand explained that they rejected a previous creator because his audience was mostly in India, the student pitched a new creator using vague, salesy claims about viewer maturity and professionals and talked about going live that month before agreeing on a price.
entries.student_email: Thanks for sharing the focus. We have an influencer who has a very mature audience mostly made up of professionals that fit what you described. Would be a great match for them, I've attached this audience demo so you can see the strong U.S. presence and overall maturity of these viewers. Let me know what you think about an integration in an upcoming video with demos for you to check out and we can look at going live this month.
entries.points: Do not use unnatural, salesy phrases like 'mature audience made up of professionals' or talk about going live before the brand even approves the creator or price. Directly address the brand's stated concern by stating the creator's strong audience location, concisely note how it aligns with what they shared, and ask if there are other factors they want to consider.
entries.rewrite: Hey, sure, we have this guy. Actually, his audience is big in this country, which aligns with the things you shared before. That being said, are there other things you'd like to consider?

quote.quote: For example, if they mention India is a thing, okay, you should counter them by mentioning, okay, this influencer is actually audience in this market, and not speak about professionals and all of that, this is not their concern.

entries.situation: The brand liked the creator, asked for his 90-second integration rate, and noted that hitting their December 11-15 window might be tight due to contract signing, product shipping, and script review.
entries.student_email: The rate for 90 second integration is 6k. Influencer already has the product, so we can skip shipping on this one and focus on hitting the 15 December window. If you're good to move forward, feel free to send the contract across too, we'll handle signing on our end, and can start working on the script right away.
entries.points: State the rate clearly, remove timeline friction by pointing out that the influencer already has the product so shipping can be skipped, and invite the brand to send the contract so signing and script work can start immediately.

quote.quote: the rate for 90 second integration is 6k, Influenza already has the product, so we can skip shipping on this one and focus on hitting the 15 December window, ah, nice, okay, I'm surprised, I'm not about it

entries.situation: The brand countered the $6k quote with $4.8k and asked to delay the post because internal management approval takes at least a week; the student countered at $5.5k, agreed to hold the post until early January, and ended with 'if this works for you, feel free to share the contract.'
entries.student_email: Paul is currently averaging around 275k views per video, and we can't go down to 4.8k. As a first collaboration we're willing to meet you at 5.5, no worries on time, we can hold the post until early January, let's not rush it. If this works for you, feel free to share the contract.
entries.points: Justifying your counter-offer with view averages and agreeing not to rush the timeline without using emojis is good, but avoid saying 'if this works for you' because it sounds like asking for permission. Frame the middle-ground rate as a steal given the creator's views and tell them to share the contract to lock it in.
entries.rewrite: I'm willing to meet you in the middle, however, for the views and everything, this is a steal actually. Feel free to share the contract, so we can lock this in, and we can move forward.

quote.quote: if this works for you, feel free to say no, I don't, I wouldn't say if this works for you, because now you're asking for permission, like you, basically you're making them a favor

entries.situation: Initial cold outreach email to a brand referencing a recent sponsorship video they did and offering to send over a creator profile with a similar audience.
entries.student_email: I came across a video from [creator] featuring [brand] and thought you might be interested in a similar collaboration on a channel that reaches an audience of [audience]. If you're open to it, I can send over the creator's profile for you to review.
entries.points: Mentioning a video where the brand was featured and offering to send over a creator profile that reaches a similar audience is a clean, effective first outreach email.

quote.quote: I came across a video from featuring this and thought you might be interested in a similar collaboration on a channel that reaches an audience off.

entries.situation: The brand asked what type of collaboration and rate they had in mind, and the student proposed 'a mid-roll integration similar to the recent one' for $6k-$7k with the earliest slot in late December.
entries.student_email: We're thinking of a mid-roll integration similar to the recent one with [creator]. The rate for this is 7k. The earliest slot we have right now is late December.
entries.points: Stating the rate and earliest slot directly shows good power dynamics, but always specify the exact integration length (such as 60-90 seconds) rather than expecting the brand to check how long a previous integration was.
entries.rewrite: The rate for a 60-90 second integration is 7k. The earliest slot we have right now is late December.

quote.quote: The rate for this is, for this type of sponsorship, or the rate for, mentioned like 60, 90 second integration. How, how much is like, like, they're not gonna go and measure them themselves, how long was it? You need to make their life easier.

entries.situation: After noticing the brand had sponsored dedicated videos, the student followed up asking if they checked out the creator or if their focus is more on dedicated videos right now, adding 'I'm happy to suggest other channels.'
entries.student_email: Did you get a chance to check out [creator]? Let me know your thoughts. Or is the focus more on dedicated videos right now? I'm happy to suggest other channels.
entries.points: Asking whether their current focus is on dedicated videos is a great follow-up question because it shows you are trying to understand their needs, but remove 'I'm happy to suggest other channels' because it sounds needy and salesy.
entries.rewrite: Did you get a chance to check out [creator]? Let me know your thoughts. Or is the focus more on dedicated videos right now?

quote.quote: the only thing I have, I would mention is happy to suggest all the channels, don't do that, very salesy, but other than that, the way how you asked a question in a follow-up, very good, very, very good

entries.situation: The brand wanted to book the late December slot but asked for a discount; the student refused the discount, held firm at $7k citing high demand for the slot, and asked for the brief.
entries.student_email: I checked with the creator, and we can go live with W/C [date]. But we need to stick with the 7k rate. Let me know if you like this slot since there is high demand for it. Please send over the brief so we can get started.
entries.points: When a brand wants the slot but asks for a small discount, hold firm on your original rate without over-explaining, note that the slot is in high demand, and ask them to send over the brief to get started.

quote.quote: But we need to stick with the 7k rate. We need to stick with the 7k rate. Let me know if you like this lot since there is high demand for it. Please send over the brief so we can get started.

entries.situation: A student's second outreach draft to an outdoor creator jokes about grilling a turtle over a fire, makes a weak transition to the offer, and asks if the creator is 'still open' to partnering with outdoor brands.
entries.student_email: Subject: squirrels payback. Body: Hey guys, honestly, that poor turtle was lucky it disappeared into the water before one of you came up with the crazy idea like grilling it over fire... Speaking of ideas that are not that crazy, we have a couple of brands that might fill those gaps as we saw in your last few videos, which made me want to check if you're still open to partnering with relevant outdoor brands... your choice, Big Dappy, or more details.
entries.points: The turtle observation is decent, but there is no logical bridge between the personalization and the offer, and the phrasing still feels overly generated by ChatGPT. Most importantly, never ask influencers if they are 'open' to working with brands; asking if they are open makes them feel overly special and creates unnecessary friction and questions. Be more direct and assertive.
entries.rewrite: I have something to present to you. If you want to say yes, good. If not, go away.

quote.quote: Big tip for you guys. Don't ask them if they are open. It will just cause more trouble, more friction, more questions. They will feel special. So don't ask them.

entries.situation: A student submits a short follow-up email to an influencer or management agency checking in on their previous email.
entries.student_email: Hey, thought I'll circle back on this. Any thoughts on that email I sent the other day?
entries.points: The follow-up is good and concise. To make it even stronger, add a light, playful reminder that you still need their details in order to bring them brand deals so they shouldn't be late.
entries.rewrite: Hey, thought I'll circle back on this. Any thoughts on that email I sent the other day? We still need something from you in order to bring those deals. Don't be late.

quote.quote: Any thoughts on that email I sent the other day? This is nice. This is nice. I will just add one more thing. You know, we still need something from you in order to... Bring those nails. Don't be late.

entries.situation: A student sends their first brand outreach email in the 3D printing / DIY construction niche with a long personalization paragraph about an article on rebuilding PLA filament chemistry for household safety with children.
entries.student_email: Subject: PLA Pure, is it safe? Body: Hey, I came across the recent article about the launch of [PLA Pure] and found the approach of rebuilding the filament chemistry particularly interesting, especially from a safety perspective for households with children. Another way to ensure safety is by partnering with creators...
entries.points: The subject line ('PLA Pure, is it safe?') is decent, or could be 'Is it really safe?', though for brands a simple 'Hey Jack, thoughts' is enough. However, the body fails because it uses an influencer (B2C) email structure for a brand (B2B). Brand contacts skim emails and care most about what is in it for them, so spending most of the email on a lengthy personalization about filament chemistry wastes precious words. Cut the personalization to one short line and devote the majority of the email to pitching the specific creators, their niche specialization, and their audience.
entries.rewrite: Subject: Hey Jack, thoughts / Is it really safe? Body: A safety perspective for household children was a good improvement on your new PLA Pure. Speaking of perspective, we have a couple of influencers that might put that new concept to the right audience. They are [Creator 1] and [Creator 2], specialized in [topic], they can also [deliverable], their videos are all about [niche].

quote.quote: Your email would be good if you're sending it to an influencer. For a brand, you missed it. Why? Because instead of making your personalization the largest part or the most important part, you use all of your precious words on personalization

entries.situation: A student submits a second outdoor creator outreach email referencing a bench and simplicity, offering to connect them with outdoor brands so they can spend less time looking for sponsorships and more time exploring.
entries.student_email: Subject: Is it that simple? Body: The bench makes you realize that happiness can be found in simplicity. And we also like keeping things simple. We connect outdoor creators like yourself with the brands that genuinely fit their content, so you can spend less time looking for sponsorships and more time exploring. If you're interested...
entries.points: This is a good email with a solid CTA ('If you're interested'). To make the offer punchier, flip the sentence structure so you lead with the fact that they are busy exploring and offer to handle their brand partnerships or bring them more brands.
entries.rewrite: Since you're busy with [exploring], let us handle your brand partnerships / let's bring you more brands. If you're interested...

quote.quote: We connect outdoor careers like your With the brands that generally fit their content, so you can spend less time looking for sponsorships and more time exploring. I would flip it, you know, since you're busy with this one, let us handle your brand's partnerships

entries.situation: The student submits two more outdoor creator emails—one about a squirrel turning its back to the view, and another joking that -14 Fahrenheit made the creator's frozen beard look like Santa—while rewording the same core offer.
entries.student_email: Draft 1 - Subject: Wrong side little guy. Body: I loved how the squirrel had its back to the view. I didn't expect a few minutes to steal the show. Seems aligned with our content focus. We connect adventure creators such as yourself with brands so you can explore instead of chasing deals... Draft 2 - Subject: Still smiling. Body: Didn't know that minus 14 Fahrenheit could make you look like Santa. Loved how you kept smiling despite those conditions, hopefully your inbox can bring a smile too. We are building... I believe your content would be a good fit. Interested?
entries.points: The hyper-personalized subject lines ('Wrong side little guy', 'Still smiling') and direct CTA ('Interested?') are strong, and rewording the offer slightly across emails is a smart way to stay out of spam. However, avoid fanboy language like 'I loved how...' and avoid comparing the creator's frozen beard to Santa—just mention the beard itself. Also test genuinely different offer angles rather than only rewording the same one.

quote.quote: I believe your content would be a good fit, interested, this is nice, this is nice, you know, from this one, Allahumma barik, it's good, just come up with different offers, this is a fanboy talk

entries.situation: A student's first outreach email to a sports media creator opens with 'Enjoyed the piece on Jalen Duren as someone who lived in Detroit', gives a take on Duren's playoff performance, and asks 'Are you open to new partnerships?'.
entries.student_email: Subject: Let him go. Body: Enjoyed the piece on Jalen Duren as someone who lived in Detroit. I would let him go if he is demanding anything near a max. His playoff performance proved he is not worth it. Speaking of being worth it, I'm currently recruiting new influencers to partner up with some brands such as [Brand 1] and [Brand 2], and I believe you would be a good fit. Are you open to new partnerships?
entries.points: Delete the first sentence about enjoying the piece and living in Detroit, which sounds like a fanboy talking about himself. Start directly with the analytical second sentence ('I would let him go if he is demanding anything near a max...'), which positions you as an expert. Also replace 'Are you open to new partnerships?' with 'Are you interested?'.
entries.rewrite: Subject: Let him go. Body: I would let him go if he is demanding anything near a max. His playoff performance proved he is not worth it. Speaking of being worth it, I'm currently recruiting new influencers to partner up with some brands such as [Brand 1] and [Brand 2], and I believe you would be a good fit. Are you interested?

quote.quote: I will let go if he is demanding anything near a max. His playoff, performance proof he is not worth it. Okay, so this one is fanboy. So we don't do this. This part is about you. Okay, this is good.

entries.situation: A student sends an initial outreach email to a self-improvement creator without a name in the greeting, includes a wink emoji after complimenting their blindfolded Rubik's cube solve, claims specific brands are a 'strong fit for your audience', and asks 'Would you like me to send over more details?'.
entries.student_email: Hey, solving a Rubik's cube blindfolded using a memory palace. That's impressive ;) Finding and negotiating brand deals yourself takes time that you could be putting back in your content and community. We take care of that side completely, working with brands like [Brand 1] and [Brand 2], a strong fit for your audience. Would you like me to send over more details?
entries.points: Always include the creator's name in the greeting (or at least 'Hi there'), and never put a wink emoji in a cold email. Do not claim brands are a 'strong fit for your audience' when you haven't seen their audience analytics yet. Focus the offer around handling brand deals so they can put time back into their content and community, and never offer to 'send over more details' in the first email if you do not actually have campaign details ready to share.
entries.rewrite: Hi [Name], solving a Rubik's cube blindfolded using a memory palace—that's impressive. Speaking of impressive, we take care of brands and we bring them, and you can get back on working on your content and community.

quote.quote: Hey, I forgot the name, so do a name, bro. Do a name. Or at least say, hi there. Solving aerobics cube blindfolded using a memory palace. That's impressive. Wink. What is this, guys?

entries.situation: After the self-improvement creator replies 'Yes, for sure' to 'Would you like me to send over more details?', the student replies with a generic script ('Right now, we are onboarding a small group of creators for upcoming brand campaigns...') and then sends a generic follow-up ('Just checking if you had a chance to go through my email') when the creator ghosts.
entries.student_email: Creator: Yes, for sure. Student Reply: Right now, we are onboarding a small group of creators for upcoming brand campaigns. Based on your channel, we think you fit what they are looking for. Let me know if you're... Student Follow-up: Just checking if you had a chance to go through my email... Third time's a charm, would love to hear back.
entries.points: The creator ghosted because you promised 'more details' about the brands in your first email, and when they said yes, you just repeated a generic onboarding pitch without giving any details. When an influencer replies asking for details, give them concrete context—such as mentioning products those brands are launching and the audience they want—and immediately ask for their analytics and rates for a 60 to 90 second integration (or ask them to send their analytics first so you can share more details). Also avoid overused follow-up templates like 'Just checking if you had a chance to go through my email'.
entries.rewrite: Brands like [Brand 1] and [Brand 2] are looking to launch their products, and they're looking for this type of audience. For that, we would need your analytics and rates for 60 to 90 seconds. Do you have those? / Send me over your analytics, so we can send you more details.

quote.quote: so brands like this, this, this are looking to launch their products, or we can mention a couple of products if you have in mind they're launching something. So, they're looking for this type of audience.

entries.situation: An AI influencer replied to initial outreach with a single word ('sure' with no capitalization or punctuation), and the student responded with a long, repetitive email asking for their media kit twice, asking for their content niche focus, and closing with 'Looking forward to connecting!' and 'Warm regards.'
entries.student_email: Hi, thank you for getting back to me. To move on further, could you share immediately? This would help me understand your audience demographics, reach and rate, so I can mark. You with the right brand opportunity. A few things I need from your end: [content niche focus, media kit and rate] Once I have these details, I can present the right brand fit for you. Looking forward to connecting! Warm regards.
entries.points: Match the influencer's brief energy instead of writing a long, repetitive email. Explicitly ask for both audience analytics/media kit and rates (since many creators lack a media kit or omit rates from it), never ask the creator for information you can see yourself by opening their channel (like their content niche), avoid needy CTAs like 'Looking forward to connecting!' with exclamation marks, and use 'Regards' instead of 'Warm regards.'
entries.rewrite: To move on further, could you share a media kit and rates? This will help matching you with the right brand opportunity. Let me know your thoughts. Regards

quote.quote: Any information you can get by yourself. Get it yourself, Yaqoob. Why ask the influencer and make him work for you when you can actually have the information?

entries.situation: An influencer sent a long reply attaching their media kit and offering a 60-second YouTube integration for $1,900. The student replied with a two-line email thanking them and asking how many campaigns they can handle per month.
entries.student_email: hey, thanks for coming back to me and sending over your media kit. Before I move forward, how many campaigns can you handle per month?
entries.points: Responding to a creator's long media-kit message with a short, two-line question asking how many campaigns they can handle per month is an effective way to gain power dynamics and make the influencer qualify themselves to you.

quote.quote: Hey, hey, little guy, we have a lot for you, but can you handle it? That's what this guy did. Allah wa barik, love it. Hi, happy to clarify. Look, boom, you're gaining power dynamics, Safi.

entries.situation: After the influencer eagerly explained they could accommodate multiple partnerships per month, the student replied asking 'Are you open to negotiating rates?'
entries.student_email: Thanks for clarifying. ... Are you open to negotiating rates?
entries.points: Never ask an influencer for permission to negotiate ('Are you open to negotiating rates?'), as it immediately surrenders your power dynamics and prompts them to demand the brand, budget, and timeline. Instead, go straight into negotiation by proposing your counter-offer directly.
entries.rewrite: Hey, your price could be good for a dedicated video, however, for a 60 second integration, that's what we can do: [X rate].

quote.quote: If he gave you the rate, give a counter offer. Say, hey, we can do it for this. Or... You can say, hey, your price could be good for a dedicated videos, however, for a 60 second integration, that's what we can do.

entries.situation: A brand manager asked for creator profiles, audience demographics targeting the US and UK, and commercial rates. The student replied with a bulleted list showing the creator's name without a link, YouTube subscriber count, a misspelled niche, geographies of 20% US and 10% India, typed-out audience age, and 'Integrated YouTube: [price]', ending with a soft CTA.
entries.student_email: Alright, thanks for clarifying, one of the greatest from our network: Creator name [no channel link], YouTube subscribers, Niche [misspelled], Our geographies: 20% US and 10% India, Audience age, Integrated YouTube: [price]. Let me know what works for you.
entries.points: Present creators to a brand in a single clean sentence: hyperlink the creator's channel to their name, hyperlink a Google Drive containing analytics screenshots to the word 'analytics' instead of typing out subscriber counts or demographics, and specify the exact deliverable and price (e.g., '60 second integration' rather than 'Integrated YouTube'). Never highlight weak or unrequested stats like 20% US and 10% India when the brand asked for US/UK, and eliminate typos because sloppiness immediately destroys trust. Using a soft CTA at the end is good.
entries.rewrite: We work with [Creator Name with channel hyperlinked], here are the full analytics [Google Drive hyperlinked], and we can do a 60 second integration for $1,000. Let me know what works for you.

quote.quote: you have a whole training to understand what's integration, what's a 60 second integration, a 90 second integration, a pre-roll, a mid-roll, a post-roll, dedicated video, you have a whole training for this, Akhi, a whole training, and you said integrated YouTube

entries.situation: A beginner student submits his first cold outreach email to an influencer pointing out a gap in their sponsorship lineup.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Noticed a gap in your sponsor lineup
Hey [first name], your [name of the video] crushed it. Yep, no sponsor on that one. That's a missed win. There are brands actually looking to lock in a creator with your kind of traction. Are you open to working with new brands for the upcoming content?
entries.points: Avoid inserting just the video title because it looks like a generic copy-paste template, remove emotional cheerleading like 'crushed it', don't insult the creator by calling an unsponsored video a 'missed win', personalize with something specific they said or did in the video, and name specific brands in your offer.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: I've noticed something
[Personalize with something specific he said or did in the video.] We have in mind these brands. Would you be interested in working with them? Let me know.

quote.quote: even if video is crushing it, we don't need to say that, right, we are just businessmen, it could be Mr. Beast in his new videos, doesn't have to, we don't have to show our emotions

entries.situation: A student submits a cold email to a tech creator about a ChatGPT model comparison video, asking if they are open to partnership ideas that 'bring value to your viewers.'
entries.student_email:
Hi [first name],
I saw your recent objective comparison of the [ChatGPT models], where you broke down the model, health tools, and the practical summary of each module stood out. Would you be open to exploring partnership ideas that bring value to your viewers?
entries.points: Cut the banned opening 'I saw', never use the buzzword 'value' (instead provide value by naming something specific), and avoid weak question CTAs or 'if' phrasing that gives the creator an easy out; use a direct statement CTA like 'If this sounds good, let me know.'
entries.rewrite:
Hi [first name],

Your recent objective comparison of the [ChatGPT models], where you broke down the model, health tools, and the practical summary of each module stood out.

We help brands and line up creators for [specific brands]. If this sounds good, let me know.

quote.quote: Yeah, don't, first of all, I don't like asking questions. And second of all is, instead of mentioning value, try to provide value by mentioning something very small.

entries.situation: An influencer's talent agency replied to a student's cold email stating they do not do affiliate deals but are open to flat-fee partnerships; the student replied with a long, ChatGPT-written paragraph praising their professionalism, explaining why flat-fee deals are good, and asking zero questions.
entries.student_email: Thank you for your prompt and professional response — it's great to hear from you back. We completely understand your position and are also interested in exploring flat fee partnerships. Our goal is to build long-term and mutually beneficial relationship between brands and creators where both parties see consistently value and mutual gains. We would encourage flat fee collaborations as they offer transparent [value], especially when the content continues to generate views over time. I look forward to hearing from you.
entries.points: Never gush over how 'prompt and professional' their reply is, cut all corporate fluff about 'mutually beneficial relationships', stop lecturing experienced agencies on how flat-fee sponsorships work, and always include a next-step question—either warming them up by asking how many integrations they can do per month, or asking for rates and analytics if they are eager.
entries.rewrite: Thank you for your response. Flat fee / CPM makes sense, no worries, totally understandable. We have [Brand A, Brand B] in mind. How many integrations can you do a month?

quote.quote: no be like okay cpm makes sense no worries totally understandable we have these these brands you know if you are afraid they will ghost you don't go for audience analytics in the first email warm them up a bit

entries.situation: A student submits a second cold email to a food creator containing links, generic praise about mixing storytelling and technique, two 'if' statements, and saying they are 'onboarding' and 'planning to reach out' to brands.
entries.student_email:
Hi [first name],
I like how your videos mix storytelling and technique, giving context about each recipe before showing the hands-on process. Noticed your video was sponsored by [Brand], and I wanted to check if you are interested in working with more brands. We're onboarding creators and planning to reach out to those brands. Let me know if you'd like me to share further details.
entries.points: Remove links and 'I like' statements, replace generic cooking praise with a specific detail from a single video, eliminate defensive 'if' phrasing that ruins power dynamics, and never tell creators you are 'onboarding' or 'planning to reach out to brands'—just state that you have specific brands in mind for them.
entries.rewrite:
Hi [first name],

[Specific comment on one video.]

Your partnership with [Brand] was very good. We have [Brand A, Brand B] in mind for you — what do you think? Should I share more details?

quote.quote: I like how your videos mix storytelling and technique, giving context, About each recipe before showing the hands-on process. Still too generic, okay? You can send to every single guy who is making food

entries.situation: A student who got zero positive replies and several 'don't message me' responses from his last 50 tech outreaches submits his new cold email about a Galaxy Gas video.
entries.student_email:
Subject: About your latest video
Hi [Name],
I just finished watching your latest video — great deep dive into [topic]! I was genuinely shocked by the difference in scale. I had no idea one can of Galaxy Gas (2000 grams) was roughly equal to 23,000 small whipped cream bottles. That really put the intent of the product into perspective. I also noticed the video wasn't sponsored. Are you open to partnerships? If so, I'd love to connect and explore potential collaboration opportunities. Looking forward to hearing from you :)
Kind regards
entries.points: Change the subject line 'About your latest video' because creators with big egos think you are criticizing their video and will report you; cut dishonest openers like 'I just finished watching your latest video', remove fangirl reactions like 'great deep dive' and 'I was genuinely shocked', drop the triple 'if/love' CTA and smiley face, and state which brands you work with directly.

Subject: Last video sparked an idea
Hi [Name],

Saw your video — one can of Galaxy Gas (2000 grams) being roughly equal to 23,000 small whipped cream bottles really put the intent of the product into perspective.

I noticed you do partnerships with [Brand]. We work with [Brand]. You with us / you cool?

entries.situation: A student submits a cold email to an AI/tech creator with a hyphenated subject line, 'hey there' greeting, 'We just saw' opener, and ChatGPT praise about how AI could become dangerous.

hey there,
We just saw your latest video and the way you laid out how AI could turn into something dangerous was powerful, especially when you walk through the prediction path. I also noticed your video wasn't sponsored...

entries.situation: A student submits his initial cold email to a study creator saying 'We are currently onboarding creators', 'We'll take care of the outreach and setup, so you don't have to', and signing off with 'Respectfully.'
entries.student_email:
Subject: you left something while you were studying

entries.situation: After the study creator replied asking for specific brand names and campaign scope, the student sent a long response full of corporate fluff without naming any brands and asked for audience analytics stating 'We're mainly looking for US, UK based audience above the age of 20', causing the creator to ghost.
entries.student_email: Thanks for getting back. I completely understand and respect your care in making sure the fit is right. We firmly believe in establishing value that suits your content and comfort. For transparency, the campaign scope involves brand integration within your study content, similar to your [past video]. We'd love to find the fit that feels natural for you and your audience. In order to better answer you, I'd like to get a better idea about your audience before moving forward. Would you mind sending a snapshot of your audience analytics? We're mainly looking for US, UK based audience above the age of 20, as that's typically what brands look for when considering them. Respectfully, [Name]
entries.points: When an influencer asks for specific brands and campaign scope, actually answer their question by naming concrete brands (e.g., Brilliant, FlexiSpot, Apple Watch) and deliverables (60-90 second integrations) instead of dodging with corporate fluff to force your analytics script; and never reveal the target audience demographics before seeing their analytics.

Thanks for getting back. We're looking for 60 to 90 second integrations, and we have brands like Brilliant, FlexiSpot, and Apple Watch in mind. Could you send over a snapshot of your audience analytics?

Best,

entries.situation: A student (Salman) submits his first two cold outreach emails to fitness creators using the subject line 'Brand Partnership Inquiry', generic praise, promises to 'handle everything' and 'boost your monthly revenue', and asking for current sponsorship rates in the first email.

[Specific personalization from video.]

entries.situation: A student (Salman) submits a cold email to a tech creator about an iPhone 17 evolution video filled with ChatGPT commentary on Apple's progress, saying 'That is exactly where many creators miss opportunities', praising 'great content like this gets the brand backing it deserves', and asking for a 'quick chat next week.'
entries.student_email:
Subject: Connecting with [Name] - Sponsorship Offer
Hi [first name],
I really enjoyed your video on the evolution of the iPhone. With the iPhone 17 having just launched two weeks ago, it's amazing to look back and see how far Apple has progressed over the years. I noticed this video wasn't sponsored. That is exactly where many creators miss opportunities. We help tech-focused creators secure more partnerships so great content like this gets the brand backing it deserves. Interested in a quick chat next week to explore how?
entries.points: Cut the ChatGPT essay about how far Apple has progressed and instead mention a concrete point from the review (like speaker size or grip); stop lecturing creators that unsponsored videos are 'missed opportunities'; remove heavy praise ('I really enjoyed', 'amazing', 'great content') because each compliment inflates the creator's rate by hundreds of dollars; and ask for a 'quick chat' without delaying it to 'next week.'
entries.rewrite:
Hi [first name],

entries.situation: During a brand upsell, the brand insisted on paying the old rate of $1,800 total ($600/video) despite the creator's views tripling. Florin shows his counter-emails declining the old rate and proposing a $1,800 base plus 30-day view milestone bonuses.
entries.student_email: Thank you for your message. Given X's growth and the performance of the previous campaign, we will not be able to move forward at the previous rate, 1800, his rate has been updated accordingly. That said, would you be able to offer to explore a structure that works on both sides if you are considering multiple placements? ... Thank you for the transparency. This makes sense on our side. ... we'd be open to structure this in a performance based way to align with the targets. For example, we would keep a base of 1800 and add performance bonuses tied to view milestone within 30 days. ... Happy to align on the thresholds that work for both sides.
entries.points: Keep negotiation emails lean and purposeful with zero fluff. Take time to ensure every line serves a strategic purpose, and maintain a firm, professional, non-needy, and non-salesy tone; when a brand gives a low offer, you can also propose creative structures like hybrid base-plus-CPM/affiliate/view-guarantee deals.

quote.quote: when you're negotiating, it's not like, you don't need to be salesy. Like, hey, if this is the last one, buy today or get one free. That's not how it works. Be professional, not needy, and everything that you say should have value.

entries.situation: After the brand rejected a hybrid deal and repeated that $1,800 ($600/video) was their max, Florin sent a pushback email without naming a new counter-number, stating that the creator raised his rate due to channel growth, noting there would be little to no agency margin at $1,800, and asking about their internal targets and conversions from the previous 450k-view campaign. The brand responded by nearly doubling their offer to $3,500 per video.
entries.student_email: We'll be interesting in moving forward. However, this guy increased his rate, and mentioned that it reflects the growth of his channel, and the trust built with, with, with his audience over the past four months. ... we understand your targets, but at the current rate, given his updated pricing after strong performance, there will be little to no margin on our end, which makes it difficult to move forward. ... Could you tell us, could you tell us more about your internal targets and the conversions discount control?
entries.points: When a brand's offer is unreasonably low compared to past campaign performance, push back firmly and politely without bidding against yourself with a lower counter-number, and use a pointed CTA asking them to share the internal targets and conversions the previous campaign drove so they are forced to confront the numbers.

quote.quote: One thing I've noticed is, throughout these negotiations, you've mentioned the price at the beginning, but you haven't even mentioned accounts or anything. You're just pushing back on them. You're doing it in a very clever way, where you're being firm, you're being polite

entries.situation: After the brand raised its offer to $3,500 per video (giving roughly $7,000 total profit across three videos), Florin shows his calm, one-sentence acceptance email matching their punctuation.
entries.student_email: Thank you for checking in with the team, we can move forward, add a trade, looking forward to the next steps.
entries.points: When a brand agrees to a rate that gives you a strong profit margin, accept it calmly and professionally without acting overly excited or using excessive exclamation marks/emojis, and do not let greed or ego about where your initial anchor started push you to haggle further and lose the deal.

quote.quote: you want to have the balance of like, you know you're making crazy profit, just close the deal, inshallah, but no excitingness, no blah blah blah, all this type of stuff, yeah, send over the contract, see what we could do, yeah, very good stuff.

entries.situation: A student submits three follow-up emails sent to outdoor fishing brands after receiving no response to the initial pitch.
entries.student_email:
Follow-up 1: Hey, wanted to bump this back up in case it got buried. Still think there's a real fit there. Happy to send over profile, content example or numbers, whatever is most useful at your end. No pressure either way.

Follow-up 2: Just making sure you saw this.

Follow-up 3: I've reached out a couple of times, but I haven't heard back, I'd appreciate a response to my email below.
entries.points: Do not beg or use overly soft phrases like 'no pressure either way' in the first follow-up, never send a one-liner like 'just making sure you saw this' (which is spam behavior), and never demand a reply ('I'd appreciate a response to my email below'), which is rude. Instead, use Follow-up 1 as a simple reminder, Follow-up 2 to adjust the offer, and Follow-up 3 as a polite breakup giving two options: tell me what you are looking for, or should I circle back in a few months.

entries.student_email:
Follow-up 1: I wanted to follow up on my previous email. I continue to enjoy your content and the positive impact it has on encouraging people to step outside their comfort zones. I would be interested to hear your thoughts about partnership opportunities.
Follow-up 2: Hi, I figured I'd take your advice and step outside of my comfort zone by sending one more follow-up.
Follow-up 3: I figured I'd take your own advice one last time. We still think a brand whose focus is on personal growth and well-being aligns naturally with the positive messages you share. Would you be interested? We have brands in mind that would be a strong fit for your audience, but we need to know if brand partnerships are something you are considering. If so, let's talk, if not, I'll stop filling your inbox.
entries.points: Never make follow-ups longer than the initial email or use needy jokes about stepping out of your comfort zone. Use 'I' instead of 'we' when expressing an opinion, and put your clear value proposition and CTA in the very first email rather than waiting until the third follow-up.
entries.rewrite: I think a brand whose focus is on personal growth and well-being aligns naturally with the positive messages you share. We have brands in mind that would be a strong fit for your audience, but we need to know if brand partnerships are something you are considering. Would you be interested?

quote.quote: Bro, this should be your first message, this should be your first message. Would you be interested? Yeah, this is your first, this is your initial email, this is follow-up, this is not follow-up.

entries.situation: A student writes a first cold email to a tech/software engineering YouTuber referencing an oddly satisfying keyboard sound in their video, saying 'I'm planning outreach in this space over the next few months,' and asking 'Should I send a few ideas?'.

You already work with some strong tech brands, but I think your software engineering content could also fit developer tools like [Brand]. I'm planning outreach in this space over the next few months. entries.situation: A beginner student in the education niche sends his first cold outreach email to a history creator about a video where Swiss farmers ambushed an army, criticizing the creator's previous sponsors as a poor fit for the education niche and asking if they are interested in a partnership.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Farmers ambushed an army

Hi [First Name],

It's hard to comprehend how a group of farmers managed to defeat one of the key armies. The Swiss historians in your comments clearly enjoyed the last update.

You've had videos sponsored by [Brand A] and [Brand B], but those brands don't seem like the best fit for an education niche. I want to connect influencers like yourself to brands such as [Brand C] and [Brand D], who are more comparable with your niche. Would you be interested in a partnership?
entries.points: Do not use a subject line that simply repeats the video title; flip it creatively. Put the strongest audience observation in the very first sentence. Never insult a creator's past sponsors or promise brands that are a much better fit when you have no brands lined up, as this sets sky-high expectations and triggers budget questions you cannot answer. Avoid the word 'partnership' if you have no brand, and soften the offer by saying 'brands such as X, Y, or something similar' to pre-handle objections.
entries.rewrite: Since they ambushed, I have something to ambush you with as well. The Swiss historians in your comments clearly enjoyed the last update, and it's hard to comprehend how a group of farmers managed to defeat one of the key armies. Since you worked with [Brand A] and [Brand B], you will probably be interested in working with brands such as [Brand C], [Brand D], or something similar as well. What do you think?

quote.quote: Since you work with these brands, you will probably be interested in working with these brands or something similar as well. Something similar basically removes pre, you know, pre-objection handling, pre-objection handling.

entries.situation: A student emails a running creator who only links his own running clothing shop in his description, including three separate CTAs, lots of first-person 'I' statements, and a line promising brands 'that don't clash with your business either'.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Thankfully, my feet are normal sized

Hello [First Name],

I actually know a guy who's got wide feet. I think I'll just point him to your recent video.

I saw that you only display your own shop in your description. Are you open to working with any brands at all?

I'm connecting people with fitness and running brands which fit your content really well, ones like [Brand A] and [Brand B], things that don't clash with your business either. Are you open to further details?

Looking forward to hearing from you soon.
entries.points: Rewrite the opening to remove repetitive 'I' statements. Never put three CTAs in one email, do not ask 'Are you open to further details?' when you have no details yet, and drop 'Looking forward to hearing from you soon' on a first email. Also remove 'things that don't clash with your business either' so the creator has a reason to reply with that concern. Structure the email as: 1) Personalization, 2) Offer connecting them with fitness/running brands, 3) Observation that they only display their own shop + one CTA ('Are you open to working with any of those brands?').

entries.situation: A student emails a privacy software brand with the subject 'Incogni is already here, I want you', mentions creators averaging 787,000 views who worked with competitor Incogni, follows up saying they generated 1.87M views on Incogni-sponsored content over the last 4 months, and sends a long final follow-up starting with 'Final follow-up from me on this' and ending passively ('if this is not something this brand is exploring right now, no worries at all').
entries.student_email:
Subject: Incogni is already here, I want you

Initial Email:
Hello [Name], ... Working with my content creators (36%), creators like [Creator] averaging 787,000 views have already shown a strong fit for privacy software with competitors like Incogni, using this creator lane successfully. Should I send the media kit? Looking forward to hearing from you.

Follow-up 1:
Just following up here. We have creators who could be a strong fit for [Brand], particularly those who already perform well with a privacy software audience—helped generate 1.87M views on Incogni-sponsored content over the last 4 months. Want me to send over the media kit?

Follow-up 2:
Final follow-up from me on this. We have creators who are already proving a strong fit for privacy... If this is not something [Brand] is exploring right now, no worries at all. If it's something you may revisit later, let me know, and we can pick things up at a better time.
entries.points: Change the overly aggressive subject line ('Incogni is already here, I want you') to a natural timeframe hook like 'Last year they helped Incogni, it's your time'. While citing 787,000 average views and competitor fit is good, never say the creator worked with a direct competitor 'in the last 4 months' because 6-month exclusivity clauses will disqualify them. Keep follow-ups to 3 sentences maximum instead of making each follow-up longer than the first email. Never write 'Final follow-up from me on this' or end passively ('no worries at all'); instead ask actively: 'If the timing is not okay, should I circle back in a month / in Q3?'

entries.situation: Student Ibrahim submits a 5-step follow-up sequence for influencer outreach to check if the messages are too generic or out of order.
entries.student_email:
1) ...Let me know your thoughts.
2) I know inboxes get hectic sometimes. Still lining up creators for the campaigns I mentioned. Let me know what you think.
3) Hi there, checking in on my previous email. I think there's some solid crossover between your builds and what we are working on. Let me know either way.
4) This is my last follow-up before I assume you're not interested right now. Let me know if timing works down the line.
5) Let's check in on this. If timing doesn't work now, no worries, let me know either way.
entries.points: Reorder and lengthen the sequence: the first follow-up ('Let me know your thoughts') is too aggressive and too short (ultra-short follow-ups look like spam); the second and third follow-ups are good soft reminders; the fourth follow-up should specify a concrete time to circle back (e.g., mid-March or next month) instead of 'down the line'; and the fifth follow-up is written as a soft check-in when the final email must be a firm breakup message stating you will not email them again.
entries.rewrite: Should I circle back in [next month / mid-March / Q2]? This is the last one I'm going to send, and that's all, I'm finishing with this one.

quote.quote: maybe make a couple of those a bit longer, especially this one, especially this one, and you're good to go. Because guys, short emails means like spam.

entries.situation: A student submits two very short martial arts / BJJ influencer outreach emails that jump straight from a one-line comment to 'Are you open to brand partnerships?' and contain links.

Connect the personalization to your pitch using a bridge phrase and state that you have specific brands in mind for their content.

We have these brands in mind that we believe would be a good fit for your content. What do you think? Let me know.

entries.situation: A student pitched a natural health creator with a generic 'science-backed' compliment, mentioned a deleted past sponsored video, pitched unrelated tech brands (Hostinger, Surfshark VPN), and asked the CTA question twice.

entries.situation: A student scheduled a cold email with the subject line 'Stay alert', claiming the Amex-Platinum partnership was the most underrated move in the Walmart story without explaining why, then pitching political creators for 'paid sponsorships and meaningful relationships'.

Hey [First Name], the Amex-Platinum partnership was the most underrated move in the Walmart story. Now let's discuss building your story. We work with political creators, helping them secure more paid sponsorships and build meaningful relationships. Open to hearing more?
entries.points: Cancel the scheduled email immediately: ditch alarmist subject lines like 'Stay alert', explain why a cited partnership worked or failed before bridging into your offer, and drop needy or bizarre phrasing like 'secure more paid sponsorships and build meaningful relationships'.
