quote.quote: Look, this partnership was the most underrated move in Walmart story. Walmart story. And that's it. You didn't say why. Give me reason. Show me. Teach me. Bro, you started super, like, confident and stuff. Give me reason.

entries.situation: A student submitted five nearly identical ChatGPT-written fitness brand emails using 'sparked an idea' in the subject lines, repeating 'I've been following [Brand] growth', inserting full YouTube video titles, using 'I work with a roster of fitness creators', and dumping average views and US/UK audience stats with 'predominantly' and 'respectively'.
entries.student_email:
Subject: YouTube integration sparked an idea / Your sparkling tropical flavor sparked an idea / Your Hero Whey launch needs the right faces

Hi [Name], I've been following [Brand]'s growth, and the way [Creator] integrated the drink into his video [Video Title] felt creative and authentic, more like genuine use than a placement, which clearly resonated with his audience.

I work with a roster of fitness creators, and I have two who I think would be a strong fit for [Brand]. Would you be open to hearing more?

[Follow-up / Variation]: [Creator 1] and [Creator 2] average [X] and [Y] views, respectively, with a predominantly U.S. and U.K. audience that aligns closely with [Brand]'s positioning. Happy to send over analytics and audience breakdown, and past campaign results if it's worth a conversation.
entries.points: Stop copy-pasting ChatGPT phrasing ('sparked an idea', 'predominantly', 'respectively') and full video titles (just say 'in his last video'); explain why a past integration worked; use 'we' as an agency and name top creators on your roster to build value; don't dump all your analytics upfront; and use a stronger, specific CTA like 'Should I send more details?' or 'Should we stick to these two, or are you interested in more creators?'
entries.rewrite: The last integration with [Creator] was great because [reason], and maybe you need more of these. Luckily for you, we work with a roster of fitness creators including [Creator 1] and [Creator 2] who would be a strong fit for you. Should I send more details, or should we stick to these two?

quote.quote: Happy to send over analytics and audience breakdown. Bro, what I have left? You send everything. Look, what else you have to send? Screenshots? Just that? Past campaign results if it's worth a conversation. And past campaign results, if you have these

entries.situation: A student wrote a first email to a DIY creator duo with the subject line 'untapped potential', opening with 'Hope you're both well, just wanted to reach out for a couple of things', praising an L-cabinets video from last year, questioning whether their irrelevantly matched video sponsor was 'by design', and offering to bring brands that better reflect what they do.
entries.student_email:
Subject: untapped potential

Hey guys, hope you're both well, just wanted to reach out for a couple of things. The custom built L-cabinets video you made last year was super helpful when I redid my bathroom wardrobe, so thanks for that. I also noticed the video sponsor wasn't entirely relevant to the project, was that by design? entries.points: Keep the subject line 'untapped potential' (and test variations of it), cut filler greetings ('Hope you're both well, just wanted to reach out...'), reference a recent video instead of one from last year, bridge personal gratitude into a reciprocal offer ('You helped me with this, let me help you with brands'), and never criticize their past sponsor's relevance or over-promise strictly niche-specific brands.

Hey [Names], the [recent project] video was super helpful when I redid my bedroom wardrobe, so thanks for that. Since you helped me with this, I have something in return and would love to help you with brands...

entries.situation: A student wrote to a sports influencer with the subject line 'open to partnerships', starting with 'saw your content recently, you hit some clutch shots in your last video, was absolutely bananas', then saying 'you do not have sponsors for most of your videos. entries.points: Replace weak subject lines like 'open to partnerships' with curiosity questions like 'Are you ready?'; cut 'saw your content recently' and silly slang like 'absolutely bananas'; avoid mocking the creator for not having sponsors on most videos; stick to one question per email; and use a standard sign-off like 'Best regards'.

entries.situation: After a brand expressed openness to seeing other athletes, a student emailed a new influencer claiming to be reaching out 'on behalf of' that brand. The influencer contacted the brand directly on Instagram to verify, causing the brand's director of partnerships to demand the student cease claiming to represent them.
entries.student_email: I'm reaching out on behalf of this brand. Would you be open to working with them, collaborating?
entries.points: Never tell influencers you are reaching out 'on behalf of' a brand when you do not have permission, because influencers or their talent agencies may contact the brand directly to verify. Instead, say you work with brands 'like X, Y, Z' or are planning campaigns with those types of brands.
entries.rewrite: We are working with brands like X, Y, Z. We're working closely / we're planning to do campaigns with these sort of brands, let us know.

quote.quote: You can say we're working closely. Are we planning to do campaigns with these sort of brands? Let us know. Because you will fall into some agencies having direct contact with the brand, for example.

entries.situation: When presenting influencers to an interested brand, a student wrote a long explanation detailing the exact US/UK audience percentages and gender breakdown to convince the brand why the creator was a match, after which the brand ghosted.
entries.student_email: This influencer is good, because he's got this many people from USA, UK. He's got predominantly male, and male, I'm guessing, is good, be good for your brand.
entries.points: Keep the pitch to a single concise sentence instead of listing out every demographic percentage in the text. Over-explaining why an influencer is a match crosses the line from selling into sounding needy and scares brands away.
entries.rewrite: We've got this guy, we've got a strong audience in the US, has a high presence in the speaking niche. So I believe there's no other fit like him.

quote.quote: Yeah, you have to keep it simple. Why? Because there's a fine line between you actually selling your influencer and you basically saying, please, please, please take my influencer, right? So there's a difference there. So you have to sound not needy.

entries.situation: The fitness niche student shows his follow-up emails, which were sent as separate email threads with new subject lines and missing punctuation.

entries.points: Never send follow-ups as new emails with new subject lines; always click 'Reply' on your initial outreach email so all follow-ups stay in the same thread. Fix missing commas and grammar using Grammarly, and replace abrupt, copy-pasted lines like 'Circling back on my last email, any thoughts?' with fuller, natural sentences.
entries.rewrite: Circling back on my last email, I wanted to check if you read this and that.

quote.quote: Circling back on my last email, any thoughts? So if we read this, circling back on my email, any thoughts? No comma, no anything. This is not good. This is not good follow-up.

entries.situation: A student in the mobile filmmaking niche shares an outreach email to a creator named Jack about his iPhone 17 Pro review.
entries.student_email:

I've been watching a few iPhone 17 Pro reviews and I agree with your conclusion that there isn't a better smartphone for video creators. Speaking of creators, I believe your content could fit for several mobile filmmaking gear brands we have in mind. I also noticed that most of your recent videos weren't sponsored.
entries.points: The subject line 'Jack, check this' is good (adding an exclamation mark makes it even better). Cut unnecessary setup fluff ('I've been watching a few iPhone 17 Pro reviews') and replace the weak 'Speaking of creators' transition by tying your agreement directly into the fact that his recent videos are unsponsored.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Hey, check this!

Totally agree with you, iPhone 17 Pro is something that video creators wish for. Would you agree with me that all of your videos deserve paid collaboration? If so, we have some brands in mind for you. Would you be open to it?

entries.situation: The mobile filmmaking student shares a second cold email with the subject line 'About that' referencing an iPhone 17 video.

Hi, Jack. I just used your iPhone 17 best in years video to win an argument. Apple has clearly shifted pro models toward filmmaking, so most people don't really need it. Keep the playful opening about winning an argument, make the second sentence more casual/humorous, and do not stack multiple pitch reasons ('your channel could be a good fit' AND 'I noticed some recent videos weren't sponsored')—pick just one. End with a simple, soft CTA like 'Let me know your thoughts.'

entries.situation: The mobile filmmaking student used a subject line ('Your amazing products could a collab be possible?') that the creator himself had shown in a video as an old email he sent to a brand 5 years ago.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Your amazing products could a collab be possible?

Hey [First Name], That was the subject line of the email you sent five years ago, which stood out to me with the line about only reviewing products that really make sense to you and your viewers. Because of that, and the content you make today, I think your channel could be a great fit for several brands we have in mind. Open to more brand collabs?
entries.points: Never put phrases like 'Your amazing products' in a subject line because it kills curiosity and looks like flattery, and the creator likely won't remember a subject line he wrote 5 years ago before opening the email. Use a short curiosity subject line like 'check this' or 'thoughts?' and mention his 5-year-old subject line inside the email body instead.
entries.rewrite:

Hey [First Name], maybe I should use the subject line that you used five years ago...

entries.situation: The mobile filmmaking student shares a fourth cold email that pastes the exact full title of the creator's video into the first sentence and says 'Since you're into content creation'.
entries.student_email:
Subject: About that

Your 'Gimbals are boring except this one' video caught my attention even though I'm more of a smartphone gimbal enthusiast. I'm asking because we are in a smartphone filmmaking niche, and are currently looking to connect brands with creators. Since you're into content creation, I think your channel could be a fit. Would you like to explore this?
entries.points: Never paste the full verbatim title of a creator's video into your email body, because mass-sending tools like Instantly use '{{video_title}}' merge tags and Google Workspace spam filters flag emails that look like automated campaigns or AI output. Paraphrase the video topic naturally, and replace 'Since you're into content creation' with 'Based on your content, we have brands that your audience would like to see.'

entries.situation: A student in the fitness niche submits three outreach emails that all follow the exact same ChatGPT-style template ('I came across your YouTube channel...', 'I noticed in a few of your recent videos that you partnered with...', 'No rush at all...').
entries.student_email: I came across your YouTube channel, and I'm loving the variety of your content, especially your latest video about trying sports that I didn't even know existed. Great fun to watch, and I definitely need to try some of them out. I noticed in a few of your recent videos that you partnered with MacroFactor and Yazio, and I was wondering if you're open to exploring additional partnership avenues. No rush at all. Just wanted to reach out and see if it's something you'd be open to chatting about. Looking forward to hearing your thoughts.
entries.points: Stop using ChatGPT to write cold emails (only use it to critique your drafts from an influencer's perspective) and never reuse the exact same sentence structure across emails by just swapping video and brand names, as Google flags repetitive patterns. Center the email and subject line around a single unique hook (like 'trying sports that I didn't even know existed'), cut 'No rush at all', and use only one CTA at the end instead of stacking three CTAs. Keeping pretentious titles like 'CEO' or 'Entrepreneur' out of the sign-off is good.

entries.situation: A student noticed a brand hiring three or four marketing positions on LinkedIn and pitched them by assuming they have a brand awareness problem and mentioning a single creator.

entries.points: Drop the assumption about newsletters and an awareness problem; hiring multiple marketing agents indicates the brand is ramping up to scale a large influencer campaign. Pitch a specific creator first and subtly mention that you have a larger roster of creators on standby ready to align with them.

entries.situation: A student pitches an automotive restoration creator with a Supra rebuild to a tool/equipment brand without personalization.
entries.student_email:
Subject: You should definitely consider him
I work with a creator whose content focus on car builds and restoration in front of 64% tier 1 audience, his recent campaign with [brand] achieved [X] views and with a full Supra rebuild, can be shown power tools or equipment during the build process, send over his demographics? entries.points: Avoid the risky subject line 'you should definitely consider him', replace 'I work with a creator' with 'we are helping a creator like him get more trusted brands', replace vague '64% tier 1 audience' with exact top-country percentages (e.g., US and UK), drop campaign view counts so brands don't demand conversion rates, and fix the broken CTA 'Send over his demographics?' to 'Should I send over his demographics?'.
entries.rewrite: We are helping a creator like him get more trusted brands... In the past, he had successful collaborations with brands like [Brand A] and [Brand B]... Should I send over his demographics?

entries.situation: A student reaches out to a cooking creator (Max) about his Nando's peri-peri chicken recreation video.

entries.situation: A student submits an initial email and two follow-ups to a cooking spray / air fryer accessories brand commercial marketing executive.
entries.student_email:

Good morning [name], [Name] from [Agency] here. Loved the championship twist with this one. The one calorie spray angle was genius. I'd love to connect you with the influencer and best-selling author of [air fryer book]. Over 55% of his audience are air fryer enthusiasts in UK and Ireland, right in your lane.
