I noticed how you use the iPhone 11 to improve your sleep. I help creators like you secure the right brand deals...
entries.points: The subject line ('How about we bring [Brand] to your audience') is decent, though a bit too revealing. Remove horizontal HTML dividers/hurdles and heavy formatting because having very few words with bulky HTML increases the kilobyte weight of the email and triggers spam filters like SpamAssassin. Fix the creepy phrasing 'I noticed how you use the iPhone 11 to improve your sleep' (which sounds like spying on him in bed) by explicitly referencing his video: 'I saw your video where you talked about how iPhone 11 can improve your sleep.' Also use 'we help' and name specific brands.
entries.rewrite: I saw your video where you talked about how iPhone 11 can improve your sleep.

quote.quote: Basically, if your email, let's say, have 20 words, it has too many, too many kilobytes, it's heavy, it's bulky, you know, and spam can recognize you, spam assassins, as spam email, because maybe you have file or something in it

entries.situation: A student submits a brand cold email about a fitness recovery device collaboration that lacks a greeting, repeats the brand's name, praises the device like a customer review, and uses wordy fluff to describe the pitched creator.
entries.student_email: I went through [Creator]'s recent video, and I saw that [Brand] sponsor him. He was on point when he talked about how [Product] measures the intensity and recovery of your workout. Not a lot of devices tell you that you need to recover more or work out more. They just tell you how many calories were used up. [Name], we collaborate with similar creators like [Creator]. His focus is on traveling and challenging the mind and body throughout various fitness challenges to teach his audience and optimize fitness. For those reasons, we think he would be a good fit for you.
entries.points: Start the email with a simple greeting like 'Hey [First Name]', avoid repeating the brand's name in the personalization, stop before sounding like a satisfied customer writing a 5-star product review, and tighten the creator pitch and CTA by removing fluff.
entries.rewrite: Hey [Name], I saw your collaboration with [Creator]. He was on point when he talked about how [Product] measures the intensity and recovery of your workout. We collaborate with similar creators like [Creator]. His content is all about fitness challenges and valuable lessons for his audience. That's why we think he might be a good fit. Let me know what you think.

quote.quote: I do not like to mention Brent's. There's a Jamie, let's say. Hey, Jamie, I saw collaboration with Mr. Beast with VPN. Make no sense. You can just say, I saw your collaboration with Mr. Beast. It's more personalized, more humanly.

entries.situation: A student submits a generic ChatGPT-written tech brand email starting with 'Hope this email finds you well', using bold text, claiming 'we think they are great' without specifics, and pitching a 'long-term value-driven relationship' and 'handpicked shortlist'.
entries.student_email: Hi X, Hope this email finds you well. We've came across your recent collaboration with X and we think they are great. We represent another influencer with similar production quality and audience that closely match your target demographics, makes them strong fit for your upcoming campaigns. We focus on building long-term value-driven relationship with the brand we work with and would welcome the opportunity to collaborate with your team. We have handpicked a shortlist of high-impact tech influencers with upcoming integration availability, that could be a strong fit, happy to share it. Warm wishes
entries.points: Delete 'Hope this email finds you well', remove bold text (which triggers spam), watch the 90-second integration to write real marketing personalization, cut all the corporate ChatGPT fluff about long-term relationships and handpicked shortlists, and simply mention two creators with a strong US audience and ask if you should send details.
entries.rewrite: Their audience is mostly USA, which could be a good fit for you, should I send details?

quote.quote: Their audience is mostly USA, which could be a good fit for you, should I send details? Yes, no, that's it, you know, this one, with similar production quality and audience that closely match your... Target demographic.

entries.situation: A student submits a home renovation brand email with the subject line 'Jack, would this be a fit?', praising how a paint remover 'efficiently strips paint without scratching', and pitching a bricklayer creator with a 45.7% UK audience.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Jack, would this be a fit?

Hello [Name], I saw your recent reel with [Creator] showcasing how the paint remover works. It efficiently strips paint without scratching and handles corners with ease. Building on this, [Creator] is a professional bricklayer with a 45.7% UK audience. We believe he could effectively promote your product. We also have a couple of creators with strong audience. Kind regards
entries.points: The subject line 'Jack, would this be a fit?' is strong, but avoid starting with 'I saw your recent reel', stop praising the paint remover like a satisfied customer (comment on the reel's ad execution instead), and simplify the creator pitch.
entries.rewrite: His video content is all about [niche], his audience is mostly UK people, could be a fit, let me know what do you think. Or: We have this guy with this much audience, and also we have a couple of other creators with audience from U.S. as well. Want me to send their details?

quote.quote: If you talk about Mr. Beast showing the product, mention what you like about the ad. Mention what you like about the veil itself, not product. We are not customers.

entries.situation: A student submits a cooking/lifestyle brand email with the subject 'Any thoughts on this?', noting their US-only shipping, saying 'I represent' creators, and asking 'If you're planning upcoming campaigns... Would you like to...'.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Any thoughts on this?

Jack's recent video featuring [Brand] stood out. The placement felt organic and fit well with his content. I saw that your shipping is currently limited to the U.S. I represent [Creators] in the cooking and lifestyle niche with predominantly U.S. based audience. If you're planning upcoming campaigns, these creators would be a strong fit. Would you like me to send...
entries.points: Keep the subject line 'Any thoughts on this?', explain why the ad placement felt organic, move the US-only shipping observation into the offer to justify pitching US-audience creators, never say 'I represent' (use 'we work with' instead), and replace weak 'If you're planning / Would you like' phrasing with 'Should I send?'.
entries.rewrite: Since I saw your shipping is currently limited to U.S., we have some influencers with strong U.S. audience. His content is all about [topic]. That's why we thought it would be a good fit. Should I send?

quote.quote: Look, I represent, this is bad word. This is no, no. This is big no, no. Guys, this is huge red flag. We work with. Why? Because if you say, represent, they figure, probably will figure it out. You represent him exclusively.

entries.situation: Student 1 (automotive car accessories niche) submits his first cold outreach email to an influencer.
entries.student_email: Hey, first name, that overhead shop crane is a very useful tool. That boat on the crane test bar got me. I noticed that only one of your last videos was sponsored. Would love to help you with that. We are planning to reach out to a few brands like this and that, international, which would perfectly fit your content for Q3 collaboration. Let me know your thoughts on that one. Best regards
entries.points: Cut the length down—there is enough material here for two follow-ups. Drop the generic first sentence and only keep 'that boat on the crane test bar got me' plus why. Never claim brands 'perfectly fit' before seeing audience analytics, say you can bring brands fitting their criteria instead of 'we are planning to reach out,' and replace the open-ended CTA ('Let me know your thoughts') with an effortless yes/no question or analytics request.
entries.rewrite: Hey [First Name], that boat on the crane bar got me [and why]. I noticed that only one of your last videos was sponsored. We can bring you brands that fit your criteria, brands similar to [Brand A] and [Brand B]—based on your content, they could be a fit, but we would need more details. Would you be interested? / If you like this, send me your analytics.

quote.quote: Perfectly fit, how do you know will they perfectly fit? You don't have their audience, right? You don't have all details. Maybe you can say, based on your content, they could be a fit, but we would need more details, please send those analytics

entries.situation: Student 2 (tech/AI niche) submits three more influencer emails ('Production nightmare', 'Patrick', and 'stuck in these connected clips') where he removed all line breaks to keep HTML clean and omitted sign-offs like 'Best regards.'
entries.student_email:
Email 2: Subject: Production nightmare. Hey, Mikey, prototypes are easy, but production is a nightmare. Valid observation on the hidden technical depth. We are lining up creators for a few long-term partnerships. I wanted to check if you're open.

Email 3: Hey Patrick, spot on about focusing on sales instead of all the technical perfection, we will actively pitch creators to premium brands in your niche, let me know if you have any open slots for Q3.

Email 4: Subject: stuck in these connected clips. Hey Jay, piecing together these connected clips is definitely a well-liked AI video right now, love your deep dives on the edge, long-term tech brand, let me know if you're open to partnering up.
entries.points: The copy itself is good, but never remove all line breaks or skip a closing sign-off. Squeezing the entire email into a single paragraph hurts readability—use line breaks between personalization, offer, and CTA. Always close with 'Best regards,' 'Kind regards,' or 'Best,' plus your name, as business email standards matter for your signature and brand. Also, minor formatting tweaks like lowercase subject lines won't close deals—your offer and negotiation are what matter.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: stuck in these connected clips

Hey Jay, piecing together these connected clips is definitely a well-liked AI video right now. Love your deep dives on the edge.

[Offer for long-term tech brand partnerships]

Let me know if you're open to partnering up.

Best regards,
[Name]

quote.quote: Coach, I used a subject line with smaller caps and I closed that influencer. It's not about subject line, bro. It's about your offer. It's about your negotiation. That small thing, you know, being like stock this, won't change anything.

entries.situation: Student 3 (productivity niche) submits three AI-written cold emails to productivity and self-development influencers ('The Prestige Trap', 'Your dad', and 'The fulfillment point').
entries.student_email:
Email 1: Subject: The Prestige Trap. Hey [First Name], The way you connect the AI UGC programs and startup equity into a path outside consulting or banking was a strong angle. I'm lining up a few creators for career and AI tools that want to reach students exploring non-traditional ways to build income. Worth a quick look?

Email 2: Subject: Your dad. Hi [First Name], The line about your dad protecting you from the life he got made the whole message hit differently. I'm working with self-development creators on partnerships with brands that fit naturally around your family, emotional growth, and personal reflection.

Email 3: Subject: The fulfillment point. The moment you admitted that the apartment, money, travel in first class seat still does not answer the deeper what's next question made the message feel honest and grounded. Your content fits naturally with self-development, mental wellness, lifestyle, and purpose-driven brands like [Brand A] and [Brand B]. Currently building a small roster... Should I send over the details?
entries.points: Stop using ChatGPT summaries that just tell a creator their video had a 'strong angle'—explain *why* it was a strong angle or simplify it to a short human reaction ('That question, what's next? Goosebumps'). Name specific brands instead of vague descriptions ('career and AI tools that want to reach students...'), which sound like volunteer work, and don't say 'I'm working with self-development creators...' which sounds like you're pitching influencers to an influencer. Finally, never say you're 'building a small roster' (making them feel special makes them quote 3x higher prices) and never ask 'Should I send over the details?' when you have no brand campaign details.
entries.rewrite: That question, 'what's next?' felt honest and grounded—goosebumps. Your content fits naturally with self-development, mental wellness, lifestyle, and purpose-driven brands like [Brand A] and [Brand B].

quote.quote: The way you connect the AI UGC programs and start up equity into a path outside consulting or banking was a strong angle. Okay, instead of what is strong angle, focus on why that's strong angle, because AI cannot do this.

entries.situation: Student 4 (DIY/design niche) submits a cold email to a brand featuring a long personalization about their software 19.1 release and pitching a huge creator with 308M+ views.
entries.student_email: I read about the AI-driven document pouring into the 19.1 release. That's the ideal workflow for showing how you can manage complex supplier invoices, materials, bank, and planning crazy builds to order... audience and creative build enthusiasts. We work with influencers in the design niche, like [Creator Name]. He has [X] subs and 308 million plus views... Are you open to explore?
entries.points: In B2B brand emails, keep personalization brief and written from a marketing perspective ('Saw this, good marketing, strong positioning, but we can help even more'), and make the offer the longest section of the email. Never pitch mega-influencers (e.g., 300M+ views costing $100k+) as a new agency—brands won't trust an unknown agency with large cash budgets and will push for commission or CPM deals instead of flat fees. Pitch $3,000–$5,000 creators first as a foot in the door to build trust.
entries.rewrite: Saw your 19.1 release—good marketing and strong positioning, but we can help even more. We work with creators in the design niche like [Creator in the $3k–$5k range]. Are you open to exploring this?

quote.quote: don't pitch, big influencers in your offer, couple of reasons, one, you are too small, okay, you are too small, they have trust issues, even if they answer you, they will be like, this, probably, he wants to take money and disappear

entries.situation: Student 5 (food/home cooks niche) submits three long brand follow-up emails that open with 'Following up on my last email about creator partnerships' and include a website URL in the signature.
entries.student_email:
Follow-up 1: Just want to follow up on my last email about a creator partnership. If getting more people obsessed with beans is something you focus on, [Creator] is an air fryer enthusiast, would love to help spread that message. For a bit of context of recent performance, his last five videos averaged 340k views and showed good engagement for his viewers.

Follow-up 2: Following up on my last email about creator partnerships. One thing worth noticing is that his audience is a crowd that assumes they can't have syrup because they are trying to eat healthy. Your syrup in his content would show them it can fit into their diet, making your product way more appealing to them. Happy to send...
[Name]
[www.website.com]

Follow-up 3: Just following up on my last email about the creator partnership. One of our creators recently collaborated with [Brand], which pulled [X views]. His content is mainly about modern Filipino comfort food, which would align well with your products.
entries.points: Shorten the follow-ups to 3 sentences (25–30 words) and don't cram multiple angles (audience fit + 340k view stats) into one follow-up. Never start with 'Following up on my last email about creator partnerships' because that line appears in the inbox preview, kills curiosity, and tells the brand you're just pitching the same creator again. Instead, open with 'It's me again' and lead immediately with a curiosity hook (like health-conscious viewers assuming they can't eat syrup, or pivoting to air fryer enthusiasts). Save past collaboration stats for initial emails, and remove website links ('www.___.com') from your signature to avoid spam filters.
entries.rewrite:
It's me again. Imagine, there are people who assume they cannot eat syrup because they are trying to eat healthy—your syrup in his content would show them it can fit into their diet. Also, we work with Air Fryer Enthusiasts; should I send them over to you?

Best,
[Name]

quote.quote: It's me again. Imagine, there are people who assume they cannot eat syrup because they are trying to eat healthy. Like, hey, you're selling those healthy syrups. And, you know, these people have no idea how good and healthy you are.

entries.situation: Student 6 (software niche, Haris) submits two final influencer cold emails using 'with this simple trick' subject lines, calling the creator 'big brain,' mentioning his own software background, and promising 'awesome prizes.'
entries.student_email:
Email 4: Subject: Your newsletters could be much better with simple trick. Hey X, so many people learn super cool skill with C because of your big brain. I came from a software background myself, and I partner with content creators to secure high-value brand sponsorships. Want to team up? [Agency Name]

Email 5: Subject: Make YouTube videos more often with this simple trick. Hey X, the mini Google Drive clone was like building with Legos, snapping a tiny piece together to show how the giant castle actually works. So, to answer a question from the title, you just make the cool video, and then brands pay you awesome prizes. Sounds fun? [Agency Name]
entries.points: Drop the '...with this simple trick' subject lines (they sound like spammy AI ads; use 'It's easier than you think' instead). In Email 4, remove 'because of your big brain' (sounds like his mom) and remove 'I came from a software background myself' (creators only care about the value you bring, not your background), though 'I partner with content creators to secure high-value brand sponsorships. Want to team up?' is strong. In Email 5, the Lego analogy is good, but 'you just make the cool video, and then brands pay you awesome prizes. Sounds fun?' is overly salesy and overpromises. Also remove the agency name.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: It's easier than you think

Hey X, the mini Google Drive clone was like building with Legos, snapping a tiny piece together to show how the giant castle actually works. [One more sentence of personalization].

I partner with content creators to secure high-value brand sponsorships. Want to team up?

Best,
[Name]

quote.quote: I partner with content creators to secure high-value brand sponsorships. Want to team up? It's nice. It is unique. Okay. Make YouTube videos more often with this simple trick. Bro, you look like you are selling AI something.

entries.situation: An influencer replied positively to cold outreach with his rate range (£800-£2,000) and platforms, and the student sent a long, overly enthusiastic reply praising his flexibility before asking for audience analytics.
entries.student_email: yeah, that's exactly the flexibility that works and gets deals closed... rather than firing one-offs, you know, we tend to push for aligned structures and opportunities... from what you said, looks like we have a few brands that would work. Before I start matching things up... it would be useful to get a quick look at your audience analytics, so just the countries, demographics, like age and gender, so I can find you the right brands... Once I've got that, I'll come back to you with a couple opportunities.
entries.points: Never act overly excited or include filler praise when an influencer or brand replies positively, as it ruins your power dynamics and makes them raise their prices or ghost you; keep your tone calm and unimpressed even if their rate is very low.
entries.rewrite: even if he says, look, my rate is a bag of chips, it would be like, yeah, yeah, I don't know, a whole bag

quote.quote: Bro's super excited, right, and this sort of takes away from your power dynamics, right, and it's the same, like, imagine you reach out to a brand, right, and you reach out to them, they're like, amazing, your influencer looks so great, right,

entries.situation: After getting the brand to agree to £4,000 for a two-month YouTube and Instagram bundle, the student emailed the influencer presenting the entire two-month package for £2,500 as a done deal; the influencer immediately pushed back claiming his Reels cost £3k-£6k and asked to do three Instagram stories instead.
entries.student_email: as promised, I've got you a deal with these people, and this is what they've proposed, and this is the term, this is what they're asking for, so I said, look, they're to pay you two and a half K to do all this... it would be a test integration, if it performs well, you know, they'd be open to making long-term, you know, long-term partnership
entries.points: Never present a multi-month bundle to an influencer upfront as a done deal, because it gives them leverage to push for more money or fewer deliverables; instead, test the waters by pitching the lower end of their stated range (such as £800-£1,000) for a single integration and dangle a second month of integrations as a reward if they meet your price.
entries.rewrite: speaking with X-Brand, you know, we're looking at $1,000 per integration, and if you're able to meet us at a price, maybe you're going to be able to get nuance [two months] for you

quote.quote: getting two months across Instagram reels, all of this is a privilege, so don't just give it to them all straight away, like, get them on one price,

entries.situation: After the brand rejected the influencer's counter-proposal for TikTok and YouTube Shorts, the student sent a short ultimatum email to the influencer stating that the brand does not do TikTok partnerships and £3,000 is the absolute maximum for the original deliverables, otherwise they cannot move forward.
entries.student_email: they don't offer partnerships with that, the absolute most they can do is 3k, um, in this month, sort of take it or leave it, otherwise, Otherwise, they can't move forward. Dude, let me know if you want to proceed.
entries.points: When an influencer keeps pushing back on deliverables or price, send a firm, concise take-it-or-leave-it ultimatum stating the maximum budget and that you will be unable to move forward otherwise; showing willingness to walk away flips the power dynamic and gets them to accept.

quote.quote: If he acts really hard to get, you know what you could do, like, you could have sucked back in a few days and be like, look, we changed our minds. It doesn't really matter.

entries.situation: The Shopify rep asked for examples of previous brand integrations the creator (James) had done, and James had never done a brand sponsorship before.
entries.student_email: James hasn't taken on any previous partnerships, he's very selective about brand partnerships, who he works with. This would be his first integration, he's particularly interested in working with Shopify since he already runs his own store on a platform. And loves how easy it is to set up. Let me know if you need anything else.
entries.points: Turn the red flag of having zero past sponsorships into a strong selling point by framing the creator as highly selective who protects his audience's trust and only wants to partner with brands he genuinely uses and loves.

quote.quote: You could be like, look, he hasn't got any partnerships because he is like, he cares about his audience and he only works with brands that he likes and he likes your brand, right? And then his audience will know.

entries.situation: Mubashir shows his initial outreach email to a second major brand that optimizes for awareness, personalizing by noting the region the rep manages and highlighting the creator's view counts and 20+ past partnerships.
entries.student_email: Hi X, notice you handle the marketing for creators in the region... I wanted to reach out on behalf of X, a creator in the space, I saw [20+ partnerships]... he gets this many views.
entries.points: Keep brand personalization simple and relevant to the contact's role (such as noting the region they oversee) rather than citing obscure product features they may not care about, and match the metrics you highlight (such as high views) to the brand's campaign goal (awareness vs. conversion).

quote.quote: brand presentation, can be this simple, and this is way more effective, brand presentation, like, it's like, brothers, oh, think it, they're like, hey, your new release of, like, this product has this, like, feature, bro, like, the influence, you might even know about that

entries.situation: The brand rep asked if Mubashir exclusively manages the creator and requested his rate for a 60-90 second mid-roll integration; Mubashir replied confirming approval to manage and pitch on his behalf, gave the rates, and recommended a pre-roll over a mid-roll.
entries.student_email: Thanks for getting back to me, we have approval to manage and pitch on his behalf. If you were to reach out directly, he would keep us looped in... his current rates are X, Y, and X [and recommending pre-roll over mid-roll].
entries.points: Proactively advising brands on campaign execution—such as recommending pre-roll over mid-roll, suggesting UTM tracking, or creating a QR code when analytics show a large percentage of the creator's audience watches on TV—builds strong trust and relationships.

quote.quote: what can build your relationship with brands is when you bring extra stuff, right? So like for example, the brand, let's say they don't have like a specific UTM, can be like, hey, how come you guys don't have that

entries.situation: When the brand still did not respond to the 12-video proposal, Mubashir sent another follow-up acknowledging they are discussing it internally, sharing the creator's prior background as a senior product marketing manager, listing exact renewal counts (with 8 placed before a higher number at the end), and proposing a call on Tuesday or Thursday.
entries.student_email: Hi X, one thing that might be helpful as you're discussing it internally: before YouTube, Creator was a senior product marketing manager at X company, where a big part of his role was taking fairly complex products and turning them into messaging that people could actually understand. We think that's one of the big reasons brands continue to renew with him. On that note, I thought it might be useful to share also an overview of total renewals so far: [29 renewals, 18 renewals, 10 renewals, 8 renewals, etc.]. At the end of the day, we know it's usually a clear sign that something's working. It would be great to jump on a call to talk through how we'd approach creator in terms of topic angles and building on what you've already done with creators in this space. We're free next Tuesday between X time or Thursday X time, let me know what works best on your end, and I'll get something over.
entries.points: Acknowledge why the brand is taking time ('as you're discussing it internally') to break the ice, spell out exact renewal numbers (putting the lowest number in the middle and a higher number at the end so the whole list looks stronger), and pitch a call with both a clear reason and specific time slots.

quote.quote: and then now you put it up again, so like the press will read it, they're like, oh, like every brand has been doing it so many times, like, so even, like, you see, even those, that, like, little stuff, he's thinking about it

entries.situation: A talent agent asked whether the student had an active paid campaign agreement or was just pitching; the student sent 3-4 cold emails to random brands just so he could claim he was 'in talks with brands' in his reply.
entries.student_email: thanks for your response. We are interested, like, we are in talks with brands, but nothing is fixed yet. But to do that, we have to know some information. We got to collect some data from influencers.
entries.points: Do not tell an influencer or agency that you are 'in talks with brands' when you have only sent cold outreach emails, because 'in talks' means brands have actually replied. Instead, state honestly that you are still in the outreach phase and ask if that is a deal breaker.
entries.rewrite: No, we're still in the outreach phase. Will that be a deal breaker for you?

quote.quote: when you say we are in talks with brands, I'll be... careful, because you're not in talks with them, you just reach out to those brands. Yes. Yeah, so don't say we are in talks, talks means they get back to you.

entries.situation: A student sends a cold outreach email to an automotive influencer starting with heavy fan praise and using conversational fillers like 'First off' and 'Quick question' inside the body.
entries.student_email: First off, nothing personal, but huge respect for taking care of not just one, but several, several legendary cars. Not many people are truly fit for that kind of responsibility. Quick question. Would you be open to explore potential collaboration? We got a few brands in mind that align with your mission and passion for the automotive world.
entries.points: Do not act like a fan or pay 'huge respect' in a cold email; keep the compliment brief and professional based on recent videos. Remove choppy transitions like 'First off' and 'Quick question' (which belongs in a subject line, not the body), place the offer before the CTA, and end directly on the CTA.
entries.rewrite: I saw your videos. You do like solid job repairing cars, a lot of knowledge. Kudos. We've got a few brands in mind that align with your mission and passion for the automotive world. Would you be open to explore potential collaboration?

quote.quote: Would you be open? We've got a few brands in mind that align with your mission and passion for the automotive world. It's not bad. It's not bad offer at all, in my opinion.

entries.situation: A student sends a cold email to an education influencer with the subject line 'Let's have relevant PARTNERSHIPS', greeting 'Hello there', a specific personalization about the Pythagoras theorem, 'we' pronouns throughout, and no clear CTA.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Let's have relevant PARTNERSHIPS

Hello there,

Never thought we would use the Pythagoras theorem to call the distance up to any number or dimension before watching your last video. We saw that it was sponsored by [Brand] and we wanted to know if you're open to new partnerships.
entries.points: Avoid all-caps words in the subject line and use curiosity or video personalization instead (e.g., 'is Pythagoras open to partnerships?'). Find the creator's real name rather than saying 'Hello there'. Keep the highly specific two-part video personalization, balance 'I' and 'we' pronouns, and add a direct yes/no CTA at the end.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Is Pythagoras open to partnerships?

I saw that it was sponsored by [Brand] and I wanted to know if you're open to new partnerships. Should I send more details?

quote.quote: We saw that it was sponsored. If by someone, we wanted to know if you're open to new partnerships, uh, you can go with simple one, should I send more details

entries.situation: A brand replied asking for an offer, and the student sent a long (>70 words), salesy second email pitching a third-division US professional soccer player with two CTAs and a media kit named with a generic abbreviation.
entries.student_email: Thanks for getting back to me. The influencer on reaching we have is [Name], who is a professional football player, who are currently playing third division of professional football in the USA. We believe [his authority] as a professional footballer combined with this [engagement with a football audience]... I've attached media kit for your review, please let me know for details...
entries.points: Keep the second email concise (50–70 words) and avoid overselling. Hyperlink the influencer's name, list key metrics (average views, engagement rate, top audience location), write just one or two sentences on why they fit the brand, attach a professionally named PDF media kit (e.g., 'Name_YouTube_Demographics.pdf'), and close with a single soft CTA.
entries.rewrite: [Influencer Name (linked)] — Average views: 100K, Engagement rate: [X]%, Major audience: US 30%. [One sentence on why the creator is a strong fit for the brand]. I have attached media kit for review, looking forward for your thoughts.

quote.quote: And then I give one sentence why this guy is good. Hatim is good because, you know, he is, I don't know, making an amazing job, Allahabadik, something like that. And that's all. That's all. If it's one influencer, you can maybe do two sentences

entries.situation: A student sends a cold email to a football influencer without a line break after the greeting, with grammar mistakes ('an upcoming campaigns', 'Let us if you're open for it'), and a weak closing line.
entries.student_email: Hey [First Name], [Team] has been the main talking point recently, and we are all waiting for the final decision. Maybe a [transfer] soon, the iconic phrase, here we go. We have an upcoming campaigns for some different brands we have in mind, and we think you are a good fit. Let us if you're open for it.
entries.points: Add a line break after 'Hey [First Name],' so the personalization starts on a new paragraph. Proofread grammar using ChatGPT so words aren't missing or mismatched. Replace 'Let us know if you're open for it' with a direct yes-or-no question ending in a question mark.

entries.situation: A student sends a cold email to an automotive dashcam brand starting with 'I really enjoyed your videos featuring [Dashcam]', pitching unnamed creators with salesy fluff at the end, and closing with 'Let me know if you'd like more details.'
entries.student_email: Hi [Brand], I really enjoyed your videos featuring [Dashcam], the way he captured its dual channel quality and compact design was a perfect match for his audience. We are reaching out as we have automotive creators with strong [reach], hands-on installs, dynamic driving footage, making [Brand] [a great fit]. Let me know if you'd like more details.
entries.points: Avoid saying 'I really enjoyed' because it sounds like a fan; use professional praise like 'Saw your last video, solid execution' while keeping the specific detail about dual-channel quality and compact design. Name two specific creators ('including [Name 1] and [Name 2] with strong UK/US reach'), trim the salesy fluff at the end of the offer, and turn the CTA into a direct yes/no question ('Should I send more details?').
entries.rewrite: Hi [Brand], saw your last video featuring [Dashcam], solid execution—the way he captured its dual channel quality and compact design was a perfect match for his audience. We are reaching out as we have automotive creators, including [Name 1] and [Name 2], with strong UK and US reach, hands-on installs, and dynamic driving footage. Should I send more details?

entries.situation: A student submits an initial cold email to Maya at Oura Ring referencing a past sponsorship with Shervin and pitching a creator named Jordan with the same lifestyle integration.
entries.student_email: Subject: A creator can solve Aura's biggest problem. Hi Maya, liked how Shervin took on the biggest hurdle for wearables by showing how naturally the Oura ring fits into his day, it's discreet, comfortable, and felt more a part of his routine. We work with creators like Jordan, who could bring that same lifestyle integration to how he fits in his everyday routine. Shall I send his profile?
entries.points: Make the subject line more curiosity-driven, shorten the personalization, remove any hyperlinks, pictures, or videos from initial emails, never pitch a creator as bringing the 'same' integration or audience as a past creator, explain how the new creator does something different to improve ROI, and replace 'Shall I' with a stronger cold-email CTA.
entries.rewrite: Subject: we can solve that problem for you. Body: Collaboration with this guy was good because he did that, but I think this could be a bit more different. Speaking of different, there's a guy who could do that—he is doing this, this, this, and in that way we can improve your ROI.

entries.situation: A student submits a follow-up email to Ciara starting with 'Maybe the first angle just wasn't quite right', pitching a workflow comparison idea, and repeating the same CTA.
entries.student_email: Hi Ciara, maybe the first angle just wasn't quite right. Here's an idea: three times the same data-heavy workflow before and after the 2.0 operation, showing how fast it runs...
entries.points: Never say 'maybe the first angle wasn't quite right' in a follow-up, because it undermines your previous offer and makes you look like you are randomly throwing influencers around. Stand behind your original creator while offering alternative creators in case the timing or current campaign focus differs, lead with the video idea, and vary your CTAs across follow-ups.

entries.situation: A student submits an initial cold email to an outdoors influencer with the subject line 'Was Tobii right?', personalization about waiting it out with Abdi, a bridge line comparing waiting to brand back-and-forth, a generic brand list offer, and the CTA 'Does this sound useful to you?'

entries.situation: A student submits an initial email to an outdoors creator with the subject line 'cool campsite, sad story', a bridge line 'What's also serious is your health', and the CTA 'You think it makes sense to explore this?'
entries.student_email: Subject: cool campsite, sad story. Body: Nice of you to share that story on Michael Adams and that campsite. That X-15 sounded pretty serious. What's also serious is your health. We're seeing brands like Hal Brands work with a lot of creators in this niche. Your cabin video could also show your audience how it can help them if they are often outdoors. You think it makes sense to explore this?
entries.points: Do not write subject lines that look like a new video title; instead, turn one specific detail from the creator's story into a question. Replace the awkward bridge line about health with a direct transition to serious brand offers, and replace opinion-seeking CTAs ('You think it makes sense?') with a binary yes/no CTA.

entries.situation: A student submits a cold email to an outdoors creator named Nate comparing swatting mosquitoes to swatting away irrelevant brand emails, and including the phrase 'outreach, out of sight, out of mind'.
entries.student_email: Subject: Don't swat this just yet. Hey Nate, unfortunate to hear about that mosquito spot, the buzzing made you feel uneasy, don't know how you did it. Like those mosquitoes, it'd be nice if you could swat away irrelevant brand emails. That's why I'm reaching out—to introduce you to brands where you can judge whether they're a fit or not. Outreach, out of sight, out of mind.
entries.points: Never compare brand outreach emails to annoying mosquitoes or talk about 'swatting away irrelevant brand emails', because it primes the creator to treat your own email as annoying spam. Remove 'that's why I'm reaching out', consider using 'Outreach, out of sight, out of mind?' as a question-style subject line, and focus on the benefits of you handling outreach and rejections so the creator only has to focus on content.
entries.rewrite: Subject: Outreach, out of sight, out of mind? Body: I'll do the outreach, I will go through rejections and everything instead of you, so you can focus on content.

entries.situation: A student submits five software-development influencer emails using a repetitive spintax offer template ('We are looking for creators who could be a good fit for collaboration with brands we target' / 'finalizing our creator roster for future brand partnerships') and one email starting with 'I noticed you're not getting paid by Anthropic yet. I've got some good news for you.'
entries.student_email: Email 1: Hello [Name], I really liked how seamlessly you integrated the Ghostty review into your latest video. Let's pick up on that. We are looking for creators who could be a good fit for collaboration with brands we target. Your content stood out, so we'd like to explore working together. Email 2 Subject: Did you get selected? Body: Your natural selection explanation in your latest video was really interesting... And now you've been selected... We are currently finalizing our creator roster for future brand partnerships. We think you could be a good fit for us. Email 3 Subject: Who thought it? Body: Hey, the duck knows a lot about AI. We liked it in our team. We are currently finalizing our creator roster for future brand partnerships... Email 4 Subject: why try at this point. Body: Having Claude remake Microsoft working in Excel was really cool... Looking at your channel, we think your content could be a fit for several of the brands we target. We'd like to explore potential collaborations for future campaigns. Email 5: Made the joke about not being sponsored by Anthropic. I noticed you're not getting paid by Anthropic yet. I've got some good news for you. Looking at your channel we think your content could be a good fit for several of the brands we target. Would like to explore potential collaborations for future campaigns.
entries.points: Place your bridge line between the personalization and the offer rather than inside the personalization. Do not use lazy spintax templates that barely change words and attract spam filters. Never imply you already have a deal waiting ('I noticed you're not getting paid by Anthropic yet. I've got some good news for you' or 'explore working together'), because creators will immediately demand budgets and briefs or think you are a scammer; always under-promise and over-deliver, and instead ask if they are interested in a couple of relevant brands you think would fit their channel.
entries.rewrite: There are a couple of brands who we think would be a good fit for you. Are you interested?

entries.situation: A brand raised concerns about an influencer's follower count and internal budget benchmarks after a $25k pitch, and the student reads a ChatGPT-generated reply offering to drop the price to $21k as a first-time pilot partnership.
entries.student_email: thanks for the update. I'm recommending the guy to the brand manager. Thank you. I appreciate you considering it. So what I understand the concern about the follower count is growth has been more recent, which is why the viewership is strong despite the follower base. That said, I understand the budgets and the internal benchmarks play a role too. If this helps the decision, I'd be happy to propose a first-time deal of 21K as a pilot partnership. Everything else stays the same. The integration, the view guarantee, the additional 20% discount, and this will allow the brand to test collaboration without the full commitment.
entries.points: Do not counter yourself by dropping your rate to $21k or $17k unprompted, as the brand likely wants a larger discount and slashing your own price makes it look like you were overcharging; instead, express willingness to make the first collaboration work and ask what budget range is comfortable for them.

entries.situation: After the student submitted several creators through a brand's form, the brand replied saying they did not match their criteria at this stage. The student replied asking which creator was not a fit and what criteria they look for so he could present matching creators.
entries.student_email: Out of curiosity, which creator wasn't a good fit, and what criteria do you look for? Happy to present more creators who meet what you're looking for.
entries.points: When a brand says your pitched creators are not a good fit, do not immediately blind-pitch more creators. Ask why the creator was not a fit and what criteria they want, pair the question with a call to action offering more creators who match, and frame it around making their job easier.

entries.situation: The brand rep did not reply to the student's question asking which creator was not a fit, so the student followed up three days later resurfacing the question to ensure future creator submissions align with the campaign.

entries.points: Avoid generic follow-ups like 'just checking in so this didn't get lost in your inbox.' Instead, resurface the specific question and reiterate the value to the brand—making sure future creator submissions align with their campaign.

entries.situation: After the brand lowballed at £3,500 for a creator whose usual rate was £35,000, the student messaged the talent agency on WhatsApp proposing £10k per integration (£30k for three integrations) and then raised his offer to £20k per integration (£60k for three integrations) before getting a counteroffer from the agency or a higher offer from the brand.
entries.student_email: On budget, we're working with 10k per integration for the test period, 30k across the 3 months. We know that's below his usual rate, but this is a test campaign... To be completely transparent, I could possibly try to push for something closer to 20k, so 60k total for three integrations, but that will be as high as I can go.
entries.points: Do not throw out a specific price first or make a firm offer to an influencer or talent agency before you have a workable offer from the brand. Instead, tell them their usual rate is too high for the brand and ask for the lowest price they can do, then say you will try to get it approved without making guarantees.

entries.situation: When the brand offered £3,500 (£1.50 CPM) for a creator averaging 2.3 million views whose rate was £35,000, the student replied explaining that £3,500 works out to a £1.50 CPM, countered with £25,000 (£11 CPM) for the main channel, and pitched the creator's second channel at the bottom of the email in case £25k was a dealbreaker.
entries.student_email: Thanks for sending over the proposal. The offer is well below his rate for his size at 2.3M average views that works out at £1.50 CPM. Considering production costs and his audience, we typically operate between a £19 to £25 CPM for his main channel. However, since this is a three-month test to assess performance, we can stretch down to roughly an £11 CPM, which equates to around £25,000 per integration. That offer is the best we can currently do as he is booked out with other sponsors and would need to add an additional video. If that offer is a deal breaker, his second channel may be a better fit. It has a high proportion of UK-based audience at 49% and averages 820,000 views.
entries.points: When a brand lowballs you that heavily on a massive creator, do not waste effort trying to push them up to £25k-£35k because the price friction is too high for a first deal; briefly dismiss the £1.50 CPM as unworkable and immediately pivot to a smaller channel or lower-priced creator that fits their budget.
entries.rewrite: you gave me one part of the CPM, it doesn't make sense, however, I've got second channel, which could be close to your budget, right

quote.quote: I probably wouldn't be even bothered with this, I probably just went boom, boom, you gave me one part of the CPM, it doesn't make sense, however, I've got second channel, which could be close to your budget, right

entries.situation: When the brand asked for the rate on the creator's second channel, the student quoted £15k (£18 CPM) and added at the end of the email that they would be happy to discuss a slight discount or bundle deal.
entries.student_email: Our typical rate for [Creator]'s second channel is £15k, which equates to £18 CPM. That price accounts for his core UK audience and a 9% engagement rate. We'd also be happy to discuss a slight discount or bundle deal too. Let me know what you think.
entries.points: State your price with confidence and never volunteer a discount in the same breath as your initial quote, as doing so undermines the credibility of your price. Let the brand ask for a bundle discount first so you stay in control of the negotiation.
entries.rewrite: Our typical rate for [Creator]'s second channel is £15k, which equates to £18 CPM. That price accounts for his core UK audience and a 9% engagement rate. Let me know what you think.

The student responded cautiously, saying the brand had never had that request and he did not want to get her hopes up.

entries.situation: After pivoting to a smaller creator whose rate was £300, the brand offered £600 with a view guarantee. The student countered with two pricing options (£1,250 flat rate or £2,000) and wrote 'Please note we don't work with VGs for this creator.'

The proposed fee is below where we typically operate for this creator with a long-term partnership recently signed. We need one of the following to make it work: Option 1: £1,250 flat rate per integration, or Option 2: £2,000. Please note we don't work with VGs for this creator.
entries.points: When communicating with brands, always use 'we' (e.g., 'we don't work with view guarantees') rather than saying 'I don't think the influencer would do this,' projecting authority as the creator's representative.

entries.situation: After the influencer replied that they are open to new brand partnerships, the student sent a reply saying they have a few brands in mind and asking for audience analytics.
entries.student_email: We have a few brands in mind that we'll be learning to work with influencers like Black in XChange for adding integration in one of these YouTube videos. Just before we get started, can we get [blank's audience analytics]?

Instead, name 2 or 3 specific example brands so they know what kind of sponsors you will pitch, and give a clear reason why you need their media kit or analytics screenshots (to see if their audience is a fit for those brands).
