entries.situation: The parenting creator (Warren) replied 'Sounds good. What do you have in mind?' and the student wrote a long philosophical reply claiming to be in talks with Lego and asking 'What type of partnerships excite you the most?' without asking for analytics or rates until two emails later.
entries.student_email:
Email 1: Hey Warren, honestly it's all dependent on the direction you want to take your content. Right now I'm in conversations with Lego, [Brand], [Brand], as well as a couple of fitness coaches looking to reach a family audience. The partnerships that work best are the ones that match the image you want to uphold. For example, I could easily envision you going 0 to 100 on an autobahn showcasing the family-safe, but sporty... What type of partnerships excite you the most?

Creator reply: Yeah, we work on a lot of different campaigns. Do you have specific campaigns in mind for me with briefs and budgets? I can take a look and work out what suits us.

Email 2: Hey Warren, it's great you're open to different campaigns, that makes things much easier. As of now, nothing is live just yet. I'm finalizing briefs with brands, and once budgets are confirmed, I will be lining up the creators. Would you be able to share your media kit and analytics?
entries.points: Cut all the flattering filler and never name a massive, unrealistic brand like Lego or ask open-ended questions like 'What type of partnerships excite you the most?'—that invites the creator to demand briefs and budgets you don't have. Close an influencer in 3 to 5 emails total: when they ask what you have in mind, state the deliverable (60-90s integration) and immediately ask for their audience analytics and rates.
entries.rewrite: Thanks for getting back to me. Right now I'm in conversation with [Brand, Brand, Brand]. We have 60 to 90 second integrations. Would you provide us with your analytics so brands know more about you, and what rates you're looking for?

quote.quote: Answers. What do you have in mind? We have integration 60 to 90 seconds. Would you send us, provide us analytics so we have better pictures so brands know more about you? Yes, here are them. What are rates you're looking for?

entries.situation: A student reached out to a travel brand via a website contact form without stating he is an agency, attached the influencer's raw media kit in his reply, wrote a wordy response when the brand asked about commission vs. flat fee, and sent a needy follow-up when ghosted.
entries.student_email:
Email 1 (Contact Form): Hi there, reaching out to get in touch with the right person on your marketing team regarding a potential collaboration opportunity. Could you kindly point me to the best contact for your partnerships? Best regards.

Brand reply 1: Let me know your social media links.

Email 2: Thanks so much for getting back to me. Here are the social media links: YouTube, Instagram, TikTok. I also attached [Creator]'s media kit.

Brand reply 2: Thank you for reaching out. I'm thrilled at the opportunity to work together. Which of our products? Let me know, and we can get things rolling. Also, would you be open to a commission collaboration? If you only work on flat fees, please share your rates.

Email 3: Thank you for your response. Rather than locking into one product right now, we would like to hear which item or category you're most focused on promoting. We can create content that aligns with your goal while showcasing your value. We typically work on flat fees. Our rate for YouTube integrations (mid-roll, 60 to 90s) is 7.5K...

Follow-up: I hope you're doing well, following up on potential collaboration... mid-roll, we're happy to explore...
entries.points: Make it clear from the start that you represent talent as an agency so the brand doesn't think you are the creator. Never send an influencer's raw media kit to a brand because it exposes the creator's direct rates alongside unnecessary fluff—only screenshot the audience analytics from the media kit and send that. When answering a commission inquiry, skip the fluff and state directly: 'We typically work on flat fees' followed by the 60-90s integration rate. Do not backtrack or beg in follow-ups.
entries.rewrite: We typically work on flat fees. Our rate for YouTube integrations (mid-roll, 60 to 90s) is 7.5K.

quote.quote: repeating himself, mid-roll, we're happy to explore, you don't need to do this, I'm needy, that's what you look like, give me money, I'm needy, please, let me close the deal, follow up to see if they ghosted you, too much explanations, too needy.

entries.situation: Cold email to a home air-purifier brand praising their product's '99.97% capture efficiency' and pitching both a single creator and a shortlist.
entries.student_email:
Subject: [Name], your opinion on this?

Hi [First Name],
I really like how [Brand]'s Air Pro and Mini Plus focus on 99.97% capture efficiency — that kind of detail makes a difference for families trying to keep their homes healthy.
We partner with family and lifestyle creators who also teamed up with brands like [Competitor], driving both trust and awareness. [Creator Name], for instance, averages [X] views with a 2.56% engagement rate, and is a great match for [Brand].
I can put together a shortlist of creators like him who would be a strong fit for [Brand]. Sounds good?
Best,
[Name]
entries.points: The subject line '[Name], your opinion on this?' is decent, but keep the email body at a 4th-grade reading level without 'really' or em-dashes. For brand personalization ('Show Me You Know Me'), do not copy product specs from their website—instead, praise a specific past influencer collaboration they ran and immediately name the creators you represent.
entries.rewrite: Saw your collaboration with [Creator] and how he did [specific thing] — it was unique. I have influencers such as [Creator 1], [Creator 2], [Creator 3]...

quote.quote: Keep it for grade, bro. You're not here to spill your knowledge. I mean, amazing stuff. Probably. I'm not sure. I'm not this guy. But use it. Use simple words, please. And also, this is not personalization that we use for brands.

entries.situation: Direct, no-personalization cold email to a geopolitics YouTuber naming brands and a recently onboarded similar creator.
entries.student_email: Hey [Name] — We're currently onboarding political YouTubers/creators for paid partnerships with brands [X, Y, Z]. Recently we onboarded [Creator] who makes similar style content to yourself and think you'd be a great fit. However, I saw your last few videos wasn't sponsored and I was just wondering if you'd be open to brand partnerships. Are you still interested? Looking forward to hearing from you. Best regards, [Name]
entries.points: Trying a direct, straight-to-the-point pitch when you have brands and a similar creator to name-drop is a good test, provided you remove the em-dash/hurdle after the greeting and cut the duplicate second CTA ('Are you still interested?'). Test 50 direct emails against 50 personalized emails, though personalized subject lines and personalized body copy typically get much higher open and reply rates.

quote.quote: What I saw, in my opinion, they don't like generic emails, even if you have brands. What I try... Nik mentioned a couple of times, personalized subject line, they like it so much, they're opening emails like crazy.

entries.situation: The student reads out a planned negotiation message offering the brand two package options at once and explicitly including 'plus the product' in the pricing.
entries.student_email: we can look into these two options. Option one would be, uh, we do 6,000 for three dedicated videos plus the product. Uh, or option two is, uh, we generally charge $2,000 for 60 second integration, but for this deal, we can offer a discount. So we'll do, uh, like 5,400 for three 90 second integrations plus the product. Let me know which option you guys would like.
entries.points: Remove any mention of 'plus the product' from your negotiation messages because the brand must send the product anyway for the creator to film the video. Additionally, never give a brand two pricing options at the same time; pitch your primary option first (e.g., three dedicated videos at $6,000) and keep the second option in reserve as a fallback only if they reject the first.
entries.rewrite: Because we're doing a three-video deal, it's not possible for us to do $1,500, but we can do $1,800 for each video (or $6,000 for three dedicated videos).

quote.quote: Right, so you don't want to give the client like options. Yes, you can save that for later in terms of negotiations. So you can give them the first option to negotiate for say three videos at 6,000, et cetera, right?

entries.situation: A student shared a cold email to Lisa at HubSpot congratulating them on ranking #8 among innovative business services companies and pitching an unnamed productivity creator averaging 100k–200k views.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Quick idea for HubSpot

Hi Lisa, congratulations for ranking eight amongst the innovative companies in business services, great recognition. I work closely with a creator in the productivity space who averages 100 to 200k views per post. Their audience consists of students and professionals from the US actively looking for better ways to improve their work. I believe he's a strong fit and can drive some significant results for HubSpot. Would you like to explore this further?
entries.points: Rated 6.5/10: the research and open-ended CTA ('Would you like to explore this further?') are good, but the email fails to connect the research and the creator's audience to why they matter to HubSpot, and refers generically to 'a creator' instead of naming the creator. Always tie the opening research hook directly to your pitch (e.g., helping them move from #8 to #1), use the creator's real name or handle so the email is memorable and credible, and spell out the exact logical chain of how the creator's audience will drive users for the brand.
entries.rewrite: Hi Lisa, congratulations on ranking number eight amongst the most innovative companies in business services. I'm emailing you to help you become number one. I work closely with Tom, who's an influencer in the productivity space where averages 100 to 100 key views per post. His audience consists of students and professionals from the US looking to improve their work. They would like to use your tool. If he speaks to you, if he speaks to them about you, you'll get more users. You will rank higher. We get closer to our number one rank. Would you like to explore this further?

quote.quote: Second thing, I work closely with a creator, I would use his name, just so that it's easier for them to remember, even if you don't mention the guy or the link, I would say like Tom or whatever

entries.situation: A student replies to a brand's request for analytics and rates by sharing average views over recent months, past collaborations, a $9,250 rate, and a CTA asking what timeline they are working towards.
entries.student_email: Shares the creator's average views over the last few months, links to past collaborations, quotes a price of $9,250, and asks what timeline they are currently working towards.
entries.points: Great email with no fluff. Mentioning average views alongside the price and ending with a timeline question CTA softens the pain of the price and keeps the conversation moving.

quote.quote: So to like, cause you mentioned the price, and price is always painful, but you wanna ask another question, like just okay, what time are you currently working towards? When would you like this to go live?

entries.situation: After being quoted $9,250, the brand replies that they only have a $5,000 USD budget. The student declines for that creator due to budget and immediately pitches another creator who fits the $5,000 budget.
entries.student_email: Hey Fulan, thanks for confirming the budget, unfortunately the 5k was too low for Fulan, and we could definitely pick it back up with him in the future, if the budget allows, however we do have Fulan, better aligns with your budget, YouTube channel, I've also attached on that, he's coming over with him.
entries.points: Excellent power dynamics. If the creator's base rate is too high (e.g., $7k-$8k) to meet the $5k budget, don't beg for $8.5k; take the first creator off the table and immediately pivot to a lower-priced creator from your roster.

quote.quote: And if you give someone an offer for something, and they want a lower price, it takes something away, right? Now this is probably, he took away the whole influence. He's like, you can't get this guy, but I got this guy.

entries.situation: The brand offered $3.5k for the second creator, but that creator backed out on the student. The student emails the brand to pass on the creator and immediately pitches a third creator with a 70% Australian audience.
entries.student_email: Hey, Fulan. Hope you had a great week. Unfortunately, you need to pass on Fulan, as the rating we offered him wasn't good enough. However, we do also have Fulan, whose audience is also 70% Australian. I've attached his analytics to email. Here's a link. Let me know if you want to move forward with Fulan.
entries.points: Pivoting immediately to an alternative creator with matching demographics without asking permission is great, but never say 'the rate we offered him wasn't good enough'—say he is unavailable so the brand doesn't offer more money for a creator who ghosted you.
entries.rewrite: Unfortunately we have to pass on Fulan, as he's not available right now, maybe we can revisit it in the future, however, we have this guy...

quote.quote: In the front line, instead of saying unfortunately to pass as the rate we offered him wasn't good enough, I would say look, unfortunately to pass on Fulan as he's not available, or I would say unfortunately to pass on Fulan as the rate wasn't good enough

entries.situation: The brand says the third YouTube creator isn't the right fit but invites more recommendations. Having no other YouTube creators ready, the student says he is checking availability with other YouTubers and immediately pitches an Instagram creator with links and analytics.
entries.student_email: Hey Fulain, thanks for confirming. I'm just checking availability with a couple of our YouTube creators. We may be open to a collaboration and we'll share them with you once that confirmation. Just to check, are you also exploring Instagram creators at the moment, or are you only focused on YouTube? If Instagram is on the table, we also work with, learn our social analytics here. And here is his profile on Instagram. Here are a couple of Chris's previous contributions. boom, let me know what think.
entries.points: Great problem-solving. When you run out of ready creators on one platform, ask if they are open to another platform like Instagram and include the creator's profile and analytics right away without waiting for permission.

quote.quote: So, he's been pitching YouTube this whole time, right? And now he doesn't have anyone ready for YouTube. A lot of people would just said, look, thanks for confirming, I'm just checking a video, being a couple of YouTube haters, and I'll get back to you.

entries.situation: The student counters the brand at $2.2k, shares specific details about the creator's upcoming videos (filming in the Ice Hotel and a video in Lapland), asks which video they prefer, and asks for the contract and brief to start working on it 'immediately'.
entries.student_email: Let's lock it in at 2.2, I'd like to send, Fulan's filming in the famous Ice Hotel in a couple of days, and next week, we'll be doing a video in Lapland, which video would you prefer to work with, if you could send me across the contract and brief, we could start working on it immediately.
entries.points: Assuming the close and giving the brand a choice between specific upcoming videos builds strong authority and helps justify the price, but remove the word 'immediately' at the end so you don't sound needy.
entries.rewrite: If you can send me across the contract and brief, I could take a look.

quote.quote: if you can send me across the contract and brief it, you can start working immediately, this is quite good, I would say the immediately part is a bit needed, I would take that out, and then, I would say, look, if you can send me across the contract and brief it, with your side, or, I could take a look

entries.situation: After the student tried to lock in $2.2k, the brand held firm at $2,000. The student accepts $2,000 by stating it is below the standard rate, but since it is their first collaboration together, they are happy to move forward and ask for the contract and brief.
entries.student_email: While 2000 is below the standard rate, as this is our first collaboration together, we're happy to move forward, please send through the contract and brief and we'll get the ball rolling immediately on our side.
entries.points: When accepting a brand's lower counteroffer after your higher anchor fails, never just cave in—frame the concession as a special one-time exception for your first collaboration so you don't look like you were bluffing and you build goodwill.

quote.quote: If you just say, oh, let's just, okay, fine, we'll just do 2k, I mean, it shows like, I mean, that 2.2 was all fluffed and you were just bluffing, right? But he gave a reason for it now, he said, look, this is below the sun rate, but I'll give you guys an exception.

entries.situation: A fitness brand replies on LinkedIn/email asking for a quick chat later in the week to discuss how their pods and data platform can drive results for the student's athlete roster. The student replies flattering the brand's data platform as a 'massive differentiator' before offering two call times.
entries.student_email: Hey Fulan, I'm glad to hear that. I agree that the data your company provides is a massive differentiator for athletes who are serious about their performance and longevity. I'm definitely around for a chat. Does Thursday 10.30 a.m. or Friday 2 p.m. works for you? If not, let me know what your calendar looks like, and I'll make it on my end, looking forward to it.
entries.points: Proposing specific call times is good, but cut out the flattering fluff agreeing that their product is a massive differentiator. Being overly agreeable weakens your negotiating position; just say 'Thanks for getting back to me' and get straight to business.
entries.rewrite: Thanks for getting back to me. I'm definitely around for a chat. Does Thursday 10:30 a.m. or Friday 2 p.m. work for you? If not, let me know what your calendar looks like, and I'll make it work on my end.

quote.quote: You know what's enough? Oh, thanks for getting back to me. That's enough. After that, we're going straight to business.

entries.situation: A student pitches unnamed travel influencers to an eSIM brand with the subject 'This is for you', noting that the creators 'haven't discussed eSIM yet on their channel', and ending with 'Let me know what you think'.
entries.student_email:
Subject: This is for you
Hi Dan, The [Creator] videos on Thailand is quite nice. The way they introduce [Brand] into the video comes across very natural as they talk about how important internet access is when traveling. Speaking of traveling, I work with travel influencers. Some of these look like a great fit because they haven't discussed eSIM yet on their channel and average [X] views from high purchasing power countries. Let me know what you think.
entries.points: Change the declarative subject line to a question ('Is this for you?'). While pitching an eSIM-free creator solves a real exclusivity pain point for eSIM brands, frame it around their upcoming travel plans where they will actually need an eSIM rather than vaguely stating they haven't discussed eSIMs yet, and use a stronger yes/no CTA like 'Should I send details?'.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Is this for you? / Is this something you're looking for?
He is traveling in a lot of countries, but he didn't work with an eSIM yet. He will be in the next country and will need an eSIM. Should I send details?

quote.quote: mean, one of the issues in the travel niche is, for example, Eastern brands, they want exclusive. But there's so many of them, so most travel influencers, they've already worked with, yeah, most esim brands, or they're working with an esim brand, right? So this, he could, like, like, he's on the right track, and I like what he mentioned there, but it's not in a good way.

entries.situation: A student praises high view counts on a brand's own YouTube channel for an iPhone 17 Pro video, then offers niche iPhone filmmakers to 'help reach more enthusiasts', followed by a multi-sentence follow-up.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Here's an idea for you
I was pleasantly surprised to see your iPhone 17 Pro video reaching such views on [Brand]'s YouTube channel. That said, I saw another iPhone videography creator featuring your gear recently. I'm curious if partnering with niche iPhone filmmakers could help reach more enthusiasts who might be in the market for these products. We work with select creators who fit that profile.

Follow-up: Just wanted to follow up on my first email. We are collaborating with filmmakers that produce high-quality short films with iPhone cameras...
entries.points: The personalization praising the brand's own YouTube video and referencing another recent creator integration is great research. However, if the brand is already getting high views, don't offer 'more reach'—pitch converting that existing hype and viewership into actual sales. Also, cut a sentence from the follow-up to make it shorter.
entries.rewrite: Since people are interested, we have a couple of guys that might convert that interest into sales. We have guys that can showcase your product in the best possible way.

quote.quote: just wanted to follow up on my first email, we are collaborating with filmmakers that produce high quality short videos with short, with short films with iPhone cameras, yeah, so I think your follow ups are good but too long, maybe remove one sentence

entries.situation: A microphone brand told a student they liked his photography-focused creator's rates and wanted to move forward, but were not 100% sure about the fit since they preferred filmmakers. The student emailed his creator telling him the brand was unsure about the fit and asking if he had upcoming projects where the microphones would make sense, and the creator stopped responding.
entries.student_email: In the meantime, we have another opportunity with XYZ. Uh, blah, blah, blah. They want to promote XYZ. However, since your content is more focused on photography than filmmaking, they are unsure about the fit. What do you think about this? Do you have any upcoming projects with these products, where these products could make sense?
entries.points: Never tell your influencer that a brand is unsure if they are a good fit. Leave out the negative feedback and go straight to telling the creator that the brand is interested in promoting their microphone and asking if they have any upcoming videos where the product would make sense.
entries.rewrite: Hey, this brand is interested, they have a microphone that they want you to promote, do you have any upcoming videos that would make sense?

quote.quote: ... and just go straight to asking, hey, this brand is interested, because they are interested, they are interested, they have a microphone that they want to, you know, they want him to promote, do you have any upcoming videos that would make sense?

entries.situation: A student reads out his draft reply to an influencer who objected that $1.9k is way below his normal rate and asked which brand and product the reel is for.
entries.student_email: The brand is about to launch a new product, and your profile might be interested for them to market their product. Based on your audience analytics, we typically work with $14 CPM, so that's why we charge 1.9K.
entries.points: The email works well as long as you include the specific product name and answer the influencer's questions while justifying the $1.9k rate with a $14 CPM based on his audience analytics.

quote.quote: Yeah, it should be fine. As long as you answer his questions, because as long as you give him what he wants, and yeah, he could be open to it later to accept the price we gave him.

entries.situation: A brand rejected a pitched creator saying they were not interested in him but to keep in touch, and the student replied defending the creator as a misunderstood short-form creator and offering to send his full list of US creators averaging over 100k views.
entries.student_email: So he's, he's, actually being misunderstood, he actually does more short form content. So, um, and also, and then after that I said, if you, we've also extended or something like this, and I said, if you, if, uh, US based creators with 100, above 100k average views is what you're looking for, let me know, and we can send our list your way.
entries.points: When a brand rejects a creator, accept the rejection gracefully and ask what specific criteria they are looking for before offering matching creators, showing you care about solving their needs rather than just pushing your roster.
entries.rewrite: Okay, cool, no problem, I understand it wasn't a fit, what are you guys actually looking for? Because I've got a couple more guys doing over 100k views, with US based audience, whatever. If this is something within the criteria, let me know, and I can send it over to you.

quote.quote: So every time you get a no, try to figure out why, and then come up with a solution to them.

entries.situation: A student submitted a brand cold email referencing a fitness recovery device sponsorship on a creator's video, summarizing what the device does in the review and listing multiple reasons why their travel/fitness creator is a fit.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Your thoughts, [First Name]
I went through [video name] and I saw that [Brand] sponsored him. He was on point when he talked about how to measure the intensity and recovery of your workouts. Not a lot of devices tell you that you need to recover more or work out more. They just tell you how many calories were used up. We collaborate with similar creators like [Creator 1] and [Creator 2]. His channel focuses on traveling and challenging my body through various fitness... For those reasons we think he would be a good fit for you.
entries.points: When personalizing a cold email to a brand around a sponsored video, comment on the marketing angle and style of the ad rather than summarizing the product review, and avoid pitching too many reasons or selling in the first email.
entries.rewrite: The way he emphasized that not a lot of devices tell you that you need to recover more or work out more was on point.

quote.quote: If you want to do a good personalization with Brent, keep in mind, talk about marketing expect, that's all, like how he mentioned, and then you just basically used his style, you know, his style of ad and your thoughts on this.

entries.situation: A student sent a cold email to a travel/adventure influencer using a generic YouTube template line ('I was watching some of your content and I noticed that your recent videos were not sponsored').
entries.student_email: Hey [First Name], Hiking Everest on three days notice is quite intense to say the least. I was watching some of your content and I noticed that your recent videos were not sponsored. Brands like [Brand 1], [Brand 2], and [Brand 3] could be a good fit for the type of content you post. Let me know if you're interested and I can share some more.
entries.points: Add a light joke to the personalization if the creator is young and casual, cut out wordy filler about how you watched their content and noticed no sponsorships, and go straight into stating you are preparing a creator roster for upcoming brand promotions.
entries.rewrite: We are preparing a roster for upcoming promotions for these brands that we have in mind. Are you in?

quote.quote: So, be like, okay, here's personalization, and be like, we are gathering or making a list of influencers or preparing roster for upcoming promotions for these brands that we have in mind. Are you in? Easy, super easy.

entries.situation: An influencer replied with interest and attached their media kit, which lacked audience age and geography. The student replied saying 'I'm exploring potential brand fits' and formally asked if they would be comfortable sharing audience geography and age, after which the influencer ghosted.
entries.student_email: Hey, thanks for sharing this one, that saves us some time. I'm exploring potential brand fits that align with your content, such as [Brand 1] and [Brand 2]. Before we move forward, would you be comfortable sharing your audience's geographics? I'm mainly looking for location and age.
entries.points: Double-check the media kit first so you don't ask for stats already included. Never say 'I'm exploring potential brand fits' because it sounds uncertain; instead state which brands fit their content, ask for their rates first to complete the picture, and casually slip in a question about the missing demographics.
entries.rewrite: Based on your content, these brands would be a good fit. Since you sent your media kit, would you send your rates so we have a complete picture? Also, I couldn't find demographics anywhere—what about those?

quote.quote: I'm exploring potential brand fits, so I'm still in Insha Allah phase, right, this is a huge problem, don't say this, I'm not exploring, we have in mind, we, you know, or maybe, based of your content, these brands would align for you

entries.situation: The tech student shared a third cold email and two follow-ups using the offer line 'I think your content could fit well with many brands we're lining up creators for' and a follow-up starting with 'We are finalizing creators roundup for Q1 campaigns and wanted to check if you had a chance to go over my previous emails.'
entries.student_email:
I laughed so hard at the joke about [Product] Pro. Too bad that the glasses are unstable when laying down. This was a good insight.
Speaking of the good insights, I think your content could fit well with many brands we're lining up creators for.
Would you like to know more?

Follow-up 1: We are finalizing creators roundup for Q1 campaigns and wanted to check if you had a chance to go over my previous emails.
Follow-up 2: Just a quick follow up in case my first email got buried. We are looking at brands like [Brand 1] and [Brand 2] and others in the content creation space that could be a good fit for your content. If this sounds like a match, let me know.
entries.points: Phrasing the offer as 'many brands we're lining up creators for' is a clever Aikido way to sound established without falsely claiming confirmed deals. However, use the squint test to fix bulky paragraph spacing, put the 'wanted to quickly follow up' phrase at the start of Follow-Up 1 so it doesn't look like a long pitch, and avoid repeating the word 'content' twice in the same sentence.
entries.rewrite:
Follow-up 1: Wanted to quickly follow up to check if you had a chance to go over my previous email, as we are finalizing our creators roundup for Q1 campaigns.
Follow-up 2: We are looking at brands like [Brand 1] and [Brand 2] and others in this space that could be a good fit for your content.

quote.quote: Speaking of the good insights, I think your content could fit well with many brands, we're lining up creators for. Good, so see this one, with many brands, we are lining up creators for. So he didn't mention brands, he aikida it.

entries.situation: A student sent a cold email to a tech/home creator praising their lighting sponsorship as 'unique' and asking 'On another topic of making differences to homes, I wanted to ask if you're open to more brands partnership like this one.'
entries.student_email: Your collaboration with [Brand] was unique. It really showed how lighting can make a difference to homes, especially for your audience in UK/Europe, where we don't always see the most sun. On another topic of making differences to homes, I wanted to ask if you're open to more brand partnerships like this one. Kind regards
entries.points: Cut generic praise like 'your collaboration was unique' because it is pure fluff, make the offer clear with a proper CTA, and don't limit partnerships only to 'making differences to homes' since your niche is defined by the creator and brands can come from any category.
entries.rewrite: Your last video where you mentioned [Product] could be good for all of the people who are not seeing a lot of sunlight—don't ask me how I know.

quote.quote: So, your collaboration with us was unique. Mabrata, it's fluff, okay, it's pure fluff, it's unique fluff, okay. Okay, you're not, you're not fanboy, you're just something, you need fluff, Abu Fluff, Allahumma bari. So, no need for this one.

entries.situation: When the influencer replied 'hey man, yes, please, let me know what you have in mind,' the student answered 'However, before I move forward, I need to clarify [qualify] you for the opportunity. Can you send your media kit and current rates for your platforms? KR' and then sent two follow-ups repeatedly demanding the rate card and analytics.
entries.student_email:
Reply: We work with tech creators for all things tech, and I believe companies like [Brand] would suit you. However, before I move forward, I need to qualify you for the opportunity. Can you send your media kit and current rates for your platforms? KR

Follow-up 1: We are looking into brands like Nebula, [Brand 2], [Brand 3] and more. If you are interested in partnering with tech brands like that, could you send over the rate card and audience analytics, so we can match you with the right opportunities. Best, [First Name]

Follow-up 2: Hi, I haven't heard back from you. Just checking to see if you got my previous email. We are closing our shortlist end of this week, could you send your rate card?
entries.points: Never tell an influencer 'I need to qualify you for the opportunity' or sign off with a lazy 'KR'—it is insulting and misapplies power dynamics. Ask for analytics politely ('in order to have a better picture, we need your analytics'), and keep follow-ups as gentle reminders rather than repeated demands.
entries.rewrite: Hey, in order to have a better picture, we need your analytics.

quote.quote: Follow-ups, they serve only one purpose. Hey, check this email above. No threatening, no, I'm asking you politely one less time. Please send me your card rate. No, we don't do this, okay?

entries.situation: A student sent a cold email with the subject line '14-day video plan question' and body: 'Hi [First Name], Your 14-day video plan guide is very practical and seems to be helping a lot of students stay on track. I have a short idea for a potential collaboration... Would you be open to a five-minute chat to see if it makes sense?'
entries.student_email:
Subject: 14-day video plan question
Hi [First Name], Your 14-day video plan guide is very practical and seems to be helping a lot of students stay on track. I have a short idea for a potential collaboration that could provide value to your audience and explore sponsorship opportunities. Would you be open to a five-minute chat to see if it makes sense?
entries.points: Do not repeat the video title in both the subject line and opening sentence, and avoid fill-in-the-blank praise that could be sent to anyone. Never pitch 'an idea' for a creator's content because creators have big egos—instead transition to brands you have in mind, though offering a 5-minute video chat is great for building trust.
entries.rewrite: Speaking of staying on track, we have some brands in mind that can help you with this. What do you think?

quote.quote: Offering five-minute call is good. Or chat, doesn't matter. You know, calling them, especially influencers, for a quick chat is good. There's nothing wrong with this because this guy is legit, he can show up himself to camera, he's not a scammer

entries.situation: A cooking creator replied enthusiastically to the student's personalization about coconut buns and said he is open to brands that align with his focused videos. The student replied parroting his concern and claiming 'I'm only looking at brands with cookware, pantry staples, and condiments, as those naturally fit your content and are the categories I specialize in,' then asked for audience analytics.
entries.student_email: Hello, I completely agree that working with brands that don't align with the content can take away from the rest. I'm only looking at brands with cookware, pantry staples, and condiments, as those naturally fit your content and are the categories I specialize in. To make sure I'm only bringing opportunities that are relevant to you, would you mind sharing a bit more about your audience analytics, specifically age range and top geographics.
entries.points: When a creator responds directly to your personalization, keep using that personalization style. In your reply, don't parrot their full sentence or box yourself into narrow brand categories ('I'm only looking at cookware, pantry staples, and condiments') since brands can come from any niche; briefly agree, name a couple of brands in mind, ask for their age and geography analytics, and follow up politely if they are slow to screenshot them.
entries.rewrite: Thanks for getting back. I completely agree. Based on your content, we have [Brand 1] and [Brand 2] in mind. If this is something you are open to, feel free to attach the age and geographies of your audience.

quote.quote: This is an answer from an influencer. So, their first word, and they give you an answer on something, this is your strongest part on your email. So, if he is talking, if he is talking about personalization, so this, this is good.

entries.situation: A student submits an automotive niche cold email to a brand and two follow-ups using the subject line 'Influencer X Brand Name', 'we saw', 'we represent', 'highly engaged', audience value assumptions, and 'circling back'.
entries.student_email:
Subject: [Influencer] X [Brand Name]

We saw [Influencer] featured in M5 build video where he positioned it as a practical alternative for friends stuck in bad habits. The way he explained the oral fixation benefits and highlighted real user numbers came across as genuine and relatable for his audience. We represent creators across the UK and US including [X, Y, Z] with highly engaged male majority audience who value practical solution and self-improvement alongside their passion for cars. Can I send over a few influencer fits for [Brand]?

Follow-up 1: Quick one, still open to influencer collabs?

Follow-up 2: Circling back for Q1. Wanted to check if [Brand] is planning any automotive influencer campaign. [Influencer], premium audience, 67% age 25+, 95% male, aligns well with performance products. Let me know if you'd like to explore this.
entries.points: Drop the overused 'Influencer X Brand' subject line, use 'I' instead of 'we' for watching videos, never claim to 'represent' creators, avoid ChatGPT fluff about what the audience values, don't ask to send influencers after already naming three, and keep follow-ups to 2-3 non-salesy reminder sentences.
entries.rewrite: Hey [First Name], I'm just following up in case you didn't see my first email.

quote.quote: He mentioned one, two, three influencers, and he said, can I send over a few influencer fits for this guy? So like, can I send more of those? No, no, no, no.

entries.situation: A student submits a travel/outdoor brand email referencing recent innovation awards, saying 'we work closely with creators', and following up with repeated call requests and 'Circling back... Is this something you want to look into?'.
entries.student_email:
Hi there, winning four major innovation awards highlights that your brand has grown. To keep the momentum going, we work closely with creators in the outdoor space, such as [Creator], with strong U.S. audience and could help you grow more. They previously worked with brands and could be a great fit for you. Are you open to a quick call to discuss how we can work?

Follow-up 1: Creators I shared in my previous message have strong UK and US audience. We can schedule a call...

Follow-up 2: Circling back... Their recent travel videos have been performing well and could... Is this something you want to look into?
entries.points: The initial email is solid, but specify how the creators will help the brand grow (e.g., well-aligned organic integrations), stop saying 'we work closely', never repeat a call CTA in follow-ups if it failed in the first email, and replace needy 'circling back' follow-ups with a casual 'either way, let me know'.
entries.rewrite: With well-aligned organic integration instead of scripted commercial with niche-down content creators that align well with your products. / Closing follow-up: Either way, let me know. If you're not interested, just let me know.

quote.quote: Give them a couple of more reasons how you're going to implement that. So, if you're going to help them grow, what are you going to do? Just mention, you know, with well-aligned audience, I mean, integration instead of like. Scripted, commercial

entries.situation: A student pitches a UK construction/tools brand with a creator focused on job site construction who has a 93% UK audience.
entries.student_email:
Subject: ... explore ...

Hello [Name], the recent content from [Creator] did an excellent job of showcasing [Brand]'s tools, demonstrating how they helped complete the oak and glass stair transformation efficiently on a real project. Following this, I work with [Creator], whose content focuses on job site constructions and reaches a 93% UK audience. We believe he would be an excellent fit to promote your products. We also work with other creators who have a strong audience in the UK and US.
entries.points: The offer is 10/10 because a hyper-niche job-site construction creator with a 93% UK audience is a dream match for a UK tool brand, proving niche alignment beats raw views. Improve the subject line by replacing 'explore' with 'something for you', keep 'we work' consistent, and shorten the personalization so it focuses on marketing rather than sounding like a satisfied customer.
entries.rewrite: Subject: Something for you

quote.quote: Whose content focuses on job site constructions and reaches a 93% UK audience? Nice. This is something. If you have right brand, bro, they'll be like, yes, thanks for reaching out. We are very interesting. So this is when Kush said, views does not matter

entries.situation: A student sends a ChatGPT-written travel brand email ('With travel content surging, brands securing strong organic integrations are winning the most... I manage a small roster of high-performing travel creators (11M+ subs)') and follow-ups asking random niche questions and saying 'You're probably playing catch-up right now, which is fair enough. Please let me know...'.
entries.student_email:
With travel content surging, brands securing strong organic integrations are winning the most. [Brand] fits naturally in this niche, as seen with [Creator] using it to verify stories and compare perspectives in regions with political instability. I manage a small roster of high-performing travel creators (11M+ subs) whose audience aligns closely with [Brand]'s core markets (US, Canada, UK). Would you be open to exploring a potential partnership?

Follow-up 1: Hi [First Name], are you mainly focused on geopolitical news creators, or are there other niches where [Brand] has seen strong performance as well?

Follow-up 2: You're probably playing catch-up right now, which is fair enough. Please let me know if the below suits what you are looking for.
entries.points: Never open with ChatGPT industry fluff or claim 'I manage a small roster'; watch a 90-second YouTube integration and make one real observation about it. In follow-ups, do not ask conversational questions when they haven't replied yet, never say 'please', and never assume the prospect is 'playing catch-up' or busy.
entries.rewrite: The way he did the backflip in his shirt was a good idea to get the attention and leave a strong picture for your brand. On that point, we have these guys. Could be a good fit. Let me know.

quote.quote: So, personalization with brands. Guys, watch integration. Watch the integrated part of any YouTube video. You know. And just watch that. It's 90 seconds. Okay? Maybe 100. Watch it and be like, say something about integration itself. Do not use JGPT

entries.situation: A student submits two automotive brand emails and follow-ups where the personalization either claims the clothes 'stay durable and comfortable' or summarizes the ad brief back to the brand ('He explained how it helps him stay healthy and energized'), and the follow-ups repeat the full sales pitch.
entries.student_email:
Email 1: Hey [First Name], The collaboration with [Creator] showed how [Brand] clothes stay durable and comfortable even while working in the workshop. Speaking of this, we work with influencers like [X] and [Y] who focus on rebuilding cars and have a strong U.S. audience. They could be a great fit for future integration. Let me show you more details.

Follow-up 1: Just following up on my last email about this collaboration with [Creator]. We work with creators who do hands-on car projects, they can fit nicely. Should I send more details?

Email 2 - Subject: How to get healthy with [Brand]
In a recent Jack video, he featured [Brand] while working on cars. He explained how it helps him stay healthy and energized during long wrenching sessions, which fit well with his content. We work with creators like [X] and [Y] who focus on hands-on car projects, can reach a large U.S. audience, they would be a strong fit for similar integration.

Follow-up 2: Just a quick follow-up on my last email, we work with a few creators... interested in collaborating with them? Happy to share more details.
entries.points: Do not write like a satisfied customer claiming clothes feel durable/comfortable from a 90-second video, and do not summarize the ad brief back to the brand—they approved the video and already know it. Tie the creator's daily environment to the product ('spend the majority of their time in workshops'), say 'might be a strong fit', and keep follow-ups to a brief reminder ending with 'looking forward to hearing from you'.
entries.rewrite: Speaking of this, we have a couple of creators who spend the majority of their time in workshops rebuilding cars. They might be a strong fit for similar integration. / Follow-up: Looking forward to hearing from you.

quote.quote: No, this pitch, save it for your first email. Then use it there. Full ops is just a reminder, guys. Shur Hashem will send more details. Same, same one. No. No, no, no, no, no. I would say in first follow up, looking forward hearing

entries.situation: An outdoor influencer agreed to a 10 EUR CPM rate by saying 'happy to do whatever you want, I still don't know what you're offering,' and the student replied saying he would present the offer to outdoor brands and share one within two weeks.
entries.student_email: Thanks, Josh, since this works, I'll start presenting the offer to brands and I should have one to share with you within the next two weeks. The brand will be related to outdoor activities
entries.points: The reply is acceptable enough to consider the influencer closed at 10 EUR CPM without sending another message now, but next time an influencer says they don't understand what you are offering, don't be vague—transparently name real example brands you will actually pitch, specify the deliverable (such as a 60-second integration), and state the target booking timeframe.
entries.rewrite: Right now, we're going to reach out to brands like [real examples of brands he hasn't worked with], and we're looking at a 60-second integration, and we'll be looking to book something within the next month or two months.

quote.quote: Now, right now, you're going to reach out to brands like XYZ, give examples, real examples of brands that he hasn't worked with, and we're looking at 60-second integration, and we'll be looking to book something within the next month, two months, whatever, simple.

entries.situation: After a brand sent a template rejection saying their budget was around 10 CPM and asking for lower-rate talent, the student pitched a creator with 327K average views at $3,200 (10 CPM) and volunteered a multi-video discount at $2,500 per video.
entries.student_email: I understand. Check out Fulan, he's averaging 327K views over his last 12 videos. We could do 3,200 USD, rate in line with your CPM criteria. [Or if we do a multi-video deal, we can do 2.5K each... he has a large US audience.]
entries.points: Opening with 'I understand' and stating '$3,200 USD, rate in line with your CPM criteria' showed good power dynamics, but saying 'check out' was too casual, over-explaining the US audience in text was unnecessary, and volunteering a $2,500 multi-video discount unprompted destroyed his leverage by signaling he would accept $2,500 for a single video.
entries.rewrite: I understand. [Creator] is averaging 327K views over his last 12 videos. We could do 3,200 USD, rate in line with your CPM criteria.

quote.quote: actually, bro, like, you're saying 3,200, and then you're saying, I'll do 2.5K each. You know what that means? You could probably do 2.5K for one video. Like, if an influencer said this to me, that's what I'm thinking straight away.

entries.situation: A student in the motorcycle niche submits his first email pitching a French motorcycle creator (30-39% France audience) to a brand by pointing out their office in Marseille and that most of their partnerships are in the US.

entries.situation: A student submits an email with the subject line 'project-based learning with [Creator]', mixing 'I work' and 'We see' in the body, with poor flow between the personalization and offer.
entries.student_email:
Subject: project-based learning with [Creator]

I noticed the recent focus on interactive learning in the app updates, which is great, since in marketing STEM, feeling hands-on is key.

I work with [Creator]. He builds an extreme example of creative problem solving. We see a strong alignment with this philosophy.

If you're open to it, I can send...
entries.points: Use a curiosity-driven subject line (such as 'is this something you're looking for?') instead of giving away the topic in the subject line. Stay consistent with 'we' instead of switching between 'I' and 'we', and transition smoothly from personalization to the offer by repeating a bridge word from the first sentence (e.g., 'Speaking of key, we have an influencer who might be key for your integration').

...Speaking of key, we have an influencer who might be key for your integration.

entries.situation: A student in the cooking niche submits a long email to a cookware brand filled with flattery, 'Simply respond with yes', apologies for taking their time ('I can imagine you must be busy'), and a claim to reserve December/January spots.
entries.student_email:
[Brand]'s solid social media presence came to my attention. Their multiple collaborations with [Influencer] surely play a part in this. He's full of energy and passion for cooking, which makes his videos very engaging and fun to watch for the audience.

Working with this kind of an influencer elevates your brand awareness. We work with a number of similar influencers in the cooking industry who could promote your pans and other cookware, such as [Influencer 1] and [Influencer 2] with mostly U.S. audience, consistent views and great engagement.

Simply respond with yes... I can imagine you must be busy, reading this won't take long, have a nice day. There are a couple of spots available for December/January content. Let me know if you're interested, I will reserve one for you.

Best,
[Large signature block with photo and website]
entries.points: Cut all introductory flattery and apologetic filler ('I can imagine you must be busy', 'reading this won't take long')—outbound outreach is about professionally annoying prospects. Keep the concise middle offer ('We work with a number of similar influencers in the cooking industry... with mostly US audience, consistent views and great engagement'), replace robotic/begging CTAs ('Simply respond with yes') with 'If this sounds good, let me know', and avoid claiming open spots if the creator has no booked integrations.
entries.rewrite:
We work with a number of similar influencers in the cooking industry, such as [Influencer 1] and [Influencer 2], with mostly U.S. audience, consistent views, and great engagement.

If this sounds good, let me know.

Best regards,
[First Name]

entries.situation: A student in the fitness niche submits an initial email and three follow-ups to a men's health brand, opening with a quote from their past integration ('1 in 4 men suffer from low T... makes you wonder if you are one of them').
entries.student_email:
Subject: Had to e-mail you after seeing it

Initial Email:
Hello [First Name],
The way [Creator] opened your integration with '1 in 4 men suffer from low [T]...' makes you wonder if you are one of them.
We work with influencers like [Creator] who has a large U.S. presence and posts educational fitness content that might interest you.
Would you be open to discussing this?

Follow-up 1:
Hello, just following up on my first email about [Creator], would this be relevant for you at the moment? Looking forward to hearing from you.

Follow-up 2:
[Creator] posted a video about daily habits that destroy [T], which I believe aligns with your focus audience. It'd be ideal to hear back before next Wednesday as his availability might change. Could share more details if useful, let me know.

Follow-up 3:
Circling back one last time as you seem invested in other projects. Wanted to check if you'd be open to taking a look at [Creator]'s details before we close this out.
entries.points: Referencing the exact hook from a brand's recent creator integration followed by a concise US-based creator offer and a simple CTA is strong (7/10). Change the misleading subject line 'Had to email you after seeing it' to 'check this', and in the final breakup follow-up, add one line about what the creator recently accomplished before closing out the thread.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: check this

Follow-up 3: Circling back one last time... [Creator] did [X] recently. Wanted to check if you'd be open to taking a look at this guy's details before we close this out.

quote.quote: We work with influencers like this who has a large U.S. presence and posts educational fitness content that might interest you. Would you be open to discussing this? Okay, the email is not bad, to be honest.

entries.situation: A student writes a second practice email to Unbox Therapy about a power bank video, saying 'Anker would be the perfect sponsor. We could easily find brands that are similar.'
entries.student_email:
Subject: That power bank in your last video

Hey Unbox Therapy, I never thought about using a power bank in that way. Anker would be the perfect sponsor. We could easily find brands that are similar. Are you open to working with brands that would integrate seamlessly into your video?
entries.points: Restructure the opening line so the specific video topic ('Using a power bank in that way...') comes first. Avoid naming a specific brand like 'Anker would be the perfect sponsor' when you don't have Anker as a client, because the creator will assume Anker is ready to sponsor them and ask for campaign details. Also avoid vague offers like 'brands that integrate seamlessly' for an unboxing channel that can feature anything.
entries.rewrite: Using a power bank in that way was something that I never thought about.

quote.quote: this make no sense because Anchor would be a perfect sponsor, Anchor, you know, kind of over promising, to be honest, what they can get from your email is like, okay, Anchor is interested in working with us

entries.situation: A student submits a cold email to a travel/finance brand ending with the CTA 'Send over your influencer requirements so we can make this happen.'
entries.student_email:
Subject: Couple of no brainers for you

Hi [First Name], Cashback, invest, economy, and these gas prices should be a no-brainer, right? We work with a couple of travel creators that are constantly on the go and could use a way to save money for the next adventure. Their US-majority audience needs to know how to do the same. Send over your influencer requirements so we can make this happen.
entries.points: The subject line 'Couple of no brainers for you' (or 'Maybe you won't regret this') works well, and cutting the confusing opening line improves the body. However, never use 'Send over your influencer requirements' as a cold email CTA—brand managers get 100+ emails a day and want you to reduce their workload by proactively pitching what they need. Reserve 'send over your influencer requirements' for follow-up emails after a discovery call.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Couple of no brainers for you (or: Maybe you won't regret this)

Hi [First Name], We work with a couple of travel creators that are constantly on the go and could use a way to save money for the next adventure. Their US-majority audience needs to know how to do the same.

quote.quote: So that's how you have to position yourself, like, I know what you're looking for, here it is. So keep that in mind. No, don't make it more work for them, make it less work for them, Inshallah.

entries.situation: A student pitches a cybersecurity brand by saying 'we work with a couple of creators that understand the importance of cybersecurity' and 'Brands like [Competitor] have already beaten you to it.'
entries.student_email:
Subject: Cybersecurity use cases

Your creators did a good job showcasing this... We work with a couple of creators that understand the importance of cybersecurity, especially when traveling, as they have shown their audience before. Brands like [Competitor] have already beaten you to it.
entries.points: Sell outcomes (the audience's response), not features (the creators themselves)—frame it as 'travel creators whose audience understands the importance of cybersecurity' and name the creators. Also, never antagonize a brand with lines like 'Brands like X have already beaten you to it.'
entries.rewrite: I have a couple of travel creators whose audience understands the importance of cybersecurity, and they can show it in the best possible way. A couple of those are [Creator Name 1] and [Creator Name 2].

quote.quote: So understand their importance of cybersecurity. I have a couple of travel creators whose audience do understand the importance. It's different. And they can show it in the best possible way. A couple of those are, ding, ding, ding, give names and there you go.

entries.situation: A student pitches the cybersecurity brand Aura with the pun subject line 'Do your sponsors have enough aura?' and jumps abruptly from data protection to travel creators.

Having Aura in 2026 is a must for protecting your data. We work with a couple of travel creators... every time they book flights, the ideal use case to demonstrate to their audience how quickly they...

entries.situation: A student submits his first three cold emails to self-improvement influencers, starting by introducing himself and his agency, asking why their last video had no sponsorships, fanboying over their engagement, listing past brands they worked with, and ending with 'Are you open to doing more collabs?'.
entries.student_email:
Email 1:
Subject: Check this out, [Influencer Name]
Hey [Name], I am [Name] from [Agency]. I saw the last video that you posted about the 7-day challenge. The four steps that you mentioned are a good reset. That's why I reached out to you, to get some crazy collaborations with brands like [Brand]. I saw your last video, which doesn't have sponsorships—is there any reason?

Email 2:
Subject: How did you build this level of engagement?
Yo Jack, week one... the way you edited the video makes it more... I love it. I'm an agency... brands like [Brand] would be a good fit. Are you open to making more collaborations? Let me know.

Email 3:
Subject: Best phone ever
Hi there, Why fight the distractions if you can delete them with a Nokia? I cannot agree more with you. I saw that you collaborated with brands [X] and [Y], but I'm confident you would be a good fit for a productivity brand like [Brand] and a few others, and I can help you with that. Are you open to doing more collabs?
entries.points: Never introduce yourself or your agency in a cold email because creators don't care. Turn your specific observation ('The four steps you mentioned are a good reset') into a curiosity subject line ('Is this a good reset?') and open directly with it. Don't ask why their video wasn't sponsored, don't fanboy, and don't list multiple past sponsors like a stalker. Pitch confidently rather than asking passively if they are open to collabs.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Is this a good reset?

Hey [Name], The four steps that you mentioned make sense...

entries.situation: A student sends a long first cold email to a BJJ/grappling creator sharing a personal white-belt injury story, praising the channel as a fanboy, and asking the creator to 'send over your pre, mid-roll rates when you get a chance.'
entries.student_email:
Hey Josh,
Love the last video on how smaller grapplers are using the Kimura now. As a white belt, I actually remember forcing one from guard once. Don't ask me how it went—I needed an ice pack. Your content stands out because it makes high-level BJJ fun, which is rare. We are currently lining up a few BJJ creators for upcoming campaigns with brands like [X] and [Y], and your channel came to mind naturally. If you are open to partnerships, send over your pre/mid-roll rates when you get a chance.
entries.points: Keep the personalization brief without telling a long personal story ('Don't ask me how I know' is enough), drop fanboy compliments and awkward phrases like 'came to mind naturally', and never ask for pre-roll or mid-roll rates in the first cold email—the first email should only aim to get a reply.
entries.rewrite: Hey Josh, Loved that you mentioned how smaller grapplers are using the Kimura now—don't ask me how I know. We are currently lining up a few BJJ creators for upcoming campaigns with brands like [X] and [Y]...

quote.quote: If you are open to partnerships, send over your pre, mid-roll rates and when you get a chance. No. I got it. It's your first email. My email was even worse. Trust me. It was super, super long. First email. It's only a response.

entries.situation: A student submits an Instagram DM to a BJJ creator that starts with a joke about a recent reel and ends with 'What's the best email to reach out?'.
entries.student_email: The Joker clap after Lord Farquaad got armbarred killed me. At the moment, we're putting together a few BJJ creators for an upcoming partnership campaign with brands like [X] and [Y], and we came across you. What's the best email to reach out?
entries.points: Because Instagram DMs have no subject line, front-load your very first words with the offer ('Partnership for you' or 'Collab for you') so it shows in the message request preview. Ending the DM with 'What's the best email to reach you on?' is excellent because it signals professionalism, avoids unnecessary small talk in DMs, and moves the conversation to email.
entries.rewrite: Partnership for you. Hey, I have a couple of brands for you that could be a good match because of your content—what's the best email to reach you on?

quote.quote: Your first line should be downloaded. Your first sentence. Partnership for you. Hey, watch the content, make sense, blah, blah, blah, could be a good fit for this. Keep it super short, keep it super quick

entries.situation: A student sends a personalized cold email to an influencer's talent/growth agency manager (Kyle).
entries.student_email:
Subject: Ads that don't feel like ads

Hey Kyle, Came across [Creator]'s channel and thought the way he makes difficult techniques simple would be a strong fit for brands like [X] and [Y]. It builds a level of trust... Let me know if [Creator] is open to...
entries.points: When emailing a talent agency or manager, you can skip heavy personalization and go straight to pitching which brands fit their creator's content. However, be cautious because talent agencies also do their own brand outreach and will often gatekeep their creator's details unless you already have a confirmed brand deal.
entries.rewrite: Hey Kyle, I saw [Creator]'s content—it could be a good fit for brands like [X] and [Y]...

entries.situation: A student submits four cold emails and a follow-up to fitness and nutrition creators (a calisthenics creator, Peter, Matthew, and Lumi) with strong, non-fanboy personalizations but vague offers like 'I'm working on something that could be helpful for your audience' and 'I've been working on concepts... share a few ideas'.
entries.student_email:
Email 1:
Subject: This could go further
Your content showed me how clear and straightforward calisthenics could be. I couldn't agree more that these workouts must be simple and easy to follow. I'm working on something that could be helpful for your audience, and thought you might like to hear a bit more.

Follow-up:
I'm following up on my previous email to ensure you received my proposal regarding a potential paid collaboration...

Email 2 (Peter):
Subject: Worth exploring
Hey Peter, The way you integrate fitness and high-protein meals is really cool. After seeing your Yaki Udon post and cookbook push, I thought of a few brands that could naturally fit your content and audience. Would you be open to hearing more?

Email 3 (Matthew):
Subject: Any thoughts on this
Hey Matthew, It is great to see how you made Korean barbecue at home without spending much time in the kitchen. People with a busy schedule really appreciate your recipes. However, we can turn this into a paid collaboration...

Email 4 (Lumi):
Subject: Could this work for you
Hey Lumi, Watching your pasta video made me think, it's amazing how simple dishes resonate so much with busy home cooks. I've been working on concepts that could align with that simplicity and really engage your audience. Would it make sense if I share a few ideas?
entries.points: Complimenting how clear and practical a creator's content is without sounding like a fanboy is ideal personalization. However, never use cryptic offers like 'working on something helpful for your audience' or 'share a few concepts/ideas'—in the AI era, creators won't know if you're pitching an app, a survey, or a sponsorship, and your follow-up about a 'paid collaboration' won't match your first email. Explicitly state that you have brand collaborations lined up for them and ask 'Are you interested?'.
entries.rewrite: Your content showed me how clear and straightforward calisthenics could be. I couldn't agree more that these workouts must be simple and easy to follow. After seeing your post, I thought of a few brands we have lined up that could naturally fit your content—are you interested?

quote.quote: I'm working on something that could be helpful for you. You, or your brand, couple of collaborations we have lined up, that could be beneficial, something, something, yeah, so insha'Allah, your offer is straight to the point, okay, offer should be clear

entries.situation: A student sent a cold email to an education influencer praising their videos as great quality, naming only one brand, and putting their agency name in the email signature.
entries.student_email: ...and I have to say, your video is such a great quality. ... keep up the good work. ... [mentions one brand] ... [Signature includes agency name]
entries.points: Do not sound like a fangirl or use generic praise that could be sent to any YouTuber; write like a businessman by referencing a specific detail from their latest video, naming a couple of brands you are onboarding influencers for, and signing off with only your first name without your agency name.
entries.rewrite: I saw your videos, solid work, [mention a couple of specific details noticed in the last video]. We are onboarding influencers for [a couple of brands'] future campaign. ... Best regards, Ammar

quote.quote: And when you say, you know, in your signature, it's enough to mention your name, you don't need to mention your agency, because you're just basically telling them, hey, go check my website, go check my LinkedIn.

entries.situation: A student sent a cold email to an automotive influencer referencing a specific comment from the creator's video ('Might be the last proper AMG') and ending the offer with 'we can start looking into solid options.'
entries.student_email: Just watch your video. This one, absolutely right. Might be the last proper AMG. ... we can start looking into solid options.
entries.points: Referencing a specific point the creator made in their latest video is strong personalization that proves the email is not automated, but do not say 'we can start looking into solid options' because it makes it sound like you have no brands and are waiting on them; instead offer to send more details or specific information.
entries.rewrite: We can send you more details, we can provide some information

quote.quote: What I would say, you know, what I would change actually, we can start looking into solid options. So basically, we're waiting for you. We're not doing anything now. You know, we don't have brands.

entries.situation: The same student showed a second automotive influencer outreach email with slightly longer personalization, the call to action 'give me the green light,' and an agency name in the signature.
entries.student_email: ... [longer personalization] ... give me the green light ... [Agency name in signature]
entries.points: Keep personalization concise, use semi-informal calls to action like 'give me the green light' only with influencers (never with brands, where you must remain more professional), and leave your agency name out of the signature.

quote.quote: When it comes to brands, don't say give us a green light. Be more professional. Be But yeah, this could be better. And also, don't mention your agency. You don't need that. Just mention name.

entries.situation: A student sent a cold email to a brand opening with 'Hope you're doing fantastic,' praising a sponsorship as a 'sharp pick and well-aligned placement,' describing themselves as 'I run a small agency working with a tight-knit group of influencer creators... speaking to very globally minded, financially savvy audience,' and offering to introduce 'one of our top creators' if 'open to exploring.'
entries.student_email: Hope you're doing fantastic. I saw your [Brand] sponsorships, sharp pick, and well-aligned placement. I run a small agency working with a fine-nit group of influencer creators in this world and space, all speaking to very globally minded, financially savvy audience. I'd like to introduce you to one of our top creators, who I think could be a great fit, let me know if you're open to exploring.
entries.points: Remove ChatGPT marketing buzzwords ('well-aligned placement,' 'tight-knit group,' 'very globally minded, financially savvy audience') and write at a simple third-grade reading level like a normal person. Never use 'I' or call yourself a 'small agency'—use 'we' and let the brand's imagination run wild (or say 'boutique agency'). Instead of vague claims about 'our top creators' or asking to 'explore,' name two specific influencers you work with and mention their views and engagement rate.
entries.rewrite: We work with [Influencer 1] and [Influencer 2], [mention solid views and engagement rate].

quote.quote: I go with two influencers, mention names, you know, we work with Farhad, we work with Dylan, and mention something about, you know, solid views, engagement rate, it's enough, keep it short, keep it nice, and that's it.

entries.situation: A student sent two cold emails to contacts at a VPN/privacy brand with the subject line '[First name], worth a shot?', greeting them with 'Hi there [First name],' writing in the opening lines 'We also reached out to Gina...', pitching 'a few influencers [Names] whose audience values safe internet browsing,' and in the second email referencing a specific privacy-scare video while saying 'We're working closely with U.S. influencers... who care deeply about online privacy.'
entries.student_email: Subject: [First name], worth a shot? Hi there [First name], Saw your video promoting [Brand], super handy for multitasking. We also reached out to Gina, but I wanted to connect with you in case you're the right person to speak with. We are reaching out on behalf of a few influencers, [Names], whose audience values safe internet browsing. / [Second email]: [References privacy scare in video] ... We're working closely with U.S. influencers who care deeply about online privacy. Would you be open to exploring collaborations?
entries.points: The subject line '[First name], worth a shot?', referencing a specific event from a sponsored video, and ending with a yes/no CTA are solid. However, drop 'there' from 'Hi there [First name]'; do not mention in the opening lines that you also emailed a coworker like Gina (either omit it completely when emailing two people at a brand, or move it to a P.S. at the end); name the creators directly instead of saying 'a few influencers'; never say you work 'closely' with creators (which invites questions about whether you manage them exclusively); and replace vague clichés like 'values safe internet browsing' or 'care deeply about online privacy' with concrete audience metrics.
entries.rewrite: Hi [First name], ... We are reaching out on behalf of [Influencer 1] and [Influencer 2] [mention something specific and strong about them]. Would you be open to exploring collaborations?

quote.quote: We're working closely with U.S. influencers. Don't mention closely, bro. Don't mention, because they can ask you, do you represent them exclusively? Do you work, do you manage them?

entries.situation: A student sent a cold email to an automotive OBD scanner brand with the subject line 'My audience are perfect for your OBD scanner,' telling the brand 'Comparing to other brands, your product is cheap and has all the required features for a fraction of the cost,' calling the audience 'budget friendly' and 'college students looking for cheap cars,' and ending with 'If you're interested, I'd like to explain how we can integrate your video into our content.'
entries.student_email: Subject: My audience are perfect for your OBD scanner. I'm reaching out on behalf of two influencers with [X] followers whose audience are missing out... Comparing to other brands, your product is cheap and has all the required features for a fraction of the cost. We believe our audience will benefit greatly as they are budget friendly, as well as one of the influencers' audience is college students looking for cheap cars. If you're interested, I'd like to explain how we can integrate your video into our content.
entries.points: Never say 'my audience' or 'our audience' because you are an agency, not the influencer, and avoid scammy words like 'perfect' in subject lines or pitches. Put personalization first by referencing a specific past brand collaboration (such as an influencer scanning a BMW M3 with their tool), followed by a single concise offer naming two creators with strong US audiences and stable views to spark curiosity. Never insult the brand or audience by calling them 'cheap,' avoid weak 'If you're interested' CTAs, and do not offer to explain how video integrations work since brands already know.
entries.rewrite: Subject: [Creator Name] worth considering for your OBD scanner / OBDX x [Creator Name]. Hey [Name], saw your collaboration with [Influencer] with your new OBD [Model] where he scanned his BMW M3, solid work. We speak on behalf of [Creator 1] and [Creator 2], with strong US audience and stable views in the automotive space.

entries.situation: Student (Hamzah) submitted a cold email to an influencer named Jack using the subject line 'What's next, Jack?', complimenting his mindset ('if you're moving, you're improving'), noting most of his sponsorships are with NordVPN, and asking if he is open to exploring sponsorships with other brands.

I was thinking we could do IG Reels, we have a few jiu-jitsu brands in mind that would be a good fit for you. However, before moving forward, we would like to know a bit more about your audience, would you mind sending us your media kit?' and was ghosted.
entries.student_email:
Initial email: Hey [First Name], just checked out your Reels on IG and love the content. Can't wait to try [that Kimura] out in training. Just wondering, are you open to sponsored partnerships? Kind regards, Mohamed.

Influencer reply: Hey Mohamed, appreciate the support, hope that Kimura gets you some nice taps in training! I'm definitely open to hearing what do you got in mind, shoot over some details or an outline of this proposal.

Student reply: Osu, no problem! I was thinking we could do IG Reels, we have a few jiu-jitsu brands in mind that would be a good fit for you. However, before moving forward, we would like to know a bit more about your audience, would you mind sending us your media kit?
entries.points: When an influencer asks what you have in mind, do not beat around the bush, repeat your initial email, or get overly excited and informal ('Osu'). Keep a professional tone, name specific brands you plan to pitch, directly ask for their rates and specific audience analytics (such as top 5 countries) or offer a call, and close with 'Let me know if you have any questions.'

entries.situation: A student submits a cold outreach email to a finance creator about an early retirement video that starts sentences with 'I watched', 'I also liked', and 'I saw', and asks if the creator is open to brand sponsorships.

And I also like how you made the huge numbers feel more real and practical. I saw the HMRC probably sponsor on it. Are you open to Morello and brand sponsorships for your channel?
entries.points: Never open with forbidden clichés like 'I watched your recent video' or 'I saw', avoid starting every sentence with 'I' or sounding like a fanboy, explain why a specific point in the video landed well, and present a concrete offer naming brands rather than asking a vague discovery question.
entries.rewrite: Your point that early retirement is really about bridging the gap landed well [followed by why it landed well]. We can work with these brands / we can get you brands like this and this and this.

entries.situation: A student in the fitness niche submits a cold email with stair-stepped line breaks ('hurdles'), a non-sequitur transition ('The orange painted nails screamed for attention. Speaking of this, we work with...'), and ends the offer with 'that could be good for your brand'.
