entries.situation: A student reads out a pitch email he sent to a brand that replied to his initial outreach, using a bulleted overview of a single creator, deliverable format, rate, and a closing CTA.
entries.student_email: To kick things off, I'd love to put [influencer name] on your radar. One of the most [this, this, that], leader in the industry, [this, this, that]. [Bullet points: overview, YouTuber name, platform, subscribers, location, audience, content style, engagement, channel link, format of the deliverable, 60-second pre-roll integration, the rate, and what it includes.] I believe the influencer could be a powerful addition to this brand's next campaign, especially given how well his audience aligns with your target market. If you'd like me to send over examples of past campaigns, happy to provide whatever helps your team evaluate the fit.
entries.points: Presenting a single creator via bullet points with deliverable details and rate (or sharing a roster via a spreadsheet) works well as long as the CPM and pricing make sense for the brand.

quote.quote: With brands, especially with brands, as long as it makes sense, you know, as long as you're not giving them a crazy CPM, then that's completely fine.

entries.situation: A brand asked for full demographics, past collaborations, and a price, and the student replied with a media kit, past collab examples, a 60–90s integration rate including a description link and pinned comment, and an offer to discuss multi-video bundles.
entries.student_email: Hey, thanks for getting back to me. I've attached our media kit as requested, which includes full demos and everything else. Here are some examples of recent collaborations... Our rates for a YouTube integration (60–90 seconds) — with a CTA link in the description and also a pinned comment... We're happy to discuss bundling options / multi-video collaboration if that is something you're open to exploring.
entries.points: Attaching the requested media kit alongside past collaboration examples, highlighting deliverables like a CTA link in the description and a pinned comment, and offering multi-video bundles is strong—just remove obvious ChatGPT em-dashes and make sure the creator's pricing structure actually leaves margin on bundles.

quote.quote: Sometimes it can be tricky, like a bundle deal. You need to look at the price of the influencer. For example, I had one case when the influencer, his normal integration was very cheap, but the shorts were more than double.

entries.situation: The brand objected that the flat fee was too high because the creator's views were unstable and offered a 25 CPM deal capped at 250k views; the student countered at 30 CPM still capped at 250k views citing primarily UK/US older male demographics and strong retention.
entries.student_email: I completely understand your concerns around unstable views... we're open to working on a performance model, and given the nature of our audience, primarily UK/US male audience, strong retention, we believe a 30 CPM, still capped at 250k, would be fair.
entries.points: Avoid sounding defensive or using vague demographic fluff that doesn't address fluctuating views; instead, cite exact audience percentages, counter higher on both the CPM and the cap (e.g., 30 CPM capped at 300k–350k), or push back against a performance deal by getting a minimum view guarantee from the creator to offer the brand.
entries.rewrite: I understand, I see where you're coming from. Given that this guy has 30% this audience, 20% of this audience, and all of this combined, we can do it at 30 CPM, capped at 300k–350k.

entries.situation: After settling on 28 CPM with the brand, the first influencer backed out of the CPM structure, so the student emailed the brand to pivot to a replacement creator with stable views and a 55% UK audience.

entries.points: When an influencer backs out of a deal structure, immediately pivoting the brand to a strong alternative creator with stable views, specific audience stats (55% UK-based), demographics, and past collaborations attached is an effective way to save the deal.

entries.situation: An influencer averaging 500k views replied to follow-ups saying 'Hi, I do YouTube ads. What are you asking for? entries.situation: A student submits his first cold outreach email to a workspace tech YouTuber under 150k average views.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Which partnership is your workload?

Konnichiwa, [Name]. Congrats on the release of your movie, moving things forward. It seems you have a lot going on from learning Japanese, making your own app to running a YouTube channel. You might align with the type of creators we are gathering for sponsorship campaign. Want details?
entries.points: Using a foreign-language greeting ('Konnichiwa') and congratulating the creator on a movie release works well to stand out. entries.situation: A student pitches an obstacle course racing (OCR) creator and names a single specific brand (Bear KompleX), stating they actively work with creators in his niche.
entries.student_email:
Subject: This could help before European Championship

Hey, impressive run in Belgium. The wheel traverse was especially insane. It looked like you were walking through the air. I noticed you're putting a lot of work into both OCR and your content, but you don't have any brand collaborations. Would you be interested in partnering with brands like Bear KompleX? They actively work with influencers in your niche.
entries.points: Tone down the fanboy praise in the opener and never name just one specific brand ('Bear KompleX') while claiming they actively work with influencers in that niche if you do not have that brand signed. Naming a single brand sets expectations that you have a deal with them ready, and the creator will ghost you once you admit you are only building a roster. Instead, mention multiple example brands ('brands like X and Y' or 'brands in this space').

Hey, impressive run in Belgium. The wheel traverse was especially insane. I noticed you're putting a lot of work into both OCR and your content, but you don't have any brand collaborations. Would you be interested in partnering with brands like [Brand A] and [Brand B] in this space?

entries.situation: A student submits a cold email to a lifestyle creator mentioning his Native collaboration, then saying he doesn't have many collaborations and claiming to be pitching creators to Nature Nate's and WHOOP.

entries.situation: A student emails a gaming chair brand using an out-of-office referral subject line ('Edward pointed me your way') and pitches a Steam Deck creator who has never showcased a gaming chair in his videos.

entries.situation: A student sends a cold email to a travel vlogger about a dodgy plane and rice fields, asking 'I'm just curious if you're open to more brand partnerships' before stating the offer.

entries.situation: A student submits three cold emails to productivity influencers: one saying 'congrats on your collab with X, you are also a good fit with Y and Z', a second offering to plan collabs with specific brands, and a third starting with 'To make good videos, you need mental clarity. I'll help you get sponsors while you focus on YouTube videos.'
entries.student_email:
Email 1: Subject: That was unexpected
Using the click to spin was a funny way to engage with your followers, well done. Congrats on your collab with [Brand], but you are also a good fit with brands like [Brand A] and [Brand B], and I can help you with that. Is this something you want to talk about? Let me know.

Email 2: I cannot agree more with you about planning everything. Don't ask me how I know. We can also plan on getting your collab with brands like [Brand]. Are you available to do more collabs apart from this one? Let me know.

Email 3: Subject: The real mental clarity
Hey, to make good videos, you need mental clarity. I'll help you get sponsors while you focus on YouTube videos.
entries.points: In the first and second emails, do not say 'you are a good fit with [Brand A] and [Brand B]' right after congratulating them on a deal, or they will ask you to introduce those specific brands immediately; instead say 'brands similar to these' or 'brands in this space, such as X and Y'. In the third email, cut the AI-sounding lecture ('To make good videos, you need mental clarity'), but keep the strong pain-solution offer ('We can help you get sponsors while you focus on YouTube videos') and add example brands plus a clear CTA ('Want to hear more about it?').

entries.situation: A student in the automotive niche sent a cold email to a major car manufacturer praising their Q-Range SUV and pitching a single small creator who gets 7K-15K views.
entries.student_email: We are impressed by this feature [Q-Range SUV]... [Creator name] creates detailed car reviews and practical insights. He frequently drives in the countryside educating his audience... Interested to see how this guy as well can support your next Q-Range project.
entries.points: Do not pitch a tiny creator to a massive car brand that does not do influencer marketing. Cut overly excited praise and fluffy content descriptions ('he frequently drives in the countryside educating his audience'), pitch two creators instead of one, use concrete marketing metrics (US audience share, consistent views, engagement rate) so the email is scannable in 3-5 seconds, and end with a stronger CTA.
entries.rewrite: I just saw collaboration [solid point]. Also, we have these guys from this space [two names, engagement rate, audience], let me know if you want something like this.

quote.quote: make sure you're sending email to someone who is doing influencer marketing, do personalization, you don't have to be like, we are impressed by this feature, you don't have to be super excited

entries.situation: A student in the geopolitics niche sent a cold email to a brand referencing an article with a surface-level takeaway ('it's great to see influencer marketing growing so fast'), pitching a top-ranked podcaster, and mentioning the creator's 10-month ongoing partnership with another brand.
entries.student_email: ...it's great to see influencer marketing growing so fast. We work with podcasters and independent creators... It has been top choice among the influencers on our roster... fit for brand, hosted by influencer, number one podcast on Spotify, Apple podcast... They all have also had successful ongoing partnership with Sama Santer for the last 10 months.
entries.points: The data-oriented offer highlighting podcast chart rankings is strong, but cut the overly excited tone ('enjoy'), replace the shallow article comment with a brief, intelligent insight about the actual geopolitics topic, name the specific influencers on your roster, and remove any mention of a 10-month ongoing partnership with another brand to avoid raising exclusivity concerns.
entries.rewrite: Collaboration, good, we have something to offer to you, this, this, this, this, should I send more details?

quote.quote: If there's like a, like something like an article about something, and your personalization method is to like, Like, say, like, an insight that you got from that article, make sure the insight is, like, interesting.

entries.situation: A student in the geopolitics niche sent a cold email to a brand opening with personal LinkedIn flattery about their multi-year company growth, describing the creator's audience as 'Millennials, Gen Z, and Boomers,' and giving a 200K-300K view range.
entries.student_email: I found you on LinkedIn, incredible to see what you built over years, from no office to LinkedIn, huge congrats to you and your team. We work with podcasters, influencers, space to help... Highly target audience, made up of Millennials, Gen Z, and Boomers... 200, 300K views... On a quick look, the audience behind both channels...
entries.points: Remove the LinkedIn flattery about watching what they built over the years because it sounds like creepy stalking; stick to business personalization. Replace generational labels ('Millennials, Gen Z, and Boomers') with exact numeric age brackets (e.g., '60% of his audience is aged 30 to 55'), and replace the wide '200-300K' view range with a specific average like 'averaging around 250K views'.
entries.rewrite: 60% of his audience is aged 30 to 55... averaging around 250K views.

quote.quote: Meetup Millennials, Gen Z, and Boomers. In my opinion, this is not professional enough. What I usually do for ages is I'll try to like, I'll look at their audience information and I'll find like the best way to summarize it in a few words.

entries.situation: A student in the healthcare/wellness niche sent a long, formal, multi-paragraph email to a doctor YouTuber including two paragraphs of personalization, a paragraph introducing their marketing agency, a formal CTA, and a full-name sign-off.
entries.student_email: Hi Doctor [Name], We share your view that wellness is an all-long time among health care... [second personalization paragraph on promoting beauty/wellness]... At [Agency], a marketing agency working with health/wellness brands to provide... Are you open to discussing such brand partnerships? [Full Name]
entries.points: Cut the email length drastically so it can be read in 3 to 5 seconds; keep the first personalization sentence and save the second personalization point for a follow-up email. Remove the paragraph introducing your agency because creators do not care who you are, simplify the CTA to 'should I send more details?', and sign off with only your first name.
entries.rewrite: We share your view that wellness is... [something specific from last video]. [Offer]. Should I send more details? [First name only]

quote.quote: at marketing agency with NFL brands to provide, bro, they don't care who you are, trust me, they don't care who you you can be night media, they don't care, trust me, they don't have time to read about you

entries.situation: A student in the education niche sent an email to an influencer with excessive line breaks, random capitalized words throughout the first half, vague personalization about Joe Rogan, confusing phrasing ('external brands', 'working with them alone'), and a Gmail auto-complete CTA.
entries.student_email: Hey, hope you're doing well. I watched your video on [Topic]. Before I Used To Think People Like Joe Rogan Are Against The System, But Clearly They're Not. I also noticed you only work with Few external brands, like [Brand 1] and [Brand 2], on both of your YouTube channels so far. Is it because you're working with them alone or you're open to exploring other partnerships? Let me know if that's something you'd like to explore.
entries.points: Combine lines so the email is compact rather than stretched out with line breaks and 'I' statements. Only capitalize proper nouns so the reader doesn't mistake your sentence for a video title. State specifically why the video showed Joe Rogan isn't against the system, replace confusing phrases like 'external brands' and 'working with them alone' with simple fourth-grade English asking if they want more partnerships, and avoid Gmail's auto-completed CTA ('Let me know if that's something you'd like to explore') because spam filters flag it.
entries.rewrite: I thought Joe Rogan is against the system, but he's not because he said [specific point]. I saw you're working with these two brands. Are you open to more partnerships?

quote.quote: Let me know. That's something you'd like to explore. This CTA is sometimes, or I think it's usual, you know, recommended by Google Gmail itself. So before, you know, when you say, when you type, let me. It gives you this. Stay away from it.

entries.situation: A student sent an outreach email to an education creator starting with 'I hope you are doing well. Just watched your video on how companies...', followed by a long personalization sentence and an overcomplicated pitch for a data-privacy brand using 'I work with...'.
entries.student_email: I hope you are doing well. Just watched your video on how companies... The way you unpack modern isolation, digital manipulation really hit, and I'm judging by the comments that your audience deeply resonates with that kind of truth-telling. I work with a brand like [Brand], which helps users protect their online data and reduce overexposure...
entries.points: Remove 'I hope you are doing well' and 'Just watched your video on...' and open directly with the specific observation ('The way you unpack modern isolation and digital manipulation really hit'), followed by a short 3-4 word tag ('plus your audience loved it'). Change 'I work' to 'We work', simplify the brand description to a third-grade reading level, and keep the whole initial email around 50 to 70 words.
entries.rewrite: The way you unpack modern isolation and digital manipulation really hit, plus your audience loved it. We work with a brand like [Brand]...

quote.quote: What I would, the length that I would go to when I'm writing a personalization sentence, it's like the way you unpack modern isolation and digital manipulation really hit, you know, hope for more videos like that in the future.

entries.situation: A large travel influencer replied to initial outreach listing 10+ major past sponsors (Universal Studios Japan, Singapore Airlines, Alipay, Chinese and Bhutan governments, Nomad eSIM 23 times) and quoting $3,000 flat fee for a 60-second integration. The student lectured them on brand budgets, countered at $1,000, got ghosted, and sent a one-line follow-up.
entries.student_email: Thanks for sharing your demographics and rates. From our experience, brands prefer to start with a smaller budget for the first collaboration. Once when they see the value you bring, long-term... [offered $1,000]. [Follow-up:] Just checking in to see if you received my previous email.
entries.points: Never insult a major influencer who has 15+ sponsors and a fair $3,000 rate by lecturing them ('From our experience, brands prefer to start with a smaller budget') and lowballing $1,000 when you don't even have a brand deal lined up yet. Either gently ask if they would do $2,000 for an initial integration or simply thank them and use their list of past sponsors as free brand leads. Also, add context to follow-ups instead of sending a one-line 'just checking in' message.
entries.rewrite: Would you go for 2k for initial integrations? [Or:] Okay, thanks for letting me know, I'll see what I can do.

quote.quote: When it comes to follow-ups, give it more context. Make it a bit longer. You know, it doesn't have to be just this, because most of the time we just copy-paste this one and easily we'll land into spam.

entries.situation: A student in the tech niche sent a cold email to an influencer introducing himself and his agency, using bold text, missing the verb 'is' ('your audience really into tech'), calling Apple and Samsung 'niche brands', asking a weak CTA ('Are you open to sponsorships?'), and signing with full name, website, and email.
entries.student_email: My name is [Name] from [Agency] Media. We notice your audience really into tech products and that's exactly the kind of niche brands like Apple, Samsung [are looking to collaborate with]. I think you'd be good for some upcoming campaigns. Are you open to sponsorships? [Full Name, Website, Email]
entries.points: Remove the self-introduction ('My name is X from Y Media'), never bold words in outreach emails because it looks spammy, fix grammar ('your audience is really into tech'), do not call giant corporations like Apple and Samsung 'niche brands', pitch 2-3 smaller realistic brands instead of tech giants, use a direct CTA like 'Should I send more details?', and sign with only your first name (no last name, website, or email).
entries.rewrite: We noticed your engagement rate and solid audience, and I think brands like [2-3 smaller brands] would work well for you. Should I send more details? [First name]

quote.quote: Yeah, what I'm saying is, I mean, maybe it's just my English, but we notice your audience really into tech. Does that sound really, like, wrong? Yeah. I feel like it should be, we notice your audience is really into tech.

entries.situation: A student sent an email typed on a phone with jagged, uneven line breaks and generic personalization ('I enjoy watching your content and learning a whole lot of great stuff').
entries.student_email: Hello [Name], I enjoy watching your content and learning a whole lot of great stuff...
entries.points: Fix jagged phone formatting so the email forms a clean, compact paragraph, and replace generic praise that could be sent to any creator with a specific detail from a recent video (such as a phone grayscale hack) followed by a simple sponsorship question.
entries.rewrite: Turn your phone to greyscale, it's a good hack. I saw your videos are not sponsored, would you be open to a couple of sponsorships? Let me know what you think.

quote.quote: Turn your phone to greyscale, it's a great hack, or it's a good hack, don't necessarily have to say great, something, something. I saw your videos are not sponsored, would you be open to a couple of sponsorships, let me know what you think.

entries.situation: A student sent an initial influencer email with 'RE:' added to a subject line referencing a segment of the creator's video, and formatted the entire email body as a single dense wall of text without line breaks.
entries.student_email:
Subject: RE: [Video segment]...

Hello [First name], [the new cookie dog... long single-paragraph block of text with CTA embedded inside]
entries.points: Remove 'RE:' from the subject line because it is dishonest (keep the rest of the subject line referencing the video segment, which is good). Use line breaks after the greeting and before the CTA to break up the bulky wall of text so it is easy to scan.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: [Video segment]...

Hello [First name],

[Personalization about the new cookie dog and offer]

[CTA]

quote.quote: Other than that, use enter. We talked about it last time. It's super easy and it's free. So you can use it here, like hello, first name, and then add the new cookie dog.

entries.situation: A student in the tech/e-reader niche submits a revised email opening with a wordy compliment ('I like how you outlined the [product]... Its small form factor makes it ideal for binge-reading e-books on the go') followed by 'We are in the process of lining up sponsorship opportunities for content like yours with brands like X and Y. Does that sound like something you'd be interested in?'
entries.student_email:
Subject: [First name], something you'd be open to?

Hey [first name], I like how you outlined the [product]. Its small form factor makes it ideal for binge-reading e-books on the go. We are in the process of lining up sponsorship opportunities for content like yours with brands like [Brand A] and [Brand B]. Does that sound like something you'd be interested in?
entries.points: Referencing a specific detail from the video is good, but avoid starting with 'I like how...' and keep the observation concise so it isn't boring to read. For the offer, avoid explaining your internal process ('in the process of lining up...'); instead, state directly that based on their content you thought Brand X would be a good match, or ask a specific question about integration length (e.g., 60–90 seconds) to get a reply first.
entries.rewrite:
Watched your video on [product]...

Based on your content, we thought [Brand] would be a good match for you. What do you think?

quote.quote: he mentioned something specific, so that's a good sign, there's a light, there's a light, okay, but don't love the aspect, check your video, watch your video, saw your video, I know it's a bad word, but, you know, don't, you don't have to start

entries.situation: The same tech-niche student submits two more drafts using nearly identical subject lines ('Hi [first name], something you might be interested in?'), starting with 'I like how you highlighted...', using slang ('By the way, the website looks dope'), and focusing heavily on praising the creator's setup ('was a nice way to make your setup clean').
entries.student_email:
Subject: Hi [first name], something you might be interested in?

Draft 2: I like how you highlighted the simplicity of using a product to manage your workload for that website. By the way, the website looks dope. We're connecting developer tools brands such as [Brand A] and [Brand B] with influencers like you...

Draft 3: Combining the dial and keyboard of the product into one enclosure was a nice way to make your setup clean. We're planning on lining up sponsorships for creators like you with brands like [Brand A] and [Brand B]...
entries.points: Do not reuse the same subject line across every draft; A/B test distinct curiosity hooks (such as 'Hey [Name], I've noticed something in your last video'). Keep personalization very brief and neutral without saying 'I like' or repeatedly focusing on 'you/your style/your setup'. Replace slang like 'looks dope' with professional wording like 'looks promising', and move casual 'by the way' remarks to the end of the email by the CTA.
entries.rewrite: I scrolled the website, looks promising. We're connecting developer tools brands such as [Brand A] and [Brand B] with influencers like you. Thoughts?

quote.quote: Your setup, your way of explaining, your style of doing things, the way how you're doing it, you, you, you. It's all about you. Okay? Yeah. You don't mention anything about him. Okay? Be a strong man. Don't say you, you, you.

entries.situation: A student drafts an email to an influencer asking them to confirm whether the 63.2% US demographic figure on their media kit is a typo compared to the 35.5% shown on their screenshot.
entries.student_email: hey name, I hope you're doing well regarding your media kit, I noticed that it states 63.2% of your audience is based in the US. However, the street shot of the demographic you shared with me shows 35.5%. Could you confirm the 63.2% bigger? Is it the updated number or is it possibly a typo? Looking forward to hearing from you, less regards.
entries.points: The draft is acceptable to send, but instead of saying 'could you confirm' (which can sound demanding), it is softer to ask whether there was a mistake/typo between the two documents or if there has been a recent audience decline.
entries.rewrite: is there, has there been a mistake on to why the media kit, the first one was 63, and the second world was 36, like, has there been a typo, or has this been just a decline on the audience

quote.quote: like, has there been a typo, or has this been just a decline on the audience, you know? Because when you say to them, can you confirm, like, hey, tell me why, tell me, tell me why is this, but it's okay.

entries.situation: An influencer averaging 50k views and posting daily claimed a past sponsor paid him $3,500. Because the student couldn't find that sponsorship on his channel, he replied asking the creator to share an example of a past sponsorship.
entries.student_email: could you share an example of a fast sponsorship
entries.points: Asking an influencer to prove a past sponsorship essentially calls them a liar and burns the bridge. Instead, counter on a CPM basis by framing it around the brand's limited budget or the standard CPM you work with (e.g., $15 CPM = $2,000 for this channel type) and ask if that budget is a deal breaker.
entries.rewrite: The brand has a limited budget / the budget that we work with is around a $15 CPM and hence it gives us $2k for this kind of channel. Would you be open to this or would this be a deal breaker for you?

quote.quote: you mentioned the budget that you work with is around this cpm and hence it gives us this number you know it gives us 2k for example what this kind of channel would you be open to this would this be a little breaker

entries.situation: A student reads out his draft cold email to a brand whose product his creator previously reviewed for free.
entries.student_email: hey Brent enjoy your products and I have seen your sponsor and creators such as creator I represent creator a in that niche with a combined following of so-and-so he also has you reviewed product in the past would you be interested in sponsoring him and so let me know
entries.points: Stop going in multiple directions at once (mentioning their other sponsorships, your roster's combined following, and the past review all together). Focus on one clear angle: you reviewed their product in the past, it went great, and you want to do more of it together.
entries.rewrite: Hey, we reviewed it in the past. It's awesome. We're gonna want to do more of that. What do you got as partnerships ideas?

quote.quote: Who problem here is that you're going in so many directions? Like you saw him from here and you also got this and you also got that and also this and he also revealed in the past fix one thing.

entries.situation: A student submits an initial brand outreach email referencing Gillian's collaboration with Elia Head, stating 'One influencer has a majority UK (33.5%) and US audience', listing all of the creator's stats and awards before revealing his name (David Greybridge-Beykov) at the end, asking 'Should I send over the demos?', and signing off with 'Yours' and a 'CEO/Founder' website signature.
entries.student_email: Hello [First Name], I recently saw Gillian's collaboration with Elia Head and saw a match for similar influencers we work with. One influencer has a majority UK (33.5%) and US audience... [lists audience stats and award wins]... His name is David Greybridge-Beykov. Should I send over the demos? Yours, [Name, CEO/Founder, Email, Website]
entries.points: Do not mention specific audience percentages if the number is under 50% (just say 'their audience is mostly from the UK and US'), state the creator's name right away instead of burying it at the end of the paragraph, withhold full stats so the prospect stays curious, keep the strong CTA ('Should I send over the demos?'), replace 'Yours' with 'Best' or 'Thanks', and remove 'CEO/Founder' and template website links from the signature.
entries.rewrite: We work with [Creator Name], their audience is mostly from UK and US... Should I send over the demos? Best, [Name]

quote.quote: So, one influencer, if you say one influencer, give name, okay? Give name, inshaAllah. Don't be like, there's one guy, you know, he is super good, maybe I'll give you his name, maybe I'll not. Be specific. They will not cut you off,

entries.situation: During a live email-writing drill for book creator Spencer Evans, a student writes an outreach email pitching sleep and wellness brands, asking for a media kit or demo upfront, and ending with 'no problem either way.'
entries.student_email: hey Spencer, these books fix my attention span, that video tells me you understand the real problem with modern attention, not just the symptoms, sleep is where attention gets rebuilt, and a reading channel is the one place a window routine doesn't sound like a wellness lecture, if you're open to partnership with sleep and wellness brands, send your media kit or demo and I'll see if there's a fit, no problem either way
entries.points: The personalization connecting reading and sleep to attention span is strong, but remove the em dash so it does not look AI-generated, drop soft language like 'no problem either way' to maintain power dynamics, and put the media kit CTA on its own line as a direct question.
entries.rewrite:
We're currently working with sleep and wellness brands that will be a good fit for your content.

Could you send over your media kit for review?

quote.quote: we don't want to sort of give the influencer the opportunity to kind of like say no to us. Like we don't want to be like too nice. You need to remember we have to maintain the power dynamics.

entries.situation: A student submits a single-paragraph cold email to Spencer Evans referencing his comment about needing a video playing to fall asleep and jumping straight into 'Open to exploring a sponsorship?' without a bridge sentence.
entries.student_email: Hi there. Love these books. Fix my attention span. You're honestly needing a video playing just to fall asleep. Really. You're honestly about needing a video playing just to fall asleep. Really hit home. That kind of relatable wind down moment. Exactly where brands love to show up. Open to explore. Doing a sponsorship.
entries.points: Break the email into separate lines after the personalization and bridge so it is easy to read on a phone, remove the em dash, and add a bridge sentence explaining what type of brand sponsorships you are offering before the CTA.
entries.rewrite:
We're potentially working with brands like XYZ.

Are you open to exploring a sponsorship?

quote.quote: That's why we clarify the type of sponsorship we're talking about in that bridge segment over here. We're potentially working with brands like XYZ. Okay, it's brand deals, it's brand type of sponsorships that we're looking at.

entries.situation: A non-native English speaking student writes a short email to Spencer Evans with broken grammar, generic praise ('I'm following your content, which is amazing'), and no clear question CTA.
entries.student_email: Hey, Spencer, I'm following your content, which is amazing. We're reading books and reading blog. I was, I was this word. I have sponsorship are interesting that will help you.
entries.points: Run your draft through AI to fix spelling and grammar before sending, dig deeper on personalization by referencing specific details from a video so it cannot be copy-pasted to another creator, and end with a clear question-mark CTA on its own line.
entries.rewrite: I was following your reading vlog and I really liked how you described the main character as this, this, and that.

quote.quote: the personalization, you shouldn't be able to transfer it from one influencer to another, that's how you know that you're going like deep enough and applying like proper personalization to that specific video

entries.situation: A student writes a long cold email to Spencer Evans with generic praise ('love the channel'), explains his role in detail, and asks for a 15-minute phone call in the first email.
entries.student_email: Hey, Spencer, love the channel. I've been watching your content and had a thought. I think that. A lot of brands that will pay for sponsor play, Spence on their video, and I've been interested in helping those connections happen. My role would be simple, find companies that align with your audience, pitch sponsor opportunities, and bring deals to you. If you like the opportunity, you take it. If not, no pressure. My goal is to help you generate additional revenue without adding work to your play. If you'd be open to talking for 15 minutes sometimes, I'd love to share a few thoughts. Appreciate your time.
entries.points: Do not ask for a 15-minute call in a first email because influencers are busy and skeptical of strangers until you have built a relationship; replace 'love the channel' with specific personalization from the video, keep the strong bridge sentence, delete the role explanation, and end with a simple question asking if they want more brand deals.
entries.rewrite:
Hey Spencer, I really liked how you had a different perspective on the main character compared to everyone else that read the book.

I've been watching your content and had a thought. I think there are a lot of brands that will pay for sponsor placements on your video, and I'd be interested in helping those connections happen.

Would you be interested in more brand deals?

quote.quote: I would basically then remove everything else in the email and then literally just change this to a CTA. Like, would you be interested in more brand deals? Would you be interested in more partnerships?

entries.situation: An influencer's sales representative/manager sent over their media kit and pricing, and the student replied trying to negotiate the rate down to $1,500.
entries.student_email: For these current campaigns... we can allocate 1.5k... is this something we can work with?
entries.points: Do not mention 'for these current campaigns' when you do not actually have an active campaign, as you will get caught if they ask what campaign it is. Instead, pick a specific metric from their media kit (such as wanting an even higher US viewership percentage) to logically justify your cap, and replace soft phrasing like 'is this something you can work with?' with firm walk-away framing like 'Will this be a deal breaker?'
entries.rewrite: Since we're looking for a higher US percentage, the max we're able to allocate is 1.5k. Will this be a deal breaker?

quote.quote: And if you don't think, you don't, you don't say if this is something you can work with, like, is this a deal breaker? This is why framing is so important, because you're positioning yourself as something who is ready, someone who's ready to, to walk away.

entries.situation: A marine and outdoor YouTube creator replied to initial outreach saying, 'Hey, yeah, I'm always open to sponsorship opportunities.' The student replied naming two fitting brands, stating the target deliverable, and asking for audience analytics.
entries.student_email: Hey, glad to hear that. I've been looking at brands like Powerpoint and Yeti that could feel well with the boating and DIY side of your content. We're probably looking at 60 to 90 second YouTube integrations. To see what will make the most sense of it for your channel, please send over your audience analytics. Mainly looking for 8th January top countries. Looking forward to hearing from you.
entries.points: Naming concrete brands that fit the creator's content and specifying the target deliverable (60-90 second YouTube integrations) before asking for analytics makes for a strong, substantive reply. However, when the email is already somewhat long, trim explanations of what analytics are (such as age, gender, and top countries) since creators already know, and cut filler sign-offs like 'Looking forward to hearing from you' so the analytics request stands alone as the clear CTA.

quote.quote: Honestly, prefer, like, when the email is already a bit long, I don't, like, tell them exactly what I want. Like, I assume they already know what is analytics, right?

entries.situation: A talent agent for a healthcare/dentistry creator replied to cold outreach asking, 'Hey, do you have a particular partnership in mind?' The student replied saying there was no specific partnership at this stage, described building a creator shortlist, buried an analytics/media kit ask in the middle, and added a list of extra questions.
entries.student_email: Not a specific partnership at this stage. We're currently building a shortlist of suitable creators for upcoming promotional campaigns, both dedicated and organic, and he is someone we're considering. Before putting his profile forward to relevant brands, we'd like to understand his audience and previous commercial work to make sure that he's a strong fit. Would you be able to share audience analytics and media kit? We'll be mainly looking at audience size, age, and range. A couple of other things that would be useful: has he worked with sponsors previously? If so, which brands? Are there any particular brands or categories he would be interested in working with? Once we assess the fit, we'll be happy to...
entries.points: Never open with 'Not a specific partnership at this stage,' as exposing that you have nothing causes the agent to stop reading immediately. Cut AI-sounding fluff about 'building a shortlist of suitable creators for upcoming promotional campaigns' and talk about outcomes that matter to them—specific brands and sponsorship opportunities in their niche. Finally, ask for only one thing per email instead of overwhelming a busy 9-to-5 talent agent with a checklist of questions.
entries.rewrite: Hey, we are looking at getting your influencer sponsored by [Brand X] and [Brand Y]. However, nothing is confirmed yet because we need a few information on your side. Before confirming anything, we need to know your analytics to see if they're aligned with what they want.

quote.quote: hey, we are looking at getting your influencer sponsored by, and you mentioned, two brands that are a very big fit for him. However, nothing is confirmed yet because we need a few information on your site.

entries.situation: After the outdoor talent agent shared Reel rates for four creators, the student countered by citing their average views over the last 10 Reels (excluding outliers), noting the quoted CPMs were too high, proposing lower target rates, and ending with 'Let me know where they can realistically land.'
entries.student_email: Hey, thanks for sharing the rates. I run the numbers against their last 10 reels, excluding outliers: [numbers]. These are well above the CPMs we typically can see in the space. Based on performance and scope of multiple reels, these are the rates we can work with: [rates]. If we can actually look closer to these rates, we can move forward and explore longer term collaboration. Let me know where they can realistically land.
entries.points: Backing up a counter-offer with the creators' average views over their last 10 Reels (excluding outliers) and pointing out that their quoted rates exceed niche CPMs is firm and effective. However, replace a weak closing line like 'Let me know where they can realistically land' with a firmer, value-driven CTA stating that aligning on those target rates will allow you to bring them more sponsorships.
entries.rewrite: If we can align on these rates, we could probably get you more sponsorships.

quote.quote: This is good. I like the email. Firm. Although the CTA is weak. CTA is weak. I would, I would actually be more firm in the CTA and like try to provide value with it.

entries.situation: Influencers replied to the student's initial outreach—where he named several brands he is in contact with—asking what each brand is looking for, and the student drafted a reply withholding campaign details until the influencers send their rates and 30-day analytics.
entries.student_email: Hey, you know, I'd like to share more information on what the brands are looking for. Before I do that, could you send your rates and analytics in the past 30 days? That would help me see which opportunities makes the most sense. And from there, we can move on to the next steps.
entries.points: Do not withhold details and immediately demand a media kit and rates from a creator who does not know you yet. Even if you do not have an official brief from the brand, give the creator plausible campaign details—such as the product, timeline, integration type, target CPM range, and language requirements—so they get interested and willingly share their rates, media kit, and availability.
entries.rewrite: We are looking into marketing their latest product, iPhone 17... we're looking for influencers, posting integrations, our target CPM is 25 to 50... we are looking for English speaking creators.

quote.quote: So, no, I think there is a better response. When they ask you for any details, even if you don't have the information, give them just any details, okay?

entries.situation: After a 3D-printing influencer replies 'Yes' to initial outreach, the student asks how many deals he can handle per month, but when the influencer asks 'What are your offers?' and 'What's your budget?', the student dodges and asks for typical rates and whether the influencer wants 'Brand Awareness and Direct ROI'.

To be honest, the budget depends on the campaign type and expected reach. Are you looking for Brand Awareness and Direct ROI?
entries.points: Asking how many deals a creator can handle in a month is a good way to warm up a stiff responder, but when they ask for your offers or budget, do not play tug-of-war—give them 'a candy' by naming brands you work with or are pitching before asking for their analytics, and never ask creators about 'Brand Awareness and Direct ROI' since those are brand goals while creators simply want to get paid for a 60-second integration.

entries.situation: A student in the health and well-being niche writes a dense, single-paragraph cold email that opens by bragging about his agency, uses complex vocabulary, tells a YouTuber 'Your videos on YouTube', bolds 'paid partnerships' in red font, places the CTA in the middle, says 'I'm looking to reach out', and lists too many brands.
entries.student_email: I represent [Agency], which brings together influencers and brands in the health and well-being sector. Your videos on YouTube have been so impactful on educational awareness, as well as on effective management on common health issues. I'm curious to know whether you'll be open to paid partnerships [bolded in red] with brand on this. I'm looking to reach out on supplement brands like [Brands], as well as on brands that empower education, like medical teaching educations... would these be a good fit to you to incorporate in your videos?
entries.points: Break the email into clean paragraphs (Greeting, Personalization, Offer, CTA at the end, Sign-off) instead of a squished 'brick'; never bold or color spam-trigger words like 'paid partnerships'; skip agency introductions and start with specific 4th-grade-level personalization without stating the obvious ('on YouTube'); and replace weak phrasing like 'I'm looking to reach out' with 'we are onboarding / preparing lists'.

entries.situation: After an influencer replies to the initial outreach, the student responds with 'In order to move forward, we require the following details' and demands a media kit/demographics, TikTok pricing, and previous brand case studies all at once, causing the influencer to ghost.
entries.student_email:
Hello [First Name], Thank you for your response. In order to move forward, we require the following details, as they will enable us to see if your content aligns with the brand's audience demographics:
- Media kit or audience information, specifically age, country.
- How much you'd charge for a TikTok video.
- Optional: Any case studies you may have from previous partnership with brands.

entries.points: Never demand multiple items at once ('we require the following details') or ask influencers for past brand case studies, which makes you look like a scammer and gets your domain reported; instead, thank them, briefly explain that you are sourcing creators for specific brands, ask only one question per email, and if the creator is stiff, warm them up first by asking how many integrations they can do per month.
