entries.situation: A student in the gaming workspace niche sends a cold email to a furniture brand with the subject 'Is this a stroke of genius?', telling them they have 'huge missed potential', pitching creators with 'more than 30% US audience', and placing the overlap note in a P.S.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Is this a stroke of genius?

I saw the new collab with [Creator], and I think it was a great way to advertise the bed frame, given he was moving. We believe there's still huge missed potential here—marketing desk and chair products would be far more useful for gamers who would constantly make good use of these types of products. We work with [Creator 1] and [Creator 2] who average 100K views with more than 30% of their audience being from the US. They play [Game 1] and [Game 2], where a single game can last up to 40 minutes. Would you like to hear more about these creators?

P.S. To avoid any overlap, I wanted to let you know I also emailed...
entries.points: Subject lines like 'Is this a stroke of genius?' only work for influencers or personal LinkedIn facts about the contact, not general brand outreach. Do not lecture the brand about 'huge missed potential', never brag about a 30% US audience (only highlight country demographics at 50–60%+), tie the 40-minute gaming session directly to needing a comfortable chair, and keep the overlap disclaimer in the P.S. (only if emailing 3–5 leads).
entries.rewrite: Most of their content is wrapped around League of Legends, for example, and I'm pretty sure those guys are sitting in the chair up to 40 minutes without moving. You need something comfortable.

quote.quote: 50, 60%. 50, you can rap it. He can be like, yeah, trust me, he's a good guy. But 60 is worth of bragging. Like majority of his audience, which is 60% is from U.S. That's good.

entries.situation: A student in the pets/animals niche sends a cold email with the subject line 'Let's earn money' and two personalizations about how fast a sheep or cow can run and a policeman holding a sheep.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Let's earn money

Hey [Name], how fast can a sheep or cow actually run? Never thought I'd ask myself that. I love the pictures of policemen holding the sheep. I might have to try that in my work. We're reaching out to brands like [Brand 1] and [Brand 2]...
entries.points: Never use 'Let's earn money' as a subject line because 'money' triggers spam filters; instead, use a curiosity question from the video ('How fast can a sheep or cow actually run?' or 'Team sheep, and you?'). Also cut the second personalization where you talk about yourself ('I might have to try that in my work'), because strangers do not care about you.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Team sheep, and you?

Hey [Name], how fast can a sheep or cow actually run? Never thought I'd ask myself that. We're reaching out to brands like [Brand 1] and [Brand 2]...

quote.quote: Hey, whoever, how fast can a sheep or cow actually run? Never thought I asked myself that. Okay, bro, instead of money, I would basically, I would basically say this, or maybe, um, sorry, um, team sheep and you?

entries.situation: A student in the construction niche sends a long cold email to a tool brand's marketing team with the subject 'Team, you are sensing creative potential here', pitching a detailed workshop renovation concept and asking 'Are you open to pilot mid-roll integration in Q4 video using this concept?'
entries.student_email:
Subject: Team, you are sensing creative potential here.

Hello marketing team, [Creator] from [Channel] did a brilliant job positioning the P2S as a practical problem-solving tool to overcome a limited setup. We work with [Creator] who is doing a farm YouTube renovation series. He will be rebuilding his workshop, a project with a car, a specialized custom storage solution... We see a strong fit to integrate the P2S as an essential tool in his workflow, showing how 3D printing... With 66% of UK audience... Are you open to pilot mid-roll integration in Q4 video using this concept?
entries.points: Change the subject line ('sensing creative potential here' can offend their marketing team) to something simple like 'This might be good' or 'Check what has happened'. Cut the lengthy workshop details because the first email is only meant to get a reply, lead earlier with the strong '66% UK audience' stat, and never use the word 'pilot' because begging them to 'just try a pilot' sounds needy and low-status.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: This might be good

We work with [Creator] who is doing a farm YouTube renovation series. With 66% of UK audience, we see a strong fit to integrate the P2S and show them how those tools can be useful.

quote.quote: Are you open to pilot mid-roll integration in Q4 video using this concept? Pilot is also bad to say. Why? Because it's it's kind of, please, please, please.

entries.situation: A student in the productivity tools/AI niche sends a cold email with the subject 'I am so sorry, Jack', joking about stealing ChatGPT tips, claiming 'multiple productivity brands campaign starting in October', saying 'You would be a fit', and then sending a follow-up with a brand-new video personalization.
entries.student_email:
Subject: I am so sorry, Jack.

I might have to steal some of those nice tips from your recent ChatGPT video. Some of them take productivity to a new plane. Speaking of which, we have multiple productivity brands campaigns starting in October, and we're looking for influencers in the AI space. You would be a fit. Interested?

Follow-up 1: Hello, ChatGPT has definitely gotten better when it comes to script writing. I appreciate your clear explanation on optimizing prompts in the last video. Speaking of...
entries.points: The apology subject line paired with playfully 'stealing' tips from his ChatGPT video is great. However, do not over-promise October campaigns if you do not have them, say 'You might be a good fit' rather than 'You would be a fit' so you do not give away power in cold outreach, and never write a whole new video personalization and pitch in your follow-up—just follow up briefly on the previous email.
entries.rewrite:
You might be a good fit. Interested?

Follow-up 1: Just following up on my previous email, just want to make sure you are interested. Let me know.

quote.quote: You would be a fit. You might be a good fit. Why? Because you are not sure. If you are sure, you will have some context. But no, if you do call outreach, don't say this. Basically, you're giving up too much power.

entries.situation: A student submits a cold email pitching an Apple-focused tech creator to Bitdefender.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Is Bitdefender reaching Apple users?

Hi [Name], Opening with the fact that one in four people dealt with a cyber incident last year was a smart way for [Creator] to make viewers feel the urgency. I work with [Creator], whose content walks Apple users through getting the most out of their devices. It's a natural place to show how Bitdefender protects their setup without slowing anything down. Want me to send over what that would look like?
entries.points: Avoid blog-style subject lines, cut long AI-sounding brand personalizations down to one short sentence, say 'we work with' instead of 'I work with', pitch one or two creators plus a sub-niche backup in case someone else already pitched that creator, and replace high-friction CTAs like 'Want me to send...' with 'Should I send...?'
entries.rewrite: We work with [Creator]... also we have these guys who might be a good fit because they do [sub-niche]... Should I send a couple of ideas?

quote.quote: Because personalization. It is important, but it should be short, especially for brands. Guys, those people are receiving 5,200 emails, right? 5,200 emails a day. He has no time to read this type of subject lines and personalizations.

entries.situation: A student submits a cold email pitching a home design and everyday tech creator to the robot vacuum brand MOVA Z70.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Did you miss a spot?

Hey, Seeing how well the MOVA Z70 cleaned up those crumbs by itself was a nice touch convincing viewers on the vacuum's independence. I work with [Creator], whose content centers on home design, renovation, and everyday tech. He can show how the MOVA Z70 rewards you by keeping your space clean after all of the effort you put into creating it. Should I send his profile over?
entries.points: Shorten the subject line from 'Did you miss a spot?' to 'Did you miss it?', use 'Hi there' when you don't have a contact's first name, and simplify wordy benefit claims into a concise one-line explanation since initial outreach is only meant to get a reply.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Did you miss it?

Hi there, ... He can show how [Product] can efficiently clean [space]. Should I send his profile over?

quote.quote: he can show how it rewards you by keeping your space clean after all of the effort you put into creating it. Okay. I will say he can show how this something can efficiently clean something.

entries.situation: A student in the automotive niche emails a brand they saw sponsoring a podcast, saying their creators' everyday job 'involves dealing with cars' and their audience likes 'car maintenance content'.
entries.student_email: Saw your brand on [Podcast], let's try some other influencers in the automotive niche. I'm working with [Creator] and a few other influencers. Their audience is based in the U.S., U.K., and Europe, since their everyday job involves dealing with cars and their audience is interested in car maintenance content. This would be the perfect audience to promote your service and products. Which profile do you want me to share first?
entries.points: Cut the length and replace vague clichés ('dealing with cars', 'interested in car maintenance') with a specific compliment on how the podcast host positioned their ad, a smooth bridge line, and a concrete sub-niche match explaining why the creator's audience actively needs the brand's product.
entries.rewrite: The way [Host] mentioned the F1 car crash and then brought up your brand was strong positioning, almost seamless. Speaking of seamless, we are working with guys who can do even better. They are Jack and John—their content is mostly about car auctions, which would be a perfect match because their audience are buying cars and need to check them before buying. Which profile do you want me to share first?

quote.quote: It'd be like the way he mentioned F1 car crashed and then brought your brand was a strong positioning, almost seamless. Good. Speaking of seamless, bridge line, which one you are missing here, right? We are working with guys who can do even better.

entries.situation: A student emails an automotive brand they saw collaborating on YouTube, adding 'We also work with many other influencers in the automotive industry. Can I send over?'
entries.student_email: Saw that you're collaborating with [Creator] on YouTube. You'll definitely like the influencer we're working with. Profiles reflect across all major platforms with audience based in the U.S., U.K., and Europe. We also work with many other influencers in the automotive industry. Can I send over?
entries.points: Maintain confident, high-status positioning: drop needy lines like 'We also work with many other influencers' and 'Can I send over?', and directly connect their past sponsorship to your specific creator.
entries.rewrite: Since you worked with [Creator], Jack would be a good fit for you...

quote.quote: Can I send over? See, can I? It's not CTA. It's this. It's this. Can I Samy, please? What did she? No, no, no. You're confident. You're not needy. You want to work with us? No. Fine, bro. We have another brand.

entries.situation: A student opens a brand email praising their '30-day return guarantee', lists multiple automotive sub-niches before pitching a creator, and lists US, UK, and European audience stats all together.
entries.student_email: Really nice idea, the 30-day return guarantee. Now all that's left to do is show it to as many potential buyers as possible. We work with influencers in the drift, off-road, and many other sub-niches in the automotive industry, with audience based in the U.S. and the U.K. Since they are all about cars, their audience is the best potential buyers based on the market.
entries.points: Do not open with customer-like praise that ruins the inbox preview, pitch your main creator offer before mentioning backup sub-niches, and tailor audience location stats to the brand's actual market (mention US stats for a US brand, European stats for a European brand).
entries.rewrite: Jack and Sam would be the best fit for your next campaign because their content is all about [X], and your product would be an amazing fit because of [Y].

quote.quote: With audience based in the U.S. and the U.K. and slightly in the U.K., don't just slap the whole audience analytics. If they are a U.S. brand, mention U.S. If they are a European brand, mention these two. Don't mention everything.

entries.situation: A student emails a brand talking about buying car parts from different countries, then abruptly pitches a Japan-based drifting creator for a VPN using filler like 'I chose to present him to you because...'
entries.student_email: Your collaboration was a good find. Buying car parts from different countries can be really frustrating. We work with [Creator], a professional drifter popular across many platforms. He's based in Japan at the moment, plus his audience is in the US and EU. I chose to present him to you because he competes in different continents, making a VPN essential.
entries.points: Ensure your opening line logically connects to your product pitch, remove internal-monologue filler ('I wanted to present...', 'I chose to present him because...'), and state the creator's value proposition directly.
entries.rewrite: Since he's competing everywhere, he would be able to mention why a VPN could be beneficial.

quote.quote: He competes in different contents making VPN essential. You can say, bro, you can say, since he's campaigning everywhere, you know, he would be able to mention why VPN could be beneficial.

entries.situation: A student submits an email starting with 'Explanation given in the video Time May Not Exist was quite clear and detailed. Never would have thought that in the time-space continuum, the past, present, and future must exist simultaneously', alongside several other emails using the exact same offer with slightly different wording.
entries.student_email: Explanation given in the video 'Time May Not Exist' was quite clear and detailed. Never would have thought that in the time-space continuum, the past, present, and future must exist simultaneously...
entries.points: Cut the opening sentence mentioning the video title and start directly with the intriguing thought, turn it into the subject line ('Does it exist?') and a playful bridge line, and remember that true A/B testing requires testing fundamentally different offer angles rather than rewording the same offer.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Does it exist?

Never would have thought that in the time-space continuum, the past, present, and future must exist simultaneously. You know what also should exist simultaneously? Our brands' partnership with your content...

quote.quote: and I would use, I would use something of this for subject finding, does it exist, does and then, bridge line, you know, what also should exist simultaneously, our friends partnership with your content, boom, and there you go

entries.situation: A student emails a filmmaking creator repeating the word 'pocket' four times, uses the bridge line 'Jokes aside', and writes 'noticed you haven't had any sponsors in your videos in the last six months'.
entries.student_email:
Subject: How you pocket the 4-2 jet?

Hello Jack, your pocket finally feels pocketable now that you've got that DJI 4P. How on earth did you manage to pocket one here in the U.S.? Jokes aside, noticed you haven't had any sponsors in your videos in the last six months. We are reaching out to creators involved in filmmaking to connect them with brands, including [Brand A] and [Brand B], and your content seems like a good fit. Are you interested?
entries.points: Keep wording simple and skimmable within 5–10 seconds rather than repeating wordplay like 'pocket/pocketable', cut weak bridge lines like 'Jokes aside', and say 'in your recent videos' or 'last two videos' instead of 'in the last six months' so you don't insult the creator or sound like a stalker.
entries.rewrite: I've seen no brands in your recent videos. I think it could be a good addition if you have a couple of those, including [Brand A] and [Brand B].

quote.quote: notice, it should be something subtle, right, like, look, I noticed you don't have any sponsors in the last two videos, right, it's like, that's something you can notice, but six months, that means that you went through every single video

entries.situation: A student reaching out to medical niche influencers submits their initial cold email for review.
entries.student_email: Hey [First Name], we love how personal your content is, especially [something], I think we can all relate to those. I saw one of your videos had sponsorship from Headspace, and I'm curious if you'll be open to working with more brands. Looking forward to hearing from you.
entries.points: Do not say 'we love' or relate the creator's video to yourself ('I think we can all relate to those'), as acting like a fan destroys your power dynamics. Use 'I' when referencing watching their video, name two specific brands instead of vaguely offering 'more brands', and never copy-paste the course template verbatim.
entries.rewrite: I saw your content. It's decent, [specific detail]... I saw one of your videos had a sponsorship from Headspace, and I'm curious if you'd be open to working with [Brand A] and [Brand B]. Looking forward to hearing from you.

quote.quote: There's nothing wrong if you say I. I love. I mean, first of all, don't say love. Because this is typical fan, okay? And we are not fans. We are basically guys who want to make money with these guys

entries.situation: A medical influencer replies 'Please only contact once you have an offer' to a generic initial email, and the student drafts a reply explaining their agency and naming target brands.
entries.student_email: Nice to hear from you. At [Agency], we specialize in connecting medical influencers to leading brands, and we plan to start outreach soon to FIGS, [Brand], [Brand]. If you're happy to be included in our group of influencers, let me know, and we can get the ball rolling.
entries.points: Mention the specific target brands (like FIGS or Notion) in the very first email so the influencer doesn't dismiss you as having no offer. In your reply, drop the self-introduction about what your agency specializes in—creators don't care who you are—and finish with a strong CTA offering to send a campaign brief, more details, or a quick call.
entries.rewrite: Should I send more details? Should I give you a brief to check out? Or should we jump on a quick call?

quote.quote: And also, this one, he doesn't care who you are, or they don't care who you are. We at this agency, blah, blah, blah. Trust me. They have multiple emails, and they don't care who you are.

entries.situation: A student pitches a tech creator to a brand, highlighting 200k average views and a 35.2% US audience.
entries.student_email: Subject: A partnership that anchors. Hello [First Name], I recently noticed that [Brand] collaborated with [Influencer]. Seeing that, we have a [Influencer Name] who averages almost 200k views per video, 35.2% US-based audience. Is this something that you'd be interested in?
entries.points: Do not mention the brand's own name when referencing their recent creator collab, and add a professional comment on why that integration was well executed. Never brag about US audience share if it is under 50% (35.2% signals a large Indian/Tier-3 audience); instead, highlight stable views, strong engagement rate (if 5%+), and why the creator's content fits the brand, ending with a strong CTA like 'Should I send more details?'.
entries.rewrite: Hello [First Name], recently saw your collaboration with [Influencer]—great execution on [specific detail]. We have an influencer, [Influencer Name], with stable views and a strong engagement rate, and since his content is all about [topic], I think he would be a great match for [product/angle]. Should I send more details?

quote.quote: Is this something that you've been interested in? So-so, so-so, be more strong, stronger. Especially, especially with brands. Those are people who are receiving a lot of emails. And you should have strong CTA, something like, should I send more details

entries.situation: A student struggling with low response rates from outdoor/hiking brands submits their initial brand pitch.
entries.student_email: Subject: [Brand] x [Influencer]. Hey X, we watched a video on [Brand]'s Featherlight pack, the way it mixes a vest and fastpack is smart. We work with [Influencer Name], a hiking backpack focused YouTuber who has viewers that are passionate about useful outdoor products. Would you be open to launch a campaign with this influencer? Kind regards, P.S. We connected with Y before, but thought that might be more in your lane.
entries.points: Say 'I watched' instead of 'we watched'. Do not compliment the brand's product features like a consumer ('the way it mixes a vest and fastpack is smart' is a 2/10 template swap); instead, compliment the marketing execution of a specific creator sponsorship integration they ran. Cut obvious filler ('has viewers that are passionate about useful outdoor products') in favor of engagement rate, view stability, and viewer comments requesting that product, use 'Should I send more details?' as the CTA, and drop the P.S. internal-referral line.
entries.rewrite: Subject: An idea for you. Hey X, I watched [Influencer]'s last collaboration with you—the way he mentioned [specific brief talking point] landed pretty well. We work with [Influencer Name], who has a strong engagement rate and stable views. In his last video, there were a lot of comments asking about backpacks, which sparked an idea for his next video. Should I send more details? Kind regards

quote.quote: So, what do you should say instead? We work with In Influencer, something good about him, strong engagement rate, stable views, audience, if it's super good, and why he is good. In his last video, a lot of comments about backpack

entries.situation: A student reaching out to an automotive restoration YouTuber submits their cold outreach email and asks if the personalization is good.
entries.student_email: Subject: Quick question: Brand sponsorship for your channel. Hey there, hope you're fantastic. I just watched your latest video and loved your style. The way you broke down the problem step by step and explained how you solved them was brilliant. It felt like I was there with you throughout the process. Quick question, are you open to sponsorships for one of your upcoming videos with a brand that aligns well with your audience? If so, I'd like to have a quick chat, won't take much of your time. Looking forward to your thoughts.
entries.points: Replace the cliché two-part subject line with a specific observation from their video. Cut 'hope you're fantastic', 'loved your style', and 'It felt like I was there with you throughout the process', which sound like an emotional fangirl. Personalization is 0/10 because 'the way you broke down the problem step by step' could apply to any YouTuber in any niche—name the exact car and repair (e.g., removing paint on an old Ford Mustang). Do not repeat 'Quick question' in the body, name specific interested brands instead of 'a brand that aligns well with your audience', and never say 'won't take much of your time'.
entries.rewrite: Subject: Restoring that old Ford Mustang sparked an idea. Hey [First Name], I just watched your video restoring that old Ford Mustang—how you solved the paint issue and removed the paint using [product] was a nice idea. We work with [Brand A] and [Brand B] who are interested in sponsoring an upcoming video. Looking forward to your thoughts.

quote.quote: Personalization, if we have zero, I'm sorry, I'm not roasting you, I'm not roasting your email, would be zero. Why? Because you can send this to every single niche, every single guy on the planet. I just watched your latest video, love your style

entries.situation: A student sends a wordy, self-important cold email to an automotive restoration YouTuber and receives a harsh rejection calling out the 30-second timestamp summary.
entries.student_email: Subject: Sponsorship collaborations. I just watched your latest video, the fuel pump issue. It was very insightful. Realizing the pump's max PSI was way too low for the engine's needs was a great catch. I specialize in developing strategic brand partnerships for premier creators in the automotive restoration space. My goal is to manage the entire process for you to focus on hands-on work that makes your content great. Would you be open to a brief 10-minute chat next week to discuss this? I won't waste your time, I promise. Thanks and regards. [Influencer reply: You do the same goofy thing that every cold email marketer does. A random video, click to a random timestamp, and summarize 30 seconds of footage to make it look like you actually know my content. Good luck on the business, but don't email me again. Try a little harder.]
entries.points: Avoid generic internet/course subject lines like 'Sponsorship collaborations' and keep video observations punchy rather than summarizing 30 seconds of footage. Delete the entire paragraph claiming 'I specialize in developing strategic brand partnerships for premier creators... My goal is to manage the entire process...'—it is unskimmable, overpromises, and reeks of desperation. Never beg for a '10-minute chat' or say 'I won't waste your time, I promise', and sign off with 'Best regards' and just your name instead of 'Thanks and regards' or a bloated signature.
entries.rewrite: The way you diagnosed the fuel pump issue was a nice clutch. We have a partnership with [Brand]—are you interested or not? Would you be open to a quick call? Best regards, [Name]

quote.quote: there's nothing wrong with best regards, it's polite, it's how everybody finish their email and name, when I see email address, when I see website, when I see number, and when I see the slogan, I don't know, my motto is, like, this, that

entries.situation: The same automotive niche student submits another cold outreach and follow-up sequence to creators (Simon and Tanner) using 'hope you're having a productive week', 'for your channel' in the subject line, and repeating the 'manage the entire process' pitch.
entries.student_email: Subject: Partnership inquiry. Hi Simon, just watched your Mudtruck video. Your persistence in diagnosing the ignition issue from the disconnecting solenoid all the way to the faulty wires was impressive. I specialize in developing strategic brand partnerships... [Follow-up:] Subject: Email regarding potential partnership opportunity for your channel. Hi Tanner, hope you're having a productive week. I'm just following up on my email I sent last week. My goal is to help bring relevant brand collaborations to you, managing the entire process so you can focus on content. Would you be open to a 10-minute chat? Thanks and regards.
entries.points: Turn dry mechanical summaries into a quick joke in your opener (e.g., comparing switching a solenoid off and on to how programmers work). Never include 'hope you're doing well', 'hope you're having a productive week', or holiday wishes ('Happy Holidays', 'Happy New Year') in cold outreach or follow-ups. Drop 'Email regarding potential partnership opportunity for your channel' as a subject line, stop begging to 'manage the entire process so you can focus on content', and ask 'Should I send more details?' or 'Should I send a brief?' instead of a 10-minute chat.
entries.rewrite: Hi Simon, how you solved the ignition issue in your Mudtruck video by just switching the disconnecting solenoid was on point—reminds me of how programmers work: turn off, turn on... Should I send more details, or should I send a brief? Best regards, [Name]

quote.quote: How you solved ignition issue with just switching diagnostic solenoid, disconnecting solenoid was on point? Or it reminds me how programmers work. Turn off, turn on. You know, you can crack a joke. I like to crack jokes in initial things.

entries.situation: A student sends a cold email to a tech brand's social media manager referencing a recent 'vibe coding' creator collaboration, using bold text and calling the pitched talent 'one of my YouTubers'.
entries.student_email: Subject: Wanted your take on this Kevin. I came across your recent collaboration with [Influencer] and saw how well his audience responded in the vibe coding space. Given the traction you already saw with [Influencer], a partnership with one of my YouTubers could scale that success to a wider, but still highly relevant community, as [YouTuber]'s audience has a passion for coding and software development. Would you and your team be open to exploring this?
entries.points: Put a comma before the recipient's name in the subject line ('Wanted your take on this, Kevin'). Do not claim you 'saw how well his audience responded' without a case study, and never say 'one of my YouTubers'—say 'creators that we are working with' so the brand knows you don't own them and stays open to Instagram or TikTok deliverables. Remove all bold formatting from initial cold emails (save bold text for highlighting deliverables and prices in offer emails), and say 'you' instead of 'you and your team' with a strong CTA.
entries.rewrite: Subject: Wanted your take on this, Kevin. I came across your recent collaboration with [Influencer]... A partnership with one of the creators that we are working with, [Creator Name], could scale that to a relevant coding and software development audience. Should I send more details?

quote.quote: so don't say my, YouTubers that we are working with, speaking behalf of, and you don't have to say YouTubers, you can say creators, you know, maybe they're interested in his Instagram channel, TikTok page, whatever it is, so it's much, much better

entries.situation: A student submits a direct message / outreach to a brand praising a 'tiny device' and promising 'creators whose audience genuinely trust their recommendation, helping brands cut through the noise'.
entries.student_email: Hi [First Name], noticed that [product] on your page. And that tiny device sure is mighty, let me tell ya. We work with creators whose audience genuinely trust their recommendation, helping brands cut through the noise. Would you be open to exploring how we could help extend [Brand]'s reach through authentic influencer partnerships?
entries.points: Cut colloquial filler like 'let me tell ya' and never overpromise with marketing buzzwords like 'whose audience genuinely trust their recommendation, helping brands cut through the noise' or 'extend reach through authentic influencer partnerships'. Stick to verifiable numbers, facts, and past brand sponsors, and finish with a direct CTA like 'Should I send more details?'.
entries.rewrite: Hi [First Name], we work with [Creator Name], who has worked with [Brand A] and [Brand B] and averages [metrics]. Should I send more details?

quote.quote: Would you be open to exploring? How we could help extend, da-da-da, reach through, authentic influencer partnership. What about this one? See, extend, this one, authentic, still over-promising, okay? Kinda, kinda spammy, kinda scam. So, there's nothing wrong, should I send more details

entries.situation: A student reaching out to luxury watch brands complains about getting no replies after a few days and submits a long first email that includes agency introduction, full creator analytics, pricing, and an offer to 'hold a September slot now'.
entries.student_email: Hi [Brand] team, we are [Agency Name], and we represent [Influencer]. [Long paragraph with full watch-niche metrics, audience demographics, pricing/rates, and: 'If the fit is there, we'll hold a September slot now.']
entries.points: Never put rates, full demographics, links, or an offer to 'hold a September slot now' in your first cold email to a brand, and cut 'We are [Agency Name]' because brands don't care about an unknown agency. Instead, use a 3-email sequence: Email 1 gets a reply; Email 2 shares the creator's channel link, subscribers, average views, engagement rate, and a one-sentence fit explanation; Email 3 provides full demographics and pricing within the creator's fair CPM range.
entries.rewrite: Hi team, [Email 1: short hook and offer to get an answer. Email 2: creator link + two sentences on subscribers, average views, and engagement rate + one sentence on why he fits. Email 3: full demographics and rate within CPM range.]

quote.quote: say subscribers, average views, average engagement rate, actually, two sentences, why he would be good, one sentence, good enough. Third email, you're not pushing, you're basically, they're more comfortable, they say, okay, yeah, he is fit, give us analytics, give us rates

entries.situation: After pitching an expensive fitness creator that was out of a brand's budget, a student follows up to pitch a cheaper creator, sends an Excel sheet of demographics, and quotes $7k—after which the brand ghosts.
entries.student_email: Student: Hello [First Name], I understand things can get busy. I wanted to follow up and see if you'd be open to working with a similar profile to [Creator 1], but at a rate that's much more in line with your budget. I'd be happy to share the profile with you if there's interest. Brand: Sorry about the delay. I went on vacation in August and returned on Monday. Of course, send me another profile you have there. Student: I hope you enjoyed your time off. Just wanted to share [Creator 2]'s profile, who is one of our professional creators. I have attached his profile for you to review. Looking forward to your thoughts. Brand: Hey, thank you. Yes, I can see the Excel attachment, seems a great fit, great demographics, what his rate for us? Student: Rates for [Creator 2] would be $7k. Let me know if you'd be happy to move forward.
entries.points: Use the 'foot in the door' method with new brands by pitching a no-brainer $1k-$5k creator first. When pivoting to another creator, do not mention 'in line with your budget' unless they explicitly gave you a number, specify the platform ('his IG profile' or 'his YouTube channel') rather than just 'his profile', and always state the exact deliverable ('for a 60 to 90 second integration') when quoting a $7k rate. Warm small talk ('I hope you enjoyed your time off') is fine once a prospect is actively conversing with you.
entries.rewrite: Rates for [Creator 2] for a 60 to 90 second integration would be $7k. Let me know if you'd be happy to move forward.

quote.quote: When it comes to foot in the door, it's not just one guy, it's something good and achievable, something that's no brainer offer. What does that mean? Guy who is, let's say, from one to five K, you know, that much.

entries.situation: The same travel niche student showed a second draft with the subject line 'New Year question', one sentence of personalization about Asian vs. European markets, followed by 'I noticed a mix of sponsored content on your recent videos. Are you currently open to additional brand partnerships?'
entries.student_email:
Subject: New Year question

Interesting to see what are markets in Asia that resemble European ones. I noticed a mix of sponsored content on your recent videos. Are you currently open to additional brand partnerships?
entries.points: Use wordplay in the subject line (such as 'New Year, old question'), write at least two sentences of personalization, avoid the repetitive '1-2 sentences + I noticed + generic pitch' formula because Google's spam filters flag predictable patterns, and always name 2 to 3 specific brands so the creator sees tangible value.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: New Year, old question

Interesting to see what are markets in Asia that resemble European ones. [Second sentence of personalization]. Based on your content, we think [Brand 1], [Brand 2], and [Brand 3] would be a good fit. Let me know your thoughts.

quote.quote: New Year question, I would change this, I would be like, New Year, old question, you know, like, wordplay. Interesting to see what are markets in Asia that resemble European ones, one more sentence, you know, at least two sentences

entries.situation: A student in the fitness niche sent a cold email reading: 'Hi, I've been following your content recently, especially your post around the half marathon and the keep moving mindset, the way you show discipline without overcomplicating things really stands out. I also noticed you've been working with brands lately. I wanted to reach out to see if you [are open to] additional collaborations that align with your fitness journey and resonate with your audience. Looking forward to connecting.'
entries.student_email: Hi, I've been following your content recently, especially your post around the half marathon and the keep moving mindset, the way you show discipline without overcomplicating things really stands out. I also noticed you've been working with brands lately. I wanted to reach out to see if you [are open to] additional collaboration that align with your fitness journey and resonate with your audience. Looking forward to connecting.
entries.points: Never use ChatGPT to write personalizations (it only reads titles/descriptions and sounds robotic); instead, watch 30-60 seconds of the most replayed spike on the YouTube timeline and use free Grammarly for grammar checks. Cut filler like 'I also noticed you've been working with brands lately', 'I wanted to reach out', and 'resonate with your audience', write casually like texting a friend, pitch specific brands, and end with a direct CTA like 'Let me know your thoughts' instead of 'Looking forward to connecting'.
entries.rewrite: Keep moving forward is exactly what I do when sending emails. Let's keep moving this offer as well. We have these brands [Brand 1, Brand 2]. What do you think?

quote.quote: Keep moving forward is exactly what I do when sending emails. You know, just freestyle it, but have something that's relatable to him. And then, let's keep moving this offer as well. We have these brands. What do you think?

entries.situation: An Australian student in the travel niche drafted an email with the subject 'Ghost cities, China' and body: 'G'day, caught by your inspirational YouTube journey video, and I'm sure it resonates with so many followers. I hope this is not the end. We noticed that your audience is big on budget travel tips, and this is something our brands really like. We have some brands in mind like [Brand 1] and [Brand 2] that would be a good fit.'
entries.student_email:
Subject: Ghost cities, China

G'day, caught by your inspirational YouTube journey video, and I'm sure it resonates with so many followers. I hope this is not the end. We noticed that your audience is big on budget travel tips, and this is something our brands really like. We have some brands in mind like [Brand 1] and [Brand 2] that would be a good fit.
entries.points: Eliminate all fanboy praise ('inspirational YouTube journey', 'hope this is not the end') and keep a neutral, professional tone. Use 'I' when referring to watching their video and 'we' for the agency, never claim 'our brands' when you don't have them, and say you 'think they might be a good fit' rather than stating they 'would be a good fit'.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Ghost cities, China

Walking that ancient building is like on a different planet, and your backpack is holding better than my future. Speaking of future, there are a couple of brands like [Brand 1] and [Brand 2] that we think might be a good fit for you. Are you interested? What do you think?

quote.quote: No fanboy talk, okay? None of those. Yoricka, you're inspirational, and then now, your last video was this, this, but we, we keep, like, neutral. We are not super inspirational, and then fanboy, we are not insulting them. You can stay professional.

entries.situation: The travel student drafted a fifth email about a New Zealand camping video talking about his own solo camping and Christmas cookies, then saying: 'The landscape of Valley New Zealand is breathtaking. It must be worth every second. I was just curious why there was no sponsor for the video, though. We have few brands like [Brand 1] and [Brand 2] in mind for your next video if you're open to paid partnerships. They are searching for adventure travel content with diverse audience. We believe you'll be a good fit.'
entries.student_email: It was cold, but the purest water you ever sipped. Baked food from sister and from mom will be something, Christmas cookie, will miss on my next solo camping. The landscape of Valley New Zealand is breathtaking. It must be worth every second. I was just curious why there was no sponsor for the video, though. We have few brands like [Brand 1] and [Brand 2] in mind for your next video if you're open to paid partnerships. They are searching for adventure travel content with diverse audience. We believe you'll be a good fit.
entries.points: Cut the irrelevant personal stories at the beginning and the generic fluff at the end ('They are searching for adventure travel content with diverse audience. We believe you'll be a good fit.'); start directly with the observation about the New Zealand landscape, the curiosity hook about no sponsor, and the specific brands in mind.
entries.rewrite: The landscape of Valley New Zealand is breathtaking. It must be worth every second. I was just curious why there was no sponsor for the video, though. We have a few brands like [Brand 1] and [Brand 2] in mind for your next video if you're open to paid partnerships.

quote.quote: They are searching for adventures, travel content. It's fluff. I can smell it. With diverse, yeah, audience. See, I knew it. We believe you'll be a good fit. My brother, fluff. Don't do this.

entries.situation: A student told a creator 'you haven't partnered with any brands' and claimed 'we work with many brands'. When the creator replied that they already have a management team but welcomed incoming deals as a middleman, the student backtracked ('We only send over incoming brand opportunities when there's a best fit') and twice demanded their audience analytics without naming any brands, causing the creator to ghost.
entries.student_email:
Initial email: Subject: The mechanic buddy
Was having a super good time with those tiny wires. Just saw your video and noticed that they are very fun to ride. Speaking of your video, I also noticed you haven't partnered with any brands for it. We work with many brands that would fit your channel. Let me know if you are open.

Follow-up 1: Circling back on this, we have many brands [that] fit your content nicely, are you open partnering with brands? Kind regards

Creator reply: Hey, I already have a management team I work with for my [channel]. You're welcome to send things my way as a middleman, if you wish, as incoming deals, but at this time, I'm not interested in partnering with another agency for brand deals.

Student reply: Thanks for the clarification. We only send over incoming brand opportunities when there's a best fit. To help us send you a right fit, share your audience analytics, age range and top countries.

Student follow-up: Just following up on my last email. We can send you incoming deals as a middleman, but to do that, we'll need your audience [age range] and top countries, send over so we can move forward.
entries.points: Never insult a creator by pointing out they have no sponsors, and never overpromise that you 'work with many brands'. When a managed creator invites you to bring incoming deals as a middleman, acknowledge their management, name the specific brands you have in mind first, and only ask for their audience analytics if they like those brands; if they ghost after your reply, send a soft close asking whether to circle back in Q2 with 'either way, let me know'.
entries.rewrite:
Reply to creator: Thanks for clarifying. Good to know you're in good hands. We have in mind these brands [Brand 1, Brand 2]. What do you think? If you find them a good fit, please send your audience so we can start cooking.

Re-engagement follow-up: It seems like timing is off, should I circle back in Q2? Either way, let me know.

quote.quote: it seems like timing is off, should I circle back in Q2, either way, let me know, you know, what I, what I found with this, either way, let me know, it's working good, because they will, they will, answer to that email

entries.situation: A student in the DIY niche wrote a good subject line ('An extra window') and casual personalization about making a hole in his wall while removing wallpaper, but pitched 'more long-term partnerships being brought to you, giving you more time to focus on your content creation', and followed up with 'if the opportunity I mentioned previously is something that you would be interested in, do let me know'.
entries.student_email:
Subject: An extra window

Hi lads, The first time I removed wallpaper, I also ended up with a hole in my wall. It's reassuring to find out I'm not the only one. I noticed that your last video was sponsored by Shopify. I'm curious if you would be interested in more long-term [partnerships] being brought to you, giving you more time to focus on your content creation. Let me know what you think.

Follow-up: Just following up on my last email, if the opportunity I mentioned previously is something that you would be interested in, do let me know, and we can discuss further.
entries.points: Keep the casual DIY personalization and subject line, but stop overpromising 'long-term partnerships' or using filler about 'giving you more time to focus on your content creation'. In follow-ups, eliminate weak 'if you would be interested' phrasing and state directly that the opportunities might be a good fit.
entries.rewrite: Follow-up: Just following up on my last email. These opportunities might be a good fit for you. Give me your thoughts.

quote.quote: If it's something that you will be interested in, do let me know, and we can discuss further, no, no, no, no, no, if, no, no. Like, these opportunities might be a good fit for you. Give me your thoughts, that's better.

entries.situation: The DIY student submitted three more outreach emails ('Everything will be printed' about a 3D printer exhaust fan, 'A nice demonstration' about a Bosch sander water glass test, and one about hidden key storage) that transitioned abruptly with 'I saw your latest video and thought...', included a ':)' smiley face, and had lengthy follow-ups.
entries.student_email:
Email 1: Subject: Everything will be printed
I thought that printing the exhaust fan for the ventilation to the printer was a smart move. It's nice to see how useful 3D printers can be on a regular day-to-day basis. I saw your latest video and thought you might be interested in...
Follow-up: Just following up on my last email. If the opportunity I mentioned interests you, do let me know and I will send over more details.

Email 2: Subject: A nice demonstration
The simple user-friendly water glass test on the Bosch sanders was a nice touch. I kind of forgot about it, but I think I will have to pull the trigger on it. As the video was sponsored by [Brand], I wanted to see if you'd be interested...

Email 3: Hidden key storage you built for the entryway shelf was a very nice feature. I'd like to think that I would be patient enough to wait for my keys every :) ...
entries.points: Instead of breaking the flow with 'I saw your latest video and thought...', bridge directly from any keyword in your personalization ('Speaking of smart moves...', 'Speaking of printing, we can print you some brand deals...'). Remove smiley faces/emojis from cold emails, and keep follow-ups much shorter than the initial email.
entries.rewrite: I thought that printing the exhaust fan for the ventilation to the printer was a smart move. It's nice to see how useful 3D printers can be on a regular day-to-day basis. What about these brands [Brand 1, Brand 2]? They would be useful as well. What do you think?

quote.quote: no smiling, no smiling, I don't have anything against them, but no, and this is too long for follow-up, this length is good, but this is too much, you know, he has to read your follow-up, and he has to read your, your first email

entries.situation: An experienced student in the holistic wellness niche who had closed several brand deals asked if he could skip personalization when pitching brand offers in a new thread to previously unresponsive creators, and showed both his initial email (written in advanced English and signed 'CMO, [Agency]') and his new thread ('Subject: A lot has changed. [Agency] closed several creator partnerships in Q4 25 with brands... As we move into Q1, we are beginning outreach with larger wellness brands...').
entries.student_email:
Initial email: Hey [Name], Recently saw [your post] explaining what to look for when buying olive oil. I'm glad to see you offer such insightful advice in the caption in simple terms, which can be so helpful. P.S. Olive oil on... I'm building a curated group of creators to pitch to wellness and gut health brands such as [Brand] for their campaigns. Your blend of diet hacks, clean eating tips, and relatable storytelling would be an excellent addition. Would you be open to partnership with similar brands?
Regards,
[First Name]
CMO, [Agency]

New thread: Subject: A lot has changed
Hi [First Name], [Agency] closed several creator partnerships in Q4 '25 with brands [Brand 1] and [Brand 2]. As we move into Q1, we are beginning outreach with larger wellness brands including [Brand 3] and [Brand 4], and are selectively bringing on a few creators. I wanted to see if you're open to exploring partnerships...
entries.points: You can skip personalization when you have concrete brand offers, though personalization is still king. Keep writing at a 4th-grade reading level, sign off with just 'Regards, [First name]' (no 'CMO' or agency name), and mention the specific product/campaign you recently closed rather than bragging 'A lot has changed' or saying 'we are beginning outreach'. If skipping personalization, use an eye-catching subject line like 'This might be good' and state directly that you are helping specific brands find creators.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: This might be good

Hey [First Name], We are helping brands such as [Brand 1], [Brand 2], and [Brand 3] actively find creators. Based on your content, we believe you might be a good fit. If you are interested, I can send you more details.

Regards,
[First Name]

quote.quote: If you have brands, you mentioned your recent campaign. You know, we recently worked on, I don't know, T-shirt, anything. Like, talk about product. It's okay to mention to your influencer. Give him something specific so he knows, like, uh-huh, this guy makes sense.

entries.situation: A student submitted two cold emails across two different niches (fitness and study productivity), both using the subject line 'Quick question [Name]', generic fill-in-the-blank personalizations ('your video about moving like an assassin made the idea of functional training feel like a fun game' and 'your tip on using 50-10 rule to study for a long time was very insightful'), and commercial-sounding vague offers.
entries.student_email:
Email 1: Subject: Quick question Adam
Hello Adam, your video about moving like an assassin made the idea of functional training feels like a fun game. Are you ready for partnership that would help to draw out the best performance from you and your audience?

Email 2: Subject: Quick question Sam
Hello Sam, your tip on using 50-10 rule to study for a long time was very insightful. I'm reaching out to see if you're open to selective partnerships with productivity and focus brands for students that fit naturally with your content.
entries.points: Stick to a single niche so you can pitch all your creators to the same brand. Replace 'Quick question [Name]' with a curiosity subject line ('Is this new way?'), avoid Mad-Libs style personalizations where only a couple of words change (instead explain *why* a tip worked when you tried it), and bridge naturally into naming specific brands.
entries.rewrite:
Email 1: Subject: Is this new way?
Hello Adam, [specific detail from video]. Speaking of fun, we have a couple of brands in mind. Based on your content, you might be a fit. What do you think?

Email 2: Hello Sam, I tried the 50-10 rule to study and it felt like the shortest time of study. Speaking of easy, this might be easy as well—we have a couple of brands in mind...

quote.quote: Look, your video about moving like assassin, you can switch it to shoulder, I don't know, super sack. Made the idea of functional training feel like a fun game. See, I made ultimate personalization, just switching your one word.

entries.situation: An Instagram design creator replied after three follow-ups saying they are open to new partnerships from March onwards and invited the student to send opportunities over. The student replied: 'I got you. Let's get things ready to go for March. We are looking into [Brand 1], [Brand 2], [Brand 3] and more. It would be great if we could understand your audience a little more so we have...'
entries.student_email:
Initial email: Hi, really respect your straight to the point style and execution, especially the series. So I'll get straight to the point too. Are you interested in incorporating some brands into your reels?

Creator reply: Hey, thanks for reaching out. Apologies for slowly replying. I'm open to new partnerships from March onwards. If you have any that you feel may be a good fit for me, then please feel free to send them my way and we can discuss further. All the best.

Student reply: I got you. Let's get things ready to go for March. We are looking into [Brand 1], [Brand 2], [Brand 3] and more. It would be great if we could understand your audience a little more so we have...
entries.points: In the initial email, drop 'really respect your' and state the observation neutrally. In the reply to the creator, mention 2 brands instead of 3 (so it doesn't look like a menu), replace the passive 'It would be great if we could understand your audience a little more' with a direct request to send their audience analytics to prepare for March, and ask for 'analytics' rather than a 'media kit' since smaller creators often don't have media kits.
entries.rewrite:
Initial email: Straight to the point style is never outdated, especially in the series. So I'll get straight to the point too. Are you interested in incorporating some brands into your reels?

Reply: I got you. Let's get things ready to go for March. We have [Brand 1] and [Brand 2], and some others as well. But to get your best fit and be fully prepared until March, send us your audience analytics so we have a better understanding.

quote.quote: We have these brands, and some other as well. But to get your best fit, and be fully prepared, until March, send us your audience, so we have better understanding. Easy. Media Kit or some analytics.

entries.situation: A brand contact introduces the student to a colleague who handles short-form creators, and the student replies to the new rep by re-attaching the creator roster link directly.
entries.student_email: thanks for the intro. Great to connect with you. As I was mentioning to the other rep, we Just wrapped up a couple of Instagram campaigns. would love to explore some fits with the brands. I've attached a roster we've made for you here. Let me know if you have any questions. ... I've attached a roster we made for you here. All these guys are great. I have audiences that perform well, some on YouTube too. Let me know if you're interested in that buff and have a great weekend.
entries.points: When a brand contact refers or CCs you to another representative at the company, re-attach the creator roster link in your reply so the new rep does not have to search back through the email chain.

quote.quote: So he reiterates the same thing, right? You want to just make it easy and post that same link. You want to not have the other rep have to go back in the CC chain and do all this extra stuff.

entries.situation: A student follows up with a brand representative after sending a creator roster by briefly recapping the offer and re-sharing the creator info instead of just writing 'bumping this'.
entries.student_email: Hope you had a great weekend. Wanted to follow up on the. Intro. We have a couple guys on Instagram would be a great fit, more info on them.
entries.points: Never send a bare 'just bumping this' follow-up that forces a busy brand rep to scroll back through the thread to find your roster; lightly recap the offer and re-include the relevant details while staying prompt without appearing overly needy.

quote.quote: You just want to make it easy as possible for them. Like just with each follow up, you kind of want to just like lightly recap everything. Just very simply, just like just like what these emails are showing. Just a very simple recap.

entries.situation: A brand rep replies that they do not currently have capacity to onboard anyone new, and the student acknowledges it politely and follows up at the start of the next month offering to refine the creator list.
entries.student_email: likewise, appreciate the update, looking forward to it. I'll circle back with you to check in with things that have opened up. Enjoy your week as well. ... wants to circle back on this as we head into the new month. Looking forward to hearing your thoughts once you've had a chance to review. Let me know how we could refine this list a bit more as to what you're looking for, or if there's anything else you need from our end.
entries.points: Do not treat a brand rep saying they lack capacity to onboard creators right now as a final 'no'; reply politely, check back at the start of the new month, and offer to refine your creator roster in case the real objection was that they did not like your initial creators.

quote.quote: So like the brother did here in the email, you follow up, but you give more solutions. That's the key here. He's giving. So that when the, when the brand re-engages, they understand that this person is in alignment with their goals.

entries.situation: A student whose email was acting up reached out to a creator via Instagram DM with heavy flattery ('I've honestly become quite a fan'), prompting the creator to question the student's track record.
entries.student_email: I've honestly become quite a fan. I love your humor and editing style, man, your ability to keep up and entertain. ... I notice you currently do not have any ongoing sponsorships, and I see that's something that can definitely be changed. Are you open to partnerships?
entries.points: Avoid reaching out via Instagram DM instead of email, and do not shower creators with fan-like praise in your first message; putting them on a pedestal inflates their ego and makes them interrogate your status instead of you vetting them.
entries.rewrite: hey, cool content, we could get you lined up with brands, interested or not.

quote.quote: Okay, already, it's like, you're giving too much. You're giving too much to this guy, you know, you're giving too much, because now, he's like, okay, you put him on this pedestal.

entries.situation: When the creator asked who the student had worked with, the student over-explained that he was taught by mentors and asked if lacking past creator experience would be a deal breaker.
entries.student_email: hey, thanks for getting back, great question, I've worked with influencer marketing in general for a while while the company of mentors was taught me. ... but I would like to ask if I can't provide substantial previous experiences with other creators, would that be a deal breaker for you? ... completely understood that it's being built as we speak. would like to add, since we recently
entries.points: Never over-explain your lack of deals or ask an influencer if your lack of experience is a deal breaker, which hands over all power; instead, flip the frame by asking for their audience demographics and rates to see if they qualify for your brands.
entries.rewrite: absolutely, man, firstly, can you share your audience demographics and rates? We'd like to see if there's a fit for the brands that we have in mind.

quote.quote: he gives them like this kind of ultimatum thing, but I would like to ask if I can't provide substantial previous experiences with other creators, would that be a deal breaker for you? It's too much, you're giving, you're giving literally all the power

entries.situation: A student shows a cold email sent to a creator who has sponsors in roughly every second video.
entries.student_email: Hey, influencer, I was watching your friend name video. Almost thought for a second that it was you drifting the streets of Japan. Looks wild. I've noticed you've been sponsored by XYZ brand recently. I actually have a few brands in mind that would be a good fit for your content. Would you be interested in your partnership?
entries.points: Cut the generic opening line ('I was watching your [brand] video') and filler reaction ('Looks wild'), start directly with the specific observation ('Almost thought for a second that it was you drifting the streets of Japan') and explain why, target the creator's pain point of inconsistent sponsorships, and end simply with 'Would you be interested?'.
entries.rewrite: Almost thought for a second that it was you drifting the streets of Japan... hey, I saw some inconsistency in your brand's partnerships. Let's fill those gaps. Would you be interested?

quote.quote: What I would change, maybe, is I would focus on pain. In his case, not a lot of brands. You said, like, second, every video-ish, he has sponsors. like, hey, I saw some inconsistency in your brand's partnerships. Let's fill those gaps.

entries.situation: A student shows a cold email to a tech creator that asks if they are currently taking on partnerships or a discovery call.
entries.student_email: High influencer. Got to say the product completes the new setup. Expensive, but nothing with new brand name, right? Overspace that content would be a great fit for the upcoming campaigns I'm working on. Are you currently talking on taking on...
entries.points: Never pitch or ask for a discovery call in the first cold email—its only goal is to get a reply. Do not passively ask if the creator is 'currently taking on' partnerships; instead, use a direct CTA tied to your offer, such as asking if they want to work with those brands or hear more.
entries.rewrite: Would you like to work with these brands? Do you want to hear more?

quote.quote: Guys, no discovery call. Okay? Obviously, we say no pitch in first email, right? Never. In cold email, we don't do pitch. That's just asking a couple of information just to get him a reply. That's the whole purpose of your first email.

entries.situation: A student shows a series of templated initial outreach emails to consumer tech brands that introduce himself by name, claim exclusive representation of an 'excited' creator, attach a media kit or list age/location demographics, and follow up with 'Just checking to see if you read my last email.'
entries.student_email: Subject: For this email, I believe my influencer is perfect match for this brand. Body: Hi, someone. Ammar's here. I know inboxes get chaotic, so I'll cut the chase. I represent a tech influencer who is excited for a partnership with you. Influencer name, Mr. Beast. Here's his media kit. Let me know if you think they are a good fit for coming campaigns. / Hi there, Ammar here. I represent a few tech influencers who are available for brand partnerships. Their content style and 25-34 years old audience across... Would you be open to reviewing them? / Follow-up: Just checking to see if you read my last email.
entries.points: Remove self-introductions ('Ammar here') since your name is in the sender field, stop claiming 'I represent' (which implies exclusivity) or that the creator is 'excited' to partner (which sounds desperate), and avoid copy-pasted templates that trigger spam filters. Use light brand personalization ('saw collaboration, some amazing stuff'), build a curiosity-loop offer around the creator's video style rather than dumping demographics, and replace the rude follow-up 'Just checking to see if you read my last email' with 'Hey, I'm following up in case you missed my email'.
entries.rewrite: Saw collaboration, some amazing stuff... In his video, he is doing [video style], it could be beneficial... Follow-up: Hey, I'm following up in case you missed my email...

quote.quote: Second one. I represent the tech influencer. That means you are representing him exclusively. Don't do this. Who is excited for partnership? That means he is asking you to reach out for them. Right? Another problem. So, inshallah, don't do this.

entries.situation: A student in the home cooking/kitchenware niche shows brand outreach emails and follow-ups that pitch the same single creator using subscriber counts and engagement rates, bulky personalizations, and repeated demands for a 10-minute call.
entries.student_email: Hey Daniel, Chef Keller's line was designed so that anyone can cook like a chef. She's a Houston baker with 1 million YouTube subscribers, 7.1% engagement rate, well above typical, her audience exact home cooking... Let me know if a quick call still works this coming week. / Hey Kate, Saw your comments on this one, making creator-led YouTube integration an evergreen part of the marketing mix with the reach and view through numbers you reported. It's clearly working... Let's have a quick 10 minutes call to discuss details.
entries.points: Stop dumping subscriber counts, engagement rates, and media kits into brand outreach. Instead, mention a couple of creators in the niche, describe what they do in their videos, and reference successful past brand partnerships. Keep personalization concise, vary your follow-ups so you don't get flagged as spam, and offer a call only as a soft option ('Would you like to hop on a call?') rather than pressuring brands for a 10-minute meeting.
entries.rewrite: We work with a couple of creators from this niche. One of them is [Creator Name]. In most of his videos, this is what he is doing. He had successful partnerships with these brands. I thought we can achieve the same results with you. Would you like to hop on a call?

quote.quote: Let's have a quick 10 minutes call to discuss details. No, no, no, no. Call is just like an option. Hey, would you like to hop on call? No, be like 10 minutes, we can book this, then. It's too much, especially for brands.

entries.situation: A student shows a fitness influencer outreach email with the subject line 'Why consistency beats freak genetics?' that says 'We are putting together a list of fitness influencers for brands such as X and Y and other similar companies. I think your content would be a great fit. What do you think? Can I ask you something?'
entries.student_email: Subject: Why consistency beats freight genetics? Body: A seven years natural body transformation is impressive. I've struggled to gain weight myself, so I genuinely respect your dedication. We are putting together a list of fitness influencers for brands such as this and that and other similar companies. I think your content would be a great fit. What do you think? Can I ask you something?
entries.points: Shorten the subject line so it sparks curiosity without revealing everything (e.g., 'Why was it?' or 'Is that the case?'). Reword the offer to 'for brands and similar companies such as X and Y' so you don't overpromise those exact brands. Never tell an influencer they are a 'great fit' because excessive praise makes them inflate their prices—say 'good fit' or 'strong fit' instead—and drop redundant double questions at the end.
entries.rewrite: Subject: Why was it? / Is that the case? Body: ... We are putting together a list of fitness influencers for brands and similar companies such as [Brand 1] and [Brand 2]. I think your content would be a good fit.

quote.quote: We are putting together a list of fitness influencers for brands such as this and that and other similar companies. I would say brands and similar companies such as this and this. So kind of let them know it's similar companies

entries.situation: A student pitching history-gaming brands shows five emails that use 'To whom this may concern' on generic website emails, repeat the exact same offer paragraph across messages, use full names in references, and open with 'We messaged Maria...' when asking for a referral.
entries.student_email: Subject: More mediocre players. Body: Hi, Christian Reesoft said that releasing on Playroom gives access to mediocre players. We can help be more specific and reach history fans. We represent influencers who host large audience in North America and Europe, the comments express how they love their take on a game. / Subject: Congratulations on your promotion. Body: We're reaching out as we saw your sponsorship with [Creator]. We work with history influencers who host large American audience enamored with their content. Comments are full of excitement with their take on history. / Body: To whom this may concern. Your video with [Creator] is what I'm concerned about. I'm looking for a person in charge of YouTube sponsorships. / Subject: Is it going to erupt? Body: Hi, your collaboration with [Creator] is what I'm concerned with. We want the right people to view so Battlefield can erupt. We work with history influencers whose audience thirst for tactical combat games... let's convert this audience into your customers. / Subject: Try to message Maria, can you help? Body: Hi [Name], We messaged Maria... Because we have something explosive. We represent history influencer who hosts large...
entries.points: Never use 'To whom this may concern'—use 'Hi there' or 'Hey there', and skip personalization entirely on generic website emails by going straight to your offer. In personal emails, use first names only, vary your offer copy across emails so Gmail's spam filters don't flag your templates, pitch how the creator's video style (transitions, jokes) drives players to the game, use 'I' instead of 'we', and put referral mentions ('I messaged Maria') at the end of the email so the prospect reads your offer first.
entries.rewrite: For promotion email: Hey [Name], congrats on a big day, hopefully there's more to come. / For generic website email: Hey there, we work with influencers...

quote.quote: To whom this may concern. Yeah, it sounds like Shakespeare. Your video with this one is what I'm concerned about. I'm looking for a person in charge of YouTube sponsorships. You can just say this. Hey, there. We work with influencers.

entries.situation: A student shows the brand outreach email in the home and lifestyle niche that earned him a reply.
entries.student_email: I hope you are doing well. I came across IG Reel where he showed how he uses the [product] integration. It got me wondering whether you're open to working with more influencers in the home and lifestyle space. We work with a small curated group of creators whose audience align really well with... entries.points: Remove 'I hope you are doing well' as it is unnecessary filler in a cold email. Consider stopping the email right after the question ('It got me wondering whether you're open to working with more influencers in the home and lifestyle space?') or cutting the templated 'small curated group of creators' paragraph so the email isn't bulky.
entries.rewrite: I came across IG Reel where he showed how he uses the [product] integration. It got me wondering whether you're open to working with more influencers in the home and lifestyle space?

quote.quote: Guys, I would try. Maybe don't listen to me. But I would try just this. This one equals I'm not a bot. But this one is I don't want to pitch anything. I'm just asking.

entries.situation: An influencer liked the second brand the student pitched and asked 'Do you have a budget in mind?', to which the student refused to give a budget until seeing audience analytics, and after the influencer walked away, the student sent a high rough estimate ($8k-$15k) and got a thumbs-up emoji.
entries.student_email: not right now. I'd like to ask you first some details regarding your audience to see if there is a fit, and then we can discuss your rates. ... okay, sure, maybe I'll come back to you when we have a budget structure that suits you. For the record, an agency handles the entire budget of the campaign. The single allocation of a budget for each channel depends. And so the quality of its audience ... but a rough estimate, considering your views, would be in the range of 8K to 15K.
entries.points: Never refuse to share a budget when an interested influencer asks for one, and do not throw out an inflated estimate without seeing analytics. Instead, hook them by quoting a budget range slightly below their typical price while saying you could go higher depending on channel quality/fit, and then ask them to send their analytics (e.g., to verify US audience share for a specific campaign month).
entries.rewrite: Budget is between 4K to 9K. We could do more depending on the channel quality or depending on fit. ... Hey, we are thinking about integration in August, for example. Our target audience right now is the U.S. market. So to make sure that you have this, can you please send us your analytics?

quote.quote: We could do more depending on like the channel quality or depending on fit or anything. Okay, so whatever. So when you have them hooked, when you have them hooked, you ask for the immediate. You ask for the analytic family.

entries.situation: A student sends a first outreach email to a Korean food creator pointing out they only had one HexClad partnership in their last 10 videos and asking if they are against working with food brands.

entries.situation: A brand asks for audience breakdown, typical deliverables, historical performance, fee range, and engagement structure in writing. The student replies starting with 'Thanks for this,' lists robotic bullet points, says 'We don't offer whitelisting yet,' and asks 'What's your main goal?'
entries.student_email: Thanks for this. Find here... age, segment, 60 seconds, 90 seconds. We don't offer whitelisting yet. What's your main goal? Awareness, traffic, ROI, fee range, engagement structure.
entries.points: Write with polite, natural flow ('Thanks for getting back to me'), attach analytics screenshots as requested, propose a specific creative angle (such as integrating the product naturally into the creator's existing series), and ask about their goals or invite them to a discovery call before dumping prices.
entries.rewrite: Thanks for getting back to me. Sure, attaching the analytics as requested, also attaching the screenshots if needed. Before I share the deliverables, I wanted to hear more about the goals—how about we jump on a quick call? This influencer actually has a series that is doing well, and we're thinking of including your product in a natural way in this series so we provide the best value possible.

quote.quote: Also, I wanted to, or did you say before the, I share the deliverables, I wanted to hear more about the goals. How about we jump on a quick call? And you just do a discovery call with them, why not?

entries.situation: Student submits a second cold email to an AI creator summarizing their entire video on the future of user interfaces.

[One short sentence on the future of user interfaces without 'I watched' or 'the way']. We are no engineers, but one thing we can engineer is opportunity. [Offer + CTA]

entries.situation: Student submits a third cold email to a gaming/tech creator about PS6 being delayed until 2029.

entries.situation: Student submits a fourth cold email to a tech creator with a long personalization paragraph and 'Are you currently open to partnerships?' as the CTA.

Subject: AI sleeps

Hey, I watched the latest... Your comparison on how it is changing the structure and how you turn it locally in a high-end consumer device demonstrates how it is taking the industry by storm... Are you currently open to partnerships?

entries.situation: Student pitches a German professor with '50%+ North American/European audience' and an end-of-month sponsorship slot in the first email to a brand.

Spot on about ToolHive vs Joe... We are building out our technical creators roster for some upcoming Q3 campaigns. Let me know if you're open to sponsorships.

Hey [Name], making pelau rice in your latest multi-cooker was a solid move. The product features seem like a natural fit. Why I'm reaching out: we work with food creators... I think his content would be a strong fit to feature a product. We also work with other creators who have a strong audience in the UK and Ireland.

entries.situation: Student emails two representatives at the same fitness brand with the exact same copy asking 'If your campaign has room, I have creators like Zahim, Mohamed...'
entries.student_email:
Subject: Enhancing performance / Extra running exposure

Saw the post about [Athlete] smashing that SkyRace event. That [Product] and 95g of carbs were a big contributor. If your campaign has room, I have creators like Zahim and Mohamed, most being in Canada, averaging [X] views per video, I would love to discuss. I'm not sure whether you handle marketing, so I thought I'd reach out to you as well.
entries.points: Never beg for budget with passive phrases like 'If your campaign has room', pitch the creator's content style and brand alignment with confidence, and never send identical copy to two people at the same company—use different personalizations and heavy Spintax on the offer to avoid spam filters.

We work with [Creator], whose content is all about [style/topic], which would make sense for your brand, and he averages strong views. [CTA] (Use a completely different personalization and Spintax offer for the second rep at the same company.)

entries.situation: Student submits two AI-generated cold emails to AI automation creators featuring bolded video titles in quotation marks ('I recently watched the video "..."') and stiff summary paragraphs.
