entries.situation: An influencer stopped responding for over a week after a brand gave pricing, and when the brand asked what the bottleneck was, the student drafted a reply inventing personal life issues for the influencer and asking permission to share other creators.
entries.student_email: Sam's schedule has been, uh, a bit uncertain lately. Uh, he has been having different, unexpected things coming up, outside of content making, so I don't want to hold things up for you. Um, I'd be happy to share other, a couple of other brands. But, you know, other, creators.
entries.points: Never deceive a brand by making up excuses about an influencer's personal schedule; once you verify the creator is unresponsive, honestly tell the brand that the creator is currently unresponsive and immediately pitch a specific replacement influencer with a strong view stat instead of asking permission to send options.
entries.rewrite: the influencer is not responsive at the moment, however, I have this influencer that pulls these numbers, last month he generated 500,000 views... Last month he did X with X brand. Would you be putting to, you know, swifting away from this influencer to this one?

entries.situation: The same student sends a second cold email to a tech creator who built a backpack-sized gaming PC, using the subject line 'Influencer, quick idea for you' and copy-pasting the same offer line.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Influencer, quick idea for you.

Building a gaming PC that fits in a backpack, as you showed in your last video could be a game changer for students, haha. On a more serious note, I've noticed that you haven't partnered with a brand in that video, are you currently open to brand deals?
entries.points: Do not use 'quick idea for you' as a subject line because creators have big egos and assume you are pitching them a video concept. Keep the subject line curiosity-driven and write a slightly longer personalization rather than one sentence plus a copy-pasted template.
entries.rewrite: Subject: Jack, what do you think about this? / Jack, let me know your thoughts / Jack, thoughts?

quote.quote: Both keep the same as we said before, I don't know, Jack, what do you think about this, let me know your thoughts, or Jack thoughts, good enough, something like that.

entries.situation: A student sends an initial outreach email to a DIY woodworking creator saying 'If I'm not wrong, I see that you have been sponsored only two times in the past six months. Are you open to partnerships?'
entries.student_email: Hey [First Name], saw your last video, and [detail] is really nice. Appreciate the fact of making it affordable for everyone with common materials. If I'm not wrong, I see that you have been sponsored only two times in the past six months. Are you open to partnerships?
entries.points: Never say 'If I'm not wrong' (which sounds insecure) and do not bluntly tell a creator they have only been sponsored twice in six months, as it reads like an insult. Instead, use Aikido to frame the observation as a question—such as asking whether having only two partnerships in six months is intentional or if they are looking for brand partners.
entries.rewrite: I saw you had two partnerships in the last six months—is that intentional, or are you looking for brands?

quote.quote: took me three seconds to see you had... Your two times partnerships in like six months. Be like, hey, is that intentional? Or you're looking for friends. That's much better.

entries.situation: The DIY woodworking creator's talent agency replied asking 'How would you like to see your brand highlighted in [Creator]'s content?', and the student responded 'Actually, I don't represent a brand. I'm thinking... I aim to get [Creator] to work with brands in line with his content...'
entries.student_email: Hi [Name], Thanks for response. Actually, I don't represent a brand. I'm thinking... I aim to get [Creator] to work with brands in line with his content, more into long-term approach. To do so, it would be great to get more information about his audience. A media kit would be ideal, but the age and country breakdown will do the job if you don't have one. 🙂 If you have any questions, feel free to ask.
entries.points: When an agency asks about 'your brand,' they mean the brand client you are working with, not a company you own. Never say 'Actually, I don't represent a brand' or 'I'm thinking,' and do not pitch a talent agency on your 'mission' to find long-term brand deals (which is already their job). Position yourself as an expert agency currently assembling a creator list for specific brands.
entries.rewrite: At the moment, we are making a list of influencers for [Brands]—are you interested?

quote.quote: Instead of saying, I don't represent the brand, and I'm thinking, you know, all of the stuff I've learned in the course, right? Because this is what is going to make you special, like a problem solver, business owner, a G, right?

entries.situation: A student sends an initial outreach email to a car detailing/restoration channel starting with 'My agency helps auto detail/restore creators into paid brand deals. You keep creating masterpiece, we do the ops... I'm going to reach out to brands like Rustoleum, Spraymax 2K, etc.'
entries.student_email: Hello [First Name], my agency helps auto detail / restore creators into paid brand deals. You keep creating masterpiece, we do the ops. I like how clean you guys made the Chevy. I'm starting a campaign and saw you guys didn't have a sponsorship on your videos. I'm going to reach out to brands like Rustoleum, Spraymax 2K, etc. Do you want to be part of it?
entries.points: Never start a cold email with 'My agency helps...' because it screams scam; always lead with personalization ('show me you know me'). Do not flatter creators like a fan ('creating masterpiece'), avoid saying 'I like' (describe a specific scene from the video instead), always use 'we' instead of 'I', and never say 'I'm going to reach out to brands' (which exposes you have no brands)—state that you are currently onboarding creators for brands.
entries.rewrite: I saw your video cleaning the Chevy and how you took care of the seats—it was a nice hack. We are onboarding influencers for brands like Rustoleum and Spraymax 2K. Do you want to be part of it?

quote.quote: even though you're only one guy plus JGPT, it's OK to see we. Why? Because agency, organization, you know, you're not just one person who do that.

entries.situation: The car restoration creator replied asking what deliverables are expected, how payment works, and the timeline. The student answered 'We usually set up brand deals with shoutouts, reels, or full video spots. Payment is either flat fee per video or based on views. And campaign starts in about two, four weeks. Can you send me a media kit to get brands?'
entries.student_email: Hi, thanks for getting back. We usually set up brand deals with shoutouts, reels, or full video spots. Payment is either flat fee per video or based on views. And campaign starts in about two, four weeks. Can you send me a media kit to get brands?
entries.points: Use proper YouTube terminology ('integrations' or 'dedicated videos', not 'shoutouts or full video spots'). Do not confuse deal structure (flat fee, CPM, commission, hybrid) with payment terms (upfront, 50% upfront, or Net 30—paid within 30 days of posting). Finally, when a creator asks multiple questions, answer them first and ask 'What do you think about it?' before asking for their audience analytics, and never say 'to get brands'.
entries.rewrite: Answer their questions regarding integrations, Net 30 payment terms, and timeline, then end with: 'What do you think about it?' before asking for audience analytics in the next message.

quote.quote: What I usually do, I answer those questions. Be like, what do you think about it? Give them some more space. Give them some more space. They like, yes, no, blah, blah, blah. And then you have power to ask for media kit, audience analytics

entries.situation: A student (Muatasim) sends an initial cold email to an automotive rebuilding creator with the subject 'Question for Chris' and body 'First name, just saw your last video rebuilding, and man, that titanium exhaust sound and looks fire. Also, noticed your last video was sponsored by [Brand], curious if you're open to more?'
entries.student_email:
Subject: Question for Chris

[First Name], just saw your last video rebuilding, and man, that titanium exhaust sound and looks fire. Also, noticed your last video was sponsored by [Brand], curious if you're open to more?
entries.points: Put a line break after the greeting, avoid Gen Z slang like 'looks fire' in favor of clear descriptive English, and stop using the exact school template ('Also noticed your last video was sponsored by X, curious if you're open to more?') or school follow-up templates verbatim so you stand out from other students. Tweak the subject line to 'Chris, question for you' or 'Chris, your thoughts on this'.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Chris, question for you / Chris, your thoughts on this / Chris, what do you think?

[First Name],

The exhaust you installed on that car changed the look and sound—now it looks and sounds amazing.

quote.quote: Here we have huge, huge copywriting skills issue. That titanium exhaust sounds and looks fire. What? I mean, yeah, it looks good and everything. It looks fire, bro. None. We are not using, That type of language, Gen Z language, right?

entries.situation: A talent agency asked 'Do you have a link or briefing for us to the specific product?' The student replied admitting they were in 'early stages of collaboration, so no final brand or brief is locked in yet.' When the agency refused to give pricing beforehand, the student replied saying he asked 'just so I can avoid any issues of coming back with an insulting offer, and because brands need target demographics to be met, it will be difficult for us to secure a collaboration unless you're open to share.'
entries.student_email:
Reply 1: Hi, appreciate you asking. We're currently in the early stages of collaboration, so no final brand or brief is locked in yet. At this point, I'm gathering interest from a selected group of creators whose content aligns with the types of campaigns we are forecasting, to see if the audience aligns with the brands.

Reply 2: Thanks for getting back to me. Understand you don't give out any pricing. I usually ask for it just so I can avoid any issues of coming back with an insulting offer, and because brands need target demographics to be met, it will be difficult for us to secure a collaboration unless you're open to share.
entries.points: Never tell an agency that you have no final brand or brief locked in yet—that is over-honest and destroys your authority. Simply state that you are putting together a creator list for brands and ask for their details. Furthermore, never say 'I' instead of 'we', never call your own potential offer an 'insulting offer' (be confident in your offers), and do not beg for rates; if they already sent their media kit/analytics, you can pitch them to brands without their rate and get the rate once a brand is interested.
entries.rewrite: We are getting a list of influencers together for [Brands]—does this sound interesting to you? If you give us more details, we can share something with you.

quote.quote: Guys, if they don't give you prices and you have analytics, analytics? That's good. That's good. You don't need, of course you need. You can still pitch guys without rates, you can get them while you are negotiating with brands

entries.situation: Student submits cold email #1 to a brand in the tennis/hydration niche.
entries.student_email: Subject: [Influencer] X [Brand] / Hi [Name], Hope you are doing great. I've noticed [Brand] significantly increasing its social media visibility, especially enjoyed... Brand digital presence growth through creative partnerships such as with [Creator]. I represent similar tennis influencers who attract large audience committed to improving their game. For example, I strongly believe [Creator] from the UK would be an excellent fit, showcase rackets and other products to his audience and tennis enthusiasts. Would you be open to expanding your collaboration? If so, I would be happy...
entries.points: Cut pleasantries like 'Hope you are doing great,' remove generic AI fluff about 'increasing social media visibility' and 'strongly believing' a creator is a fit, and use a curiosity subject line with a concise discovery pitch.
entries.rewrite: Subject: Jack, thoughts? / Hey Jack, I checked your LinkedIn and saw you got promoted—all the best. To get momentum in your new position, we have a couple of creators that could work really well with your brand. Let me know what you think. (Or shorter approach: Hey Jack, I was wondering, would you be the best person to talk about collaborations or potential partnerships? If yes, let me know.)

quote.quote: Hi, who... You are doing great. It's a first mistake. If you are doing brand outreach, especially brand outreach. Why? Making your email longer for no reason. And it's kind of, you know, fluff. So cut the chase.

entries.situation: Student submits cold email #2 to a hydration brand using the subject line 'Tennis X Hydration' and pitching European creators averaging 50k views.
entries.student_email: Subject: Tennis X Hydration / I've noticed [Brand] gaining traction on social media thanks to your partnership with common creators such as [Creator 1] and [Creator 2]. I was curious if you were open to expanding your creator collaboration. I'm currently working with similar European influencers who average over 50k views per reel... If interested, I'll be happy to send over his analytics.
entries.points: Never use '[Creator Niche] X [Brand Niche]' as a subject line because it is confusing. When pitching smaller creators (e.g., 50k average views), flip the script by highlighting their specific high engagement rate (e.g., 7.39%), and end with a stronger CTA than 'if interested, I'll be happy to send over his analytics.'
entries.rewrite: We work with a similar European micro-creator—he might have 50,000 views on average, but his audience is strongly engaged with a high engagement rate of 7.39%.

quote.quote: he might have 50k thousand, 50,000 views in average, but his audience is strongly engaged, with high engagement rate, and give the number, 7.39, for example, right, and that way, you can really show the value in your offer

entries.situation: Student submits cold email #3 to a tennis brand with the subject line 'New faces for [Brand]' and claims the creator's audience 'places great importance on their equipment.'
entries.student_email: Subject: New faces for [Brand] / It's great to see [Brand] increasing its social media presence... [Creator] has a highly engaged audience who places great importance on their equipment. To name a couple, I believe [Creator 1] from France and [Creator 2] from the UK would be an excellent fit to showcase rackets to their viewers. Are you the right person to discuss with? If not, who can I contact at [Brand]?
entries.points: Avoid 'New faces for [Brand]' because 'new face' implies a brand ambassador rather than an influencer integration. Do not make up generic claims about what a creator's audience cares about as if you know them personally, explain why the creators are a fit, and avoid repeating the brand's name at the end.
entries.rewrite: If you're not the right person, sorry to bother you—would you like to connect me with someone?

quote.quote: You have no idea who they are. You're talking about audience as you know him, like he plays great importance of their equipment. Like you spoke with those guys. Don't do this. It's flat and it's easily noticeable, right?

entries.situation: Student submits an initial outreach email to a history and geopolitics YouTuber.
entries.student_email: Subject: Your sourcing on that Siberian intervention / Hey [Name], the way the Czechoslovak Legion made its way through Siberia... We specialize in the historical and geopolitical niche, and we target well-researched documentary and long-form video creators and their fan bases for brand deals. Would you be interested in getting more brand deals?
entries.points: The curiosity subject line about their video sourcing and the personalized opener are good, but cut the wordy explanation about your agency's niche and replace the generic survey question ('getting more brand deals?') with a direct CTA naming example brands.
entries.rewrite: Would you be interested in working with brands such as [Brand A] and [Brand B]? Our main focus is to bring more creators who do [A] to brands like [X, Y, Z]—are you interested?

quote.quote: We specialized, yeah, and I know why. In historical geopolitical image, and we target well-researched documents and long-form videos creators. And their fan bases for brand deals, this is fluff, okay, kind of too long to be honest

entries.situation: Student submits outreach email #1 to a productivity influencer referencing a macOS Finder toolbar trick.
entries.student_email: Subject: You could do that / Hi [Name], didn't even know that dragging the mail app directly into Finder toolbar to drop files was possible, that's a very helpful trick. Now let me help you find your next sponsor / brand association...
entries.points: Great short curiosity subject line (just add an exclamation mark), specific video personalization, and smooth transition into the sponsorship offer.

quote.quote: you could do that, nice, this is good, I would do it, just add an exclamation mark, hi, didn't even know that dragging the mail app directly into Finder toolbar to drop files was possible, that's a very helpful trick, good

entries.situation: Student submits outreach email #2 to a productivity influencer referencing 'wabi-sabi' and ending with 'Should I go into more details?'
entries.student_email: Subject: Is it worth it? / Hello [Name], the wabi-sabi point you mentioned really hit, good perspective to have on life. Speaking of things, we're building a roster of creators to match with brands for future campaigns, and your content stood out. Should I go into more details?
entries.points: Good email overall, but add one specific detail explaining why the 'wabi-sabi' point resonated, and specify 'details on how that will work' in the CTA so the creator does not ask for campaign details you do not have yet.
entries.rewrite: Should I go into more details on how that will work?

quote.quote: If you mention details, they will ask for details and you don't have them. So be careful. Maybe, you know, details about campaigns or should I mention more or should I go into more details? How that will work?

entries.situation: Student submits outreach email #3 to a productivity influencer with the subject 'New series, new brands' and names specific brands alongside the CTA 'Worth a quick look?'
entries.student_email: Subject: New series, new brands. / Hello [Name], really interesting to see Mark's series on changing your life. Hope there's more content like that in the future. It's great to see that level of detail—made me think brands like [Brand A] and [Brand B] would be a natural fit for you. Worth a quick look?
entries.points: Avoid putting 'brands' in the subject line since creators are tired of it; use a curiosity hook instead. Also avoid pairing specific brand names with 'Worth a quick look?' because it implies you already have live offers from those exact brands, causing creators to demand budgets, timelines, and talking points.
entries.rewrite: Subject: We saw the new series, but are you ready for this? / ...It's great to see that level of detail—made me think brands in this space would be a natural fit for you.

quote.quote: New series, new brands. Nice. Maybe I wouldn't mention brands because they are kind of tired. Those. I would mention something else. Maybe new series. Okay, we saw new series, but are you ready for this? Maybe something like that.

entries.situation: Student submits outreach emails #4 and #5 to productivity influencers using creative transitions from an ice bath scene and a broken microphone mid-sentence.
entries.student_email: Email 4 - Subject: It was that cold. / Hey [Name], seeing you get in the ice bath was scary. That did not look like a good experience. On the contrary, we can give you a good and smooth experience by... No random deals, only brands that make sense. // Email 5 - Subject: Is it worth that? / Rest in peace, your mic. It was unexpected when it died mid-sentence. Let's help you buy a new one. We are on the lookout for creators to pair...
entries.points: Clever, natural bridges from specific video moments (the scary ice bath and the mic dying mid-sentence) directly into the agency's value proposition—just keep the CTA slightly less risky and scale up volume.

quote.quote: Hey, seeing you get in the ice bath was scary. That did not look like a good experience. On the contrary, we can give you a good and smooth experience by nice. No random deals with brands that make sense. Good, good.

entries.situation: Student submits cold email #1 to an AI software brand pitching three AI creators with '@handles' and 'a consistent 60k to 140k views.'
entries.student_email: Subject: Had you in mind for this one / Hi [Name], Using a real workflow to show Seedance 4K in action was a smart move — it makes the tool feel native rather than a product demo. We work with @[Creator1], @[Creator2], @[Creator3], three AI specialists pulling a consistent 60k to 140k views per reel. They have worked with similar brands before, and we believe they'd be a great fit for [Brand]. Would it make sense to explore something together?
entries.points: Remove AI tells like em-dashes, drop the '@' symbol before creator channel names, replace wide view ranges ('60k to 140k') with either a single combined average or 'up to 140,000 views per reel,' omit the brand's name in the closing line, and tighten the CTA to 'Should we explore this?'
entries.rewrite: We work with [Channel 1], [Channel 2], and [Channel 3], three AI specialists pulling up to 140,000 views per reel. They have worked with similar brands before—should we explore this?

quote.quote: It takes the tool, feel native rather than a productive demo. I don't trust it since it's M-Dash here, to be honest. We work with. At, at, at. You don't need to. To do at, you just mention names

entries.situation: Student submits follow-up #1 to a football brand leading with ' averages 150k views on Instagram with 5% engagement rate, which aligns naturally with [Brand]'s goals of gaining trust with Gen Z. Would you be open to seeing his media kit?'
entries.student_email: Hi [Name], [Creator] averages 150k views on Instagram with 5% engagement rate, which aligns naturally with [Brand]'s goals of gaining trust with Gen Z. Would you be open to seeing his media kit?
entries.points: Flip the sentence order so the brand alignment comes first and the hard numbers (150k views, 5% engagement rate) come at the end of the sentence where they stick. Cut generic 'gaining trust with Gen Z' fluff, and make the media kit CTA punchy or playful.
entries.rewrite: Hi [Name], [Creator] aligns naturally with [Brand] and averages 150k views on Instagram with a 5% engagement rate. I packed his media kit—sending it to you right now (or: by the time you're reading this email, his media kit is ready—should I send it over?).

quote.quote: Would you be open to seeing his media kit? I will make a joke about it, like, I packed his media kit, I'm sending it to you right now, maybe something like this.

entries.situation: Student submits cold email #3 to a football brand asking if the recipient is the right person to contact regarding partnerships and mentioning creators who specialize in backyard trick shots.
entries.student_email: I was wondering if you are the right person to contact regarding partnerships. We work with a couple of football creators who specialize in backyard trick shots...
entries.points: This right-person discovery email with a specific creator angle ('backyard trick shots') is solid—just trim it slightly to make it even shorter.

quote.quote: I was wondering if you are the right person to contact regarding partnerships. We work with a couple of football creators who specialize backyard trick shots. Da, da, da, da, okay, this is not bad. I'll just make it a bit shorter.

entries.situation: A student submits a third cold email draft with the subject line 'Not sure if you are open to this', good personalization about college friendships, a repeated line about videos not being sponsored, 'I have a few brands in mind', and a CTA asking for insights.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Not sure if you are open to this

Hey [First name],

The advice you share in your videos are very relatable and genuine, especially your points about how easy it is to fall into party lifestyle through certain friendships in college. I noticed that most of your videos aren't sponsored. Is that something you might be open to exploring? I have a few brands in mind. If this sounds like something you'd consider, feel free to send over your insights.

Best regards,
entries.points: The subject line, specific personalization, and 'We have a few brands in mind' offer are good, but stop repeating the exact same 'I noticed that most of your videos aren't sponsored' line across emails or spam filters will catch you. Strip out the request for insights in the first email—use the initial email strictly for discovery and move analytics or availability questions to the second or third email.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Not sure if you are open to this

Hey [First name],

The advice you share in your videos are very relatable and genuine, especially your points about how easy it is to fall into party lifestyle through certain friendships in college. We have a few brands in mind. Would you be open to partnerships?

Best regards,
[Name]

quote.quote: Next email, it's all about analytics and stuff, okay? Or if a guy is a bit stingy, replace this move with an extra move, okay? Be like, okay, let me move analytics here. This is, let me ask availability.

entries.situation: A student emails a goalkeeper creator ('I hope the session went well and you made some amazing saves... I have some brands in mind... let me know if you're interested'). When the creator replies 'Sure, let me know, what do you got?', the student ignores the question and replies asking for audience age, nationality, engagement rate, past brands, and rates.
entries.student_email:
Initial Email:
Hey [First name], I hope the session went well and you made some amazing saves. I'm currently looking for goalkeeper influencers for some brand collaborations. I have some brands in mind that I want to reach out on your behalf. But before that, let me know if you're interested.

Creator Reply:
Sure, let me know, what do you got?

Student Reply:
Great to hear back from you. To move forward, could you give me some info on your audience first? Can you send over details like age, nationality, and engagement rate? Also what brands have you worked with and could you also tell me your rates?
regards
entries.points: Make the initial personalization more specific than 'amazing saves' (which applies to every goalkeeper). More importantly, when a creator asks 'what do you got?', answer their question first by naming a few relevant brands instead of blindly pasting a script demanding analytics and rates. Never ask for metrics you can find yourself (like average views or engagement rate), and ask only one question per email.
entries.rewrite: Thanks, great to hear back from you. Since your content is based on [topic], we have brands such as [Brand 1], [Brand 2], and [Brand 3]. Let me know what you think.

quote.quote: Thanks, great to hear back from you. And then, explain what you have. For you, and since your content is based about this and that, we have brands such as this, this, this, and this. Let me know what you think.

entries.situation: A student in the filmmaking niche opens with '[Name] from [Agency Name]. Love how you get to travel to beautiful places showcasing smartphone videography. It obviously makes for great images, but made me wonder about the audio side. We focus on mobile filming and aim to work with wireless microphone and lighting gear brands... Would you be interested in a collab where you review audio and lighting gear?'
entries.student_email:
Subject: What about audio and lighting?

Hey [First name], [Name] from [Agency]. Love how you get to travel to beautiful places showcasing smartphone videography. It obviously makes for great images, but made me wonder about the audio side. We focus on mobile filming and aim to work with wireless microphone and lighting gear brands. I believe you could be a good fit for them. Would you be interested in a collab where you review audio and lighting gear?
entries.points: Drop 'from [Agency Name]' so you don't invite extra questions, and stop using fanboy words like 'love' ('more love, less money'). Make the transition from your observation to the offer smooth ('Speaking of audio, we have a couple of brands in that space...'), and do not box yourself into tiny sub-niche products like wireless mics and lighting gear when creators can promote broad non-niche brands too.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: What about audio and lighting?

Hey [First name],

The way you are doing videography with a smartphone proves that you don't need cameras, which made me wonder about the audio side. Speaking of audio, we have a couple of brands in that space that would be a good fit for you. Let me know.

quote.quote: If you say this, the audio side, speaking of audio, we have a couple of brands in that space that would be this and that good fit for you. Let me know. Make it nice

entries.situation: A student in the combat sports niche sends an HTML-formatted email with heart emojis, saying 'I've been following your content for a while now, and I love what you are doing. I don't want to waste your time, so I'll go straight to the point of my email. Sponsorship or sparring? Let me know because I can do both... Now that you've chosen sponsorship, shoot me a reply... PS: don't beat me up 😢'.
entries.student_email:
I've been following your content for a while now, and I love what are you doing ❤️. I don't want to waste your time ❤️, so I'll go straight to the point of my email. Sponsorship or sparring? Let me know because I can do both. Just so you know, [weight class joke]... Now that you've chosen sponsorship, shoot me a reply to this email to get things going, and then we can explore some appropriate options for you. I look forward to hearing from you.

Best regards,
[Name + website/HTML signature]
PS: don't beat me up 😢
entries.points: Strip out HTML formatting, websites, and heavy signatures that trigger spam filters. Never use fanboy language ('I love what you are doing'), emojis, cringe jokes ('Sponsorship or sparring?', 'PS don't beat me up'), or low-status apologies like 'I don't want to waste your time'—your offer is valuable, so position yourself with authority and use a straightforward personalization, offer, and CTA.
entries.rewrite:
Your recent video about [upper hook or spinning kick] was informative. Are you open to partnerships? Let me know.

Best regards,
[Name]

quote.quote: I don't want to waste your time, we don't say that, never. Why? Because our offer is too good, he is wasting our time looking for sponsors and stuff. If you position yourself as something that's not worth it

entries.situation: After the brand countered at $3,500 for a dedicated video due to low US audience percentage and the first creator declined, the student pitched two smaller replacement creators for dedicated videos ($1,600 and $2,600) and pitched the original creator for an integration ($2,500).
entries.student_email: Hi, Fulan has declined this proposal. However, [Creator 2] can have the video published in early December. We have attached his audience demographics and the proposed rate for a dedicated video is 1,600. Also, Bulan is open to a dedicated video at a rate of 2,600. We have also attached his audience demographics. Regarding Fulan, would you be open to an integration at a proposed rate of 2,500?
entries.points: Pivoting immediately with two cheaper replacement creators who can meet the brand's early December timeline, pitching the original creator for a cheaper integration, and using 'the proposed rate' instead of 'his rate' are all strong moves. However, the email repeats 'we have attached his audience demographics and proposed rate' and should be formatted more cleanly using spacing or bullet points.
entries.rewrite: I've got these two guys, [links to channels], this is the price, and I'm going to attach both the analytics for you.

quote.quote: So we mentioned earlier, don't say the guy, this is his price, this is a bit better, the proposed rate, this is a bit better, there's no like deception or anything like that in there, the proposed rate for a dedicated video is 1,600

entries.situation: A brand responded to the student's $7,000 three-creator bundle with an eager, lengthy email countering at $6,000 plus 20% affiliate commission and asking for earliest publication timelines, and the student simply replied with the timelines.
entries.student_email: The confirmed timelines are below: mid-November, 10-16, and start production of November. Let me know your thoughts, and we can share them.
entries.points: When a brand sends a long, polite email begging to close at their counteroffer ($6,000 instead of $7,000), you hold the leverage. Never just accept their lower price flatly and hand over the timelines—that surrenders your power dynamics (and here the brand ended up dropping one of the three creators over timing). Always frame accepting a lower counteroffer as a one-time favor so the brand owes you goodwill and expects to pay the original full rate on future upsells.
entries.rewrite: Look, usually we wouldn't do it for this, but because this is our first time / we value our partnership with you, we'll do this just for you this time, and for future collaborations we'll do it at the original price. The confirmed timelines are below...

quote.quote: so you go, look, we don't usually do this, but because, let's say you were working for them for a long time, you go, you know, we value your partnership with you, and we've worked with you for long, we'll do this just for you

entries.situation: A student reads out a draft email to upsell the same creator to a brand after a high-ROAS first integration.
entries.student_email: Hey, we have an upcoming slot, end of January, would love to have you guys on the channel again. Let me know if this is something you'll be hoping to explore.
entries.points: Strengthen the upsell email by referencing the successful first collaboration, including the topic of the upcoming video, and pitching a 3-to-6 video bundle instead of just a single slot since the creator already proved profitable for them.
entries.rewrite: Include that we had a successful collaboration, include the topic of the upcoming video, offer a 3 to 6 video bundle deal instead of one slot, and optionally mention: also we have a couple of other guys that you might be interested in.

quote.quote: To be honest, I would not limit myself to one, maybe offer like three, six bundle deal, it's much better, because they did good.

entries.situation: A brand rejected the pitched creator saying they were moving forward with another agency that offered the same creator closer to their budget, and Kamil ignored that statement and immediately pitched two replacement creators.
entries.student_email: I'm attaching both media kits. ... Same formats, 1.6, I'll share a quick brief, I'll set a timer to get a video out fast, let know your thoughts.
entries.points: Do not ignore a brand's claim that another agency offered the same creator for cheaper; ask curious follow-up questions about what price and deliverables the other agency offered so you can gather market intelligence and sound conversational.
entries.rewrite: What does that mean exactly? I'm just curious how much they offered him, or the prices and what are the deliverables.

quote.quote: like, okay, what does that mean exactly? You know, I'm just interested. I'm just curious how much, you know, they offered him. Or the prices and what are the deliverables. And just get a sense of what other agencies are doing.

entries.situation: A brand pushed back that $1,800 worked out to a $30 CPM unless paired with a 70k view guarantee and suggested a prorated structure; the student countered with a hybrid structure ($1.5k base with a 40k/56k view guarantee plus $30 CPM) and firmly walked away when the brand kept lowballing.
entries.student_email: We can do a hybrid structure 1.5 with 40K and 30 CPM from the case. ... I understand it's different from what you're looking for, but please let me know if anything changes on your side.
entries.points: Countering a brand's prorated/view-guarantee pushback with a hybrid structure (lower base plus view threshold and CPM) is good, and when a difficult brand chronically lowballs every creator, stand firm on your maximum offer and be willing to pass.

quote.quote: And don't have high expectations from this brand, to be honest. Yeah, I'm good at the call. Do you have any other questions? I think you've done a good job, to be honest.

entries.situation: When influencers replied asking 'What do you have in mind?', the student told them he was planning to reach out to certain brands on their behalf and asked them to send their media kit, causing the influencers to ghost him.
entries.student_email: oh, we have these influencers in mind, so I stated the influencer, I mean this brand in mind, we're planning to reach out to this brand, and then I asked that [send me your media kit].
entries.points: Never tell an influencer that you are planning to do outreach to brands for them or reply to 'What do you have in mind?' by asking for a media kit, and avoid people-pleasing ChatGPT phrasing; instead, act like the brand and ask directly for their deliverable rates.
entries.rewrite: Hey, we're actually looking for 60 to 90 second integrations, please share the rates with me. Also, are you open to a dedicated video?

quote.quote: Like, just pretend you're the brand, bro, like, hey, yeah, give me your rates, like this, none of your business, wow. How I'm going to do things. I'm not going to tell you that.

entries.situation: The talent manager ignored the student's first request for analytics and replied guardedly asking if the student was going through another agency/platform or brand direct, and said the creator doesn't want supplements. The student replied thanking him, saying 'noted', and asking for audience analytics a second time.
entries.student_email: Thanks for coming back, noted on NordVPN and supplements, reach out directly to brands, not through [agency/platform], to make sure we only bring relevant opportunities, does Mike have audience analytics we could look at, that will help align the right campaigns for this channel
entries.points: Do not say 'thanks for coming back' or 'noted' when a manager is being dismissive, and do not robotically repeat a request for audience analytics that they just ignored. Address their skepticism directly by stating you reach out directly to brands and asking if they only work through their existing platform, which flips the power dynamics and gets them to justify themselves.
entries.rewrite: We reach out directly to brands when we think there's a fit. Is that something you are not interested in, or do you only work with brands through [agency/platform]?

quote.quote: And you say, thanks for coming back, no, you need to flip it, need to bring the power dynamics your way, like, hey, we reach out directly to brands, directly, not even noted on the supplements

entries.situation: Billy sent a very long, eager reply detailing his September availability and how he uses DJI drones. The student replied thanking him for mentioning DJI drones, asking for his rates for a 60-second integration and a dedicated video, and saying 'We can definitely do something epic with a DJI sponsor.'
entries.student_email: Hello, Bill, thanks for mentioning your use of the DJI drones, that would definitely help our case. What are your rates for a 60 second integration and a dedicated YouTube video? We can definitely do something epic with a DJI sponsor, I'm curious to know...
entries.points: When an influencer writes a long, needy reply, do not give away your power dynamics by thanking them for rambling or saying 'we can definitely do something epic with a DJI sponsor.' Keep a high-status frame where you are evaluating whether their rates make sense first so they fear quoting too high. However, asking for rates on two specific deliverables (a 60-second integration—or specifying pre-roll/mid-roll—and a dedicated video) is very effective because it signals volume and professionalism.
entries.rewrite: Hello Bill, DJI drones would be a good fit, but first, what are your rates for a 60-second integration and a dedicated YouTube video?

quote.quote: 60 seconds and dedicated. This is very good. And I think, uh, coach Kushten was mentioning this a lot on the fact that you mentioning two things like, hey, 60 second integration, very precise 60 seconds.

entries.situation: Billy quoted $4,000–$6,000 for an integration (despite averaging 50k views), and the student tried to negotiate him down to $1,000 by saying 'that's something the brands like to see, consistency... at least 30% from the US, UK, Europe... yours is only around 20 to 25%... it would be hard to sell with the rates you provide. If we can adjust the rates to 1k, it would be easier to get something booked. How would you like to proceed?'
entries.student_email: Hey, thanks for getting back to me with your rates, I understand that the audience's geographic changes based on where the video is recorded, but that's something the brands like to see, consistency, at least 30% from the US, UK, Europe. And also, from what I can see, yours is only around 20 to 25% at the moment. It would be hard to sell with the rates you provide. If we can adjust the rates to 1k for 1 video, it would be easier to get something booked. How would you like to proceed?
entries.points: Never frame yourself as a weak middleman by saying 'the brands like to see', 'it would be hard to sell', or 'it would be easier to get something booked'—always say 'we need to see' and 'so we can confirm internally.' Do not insult the creator by pointing out their 20–25% audience stat; just state your 30–50% requirement and your $1k counteroffer so they connect the dots themselves. Finally, replace 'How would you like to proceed?' with 'What do you think?' so you remain in control of the process.
entries.rewrite: We understand that the audience's geography changes based on where the video is recorded, but consistency in the audience is something we need to see. We were expecting 30 to 50% from the US, UK, and Europe; however, we can make it work if we adjust the rate to $1k so we can confirm internally and see if we can get something done for the summer. What do you think?

quote.quote: you should never say, hey, the brand likes to this, the brand wants this, brand. Don't make them feel like you're a middleman. Here, you should have said, but that's something, that consistency in the audience is something we need to see.

entries.situation: A brand replied to cold outreach with a short note asking the student to send the creator over with 6 bullet points of information (geography, demographics, gender, average views, rate, past samples). The student responded with a massive email describing the creator's entrepreneurship content and how the fit works alongside the bullet points.
entries.student_email: Thanks for getting back to me, our creator is... he covers topics like entrepreneurship, buying businesses, building companies, lessons from fake business, and real world CEO insight, essentially a place where he shares candid, experience driven content for business owners. Here is a link for more details... [6 bullet points]... the way I see this fit... Looking forward to hearing from you.
entries.points: Match the email length and tone of the brand. When a brand sends a brief message asking for 6 specific bullet points, do not write long paragraphs over-explaining the creator's content and why they fit—that signals you are an inexperienced newbie and kills their interest. Send a one-line intro, the exact bullet points requested (adding 'Content: entrepreneurship, business operator' as a short bullet if needed), and 'Looking forward to hearing from you.'
entries.rewrite:
Here is the link to his channel and some additional details, as requested:
[6 bullet points]
Looking forward to hearing from you.

quote.quote: Match the email size of the brand. Allahumma bariq. Allahumma bariq. Bro, the, the brand sends you like, a few words, and some bullet points, and your email is huge, huge.

entries.situation: The influencer agreed to $5k for the first video depending on the product and asked which brand it would be before the student had secured a brand.

entries.situation: After the student quoted $2k for a 60-second integration, the brand rejected the pitch saying their 20 CPM cap was too far below his asking rate. The student invited them to share their offer anyway ($800) and countered at $1,200 by explaining tech niche CPMs (25-40 CPM), ultimately closing a 2-video bundle for $2k plus 15% commission.

Okay, 1,200, let me know your thoughts
entries.points: When a brand says your creator is too expensive for their CPM cap, don't walk away; keep a warm, confident tone, invite them to share their best offer, and justify a counteroffer using niche-specific CPM benchmarks to turn a 'no' into a bundle deal.

entries.situation: A brand expressed concern that booking an influencer with no prior sponsorship examples could be risky. The student replied to reframe being one of the creator's first sponsors as a benefit and quoted $4k while offering backup discounts, Shorts, or Reels if it underperformed.

For the 60 integration, we're asking for K. Okay. In case something goes wrong, we can always give some discounts or offer something else in package, shorts, reels, etc.
entries.points: The student used strong Aikido by turning a lack of past sponsorships into a positive (leaving a stronger impression on an untapped, loyal audience) and de-risking the $4k offer with backup deliverables like Shorts, Reels, or a free newsletter slot.

entries.situation: After the student quoted $4k, a stingy brand countered at $2.5k with a 100k view guarantee within 45 days. The student stepped down firmly to $3.3k because of the view guarantee, and when the brand said $2.8k was their absolute maximum, the student accepted $2.8k only without the view guarantee.
entries.student_email: I spoke with my influencer, and we do care about the relationship the most... since it's a bundle deal, and you're looking for a long term, when we can lower the price, since you're asking for a view guarantee, the best we can do is 3.3k. ... We can accept 2.8k... but without new guarantee. If that's acceptable, then we have a deal.
entries.points: The student maintained strong power dynamics by refusing to cave from $4k to $2.5k, stepping down gradually to $3.3k due to the view guarantee, and only accepting the brand's $2.8k ceiling by removing the view guarantee entirely—even if the creator would have agreed to it.

entries.situation: A student submits an initial cold outreach email sent to a tech/AI YouTuber named Andrew referencing a Fitbit tennis heart-rate bit and asking if he is open to working with more brands.

entries.situation: The motorsport student shows additional brand outreach drafts to contacts named Justin, Georgia, and Jack using nearly identical templates pitching a restoration/mechanic creator.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Thoughts on that? / An idea for your next campaign / Quick one for you, Jack

entries.situation: A student submits a productivity/tech brand outreach sequence with the subject line '[Brand] X [Agency]', praising the engineering of a hybrid phone mount, offering three unnamed creators, and putting a tailored content concept in the second follow-up.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Norvipian X Miskeen Agency

Hey, Brandi. The engineering on the new hybrid mount looks incredible. Turning a simple phone mount into a full cinematic rig that holds an SSD and mic is a serious flex. Believe we can add to that. We work with creators within the tech space that are already creating content around products similar to yours. We actually have three creators in mind that would work really well with the direction you are going. Would now be a good time for you to send over the list?

Follow-up 1: Hey, Brandy, dropping a quick note here in case you've been tied up. Let me know if you want to look at those three creators.

Follow-up 2: We thought out a quick content concept tailored specifically for the new hybrid mount. The idea is zero to cinematography, visually demonstrating how quick to pair it...
entries.points: Never use '[Brand] X [Your Agency]' as a cold email subject line because prospects do not know or care who your agency is and will block you. Keep personalization short and marketing-focused rather than praising product engineering like a customer. Include creator names or a specific integration concept in the initial email (such as how a high-energy creator will showcase a product mid-video) rather than waiting until the second follow-up when it is already too late, and use a direct CTA instead of asking 'Would now be a good time?'.
entries.rewrite: Should I send? / Hey, I'm sending the list right now. What do you say?

quote.quote: Second follow up. We thought out a quick content concept, Taylor, specifically for the new hybrid mount. Yes, but it's kind of too early or too late. Because, no, I did, I said no to your creators and you're offering me ideas.

entries.situation: A student submits a first cold email to a tech/gaming creator commenting on their black-and-white setup, asking if they are open to more partnerships 'like that', and ending with two closing lines.

entries.points: Avoid generic personalization that applies to anyone, keep the tone professional rather than joking, do not ask if they want sponsors 'like that' (since the past sponsor may have paid poorly) and instead name a few example brands, avoid excessive blank lines between every sentence, drop redundant closing lines like 'Looking forward to hearing back' in cold outreach, and proofread carefully for missing words.
entries.rewrite: Can I share more details if it's something you'll be open to?

Can you share a quick snapshot of your audience breakdown? Brands usually ask for this information when they want to work with creator.
entries.points: Do not rush into asking for both audience demographics and rates immediately—ask one question or ask about their monthly integration schedule; drop the word 'strong' from 'strong potential fit' to maintain power dynamics; and remove patronizing explanations teaching creators why brands want analytics, using a brief reason that isn't copied verbatim from the course.

entries.points: Avoid robotic ChatGPT phrasing and over-explaining your internal review process; simply thank the creator for sending their analytics and rates and let them know you will follow up with more details in a couple of weeks.

entries.situation: A student sends a cold email to a videography influencer (which landed in spam) with the subject line 'Partnership opportunity', starting with a lowercase letter, calling themselves a 'big fan' who 'loved' the Gen Z video, and saying 'I couldn't help but notice that you didn't get any sponsors on that particular video'.

big fan of the content. I especially love your recent video on Gen Z. It's really interesting seeing how the future generation is navigating the industry. I couldn't help but notice that you didn't get any sponsors on that particular video.
entries.points: Capitalize the start of sentences properly, drop 'Partnership opportunity' as a subject line, stop acting like an emotional fan ('big fan', 'loved'), and never use dramatic phrasing like 'I couldn't help but notice you didn't get any sponsors' because it insults the creator's ego.

entries.situation: A student submits their first cold outreach email to a tech/PC desktop setup brand praising a previous YouTube sponsorship and pitching a creator for the upcoming holiday season.

entries.situation: A student pitches a 3D printing brand, praising their Red Dot Design award twice, telling the brand what their ideal demographic is based on Facebook ads, and forgetting a line break before the P.S.
entries.student_email: Hey [First Name], I was impressed to come across the new award-winning [Brand/Product]. We thought our huge 3D printing audience aged 18 to 34 would be an excellent fit for you after seeing your campaign reach on Facebook for the age bracket. I represent a YouTube influencer with an engaged following that we believe is ideal for your company. Would you be willing to look into a potential partnership? PS, congrats on winning the 2025 Red Dot Design Award! Best regards, [Name]
entries.points: Do not give away power dynamics by saying 'I was impressed' and congratulating the company twice on an award. Never lecture a brand on what audience fits them best, name the specific creator you are pitching, and add a line break before any P.S.
entries.rewrite: Saw your collaboration with [Creator]. I wasn't surprised when I saw you are an award winner. I represent [Creator Name] who is doing [X] with an engaged [specific audience] following...

quote.quote: there's a button called enter, that's how you spell it, one of the easiest words, use it inshallah, here, when you come after a question round, one click, and this goes, PS, congrats on winning

entries.situation: A student sends a long travel/eSIM brand outreach email pitching two separate creators in detail ('We represent... We also represent...') and including a mission statement at the bottom.
entries.student_email: Hello [First Name], We saw your partner up with [Creator]. He hit the nail on the head talking about how [Brand] saves you the hassle of replacing your SIM and searching for free Wi-Fi. We represent [Creator 1] who has a mainly US-based audience with a solid 8% engagement rate. He just finished going around [Country], and he'll also be going to [Country] and bouncing all over the place, which we believe would be a great stage to showcase [Brand]'s conveniency and travel-friendly features. We also represent [Creator 2] who goes around Europe and has a UK-based audience making him a good fit to present [Brand] to his audience. Our mission is to...
entries.points: Never pitch two creators in Separate paragraphs in the initial email or dump every detail upfront, or the brand manager will stop reading and you will have nothing left to share when they ask for details. Pitch one creator slot succinctly, cut the 'our mission' line, and reduce the email length by 80%.
entries.rewrite: Hey [First Name], saw your collaboration with [Creator]. We work with [Creator 1], who has a mainly US-based audience with a solid engagement rate. He just finished going around [Country] and he'll soon be going to [Country]. Should I send more details?

quote.quote: So as we said, personalization, we have name, name, know, hi, name. Personalization, offer. No, no more, no more place for offer. That's it. You just have one slot here. It says offer.

entries.situation: A student addresses two people at once ('Hey Shaghoff and Sherry') in a tech brand cold email and 3 follow-ups, bolds the creator names, states that tech creators focus on gadgets/IT, and uses generic template follow-ups.
entries.student_email:
Hey Shaghoff and Sherry, I noticed you recently collaborated with [Creator] where [Brand]'s products were highlighted. I'm working with a number of tech influencers, such as **[Creator 1]**, **[Creator 2]**, and others, who focus on gadgets and IT products. I believe they could extend reach to a highly relevant audience and add value to [Brand] products. Would you be open to discussing potential collaborations? Warm regards, [First Name]

Follow-up 1: Hi Shaghoff and Sherry, Just following up on my last email regarding partnership opportunity. Is this something you're interested in? I believe this will drive growth and bring value to your brand by showcasing your product to an engaged audience.

Follow-up 2: Hey Shaghoff and Sherry, I'm reaching out to see if you had the chance to review my email about partnership...

Follow-up 3: Hi Shaghoff and Sherry, I'm just sending this quick message to ask if you might be open to discuss ways we can collaborate to have products exposed to a highly engaged audience through our trusted creators. Is this something you're open to discuss?
entries.points: Email only one person at a time, never bold creator names or change font formatting, add one specific sentence on how the previous creator highlighted the product, replace obvious niche descriptions with concrete metrics (strong US audience, stable views), and avoid generic template follow-ups.
entries.rewrite: Hey Sherry, I noticed you recently collaborated with [Creator] where [Product] was highlighted [add one specific sentence on how/why]. We work with a number of tech influencers, including [Creator 1] and [Creator 2]. We believe they could extend your reach because of their strong US audience and stable views. Should I send more details?

quote.quote: Maybe extend the reach, why, also why, said it why, because of their strong US audience, because of their stable views, because of their strong engagement rate, because, I don't know, they are this, they are that

entries.situation: A student pitches a mattress brand with the subject line 'Q4 partnership: Market your mattresses using YouTube creators', puts a question in the middle of the email, switches from 'I watched' to 'We are working', and ends both the initial email and follow-up with 'Is now a bad time to talk to you about partnerships?'
entries.student_email:
Subject: Q4 partnership: Market your mattresses using YouTube creators
Hey Marketing Team, I watched [Creator] talking about your mattresses in a few of his videos, and thought the scripting on this one was well done. I was curious if you're looking for more creators in this niche. We are working with similar DIY content creators, mainly older US viewers with +50k average views, planning their upcoming projects, and it would make sense for their viewers to hear about your mattresses. Is now a bad time to talk to you about partnerships?

Follow-up 1: Hey Marketing Team, Just reaching out to you again because our content creators have a strong reach to your target audience. We have some space for campaigns in Q4 and are looking forward to working with you. Is now a bad time to talk to you about partnerships?

Follow-up 2: Hey Marketing Team, I want to follow up with you here... Are you still interested in new creators with 50k+ UK/US viewers talking about mattresses? Thank you.
entries.points: Make Q4 subject lines short and intriguing ('Q4 is here, are you?') instead of giving away the whole pitch, start personalization directly with the verb ('Watched [Creator]...') to avoid pronoun inconsistency, put only one CTA at the very end, and never ask 'Is now a bad time to talk?' because it makes it easy for the brand to say yes and ignore or spam you. End with 'Let me know' instead.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Q4 is here, are you?
Hey Marketing Team, watched [Creator] talking about your mattresses in a few of his videos, and thought the scripting on this one was well done. We're working with similar DIY content creators [mention creator name and something specific about their content]. Let me know if you're looking for more creators in this niche.

quote.quote: they're getting offers every single day for Q4, I don't know, Q4 is here, are you, question mark, something like that, but this is too revealing, okay, what if they finished, they're not interested anymore

entries.situation: A student sends an outreach email to a brand pitching a specific YouTube creator with a link to their channel.
entries.student_email: Hey, Lane, hope you are doing well. I'm reaching out on behalf of [Influencer] on YouTube. Below is a link to his channel [link]. Looking forward to hearing what you think.
entries.points: Reserve pleasantries like 'hope you are doing well' for warm leads rather than cold outreach. Avoid saying 'I'm reaching out on behalf of' if you do not have exclusivity or have not told the creator you are doing outreach for them, as it invites tricky questions; instead, simply introduce the creator and ask what they think. When linking a channel to a warm lead, hyperlink the creator's name rather than pasting a raw URL.
entries.rewrite: I'd like to introduce this influencer, what do you think about this guy?

quote.quote: The way that I like to do it usually when I'm linking the channel is I'll put the guy's name, hyperlink it, I think it just looks a little smoother, and then just put his name on the hyperlink his channel into the link.

entries.situation: A brand says $3.5k for a 60-second integration is high for a creator of his size and asks how flexible the agency is, and the student replies saying $3.5k is already below standard rate while repeating that they are flexible without offering a new number.
entries.student_email: Thanks for your questions. Audience breakdown is attached below. Regarding the 60-second integration, 3.5k is already below his standard rate. However, we're flexible and open to find a price that works for both of us. Let me know your thoughts on what price point works best for you.
entries.points: Saying you are flexible while not actually dropping the price contradicts yourself and drags out the negotiation, and repeatedly asking 'what price point works best for you' sounds needy. When a brand asks how flexible you are, lead the negotiation by making a small calculated price drop (such as from $3.5k down to $3.25k or $3k) and justify the discount here as a gesture to start a long-term first-time partnership.
entries.rewrite: We could do 3.25k [or 3k] because this is our first integration with you, so we can have a long-term partnership.

quote.quote: Because they're trying to negotiate, and you're saying you are, you're flexible, but then you're not negotiating, you're not going down the price, do understand? So it's like, you're, you're, you're here, he's, with this email, he actually made it a bit longer

entries.situation: A student reads out a line he sent to the talent agent of an influencer who had never done a brand sponsorship before, pitching the first collaboration as social proof for future deals.
entries.student_email: since X isn't sponsored by any brands yet, I think that this first collaboration would be a social proof for upcoming deals, and it would be good.
entries.points: Pitching a first sponsorship as 'social proof for upcoming deals' to an agent isn't terrible, but it is unnecessary—if the creator wanted sponsorships, their agency would already have leveraged their reach to get them deals. A simple casual inquiry asking if they are open to exploring a deal is enough.
entries.rewrite: hey, I have a deal, are you open to it, are you open to exploring

quote.quote: I'm just going to keep it casual, like, hey, I have a deal, are you open to it, are you open to exploring, that's it, inshallah.

entries.situation: In the second email of the thread, the brand rep (Shaylin) asks the student to share the creator's social media links and the proposed integration format.
entries.student_email: As mentioned before, briefly, the men's self-improvement influencer focuses on helping young men reach their maximum potential, has 30k subscribers... they enjoy taking tips and are highly interested in products for brands... Based on the brand's goals, sales through... Looking to explore 60 to 90 second integrations, and potential extensions of the collaboration, such as an Instagram Reel, for example.
entries.points: Skip the storytelling paragraph describing the creator's self-improvement niche, subscriber count, and how much the viewers love brand tips—viewers watch for the creator, not the sponsors. Simply paste the channel link and raw stats, state that you are looking to do a 60 to 90 second integration (or a specific series/dedicated video), and aggressively pitch a bundle of Shorts or Instagram Reels.
entries.rewrite: [Channel link] Here are the stats. We can do a 60-90 seconds integration, also we can offer you a bundle of shorts, this and that.

quote.quote: Or you can skip the entire part, like this part, you can skip it completely, channel link, you could basically start from here, looking to explore 630 to 90 seconds, okay, potential extensions of the collaboration, certain Instagram Reel, for example

entries.situation: In the third email of the thread, the brand rep (Shaylin) asks the student to share the creator's rates, and the student responds with a long email repeating the subscriber count, justifying the $2,000 rate, and offering to lower it if budget is an issue.
entries.student_email: Thank you for getting back to me, really glad to hear that... For this collaboration, we'd like to focus on a YouTube sponsorship integration... currently has over 32k subscribers on YouTube with a strong and loyal following... [2k rate]. The rate reflects both the strengths of his audience engagement and organic alignment between... If budget is a consideration, we're happy to discuss and find a structure that works for both sides.
entries.points: Stop repeating the creator's subscriber count and cut all the pleasantries. State the rate for the YouTube integration directly, and invite the brand to share their budget if they want a bundle so they reveal their cards first. Never justify your price when asked for a rate, and never pre-emptively offer to discount if budget is a consideration.
entries.rewrite: Sure, here are the rates: [rate for the YouTube integration]. Also, feel free to share the budget with me for a bundle, if you're interested in that, and I can see, based on the budget, what type of bundle I can make.

quote.quote: you give them the rate for the YouTube integration, and you say, also, feel free to share the budget with me for a bundle, if you're interested in that, and I can see, based on the budget, what type of bundle I can make.

entries.situation: An influencer averaging 85k views with no prior sponsorships replied 'yes, I would be interested' to an initial outreach email, and the student drafted a reply vaguely mentioning having brands in mind and asking for analytics before moving forward.
entries.student_email: thanks for responding. We have a few brands in mind. However, before moving forward, we need to understand a bit more about your audience. Can you send us your analytics?
entries.points: Instead of keeping the brands vague and sounding pushy by demanding analytics before moving forward, name 3 to 4 specific brands that sponsor similar creators in his niche (making sure he hasn't worked with them yet) to build trust, and softly ask for his rates and media kit only if he is interested.
entries.rewrite: if you're interested, please let me know, along with any useful information such as the rates, media kit, and all.

quote.quote: I'm going to say something like, if you're interested, please let me know, along with any useful information such as the rates, media kit, and all. And why I do this? Because I don't want to sound pushy, you know.

entries.situation: The travel niche student shows three follow-up emails sent to a brand rep after getting no reply to the initial email.
entries.student_email:
Follow-up 1: I wanted to reconnect regarding my previous email in case it didn't reach you. Could you share whether this remains relevant... Recent brand collaboration featuring [Creator] achieved strong results supported by around 150,000 views and highly engaging audience.
Last follow-up: ...if someone else manages influencer marketing... Thanks in advance / Best regards / Wishing you the best
entries.points: Drop the stiff AI phrasing ('Could you share whether this remains relevant?'), stop repeating the same creator offer in later follow-ups, do not ask if someone else manages influencer marketing when emailing a qualified rep, and do not rely on changing sign-offs like 'Wishing you the best' to get replies.
entries.rewrite: Hey, you might be in a hurry, maybe you missed my email. Anyways, here's what I said in it... I'm guessing this guy's not a really good fit for your brand. By the way, also we have this sub-niche... Maybe the timing is not right. Should I circle back?

quote.quote: What I usually do with follow-ups, first is just a reminder, check my email, this and that, there's a reason why you should check my email. Second, Brent, might be a different offer, guys.

entries.situation: The gaming niche student submits a second influencer email and follow-up talking about point-blank shooting, wanting to add the creator to a roster, and joking about Men in Black.
entries.student_email:
It is confusing shooting from the point blank range, and you really don't know what is going on... I'll bring you an offer that is simple and clear. Your content seems like fit for brands like [Brand 1] and [Brand 2]. We want to add you to our roster. Are you up for sponsorship?

Follow-up: I wanted to check if you received my email, and yes, nobody remembers Men in Black, by the way.
entries.points: Stay formal and businesslike in gaming/entertainment niches instead of acting like a gamer fan, say 'brands including' or 'similar to these' rather than 'brands like' so you don't falsely imply existing partnerships, remove 'we want to add you to our roster', and lead by agitating the creator's sponsorship pain.
entries.rewrite: I noticed that you haven't had any sponsors in your last five videos, your content seems like a good fit for brands including [Brand 1] and [Brand 2]. Are you open for this?

quote.quote: I would say for brands including, this might be less, less dangerous because if you mention brands like this and this, they will sometimes get on the idea that you're working with that. So say including, you know, send similar to these.

entries.situation: A student submits his first cold outreach email to a Linux/tech coding YouTuber.
entries.student_email: I watched your latest video about your Linux experience. I got to say as someone with a bit of background in Linux, it's refreshing to see people exploring, discovering the Penguin world for the first time. On that note, I happen to notice that it was a partnership with [Brand]. We're organizing a partnership round soon and we're planning to connect with brands such as [Brands]. Would that be something you'd be up for? Warm regards
entries.points: Avoid the banned phrase 'I watched your latest video' and overusing 'I'. 'Discovering the Penguin world' and the transition 'On that note' are good, but never say 'we're planning to connect with brands' because it reveals you have no brands yet, and avoid weak CTAs like 'Would that be something you'd be up for?' that invite a 'no'.
entries.rewrite: We are preparing a list of brands / we are making a list of influencers... Should I send more details?

quote.quote: So, yeah, when it comes to this one, what I would change is, we are preparing list of brands, we are doing this, we are doing that, you know, that's better, because you don't reveal, I don't have brands, I just started

entries.situation: The same student submits a second cold email to another coding creator about learning programming with Python.
entries.student_email: Hi [First Name], Just watched your video on how to learn programming, and I have to say it was a rather refreshing take. The point about starting with Python was spot on, and [tool] makes it such a great... I really enjoyed... On a related note, I noticed it was an ad with [Brand], and aligns with what we are preparing. We are setting a partnership round with [Brands]. I wanted to see if you'd be interested in joining this round.
entries.points: Do not repeat formulaic patterns across your emails ('just watched', 'I have to say', 'refreshing'). Cut out overly formal or fangirl praise ('it was a rather refreshing take', 'I really enjoyed') and stop saying 'what we are preparing'; instead, state directly that you have specific brands in mind for their channel and ask what they think.
entries.rewrite: We have these brands in mind for your content, for your YouTube channel, so do you have contact with them? / We have brands in mind based on your content. What do you think?

quote.quote: what is the issue, I've got to say, I have to say, oh, okay, sorry, you know, it's pattern, right, you're repeating yourself, just watch your video, I have to say, I have to say, it was rather a refreshing take

entries.situation: An automotive creator replies with a $7,000 rate for a 60–90s integration; the student immediately asks for analytics, then replies 'Your content is definitely top-notch. However, the budget we have here caps at 4K', and after the creator says to reach back out when a specific campaign is ready, replies 'Totally understand, I'll circle back once there's a campaign'.
entries.student_email:
Reply 1: Thanks for getting back to me. We're continuing working with brands like [Brands] to help us confirm if the brand would be a good fit. Could you share honest analytics of the countries and age groups?

Reply 2: We appreciate you sharing your audience and rate. Your content is definitely top-notch. However, the budget we have here caps at 4K, can we make something happen around that range?

Reply 3: Totally understand, I'll circle back once there's a campaign that aligns well with content and audience.
entries.points: When a creator quotes an inflated rate upfront, ignore the number at first and warm them up by asking how many integrations they can do before requesting analytics. When negotiating, never flatter them ('top-notch') right before dropping a lowball cap without justification; instead, lead with the negative reasons first (analytics/sponsorship volume) and end with the offer ('would you be open for 4K? Would this rate be a deal breaker for you?'). Finally, when a creator or brand says to come back when you have a specific match, do not reply until you actually have the campaign or influencers ready.
entries.rewrite: Thanks for sharing your rates. By looking at [reasons based on analytics/brands]... would you be open for 4K? Would this rate be a deal breaker for you?

quote.quote: Don't answer to that email, okay? Be like, just ghost them, look for influencers, be like, okay, thanks for letting me know, clarifying. Here are the influencers. Same here. Here, once when you have specific campaign ready, ghost them.

entries.situation: A student submits a thread with a DIY snowplow creator: subject 'Let's Talk Collab [First Name]', opener 'your snowplows could actually come in handy in winter', and after the creator says interest 'depends on the deals, on what kind of companies', the student ignores the question and demands audience analytics, then sends a long follow-up asking for average views and explaining that 'brands usually request them'.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Let's Talk Collab [First Name]

Hi [First Name], your [DIY] snowplows could actually come in handy in winter. I noticed your videos were not sponsored. Would you be open working with brands?

Creator: Hi, if you can provide me with a non-exclusive deal, then I would definitely be interested in considering.

Student: A non-exclusive deal works. Would you be open to managing multiple deals in a month?

Creator: If you can pitch good deals to me, then that would be great, depends on the deals, on what kind of companies.

Student: To better align potential deals, could you please share your audience analytics?

Follow-up: I'm following up on your audience analytics, for now, I just need a quick overview (age, geo breakdowns) and average views, screenshots or media kit would be ideal, brands usually request them, this way I don't need to ask you again...
entries.points: Do not capitalize every word in the subject line ('Let's Talk Collab'), avoid stating obvious facts in personalization ('snowplows come in handy in winter'), and never copy templates from free YouTube videos. When a creator asks what companies you have in mind, do not ignore their question and demand analytics right away—name example brands first and casually ask for analytics 'in the meantime' so you don't sound suspicious. Never ask for average views (which are public) or over-explain why you need a media kit in follow-ups.
entries.rewrite: We have these brands in mind—brands like [Brand 1], [Brand 2], [Brand 3], what do you think about it? In the meantime, could you share some analytics?

quote.quote: so this follow-up is a bit longer, and over-explaining, I need quick, okay, so this one, you know, audience analytics, this is that, and average views, bro, you don't ask for average views, you can, you can find them on your own, it's public

entries.situation: A student submits a cold email to a fitness brand asking how to make his offer more valuable without sounding too salesy or casual.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Quick note on your integration with [Influencer]

Hi [First Name],

Mentioning his own personal story with [Brand] in his integration added a nice touch of authenticity.

Noticing your interest in the fitness niche brought to mind [Creator], one of the creators we work with. He could talk about the struggle of eating enough calories while bulking being solved by consuming more [Brand].

Would you be open to exploring this?
entries.points: Shorten the subject line so it does not give away the whole email, refer to the brand's integration into the influencer's video (not the influencer's integration), make the personalization specific enough that it cannot be copy-pasted to any brand, and replace the detailed ad-concept pitch with a short curiosity hook mentioning a couple of creators with a strong US presence and engagement rate.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Quick notes

Hi [First Name],

Mentioning his own personal story with [Brand] in your integration in his video [plus specific detail from the video].

We work with [Creator 1] and [Creator 2]—they have a strong U.S. presence and solid engagement rate. We also work with creators in [another sub-niche] that you might be interested in.

Would you be open to exploring this?

entries.situation: A student pitches a smaller German/DACH drift-build YouTuber (300K average views) to an automotive brand that recently sponsored a much larger German creator with similar content.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Another YouTuber channel to deepen your [German reach]

With [Influencer] already on board, [Brand] is clearly taking YouTube in Germany seriously. We have [Creator with hyperlink], a drift-build channel averaging around 300K views per upload to a majority DACH audience.
