entries.points: Do not pitch a smaller creator with identical content as a duplicate of a massive creator the brand already sponsored, avoid assuming their German expansion or previous sponsorship went well, remove hyperlinks and specific view counts from the first email, and frame the initial email as an open-ended curiosity hook rather than an information dump.
entries.rewrite: If you are exploring [this sub-niche], we also have some guys with a high audience from these countries.

entries.situation: A student submits two tech-niche cold emails (one to a rugged gear brand and one to an IT/cloud learning platform) that reference product launches/specs and list multiple creator content formats.
entries.student_email:
Email 1:
Subject: Gear this tough
Hi [First Name],
[Product launches] are landing at the perfect moment—whether filming outdoors when traveling where reliable MIL-SPEC drop protection matters...
We work with creators who naturally test gear in tough locations—travel shoots, rainy hikes, build logs, and mobile setups where content performs because audiences immediately see the...

entries.situation: A student submits a self-improvement brand cold email with the subject line 'A strong fit for [Brand]', generic personalization, a 4.6% engagement rate stat, and 'Happy to share more details. Let me know.'
entries.student_email:
Subject: A strong fit for [Brand]

Hello [First Name],

I noticed [Brand]'s recent creator collaboration and it's clear the brand is actively expanding through influencer partnerships.

I work with [Creator 1] and [Creator 2], a YouTuber whose content aligns closely with [Brand]'s mission and vision. With a 4.6% engagement rate and consistent viewership, he is a strong fit for your audience.

entries.points: Soften bold claims like 'A strong fit' to 'Might be a good fit' so prospects do not instinctively disagree, replace generic observations that the brand uses influencer marketing with real personalization, do not cite specific engagement rate numbers (especially a mediocre 4.6%; just say 'strong engagement rate' and 'stable views'), and replace passive closings like 'Happy to share more details' with a direct question like 'Should I share more details?'.

Subject: Might be a good fit for [Brand]

[Specific personalization]

We work with a couple of guys like [Creator], who has a strong audience in [country/region] with stable views and a strong engagement rate—he might be a good fit for your audience.

entries.situation: A student reads out a draft email to a talent agency requesting analytics for Influencer B and asking for rates and analytics for Influencer D.
entries.student_email: hey, thanks for sharing the rates, we would like to move forward with this influencer B right now? entries.situation: A student submits a cold email pitching a fitness creator to a sleep-mask brand in the health and fitness niche.
entries.student_email:
Subject: had to email you after seeing it

Hi, [first name]. Your campaign with [influencer] in his video about ditching the weight, chest, workouts, remind me of a man I speak to sometimes, [creator name]. His subscribers are into working out. So I believe they'd like a mask that can improve their sleep and get them closer to their fitness goals. Open to explore this idea? Cheers, [first name]
entries.points: While the subject line ('had to email you after seeing it') and CTA ('Open to explore this idea') are decent, the opening line ('remind me of a man I speak to sometimes') is vague, sloppy, and overly casual, and saying a fitness creator's subscribers 'are into working out' states the obvious with zero value; instead, cite specific audience demographics like country percentage.
entries.rewrite: Most of his audience are gym enthusiasts from US, roughly 70%, something like that.

quote.quote: I like, still like to stick to personalization, to offer, and CTA. Everybody knows that, right? So your personalization is also an offer, like integrated offer. A bit, you know, interesting approach, but I think it's too casual, too, you know, laid back.

entries.situation: A student submits a formal, corporate-sounding brand outreach email filled with filler phrases ('constantly maintain strong engagement rates', 'yield significant results').
entries.student_email: We have been following your previous influencer marketing campaigns, with influencers like [name]. We believe our network of influencers would be an excellent fit to enhance your brand awareness and sales. Our influencers focus on U.S. audience and constantly maintain strong engagement rates, which makes us confident that integrating your product into upcoming content will yield significant results. I will be happy to send over a few influencer profiles... Best regards
entries.points: Avoid stiff, essay-like corporate language that reads like a terms-of-service policy; keep brand outreach under 50-70 words at a simple reading level, personalize from a marketing perspective on why their past integration worked, state the creator fit concisely, and treat the first email like a low-pressure discovery call.
entries.rewrite: Our influencer mainly focus on U.S. audience. They have strong engagement rate. Would you think that would be a good idea? Let me know.

quote.quote: What do you do with personalization? You speak from marketing aspect. Okay. Stalk collaboration with this guy. How he did that, the way he do, you know, this one, this one. Explain why that integration, in your opinion, was a good approach.

entries.situation: A student in the PC/gaming niche pitches a brand by praising their past integration as 'natural, clean', saying their creators 'reach similar PC focus audiences', and stating 'Our creators range from [X to Y]'.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Quick thoughts for you

Hello, [first name]. I saw your sponsor integration for [creator] and [creator]. It left a strong impression—it felt natural, clean, and focused on what builders actually value. We work with U.S.-based gaming YouTubers who reach similar PC focus audiences, maintaining stable views and strong engagement rate. Our creators range from [X to Y], making them a solid fit for your community of builders and tech enthusiasts who appreciate performance done right. Let me know if you'd like a short overview of the creators.
entries.points: Do not flatter the brand like a fan, do not say your creators reach the exact same audience they already reached with another influencer, never give a subscriber or view range ('Our creators range from 50k to 100k') because it reveals a tiny roster and inconsistent views, and talk about what the specific creator does rather than making assumptions about their audience.
entries.rewrite: Here is John. He is doing this. He is doing that. He would be a good fit because [specific reason]. Let me know if you'd like a short overview of the creators.

quote.quote: Don't say this. Our creators range from. Don't give range, especially with views. Like, our creators range from 50k to 100k. So, you know, maybe, maybe sometimes good, maybe sometimes, you know, you know the rest, right? So, don't use range. Range is not good.

entries.situation: A student submits an overly compressed, aggressive 'Hormozi-style' AI-generated email pitching a 'gamer lockdown kit' video and ending with '— happy to send names plus timing, or when we can slot this for early Q1, your call.'
entries.student_email:
Subject: Hey

[First name], we've been tracking [brand] platform, especially application allowlisting and ringfencing. We work with [creator], and they can show that working in real gaming workflows with a video: gamer lockdown kit, before and after on screen, and give viewers a free kit they can use today — happy to send names plus timing, or when we can slot this for early Q1, your call. Warm regards, [first name]
entries.points: Do not over-apply power-dynamics or ask ChatGPT to write in an aggressive 'Alex Hormozi' tone that makes the email cryptic and the CTA confusing; short only works when the email is clear and valuable. If you know the creator's upcoming video topic, simply state what video the creator is making and why the brand's product fits.
entries.rewrite: He is making a video about [topic], and that's why we thought your product would be a good fit. Let me know what you think.

quote.quote: Yaani, there might be a longer email than this, that might be better. Just because it's short doesn't mean it's good. So, it's all about putting your value into the email and not wasting words.

entries.situation: After the student agreed on a price with a brand and asked the influencer for his shipping address, the influencer demanded visibility into the brand's direct contract and total budget without the agency cut (worried the brand might be paying $5,000 while he only gets $1,500). The student read out his reply, after which the influencer ghosted for seven days.
entries.student_email: I completely understand where you're coming from. It's a fair question. Especially if you've not worked with an agency before, just so you're clear, this is the standard across the industry. Agencies handle the contracts and budgets directly, the brands and creators are contracted through agencies for the agreed rate. The brand agreement isn't something creators are involved in, that's handled on our end, best regards
entries.points: The student's reply was alright in stating industry standard, but it lacked a call to action and was too brief for an inexperienced creator who needed a fuller explanation. In this situation, write a semi-long email explaining that: (1) unlike an exclusive talent management agency that takes a percentage cut from a creator's gross rate, your agency is paid by the brand to source multiple influencers; (2) just like a travel agency doesn't disclose wholesale ticket costs, the brand's total budget is between the brand and the agency; and (3) the agency is offering the creator the agreed rate, so if he doesn't want it, you can give the deal to another creator.
entries.rewrite: Had we been managing you exclusively, that would be a different story. Then we would take the cut from you, and you would also know the gross rate. Because of our model and the brand's willingness to work with us, we are sourcing many influencers for them, not only you. The brand is paying us, and we are paying you and giving you the offer at our agreed rate—so if you're not happy with the price, that's fine, we can pass it to someone else.

quote.quote: You need to explain to him that whatever the brand is willing to pay me, the agency, for working with them, for providing them influencers, not influencer, influencers, is none of his business.

entries.situation: Student reads a cold email to an automotive dashcam brand referencing a creator catching license plates within five meters and pitching an American muscle car creator with a 46% US audience.
entries.student_email: Hello there. Someone's use of the, to catch license plates within five meters was a smart way to show the camera's real world value. The details hits home for anyone worried about the car safety, about car safety. That same approach could work with this guy. Here, we've used classic American muscle cars, and they post every week or two. Here's 46% of U.S. audience fits your U.S. goals. Open to a few ideas.
entries.points: Shorten the personalization so it is easier to read, keep the smooth integration of the 46% US audience stat, and use a more direct CTA (like booking a slot or asking if they need more details) rather than asking 'Open to a few ideas?' after already naming the creator.
entries.rewrite: should we book a slot for you? Do you need more details?

quote.quote: Go for something more direct. You know, should we book a slot for you? Do you need more details? If you are something, something, you know, always go for that one. If you give names, don't mention ideas in CTA. It's kind of repetitive.

entries.situation: Student reads a first follow-up email to an automotive brand proposing a pilot campaign to test how the creator's style fits the brand.
entries.student_email: Hey there, we were thinking of running a pilot first. The way you can see how the creator's style fits your brand and see how it works.
entries.points: Proposing a pilot in a follow-up is strong, but strengthen it by adding a concrete example of a past collaboration where that creator ran a pilot with another brand that turned into a long-term retainer.
entries.rewrite: we were thinking of running pilot first, the same way influencer had collaboration with this one. And guess what? I don't know, six months retainer. It was working good.

quote.quote: Like, okay, we were thinking of running pilot first, the same way influencer had collaboration with this one. And guess what? I don't know, six months retainer. It was working good.

entries.situation: Student reads a second follow-up email to a brand sharing that the creator averages a 5% engagement rate and asking if that is a fit.
entries.student_email: hello there, adding one more point here, he averages, yeah, okay, five engagement rate, could this be fit for you?
entries.points: Do not follow up with ordinary view counts or a 5% engagement rate as if they are extraordinary; instead, frame a smaller or nano creator around having a highly engaged, trusting audience that makes for a great low-risk test.
entries.rewrite: by the way, he is, you know, nano influencer, is this type of influencer, and it's a nice way to test waters, because most of the time, you know, influencers, with this amount of you, have a more engaged audience, they trust them more

quote.quote: if you want to mention, Mention this amount of views, something to mention like hate views and stuff, if it's not extraordinary, don't do it.

entries.situation: A brand replied asking 'Can you share a link to content so I can take a look?' and the student replied with just 'Here's the link. Let me know if I should send over his analytics,' followed by two follow-ups when the brand didn't answer.
entries.student_email: Here's the link. Let me know if I should send over as analytics. Follow-up 1: Just wanted to follow-up to see if you have a chance to take a look. I would be like to know what you think. Follow-up 2: I wanted to quickly follow up. Does fit for you looking for it? If not, if there's any specific type of influencer, like a potential population, if not, either way, let me know.
entries.points: Once a brand replies, switch from copywriting to sales: hyperlink the creator's name (Ctrl+K) to their channel and sell the outcome—mentioning their past campaign results and why their content matches the brand—rather than dropping a bare link. If they ghost afterwards, a recovery follow-up asking if they want a different type of creator works well.
entries.rewrite: His last campaign did this, for this brand, with this brand. His content is all about backflips. He would be an amazing match for your brand.

quote.quote: Like, thanks, can you share link content so I can take a look? You have to say something. His last campaign did this, for this brand, with this brand. His content is all about backflips. He would be an amazing match for your brand.

entries.situation: Student reads a cold email to a solar/electrical brand saying 'We happen to work' with a creator 'who is planning a series' and ending with 'Should I send over more details?'
entries.student_email: Showcase how an illustration can swap the electric panel in solar, in his solar home review, then highlight the easy plug and play design. We happen to work with this creator who is planning a series. I think his content would fit your product well. Should I send over more details?
entries.points: Explain why the past integration's plug-and-play angle worked for non-technical viewers, drop weak phrasing like 'We happen to work' and 'is planning a series' in favor of 'is filming' or 'is going to do,' and replace overused CTAs.
entries.rewrite: creator highlighted how it's easy and plug and play, nice way to something, something, to all of the audience who are not tech

quote.quote: or creator highlighted how it's easy and plug and play, nice way to something, something, to all of the audience who are not tech something, right. Give a reason why that ad would work. We happen to work. Wrong choice of words.

entries.situation: A student reaches out to a brand contact regarding an upcoming Samsung S26 campaign to ask if KPIs and timelines have been finalized.
entries.student_email: Hey, [employee name] mentioned, I should reach out to you regarding upcoming campaigns for influencer marketing. We previously spoke about the Samsung S26 campaign. Can we share some more details if KPIs and timelines have been finalized?
entries.points: Keep the initial campaign inquiry short and focused on discovering the brand's KPIs and goals so you can tailor your subsequent influencer pitch.

quote.quote: Okay, so not much here. As I said, keep it as short as possible. They just want to see like, maybe they want to see what kind of goals they have so they can tailor their pitch.

entries.situation: The brand references a recent high-performing Samsung video on the creator's channel and asks for the channel's media kit and integration fees.
entries.student_email: Yes, as mentioned, we'll be featuring the Samsung S26. So the title will be similar. The rate for a similar integration to the one shared is 2,500. Let me know if you'd like to lock in the slot.
entries.points: Always answer every part of a brand's request; along with stating the rate and a call to action to lock in the slot, make sure to attach and explicitly mention the requested media kit.
entries.rewrite: Yes, as mentioned, we'll be featuring the Samsung S26. So the title will be similar. The rate for a similar integration to the one shared is 2,500. Media kit, as requested, is attached. Let me know if you'd like to lock in the slot.

quote.quote: so always make sure to, to like send, send whatever they're looking for, so, especially media media kit, like, media kit is something very important, you know, and, uh, and, and yeah, maybe include that, okay, media kit, as requested is a test

entries.situation: The student responds to the brand's $800 lowball offer after initially quoting $2,500.
entries.student_email: Unfortunately we cannot move forward at 800 as this is quite far from the mentioned rate. For the first collaboration, the best we can do is 1,800. Let me know if we can move forward.
entries.points: Show flexibility when countering a lowball offer by dropping the price to a middle ground framed as a special concession for the first collaboration.

quote.quote: because this is our first time, you know, for the first collaboration, we are willing to drop the price to 1,800. We are willing to find the middle ground that both of us can move forward, like a win-win deal, you know.

entries.situation: The brand counters the student's $1,800 offer with $900 plus a 15% affiliate commission.
entries.student_email: If we include a 15% affiliate commission, we'd be willing to move forward at 1,300. Let me know if you'd like to proceed.
entries.points: Leverage the brand's higher affiliate commission offer to meet them closer to their budget on the flat fee while still holding above their lowball number.

quote.quote: so he agreed to the 15% so he can show the brand that, okay, we understand what you're trying to do. You want to lower the risks. Maybe your budget is capped for this month, this quarter.

entries.situation: A student reads out a cold email to an outdoors/van-life creator that wishes the creator a happy birthday and ends with a weak call to action.
entries.student_email: Hi [First Name]. Those remote areas around British Columbia were a solid find. Happy birthday, by the way. I wanted to talk about your van life and outdoor trips, [XYZ] and other relevant brands could fit well with the content you're putting out. Let me know if you're interested in potentially working with them.
entries.points: Never wish an influencer 'Happy birthday' (it looks needy and violates Islamic principles), focus your personalization on one specific moment from watching five minutes of the video, connect the offer directly to that video's topic, and replace soft CTAs like 'Let me know if you're interested' with a strong direct question or a request for analytics.
entries.rewrite: Since your last video was about [this and that], these brands would be a good fit for those type of videos, what would you say? / If you're interested, send me your analytics.

quote.quote: Call to action or CTA should be always strong for the initial email. Okay? So that's the equation. Strong, strong, strong. How strong? Are you interested? What do you think about it? Those type of stuff. Do you have some free slots?

entries.situation: A student pitches a saltwater fishing creator to a fishing gear brand using a long email that lists subscriber counts, TikTok/IG metrics, total lifetime views, and 'combined roster followers', and claims to 'represent' the creator.
entries.student_email:
Subject: A saltwater creator with 625 million views for [Brand]
[Location] spring is saltwater country, and [Brand]'s fishing section is right in the path of the audience that lives for it. The question is whether the right creators are putting your gear in front of that audience right now. We represent [Creator], a saltwater and freshwater creator with 458,000 YouTube subscribers, [X] on TikTok and [Y] on Instagram, and over 625 million total views. High energy, challenge-based content that Southwest Florida anglers already watch and share. We also represent a broader roster of fishing and outdoor creators with over 1 million combined followers. If you're open to looking beyond a single partnership, would love to send over numbers and content if you're open to taking a look.
entries.points: Use a curiosity subject line like 'Hey Jack, thoughts' so they open the email, cut the long opening fluff under 30 words, say 'we work with' instead of 'we represent', omit subscriber counts, total lifetime views, and combined roster followers (brands care about single-video views and audience fit), mention sub-niche creators briefly, and end with a simple CTA: 'Should I send his details?'.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Hey Jack, thoughts
We work with [Creator], a saltwater and freshwater creator, with high energy, challenge-based content that Southwest Florida anglers already watch and share. Also, we work with [sub-niche] creators. Should I send his details?

quote.quote: To be honest, I would say, we work with Mr. Beast, a saltwater and freshwater creator, with high energy, challenge-based content that Southwest Florida anglers already watch and share. I think this is enough.

entries.situation: A student submits an initial brand outreach email and follow-up in the gaming/sci-fi niche that repeatedly starts sentences with 'We' and lacks smooth copywriting.
entries.student_email:
Initial: Hello, we have been following your campaign for [X]. We noticed that collaboration with influencer [Y]. We have influencers in that and this niche, would you be open to potential collaboration?
Follow-up: I hope you are well. We have creators who specialize in this and are also with a general tech niche. The majority of their audience is in the US, UK, and Canada. I look forward to hearing from you, and I'm happy to provide more information. Thanks.
entries.points: Stop repeating 'We... we... we...' like a caveman (use 'I'), explain specifically why the brand's past influencer campaign worked (e.g., 'seamless and natural'), reuse a keyword from that compliment in your bridge line ('Speaking of seamless...'), reference results or case studies from creators in your offer, and drop filler like 'I hope you are well' from follow-ups.
entries.rewrite: Campaign with [Creator] was top, the way he mentioned [X] was seamless and natural. Speaking of seamless, we've been working with this guy, he's been achieving good results with brands like [A] and [B]. Probably he would do the same for you as well.

quote.quote: Hey, we've been working with this guy, he's been smashing it, he's been, you know, achieving good results with brands these and these. Probably he would do the same for you as well. So you can use case studies of other influencers

entries.situation: A student pitches a brand using the subject line 'Promising creators from [niche]', opens with 'I hope you are well. We noticed that you helped your members save 2.5 billion', and claims 'We represent creators... they are perfect candidates'.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Promising creators from [niche]
I hope you are well. We noticed that you helped your members save 2.5 billion, which is impressive. We represent creators in that niche, they are perfect candidates for your products and I'm sure they will help your members gain even more savings. Looking forward to hearing from you.
entries.points: Do not reveal that you are pitching creators in the subject line, cut 'I hope you are well. We noticed...' and open directly with the punchy stat ('$2.5 billion saved by your members is outstanding. That is called trust. Speaking of trust...'), never claim 'we represent' unless your agency email is in the creator's bio, and explain why the creators fit rather than just calling them 'perfect candidates'.
entries.rewrite: 2.5 billion dollars saved by your members is outstanding. That is called trust. Speaking of trust, we have some creators who can do [this and that]...

quote.quote: Switch this, bro. 2.5 billion dollars saved by your members is outstanding. That is called the trust. Boom. Speaking of trust, we have some creators who can do this and that, blah, blah, blah, and that would be good.

entries.situation: A student submits two gaming brand outreach emails with subject lines 'Creators for [Brand] and more' and 'Heat and Lost Eden', sounding like a fan of the game updates and using weak CTAs.
entries.student_email:
Email 1 Subject: Creators for [Brand] and more
Hi [Name], I think the latest heavy cavalry update will bring even more excitement to this game. Speaking of exciting things, we represent creators in gaming, sci-fi niches who have viewerships from USA, UK, and Europe, they would be great candidates for not just [Brand], but also brands like [X] and more.
Email 2 Subject: Heat and Lost Eden
Hi, we have been reviewing transition to Heat era and the launch of season one Lost Eden with interest. We represent creators in gaming...
entries.points: Replace spoiler subject lines like 'Creators for [Brand] and more', avoid sounding like a customer reviewing game updates or repeating 'we, we, we', stop claiming 'we represent', and finish with a frictionless CTA like 'Should I send more details?'.
entries.rewrite: Hey, I have a couple of these guys. They achieved good results. Should I send more details?

quote.quote: Initial brand outreach, creators for this and more. Bad, bad, bad, subject line is bad. Hi, someone, I think the latest heavy cavalry update will bring even more excitement to this game. Okay, you sound like a satisfied customer to be honest

entries.situation: A student emails three people at the same jump-rope fitness brand simultaneously, using title-case or bizarre subject lines ('Thoughts For Increasing Exposure, Jack', 'Can I See Your Thoughts', 'Jack, NordVPN, MrBeast'), pointing out that the brand's posts average under 100 likes, and reusing the same personalization across contacts.
entries.student_email:
Email 1 Subject: Thoughts For Increasing Exposure, Jack / Can I See Your Thoughts
Hey Abby, I like how Davey showcased some of your ropes. It landed better showing how much weight he lost as well. On that note, you average 96 likes. I have [Creator]. His content is solely running focused. His lifestyle audience would benefit from this given his average views are 200k plus. You can have more people interested in your ropes. Can I send his profile over?
Email 2: Hey Abby, I've reached out to others and wanted your opinion. I saw David's weight loss... you average under 100 likes... I would bring [Creator] who makes running content...
Email 3 Subject: Jack, NordVPN, MrBeast
Just wanted your thoughts, the people you've platformed to show your ropes, shows the effectiveness on the product. I wanted to bring [Creator] to you. His content is running focused bringing fitness health enthusiasts to his videos type to benefit from cardio products.
entries.points: Email only two people per company at a time with completely fresh personalization for each person, don't capitalize every word in the subject line or use nonsensical combos, never point out that a brand's video flopped ('you average 96 likes'), bridge smoothly from the compliment ('Speaking of landing...'), and structure the offer so the strongest proof (200k+ average views) lands at the very end right before 'Can I send his profile over?'.
entries.rewrite: Hey Abby, I like how Davey showcased some of your ropes. It landed better showing how much weight he lost as well. Speaking of landing, [Creator] can land really well. You can have more people interested in your ropes because his content is running focused and on top of that he is making 200k views. Can I send his profile over?

quote.quote: On that note, which note? It's a better way to say. It lands. Speaking of landing, these influencers can land really well. On that note, you average 96 likes. What is this? You average 96 likes. Where? It's confusing.

entries.situation: A student sends cold emails and follow-ups to AI/software developer influencers using a mystery subject line ('It stops there'), asking survey-style questions about why they haven't had sponsors, and copying generic one-line follow-ups from the course.
entries.student_email:
Email 1 Subject: It stops there
Hey, impressive AI workflow library you built there, can it automate this thought, though? It seems like you haven't had any partnerships in your last few videos, do you mind [sharing why]? I think you would be a great match for companies similar to PostHog and CodeRabbit. We'd like to support you with that. Would you like to hear more?
Follow-up 1: Hey, just following up in case you missed this.
Follow-up 2: Just making sure my emails are reaching you.
Email 2 Subject: It stops here / Loop engineering
Nice, I might use the SEO loop you showed there, does one of your loops cover this though? Looks like you haven't had any sponsors, although I think you'd be a great match for companies like [X] and [Y], we're looking for peers to add to our brand marketing roster, and would like to offer you a spot.
entries.points: Mystery subject lines like 'It stops there' are good when varied, and naming specific fit brands (PostHog, CodeRabbit) works well, but stop using templated personalization questions ('can it automate this though?'), never ask survey questions about why they lack sponsors (treat no sponsors as the pain point your offer solves), and never copy-paste generic course follow-ups ('Hey, just following up in case you missed this') because they will put you straight into spam.
entries.rewrite: I think you would be a great match for companies similar to PostHog and CodeRabbit. We'd like to support you with that.

quote.quote: Hey, just follow up in case you missed this. Guys, don't do this. It's from the course and everybody is using those. To be honest, go back and read about follow-ups in general. Get the idea, and then make your own follow-ups

entries.situation: Automotive niche student submits a first outreach email to a car creator about importing an S4 Turbo S from Japan.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Quick idea

I saw you recently got the S4. Turbo S from Japan. That's unusual instead of the UK salvage road. That's smart to tap into Japanese salvage cars, but the difference in fact and condition speaks for itself.

I've noticed your last videos were not sponsored. Does the idea to work with different brands interest you?

Let me know.
entries.points: Never open with the overused phrase 'I saw', which immediately signals a partnership pitch; use creative synonyms. Make sure personalization connects with the creator ('show me you know me') without critiquing their decisions or hurting their ego (such as calling their import choice 'unusual'). The offer and 'Let me know' CTA are decent, but remove large blank gaps between paragraphs.
entries.rewrite: as for this one, this one, I don't know, amazing. Colors, this and that. Looking forward to seeing your videos.

quote.quote: I've noticed your last videos were not sponsored. Does the idea to work with different brands interest you? Let me know. Okay, this is decent, Allahumma barik. I would maybe use this one, a bit different. I would change it, but this part is decent.

entries.situation: Automotive niche student submits a second cold email praising a creator's 4Runner transformation and asking if they want to work with more brands.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Quick idea

I've seen your last video about the Forerunner transformation, what an impressive job. That smoky blue and bronze rims just looks brand new from the factory.

I've seen that you're sponsored by this brand. Would you be interested to work with more brands?

Let me know.
entries.points: Avoid fanboy praise and fluff like 'what an impressive job' and describing the paint and rims; tone it down to 'decent job'. Strengthen the shallow offer by naming specific brands in mind that align with their content and noting that those brands are actively looking for creators in Q1. Close with 'Looking forward hearing your thoughts' instead of 'Let me know'.
entries.rewrite: Based of your content, we had these, these brands in mind. What do you think? Looking forward hearing your thoughts.

quote.quote: I've seen your last video about the Forerunner transformation, what an impressive job. Okay, you should. could use this one, this is fanboy, okay? That smoky blue and bronze rims just looks brand new from the factory. Bro, this is fluff, okay?

entries.situation: MMA niche student submits a first cold email saying the creator's video popped up and reminded them to reach out, claiming to have MMA brands, and apologizing in a P.S. for not finding the creator's name.
entries.student_email: Hello [first name], Saw your video popped up recently — and it reminded me to reach out. Really entertaining and easy to watch. Quick question, are you open to brand collabs? Most of your content isn't sponsored, and I have a couple of MMA brands that could fit your style. If it sounds interesting, I can explain more. Best, [name]. P.S., I didn't catch your name anywhere, so apologies for keeping it informal.
entries.points: Treat the opening line as your 'golden sentence' visible in the inbox preview—never waste it on unprofessional filler like 'Saw your video popped up recently, and it reminded me to reach out' or 'Really entertaining and easy to watch.' Cut 'Quick question' and place the collaboration question at the very end of the email so it is the last thing they remember. Do not claim 'I have a couple of MMA brands' when you have none; say 'We have a couple of brands in mind' and name 1 to 3 brands. Remove weak conditional phrasing like 'If it sounds interesting' that invites a 'no', and never apologize in a P.S. for not finding their name.
entries.rewrite: We have a couple of brands in mind [mention 1-3 brands]. Are you open to brand collabs? Let me know.

quote.quote: Popped up recently and reminded me to reach out. It's unprofessional. It's unprofessional. Apology, 100%, 100%. It's unprofessional. Like, you know, your video was so good that made me reach out, but I have influencer marketing agency, and I do that daily.

entries.situation: Fitness niche student submits an outreach email with the subject line 'Your home gym is the winner' and body text about the creator's dog riding on a bike.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Your home gym is the winner

You have a brave, brave dog, going on a bike, ride along, a little daredevil. In your videos, I see you have sponsorships, and I wanted to know if you are ready for other similar opportunities. Speak soon
entries.points: Never start subject lines or openings with 'Your...' or 'You...', and never jump from one topic in the subject line (a home gym) to a completely unrelated topic in the opening line (a dog on a bike). Reference a specific item or action in lowercase (e.g., 'a backwards cap') in the subject line and continue that exact thread into the body and offer. Replace poetic 'haiku' phrasing and 'Speak soon' with a direct offer naming brands in mind and 'Best regards'.
entries.rewrite: I also noticed, let's say, you're working with these brands. Based on your content, we have these brands in mind. Do you want to work with more brands? Best regards

quote.quote: Yeah, and then, you should continue the same flow with the backward cap, okay, not, do not talk like, high buildings surround you, you walk in middle of night, moonlight behind you, make no sense, right? Make no sense. Jumping from topic to topic.

entries.situation: Student submits an outreach email with the subject line 'On the table.' calling the creator's explanation 'enlightening' for a 'layman' and saying 'I am looking at some brands. There might be a good fit for integration work. How does that sound? Thanks.'
entries.student_email:
Subject: On the table.

The explanation regarding lats was enlightening. Makes it easy for a layman to understand complex topics. I am looking at some brands. There might be a good fit for integration work. How does that sound? Thanks.
entries.points: Write emails at a 4th-grade (11-year-old) reading level rather than using complex words like 'enlightening' and 'layman'. Never call yourself a 'layman', which destroys your power dynamics and makes you sound inferior. Eliminate weak, hesitant language like 'I am looking at some brands', 'might be a good fit', and 'How does that sound?'—be confident and direct ('we're looking at these brands'), connect the subject line to the body, and sign off with 'Best regards' instead of 'Thanks'.
entries.rewrite: we're thinking about some brands, we're looking at these brands... Best regards

quote.quote: If you say I'm looking at brands, that might be a good fit, even that like might be a good fit. That is too, but like, how does that sound? Might be a good fit. All these words, they don't like, there's no confidence there.

entries.situation: Fitness niche student submits an outreach email comparing Eugen Sandow vs. Ronnie Coleman, adding 'Oh, well', and saying 'I further notice that you've not done any integration and sponsorship work in most of your videos. Is that something you'll be interested in?'
entries.student_email:
Subject: Interesting feat about new versus old

I was looking at your video about old versus new bodybuilders, and now I have to say, if you were to showcase Eugen Sandow versus Ronnie Coleman, Sandow doesn't stand a chance. Oh, well. I further notice that you've not done any integration and sponsorship work in most of your videos. Is that something you'll be interested in?
entries.points: Cut poetic or spoken conversational filler like 'and now I have to say' and 'Oh, well'—emails should be casual and natural, not filled with spoken interjections. Avoid robotic transitions like 'I further noticed', and instead of merely pointing out that they lack sponsorships, pitch a clear solution ('we can help you with that, we have brands in mind for your content').
entries.rewrite: I was looking at your last video about this, and this... we can help you with that one, we can, let's change it, we have brands in mind for your content.

quote.quote: I further noticed that you've not done any integration and sponsorships work in most of your videos. Then you can, you can really offer, we can help you with that one, we can, let's change it, we have brands

entries.situation: Student submits an outreach email with the subject 'Distractions, focus, and consistency loops', complimenting the creator's minimalistic setup ('As they say, less is more') and asking 'I noticed that you haven't had any sponsorships in your videos. Is that by design, or are you looking to get sponsored?'
entries.student_email:
Subject: Distractions, focus, and consistency loops

I saw your video about how to stop wasting your life, a simple but good concept. Also, your setup is very minimalistic and simple. And it works because there is more focus on the content. As they say, less is more. I noticed that you haven't had any sponsorships in your videos. Is that by design, or are you looking to get sponsored? Kind regards
entries.points: The curiosity-loop subject line and 'less is more' personalization are decent, though slightly long. However, asking 'Is that by design, or are you looking to get sponsored?' only points out the creator's pain (no sponsors) without offering a solution. Instead, play off 'less is more' to pitch the solution directly: you noticed they have fewer sponsorships recently, so let's make it more with specific brands in mind for the new year.
entries.rewrite: As they say, less is more. You know, I've noticed that you have less sponsorships in your recent videos. Let's make it more. We have some brands in mind for you. Kind regards.

quote.quote: He's given like half the offer, and he's mentioning like the pain, but he's not giving him the solution, right? He said, oh, I noticed you don't have sponsors, like, but he's not giving him like, but I can do this for you.

entries.situation: Student submits an outreach email about a flexibility video hurting their back, then asking 'I noticed that you haven't posted a lot of videos lately. Are you looking to make a comeback in terms of posting more videos? If that's the case, how does brand integration sound?'
entries.student_email: Your video about flexibility ladder is good, however, just watching that video hurts my back, no joke. I noticed that you haven't posted a lot of videos lately. Are you looking to make a comeback in terms of posting more videos? If that's the case, how does brand integration sound?
entries.points: Do not jump abruptly between disconnected topics (back pain, posting inactivity, brand integrations) without a natural transition. Never ask a creator if they are planning to make a comeback—if they aren't coming back, you cannot work with them anyway. Assume they will post again, pitch an idea or brands for their next video, and lead them confidently instead of asking hesitant questions.
entries.rewrite: For your next video, I've got an idea for your next video... we have some brands that could be a good fit, let me know.

quote.quote: Are you looking to make a comeback in terms of posting more videos? If that's the case, how does brand integration sound? It's all over the place, my brother. You talk about back pain, then you talk about videos, then you talk about brand integration.

entries.situation: A student reads out his first cold email to a wellness/supplement brand (Rachel) pitching fitness creators.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Hey Rachel, can I run something by you?

I came across [Creator]'s recent collab with Athletic Greens and thought they were really well done. I hadn't realized DS-01 contains 24 different probiotics and prebiotics. It feels like many fitness-focused audiences still haven't been meaningfully introduced to the benefits of DS-01, even though gut health is the top priority for them.

We work with a couple of creators whose audience strongly aligns with your mission:
- [Creator 1]: highly engaged, fitness-focused audience
- [Creator 2]: very interesting channel, fitness critics...

Would you be available to review their audience stats this week?
entries.points: Shorten the subject line, use the brand's colloquial name (e.g., 'AG1' instead of 'Athletic Greens'), and stop writing like a customer praising product ingredients (probiotics/prebiotics). Write like a sharp marketing manager: cut filler words like 'mission', 'fitness-focused', and 'very interesting channel', back up claims of high engagement with specific numbers (e.g., 15% engagement or US audience), and use a short, low-friction CTA without 'this week' constraints.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Can I run something by you, Rachel?

[Personalization referencing recent AG1 collab from a marketing angle]
[Mention two creator names with concrete metrics like US audience, 15% engagement rate, or stable views]

Mind if I send some audience analytics?

quote.quote: do you mind, or maybe mind if I send some audience analytics, or maybe just, mind if I send some analytics, question mark, that's all, keep it short

entries.situation: A student shows a second cold email to a brand contact (Sean) claiming a past creator had 'organic alignment' and that the student's creators 'would be an equal strong match'.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Hey Sean, can I share an idea?

Hey Sean,

I saw your recent integration with [Creator], organic alignment with his audience. We work with a few fitness and cooking creators who would be an equal strong match and would love to share with their communities.

Looking forward to sharing more details.
Best,
[Name]
entries.points: Don't state things you cannot know as objective facts—such as claiming a past collab had 'organic alignment' or that your creators 'would be an equal strong match'. Instead, compliment the execution from a marketing manager's perspective ('solid execution, nice work') and frame creator fit as your agency's opinion ('we believe', 'we are confident'). Also avoid ending with a passive statement like 'Looking forward to sharing more details.'
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Sean, can I share an idea?

Hey Sean,

I saw your recent integration with [Creator] — solid execution from the angle of a marketing manager. We work with a few fitness and cooking creators who we believe would be a strong match...

quote.quote: Be like, I saw recent integration with this guy. Say something about it, people like compliments, okay. Solid execution, nice work, amazing stuff, however you like. And then say, from the angle of a marketing manager, okay.

entries.situation: A student submits a third cold email to a food/cooking brand (Ashley) praising a chicken pot pie recipe and Smokey Chipotle flavors.

Subject: Hey Ashley, can I share something about Smokey [Product]?

I recently saw [Brand] featured in [Creator]'s video and really enjoyed the roasted chicken base recipe he used to make chicken pot pie. I'd love to share two chef channels whose audiences align naturally with your brand's voice:

Delete filler paragraphs claiming consumers 'are still unaware of great flavors', and strip out ChatGPT buzzwords like 'align naturally with your brand's voice', 'unique chef', and 'trusted name'.
entries.rewrite:

- [Creator 2]: a name in the cooking niche with consistent viewership

quote.quote: I believe many people are still unaware of great flavors like smokey chip dough and their other products simply because they haven't discovered better than the hot. Cool. That said, I'm going to remove this line. It never existed in this email, insha Allah.

entries.situation: A student submits a tech brand outreach email that opens with 'Congratulations on...' and ends by asking to share a list of influencers after already naming three creators.
entries.student_email:
Subject: [First name], a new idea to explore

Congratulations on [recent launch]! We believe that some of the creators we are in contact with, such as [Creator 1], [Creator 2], and [Creator 3], could benefit [Brand] by reviewing your latest [product].

Would you like me to share a quick list of influencers who would be a strong fit?

Kind regards
entries.points: Trim 'new' or 'explore' from '[First name], a new idea to explore' to make the subject line less salesy. Never start a cold email with 'Congratulations!'—it looks like a scam in the inbox preview and triggers spam reports; instead, start directly with 'Your recent launch of [X] was...'. Finally, if you already named three specific creators in the body, don't ask 'Would you like me to share a quick list of influencers?' in the CTA.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Jeff, an idea to explore

Your recent launch of [product] was...

quote.quote: You know, this email, the way you started it, with the congratulations on this, it's like, you know, you know, you get those spam emails from, like, Nigeria and stuff, congratulations, you earned a million thousand, whatever.

entries.situation: A student who was roasted the previous week submits an improved tech brand email with the subject line 'Jeff, how did this get past you?'
entries.student_email:
Subject: Jeff, how did this get past you?

Hey Jeff,

[Brand] launching [feature] earlier this year caught my attention as it opened [product] not just to web designers, but to app developers as well.

I work with a few creators who talk about tech and software, and I think [Creator] would be a natural fit for their audiences. For example, [Creator] has over 50% of his audience from the UK.

Should I send more details?
Thanks
entries.points: The subject line ('Jeff, how did this get past you?'), the product launch personalization, the UK audience stat, and the CTA ('Should I send more details?') are solid. To improve it further: say 'We work with' when referring to your agency (and 'I think' for your personal view), and replace vague descriptions like 'creators who talk about tech and software' with specific topics from their last three videos framed around how the brand benefits.
entries.rewrite: We work with a few creators [mention specific topics from their last 3 videos], and I think [Creator] would be a natural fit for his audience. For example, [Creator] has over 50% of his audience from the UK. Should I send more details?

quote.quote: When. you talk about agency, you will say we. When you're typing emails, watching videos, sending invoices, it's just you alone, you don't need extra help. We work a few creators who talk about tech and software, and I think this is good

entries.situation: A student submits a cold email to a high-protein food brand with the subject 'Which flavor should I choose?' and raves about their 'cracked pepper with roasted garlic' flavor.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Which flavor should I choose? [Brand]

Hey Jennifer,

Congratulations on the new flavors that [Brand] just released! The cracked pepper with roasted garlic really struck the appeal to... doesn't seem like a boring old pack of...

Is [Brand] looking to promote these flavors to appropriate audiences on social media? If so, we have a roster of high-protein recipe creators that are ready to potentially showcase your products to their mostly American viewers.
entries.points: Never write a subject line like 'Which flavor should I choose?' or rave about product flavors ('cracked pepper with roasted garlic') like a retail shopper—brands skim cold emails and will just think you want a link to buy the product. Instead: (1) use a casual, curiosity-loop subject line like texting a friend ('Your thoughts on this?', 'What do you think about it?', 'Check this'); (2) personalize around a specific past creator integration and how it was executed; (3) name two specific creators the brand hasn't worked with yet along with one golden metric (US audience, engagement rate, stable views); and (4) close with 'Should I send more details?'
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Your thoughts on this? / What do you think about it? / Check this

Saw your collaboration with [Creator] — solid job, the way he presented [Brand] while [specific action in video] was super unique and a natural fit.

Speaking of promotions, we work with [Creator 1] and [Creator 2], who have [golden metric: US audience / strong engagement rate / stable views].

Should I send more details?

quote.quote: it should be like, you're texting your friend, your thoughts on this, what do you think about it, give me your idea, check this, that's good subject line, it's catchy, they have no idea what's happening, and there is something called curiosity loop

entries.situation: A student submits two productivity brand outreach emails and a follow-up that copies a subject line from the course, promises creators 'would be happy to speak about' the brand, bolds 'Best wishes', and ends the follow-up with 'Let me know what I can do on my side. Have a great rest of your day! :)'
entries.student_email:
Email 1:
Hi [First name], I came across [Brand] and thought the adaptive training plans are a handy way to keep momentum going. We work with [niche] creators such as [Creator 1] and [Creator 2] with strong, engaged US/UK audiences who would be a fit to feature [Brand]. Should I send more details?
**Best wishes,**

Email 2:
I came across [Brand]... Your integrations are plenty. We partner with creators with a strong UK/US audience, such as [Creator 1] and [Creator 2], who would be happy to speak about [Brand]. Should I send over their analytics?
Best wishes,

Follow-up:
Hello, did you get a chance to check out my last email? Let me know what I can do on my side. Have a great rest of your day! :)
Best wishes
entries.points: Don't copy subject lines verbatim from the course because many other students use them. Don't praise product features ('adaptive training plans') instead of marketing, and don't bold 'Best wishes'. Never tell a brand that creators 'would be happy to speak about' them before checking if the creator actually wants to work with that brand; say 'we are confident they would be a good fit' instead. Finally, never say 'Let me know what I can do on my side', 'Have a great rest of your day', or use smiley faces in follow-ups—it destroys your power dynamics and makes you sound desperate.
entries.rewrite: We partner with creators with a strong UK/US audience, such as [Creator 1] and [Creator 2], who we are confident would be a good fit. Should I send over their analytics?

quote.quote: subject line from course are big no-no because you... A bunch of other guys will use it, right, and I will just use something different, and I will close the deal

entries.situation: First cold outreach email to a graphic design Instagram creator who posts logo tutorials.
entries.student_email:
Subject: the logo goat

Hi [First Name], I'm into the whiteboard setup, I see that you are doing, taking it back to basics. I noticed you've done a couple of on-brand ads with [Brand 1] and [Brand 2], et cetera. Are you open to working with more? Let me know. Best regards.

Make the personalization sniper-accurate to one specific video so it cannot be reused on anyone else, stop listing the brands they already worked with for no reason, and present a concrete offer with specific brands instead of vaguely asking 'Are you open to working with more?'.

entries.situation: Second cold outreach email to a graphic design Instagram creator who recently hit 200+ posts.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Congrats on 200+

Your IG is genuinely a gold mine of resources, I have loads saved even though I never end up using them. I notice in a lot of them, you promote services, but most are without sponsors, are you interested in more paid partnerships?
entries.points: Cut fanboy flattery like calling their page a 'gold mine of resources' that you save all the time—keep the tone strictly business. Fix the logical contradiction of saying 'most are without sponsors' and then asking if they want 'more paid partnerships'; instead, use the lack of sponsors as a transition to pitch specific brands you have in mind. Always re-read your draft from the influencer's perspective before sending.
entries.rewrite: I notice a lot of you promote services, but most of them are without sponsors. We have those sponsors. We have in mind these brands. Let me know what you think.

entries.situation: Cold outreach email to an educational creator covering economics and history ('free trade' breakdown).
entries.student_email: I watched your free trade breakdown. The way you broke down the history of the concept and where we are with it now was a refreshing historical approach. We are starting our brand outreach for this coming season. Would you want to join our selected creator list?

Never say 'We are starting our brand outreach for this coming season' or invite them to 'join our selected creator list'—saying you are just starting signals you have no brands and no experience.
entries.rewrite: The way you broke down the history of the concept and where we are with it now was a unique approach.

entries.situation: Cold outreach email to a YouTube food-challenge creator.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Question about your YouTube food challenges

I was browsing through your recent videos. It's interesting how you turn time-based constraints into an actual storyline. You must have an iron stomach for real.

I've seen a few brands lean into that style recently, so I wanted to ask directly. Do you ever consider brand partnerships that naturally fit into those challenge style videos?

Totally fine if not, just wanted to reach out and ask.
entries.points: Don't write 'Question about your YouTube food challenges' as the subject line—write the actual curiosity-inducing question itself. Cut fanboy lines like 'I was browsing through your recent videos' and weird personal remarks like 'You must have an iron stomach for real'. Pitch specific brands that fit their challenge videos and replace the weak 'Totally fine if not, just wanted to reach out and ask' with a direct CTA.
entries.rewrite: It's interesting how you turn time-based constraints into an actual storyline. Since your channel is all about this, we thought brands like [Brand A], [Brand B], [Brand C] would be a nice fit for you. Let me know.

quote.quote: Question about your YouTube food challenges, okay, so, this subject line should be your idea. Be like, hmm, which question should I ask him about YouTube food challenges? And then, make the question, and put it in your subject line. Do not over-explain

entries.situation: Cold outreach email and two follow-ups to an automotive creator building a V2 drift truck.
entries.student_email:
Hi [First Name], we saw your drift truck V2 paint job. The purple to black shift, depending on the angle, turned out solid. You work with a brand like [Brand 1] and [Brand 2]. We got a few brands in mind in the automotive and shop equipment space that could help fund the wide body build or full double down prep.

Follow-up 1: Hi [First Name], following up to see if you had a moment to consider this, would be great to connect if the timing is right.

Follow-up 2: Just looking back on my earlier message, I think there's some solid crossover between your builds and what we are working on.
entries.points: Remove 'We saw your drift truck V2 paint job' and start directly with 'The purple to black shift depending on the angle turned out solid on your new V2 drift truck' (plus a light joke like 'that's probably plus 20 horsepowers'). Drop the robotic 'You work with X, we got Y' phrasing and name the specific brands that can fund their build. Avoid ultra-short 1-line follow-ups that trigger spam filters; write 3-sentence follow-ups that remind them of the brands mentioned and include a clear CTA.
entries.rewrite: The purple to black shift depending on the angle turned out solid on your new V2 drift truck—that's probably plus 20 horsepowers. Since you started your full double down prep, we got you—there are a couple of brands you might be interested in: [Brand 1], [Brand 2].

quote.quote: Something, something, something, from your subject, from your personalization, or maybe this, since you started your double prep belt or something, full double prep, we got you, there are a couple of brands you might be interested in, these are, da, da, da

entries.situation: Cold outreach email and follow-up to a classic car restoration creator working on a 1966 Mustang Fastback.
entries.student_email:
We caught your video on the 1966 Mustang Fastback build. The vanilla bean concept is smart, taking an inline-six automatic and turning it into a practical daily driver classic is a solid angle that sets it apart from the usual V8 builds. I know you partner with brands like [Brand 1] and [Brand 2], both strong fits. I have a few others in mind that could align well with your channel and help support future build projects. Would you like me to keep you in the loop for the next campaign we are running?

Follow-up: Hope all's been good your side. Just looping back to see if sponsorships are something you're looking at this season.
entries.points: Don't use ChatGPT to summarize video transcripts into robotic technical compliments; watch 30 seconds of the video and write your genuine first thought. Don't praise their existing sponsors—instead lead with helping speed up their future build projects and name specific brands that would be a good fit. Replace weak CTAs ('Would you like me to keep you in the loop...') and passive follow-ups ('Just looping back to see if sponsorships are something you're looking at this season') with direct CTAs and build-focused follow-ups ('those builds won't finish themselves').
entries.rewrite:
To speed up those future build projects, we have something for you. Brands like [Brand 1] and [Brand 2] probably would be a good fit. Let me know what you think about this.

Follow-up: Those builds won't finish themselves—I'm following up on my previous email.

entries.situation: An automotive niche student submits a cold email to a brand referencing a past creator integration without naming the creator, then pitching a car-building creator with an 8% engagement rate.

Also bringing up to 500 coffee options was a good way to show the value of subscription. One creator we can bring for trade is this guy. He repairs and builds cars with a chill weekend project style. Nothing overcomplicated. No screaming, shouting, and an 8% engagement rate. Want to see more details first. Best regards

Avoid repeating the brand's name in the offer ('One of the creators we can bring to you' instead of 'for [Brand]'), tie the creator's specific style ('chill weekend project style, no screaming, shouting') directly to how it aligns with the brand, and drop the word 'first' from the CTA.

entries.situation: A student submits a final break-up follow-up to a brand saying 'I'll think this is a pass for...' and 'If things change, I'm one reply away.'
