entries.student_email: Hi Robert, Abraka Drywalls' use of the Ultraflex trowel in a real job is a perfect example of authentic product demonstration. The trowel makes skimming easier and delivers neat finish. OX Tools is running campaigns aiming at UK tradesmen to raise awareness of new products. Kirk Johnstone, a UK plastering creator we work with, averaging 2K views... He can demonstrate OX Tools in real plastering jobs, driving awareness and credibility. Do you want to view Kirk's audience information?
entries.points: Keep cold emails around 50 words max. Cut customer-sounding product fluff ('makes skimming easier and delivers neat finish'), don't explain the brand's own campaign to them, and don't mention low view numbers like 2K views. Upgrade the CTA to a cliffhanger choice ('Should I send his details only or a couple of more creators that we work with?'), never email the same person twice with the same pitch, and completely change the personalization when emailing two different contacts at the same company.
entries.rewrite: Hi Robert, Abraka Drywalls' use of the Ultraflex trowel in a real job is a perfect example of authentic product demonstration. Kirk Johnstone, a UK plastering creator we work with, can demonstrate OX Tools in real plastering jobs, driving awareness and credibility. Should I send his details only or a couple of more creators that we work with?

quote.quote: If you're sending to two people from the same company, which probably you try to do that, like to A and B, I usually change personalization completely. It's a new thing, right? And then, offer could be the same or similar.

entries.situation: A student submits a cold email to a travel fintech brand with the subject line '[Brand] product features and [Creator]', opening with 'I hope you are well. I've reached out to your marketing manager...', claiming their creators 'are perfect for demonstrating these features', and ending with 'Could you point me to the best person?'
entries.student_email:
Subject: [Brand] product features and [Creator]
I hope you are well. I've reached out to your marketing manager, but wanted to connect regarding specific product features. I came across [Creator]'s video, and it really showcased digital card tracking and fee-free card exchange. Our creators, like [Creator 1] and [Creator 2], are perfect for demonstrating these features to their travel audiences. Could you point me to the best person?
entries.points: Replace policy-sounding subject lines with short curiosity hooks ('[First name], check this', '[First name], thoughts', 'Did you lead this?'). Cut 'I hope you are well' and move any mention of reaching out to another colleague out of the first line. Never just claim your creators 'are perfect'—explain specifically why their content fits. Finally, start outreach with top executives (CEO, COO, CFO) or marketing managers rather than pitching non-marketing gatekeepers, and if you do ask a gatekeeper for a referral, simply ask who to reach out to without pitching the full offer.
entries.rewrite: I've been struggling to find the right guy. We have a couple of influencers we believe would be a good fit for your brand. Who should I reach out to?

quote.quote: Okay, something product features and something creator. Subject line is bad. Okay? You know, it's been like policy stuff. No. First name, check this. First name, thoughts. Take, take inspiration from this guy. Did you lead this?

entries.situation: A student submits a brand outreach email with the subject line 'Influencer partnership', praising how the brand's gear 'revolutionized travel vlogging', pitching three different creators with subscriber counts and gear usage, and ending with 'Would you be open to exploring a partnership?'
entries.student_email:
Subject: Influencer partnership
I hope you're well. I saw the Tech I Travel With series featuring [Brand], and it's a perfect showcase for how your gear has revolutionized travel vlogging. [Creator 1] and [Creator 2] are cinematic specialists who already use [Brand] to level up their production, while [Creator 3] (2.25 million) uses [Product] as his primary tool in the field. They can authentically demonstrate both the professional quality... Would you be open to exploring a partnership?
entries.points: Never use 'Influencer partnership' as a subject line because it comes straight from the course, is heavily overused, and gets filtered by AI inbox tools. Cut the overly salesy, multi-creator pitch—save detailed roster breakdowns for the second or third email after the brand replies—and don't ask a marketing manager 'Would you be open to exploring a partnership?' since finding partnerships is already their job.
entries.rewrite: I watched this video, saw your app. Here I am. I have this guy, he's an amazing fit for you, and here is why.

quote.quote: Would you be open to exploring partnership? No, no, no. Guys, if you're reaching out to digital marketing manager, influencer marketing manager, they are. That's their job to find good match. So don't ask those questions. Go straight to the point, okay?

entries.situation: A student who hardly gets brand responses submits a multi-paragraph, book-length cold email praising a robotic vacuum's UV stain detection, RGB camera, mopping power, and self-cleaning base.
entries.student_email: I just went through the announcement of [Product], and it genuinely feels like one of the most interesting product leaps in the robotic vac category. The way it blended UV stain detection and RGB camera, high-intensity mopping power, and self-cleaning base gives creators a lot to work with. It's the kind of tech that naturally lends itself to visual, trust-building content. Several of our creators already produce strong results in areas like hidden mess cleaning, pet-friendly home routines, and smart home optimization. The stain-reveal visuals and the proof-of-clean angle would translate perfectly into before-and-after tests, real-time demos, and educational content that their audiences constantly engage with. I'd be keen to see whether there's room to collaborate around [Product] or any upcoming launches...
entries.points: Demolish book-length cold emails down to under 50 words written at a 10-year-old reading level, because the only goal of the first email is to get a reply. Strip out all ad-copy fluff listing product specs and keep just one brief personalization line, one sentence on the creators' niche results, and a simple yes/no CTA ('Should I send more details?').
entries.rewrite: I just went through the announcement of [Product], and it genuinely feels like one of the most interesting product leaps in the robotic vac category. Several of our creators already produce strong results in areas like hidden mess cleaning, pet-friendly home routines, and smart home optimization. Should I send more details?

quote.quote: This is why you're not gathering sponsors. No one is reading books in emails, okay? If you want to read book, you probably sit down, open it, and you usually, we usually choose books that we want to read

entries.situation: The same student submits multi-paragraph brand follow-ups pitching individual UK comedy creators in full detail before getting a reply.
entries.student_email: Bringing this back to you because something interesting popped up... Following on from my last note, I wanted to share two UK creators who would fit really naturally into this style—light, memorable, and easy for viewers to recall. First guy: UK-based comedy creator...
entries.points: Follow-ups are short reminders meant to direct the recipient back to your first email, not multi-paragraph pitches. Keep the follow-up to a single sentence ('Following on from my last note, I would like to share two UK creators who can fit naturally into this style') plus a strong CTA, and save detailed creator profiles for after the brand replies or gets on a call.
entries.rewrite: Following on from my last note, I would like to share two UK creators who can fit naturally into this style.

quote.quote: I would like to share two UK creators who can fit naturally into this one. And then CTA, strong, no, strong as coffee. First guy, UK based comedy creator. nah, nah, nah, nah, This is for email once when they are interested.

entries.situation: A student submits a cold outreach email to a finance creator named Nolan pitching brand collaborations with Morning Brew and Public.
entries.student_email:
Subject: You were right about that sort of flop.
Hi, Nolan. Calling the recent oil crash, a micro shift, not a pullback, stood out. You'll reframe volatility into a clear long-term opportunity. That kind of simple breakdown aligns with brands like Morning Brew and Orpublic. We help creators in finance land long-term brand collaboration. You want me to map a few sponsor ideas for your next upload?
entries.points: Cut the specific topic out of the subject line to create a curiosity loop, simplify 'land long-term brand collaborations' to 'get more partnerships' so you do not overpromise, put a line break before the CTA, and avoid mentioning 'sponsors' in the CTA when you do not have a sponsor yet so they do not immediately demand a budget.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: You're right about that.
Hi, Nolan. Calling the recent oil crash, a micro shift, not a pullback, stood out. You'll reframe volatility into a clear long-term opportunity. That kind of simple breakdown aligns with brands like Morning Brew and Orpublic. We help creators in finance get more partnerships.

Are you interested in this one? How does this sound to you?

quote.quote: This CTA as it is could be a little bit dangerous because you are mentioning sponsors instead of them, you know, if you have no sponsors, CTA should be like leaning more toward, are you interested in this one?

entries.situation: A student in the finance niche submits three follow-up emails to an influencer that repeatedly mention sponsor options, compare the creator to similar creators who monetize, and promise to help land paid sponsors.
entries.student_email:
Follow-up 1: Just resurfacing this, open to seeing what sponsors options could look like.
Follow-up 2: I've seen similar creators monetize... wouldn't need to outline a fits for you.
Follow-up 3: I can help you start lending paid sponsors aligned with your previous, with your years. Should I move forward?
entries.points: Stop mentioning 'sponsors' in every follow-up, never compare creators to other creators because of their ego, and avoid scammy 'I can help you land paid sponsors' phrasing. Use a 4-email follow-up structure: (1) soft check-in on the ideas/brands from email one, (2) acknowledge their busy inbox and ask their thoughts, (3) low-friction 'Either way, let me know', and (4) ask whether to circle back in a future quarter.
entries.rewrite:
Follow-up 1: I'm following up on my previous email. Are you interested to see what kind of ideas I have in my mind? What do you think about these brands that I mentioned above?
Follow-up 2: You've been getting a lot of emails, I get it. But what about this one? Let me know, what do you think?
Follow-up 3: Checking in on you again in case my email landed in spam. What do you think about these brands that I mentioned? Either way, let me know.
Follow-up 4: Okay, I get it, you are not interested or maybe timing is not good. Should I circle back in Q3?

quote.quote: I would say fourth email with influencers, I think that's enough. And more like, okay, I get it, you are not interested or maybe timing is not good. Should I circle back in Q3 in a couple of days? Let me know.

entries.situation: A student in the productivity/tech niche submits two influencer outreach emails generated by ChatGPT that quote full video titles and use robotic AI phrasing.
entries.student_email:
Email 1 Subject: Quick idea from your latest Apple video.
I love your recent M5 and Max feels like cheating video. The way you break down performance versus price really helps viewers make sense of it. Since you work with Bellroy and Moano, I thought brands like Twelve South, Elgato or Obsidian could similarly resonate with your audience. Would you be open to a quick chat about potential collaboration?

Email 2: Hi, Luke. I enjoyed your Cool Tech under 1,500 video. They make discovering practical gadgets so easy. The way that... I was wondering if you're considering featuring brands like this and this.
entries.points: Make the subject line vaguer to spark curiosity, and never copy-paste ChatGPT-written emails that quote full video titles ('I love your recent [Title] video') and use cliches like 'The way you break down...'. Write like a real human and only use AI to critique your draft without rewriting it.
entries.rewrite: Subject: Something from your latest video / Watching that video gave me an idea

quote.quote: if you are using AI, I cannot stop you from using ChatGPT, don't let me rewrite your email. Use it more like, hey, would you let me know what is working, what is not, how should I improve my email without changing it?

entries.situation: A student in the tech niche who keeps getting ghosted by brands submits a long cold outreach email to a brand marketing manager along with a fifth email to another marketing manager.
entries.student_email:
Email 1: I am Ammar, I saw Tina's demos of [Brand]'s model console feature and thought it showcased the product well. I'm reaching out on behalf of an influencer, whose audience includes tech-savvy professionals and enthusiasts who actively seek out the latest AI discovery and automation tools, similar to Tina's followers. I'd like to explore potential influencer partnership or campaign and determine whether the creator I have in mind is a good fit for marketing's priorities. Looking forward to hearing their thoughts.

Email 5 Subject: Replacing a week of work, what comes next?
Hi, we spotted recent work with [Creator], where they discussed the platform's ability to replace nearly a full week of work using Cloud Work Stack. On the other hand, we represent the creator...
entries.points: Keep brand outreach short (around 50 words), cut self-introductions ('I am Ammar'), avoid saying 'we spotted' or 'on behalf of an influencer', strip out corporate fluff about 'determining marketing priorities', and make the offer a simple, direct discovery pitch.
entries.rewrite: I have this guy who would be [X, Y, and Z]. In our opinion, it's good. What do you think? Let me know.

quote.quote: I'd like to explore potential influencer partnership or campaign and determine whether the creator I have in mind is a good fit for marketing's priorities. Looking forward to hearing their thoughts. Guys, what is this? What is this? What do you think? This is fluff.

entries.situation: The tech-niche student submits three brand follow-up emails: the first says 'No worries at all if the timing or fit isn't there. Please let me know', the second is copied verbatim from the course, and the third asks if the brand has any questions.
entries.student_email:
Follow-up 1: Just resurfacing this to the top of your inbox in case it was missed. Would love to share a few details about the creator we have in mind for [Brand]. No worries at all if the timing or fit isn't there. Please let me know.
Follow-up 2: Hi [First Name], Just checking in to see if you had a chance to review my last email.
Follow-up 3: Top of the morning, Jack. Circling back to see if you have any questions about my previous message or messages. I'm looking forward to speaking with you.
entries.points: Do not undermine your first follow-up by saying 'no worries if the timing or fit isn't there' right before 'please let me know'—instead project confidence. Save 'let me know if you have any questions' for the first follow-up rather than the third when the prospect is ignoring you, and add a closing follow-up at the end.
entries.rewrite: Follow-up 1: We are confident this collaboration could bring [X and Y]. What do you think? Please let me know. / Hey, I'm following up on my first email, let me know if you have any questions.

quote.quote: Questions are for this guy, for first follow-up. Hey, I'm following up on my first email, let me know if you have any questions. You know, questions in third follow-up, where the guy obviously is not that interested

entries.situation: A student submits two influencer outreach emails with fanboy subject lines ('Keep up the great work', 'Jack, hope you made it') and repeatedly tells the creator their channel is a 'great fit'.
entries.student_email:
Email 1 Subject: Keep up the great work
Hey, comparing and reviewing [Product] and their features helps the audience understand the difference and keeps them engaged. Keep up the great work. We see you've been working with brands... Therefore, I think your channel could be a great fit for a couple of brands we have in mind. Would you be open to discussing this?

Email 2 Subject: Jack, hope you made it.
Testing the design using 3D printing was a smart move, but I hope the final aluminum version actually improves the cooling of the [item]. The type of content you make today makes your channel a great fit for several brands we have in mind. Would you be open to brand partnerships? Share your thoughts.
entries.points: Never use fanboy praise like 'Keep up the great work' or overly familiar subject lines like 'hope you made it'—keep your tone professional because the creator does not know you. Never tell an influencer their channel is a 'great fit', because flattering their ego causes them to inflate their rates by thousands of dollars.
entries.rewrite:
Email 1: Comparing and reviewing features was a nice idea. I'm sure your viewers loved it. I'm wondering if you would be open to more partnerships...
Email 2: On the other hand, let's make your life a bit easier. We have a couple of brands in line, and we thought they could align with your content. What do you think?

quote.quote: Guys, no matter what you do, don't put this in subject line, okay? Keep up the great work is a fan email, is not a marketing agency email, okay? Keep up. the great work. I'm your huge fan. Don't do this

entries.situation: A student reaches out to a tech influencer with the subject line 'Tec Brands, Profitable Collab', a generic opener about a keyboard video, confusing phrasing saying 'We are currently looking to sponsor influencers', and name-dropping mega-brands like AMD, MSI, and Apple.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Tec Brands, Profitable Collab

Hi [first name or team],

Just saw your most recent video and the keyboard feature were really nice. I liked how you describe its features.

We are currently looking to sponsor influencers and I think your channel is comparable with the niche we are in. We are looking at working [with brands] such as AMD, MSI, Apple, and much more.

Let me know if you're interested so we can go further.
entries.points: Drop overused openers like 'Just saw', avoid generic fanboy compliments that could be sent to any tech creator, do not say 'we are looking to sponsor influencers' (which makes you sound like the brand paying out of pocket), and do not name-drop unrealistic mega-brands like Apple. Instead, state that you are gathering a list of influencers for upcoming campaigns with realistic niche brands.
entries.rewrite: We are gathering, we are collecting, we are whatever, list of influencers for upcoming campaigns for these, these brands, and much more.

quote.quote: Just saw your most recent video and the keyboard feature were really nice. I liked how you describe its features. So, guys, from one to 10, how bad this personalization is? How ChetGPT this personalization?

entries.situation: A student (Zhir) with a warm travel/eSIM brand lead emails a creator praising their past ad ('Showing how you use the service yourself is much better than just sugarcoat stating the obvious') and asks if they can take on a 60-90 second integration for December/January.
entries.student_email:
Subject: [Brand] X [Influencer]

Hey [Name],

The ad you did for [Brand] was very clever. Showing how you use the service yourself is much better than just sugarcoat stating the obvious.

We want you to do something similar for [Brand]. We are in talks [with them]... Can you take on a 60 to 90 second integration for December/January?
entries.points: Using actual names in the '[Brand] X [Influencer]' subject line is good and the email got a reply, but avoid saying 'Showing how you use the service yourself is much better than sugarcoat stating the obvious' as it gives away power dynamics; depersonalize the compliment ('Showcasing the product is much better than just talking about it'). Combine 'We want you to do something similar' and 'We are in talks' into one smooth sentence, and avoid restricting the pitch to a 60-90 second integration if dedicated videos (which pay much more) are an option.
entries.rewrite: Showcasing the product, you know, is, you know, much better than just talking about it.

quote.quote: instead of saying, showing how you, just say, you know, showcasing the product, you know, is, you know, much better than just talking about it, you know, it's like the same thing, but it's not like attached

entries.situation: A student writes to a marathon runner: 'Your last marathon at 3:15 pace really stood out. Holding that over 40 kilometers is impressive. I'm currently selecting creators for our next brand outreach... If this sounds relevant, I can share more.'
entries.student_email:
Hi [first name],

Your last marathon at 3:15 pace really stood out. Holding that over 40 kilometers is impressive.

I'm currently selecting creators for our next brand outreach... If this sounds relevant, I can share more.
entries.points: Replace stiff ChatGPT flattery ('Holding that over 40 kilometers is impressive') with a light human joke about their pace. Use 'we' for agency actions ('we are selecting') and 'I' only for solo actions ('I saw'), and rotate 3 to 5 versions of your offer and CTA so identical templates don't send you to spam.
entries.rewrite: Last marathon, how you did it, your approach, your tips, this and that. I wish I can run more than 100 meters with the same pace.

quote.quote: See, the same thing, you will end up in spam. We spoke about it, right? So, have three to five versions of this one. And as agency, we. As something that you can do alone, I saw, I'm writing, I'm doing, it's only you.

entries.situation: A student couldn't find a gaming creator's email, so he messaged him during a live stream and followed up via Discord DM. The creator replied positively ('Hey, yes, depends on the brand, and what you guys have in mind'), and the student responded with a long wall of text naming Logitech, Razer, and HyperX, explaining he wants to pitch him, asking multiple audience/media kit questions at once, and adding a smiley emoji, causing the creator to ask 'So you're from an agency or...'
entries.student_email:
[Initial Discord DM:] I have seen your last stream, and I thought that is a kind of absurd. I also noticed that stream wasn't sponsored, are you up to working with brands?
[Creator:] Hey, yes, depends on the brand, and what you guys have in mind
[Student Reply:] Thanks for getting back to me. We are actually thinking about pitching you to some brands like Logitech, Razor, HyperX. We also got a few more brands in mind to make sure this is a good match. I would like to get a better understanding of your audience... [asks multiple questions + smiley emoji]
[Creator:] So you're from an agency or...
entries.points: Reaching out via livestream and Discord DM when no email is available is great creativity, and the short initial message worked well. However, once the creator replies, do not bombard them with your internal pitching process and multiple qualification questions in one run-on paragraph. Use line breaks, take it piece by piece with one question at a time (e.g., naming a few brands and asking what they think, or asking for audience analytics), and avoid graphic emojis.
entries.rewrite: To make sure it's a good match, would you share your audience? / Some brands like this and that, what do you think?

quote.quote: What I don't like with this email, with this here answer is reply, da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da No, we are not doing it. Piece by piece. To make sure it's a good match, would you share your audience?

entries.situation: When a creator/manager replies asking to learn more about the specific brands the student represents so they can evaluate alignment, the student replies: 'Thanks for getting back to me. To clarify, I'm not representing any brands yet. Brand outreach begins next month... We are planning to approach...'
entries.student_email:
[Creator/Manager:] We'd love to learn more about specific brands you are representing here, we can then evaluate if there is a potential alignment and look to explore partnership development, looking forward to continue the conversation, high regards.

[Student Reply:] Thanks for getting back to me. To clarify, I'm not representing any brands yet. Brand outreach begins next month... We are planning to approach... I think they could align well...
entries.points: Never tell an interested creator or manager that you are not representing any brands yet and won't start brand outreach until next month—that immediately kills the conversation. You do not have to answer a question on their exact terms; steer the conversation by saying you have a couple of brands in mind that would fit their channel and ask qualifying questions like how many integrations they can take on.
entries.rewrite: We have brands, for you we have brands in mind... We have couple of brands that would be a good fit for you, how many you can do?

quote.quote: So, okay, I'm not telling I don't have brands. We have brands, for you we have brands in mind, it's a much better answer. We have couple of brands that would be a good fit for you, how many you can do

entries.situation: A student submits a cold email to a tech creator (Liam at CreativeTag) with a long AI-sounding compliment and a pitch stating 'I connect brands with creators'.

I connect brands with creators with whose audience rely on tools like these. So I wanted to ask if brand collaboration would interest you.

entries.rewrite: I like how Credit Act focuses on practical buying advice and testing, especially, watch this before you buy videos.

entries.rewrite: We've been in this space for some time. And we are helping influencers get more collaborations, get more partnerships.

entries.situation: A student pitches a DIY/construction brand with the subject line 'did you take charge on this', a drawn-out compliment on a past sponsorship, and an offer proposing 'a very similar YouTuber' targeting a 'very similar yet different audience'.
entries.student_email:
Subject: did you take charge on this

Hi, [Brand's] YouTube integration was really on the spot. Having [product] naturally embedded into the video made for sponsorship segment that can never be skipped. Kudos to the team behind it. I am proposing a very similar YouTuber, also in the DIY space, but much better views and engagement rate. He works on wide range of projects, including metal and steel restorations, allowing us to target very similar yet different audience.
entries.points: Make the subject line shorter and more intriguing, keep the entire brand email around 50 words, cut fluff like 'Kudos to the team behind it', and never pitch a creator as 'the exact same thing' a brand already sponsored—lead with unique benefits like stable average views, long-term partnership potential, or what the creator is uniquely known for.
entries.rewrite: Subject: is this for you / something for you / you should check this one

quote.quote: did you take charge on this, you know, I would make it, I will make it a bit shorter, maybe, is this for you, or something for you, you should check this one, you know, those things, to keep that curiosity.

entries.situation: A student submits several influencer outreach emails in the travel/camping niche that all follow the exact same copy-paste template starting with 'Just watched your [video]...' and ending with 'Are you currently open to brand partnership? Let me know.'
entries.student_email: Just watched your Simpsons Florence Luxury Resort video in Kandy. The mix of nature and experience in your last video made the trip feel really immersive. I believe brands like Booking.com, Samsonite, and DJI would align with the luxury travel and family adventure content you are creating. Are you currently open to brand partnership? Let me know.
entries.points: Delete 'Just watched your [video]' so the email opens directly with the observation (creating curiosity instead of immediately screaming sponsorship), trim fluff from the brand fit sentence, use a single direct question CTA ('Is this something you're looking for?'), and vary your email structure so spam filters do not flag repetitive copy-paste patterns.
entries.rewrite: The mix of nature and experience in your last video made the trip feel really immersive. Brands like Booking.com, Samsonite, and DJI would align well with content you are creating. Is this something you're looking for?

quote.quote: I struggled also with I saw, I checked, blah, blah, blah. You type everything and you just remove the part. It's easy. Like perfect mix of adventure and comfort on the road in your last video. Boom.

entries.situation: A student sends a very long email to a travel brand naming two past YouTube sponsors, describing the creator's audience in detail ('border crossing, travel, remote transport... accidents, dispute'), and citing a 4.4% engagement rate and 1M views on the creator's last video.
entries.student_email: We've noticed your recent partnership with [Creator 1] and [Creator 2] on YouTube. It seems like you are balancing targeting between frequent and beginner travelers, and that's a smart move. The audience of the creator that we represent follow hidden destination adventure, border crossing, travel, remote transport, and off-grid in Americas. They're actually the type of travelers who need to think ahead about accidents, dispute. With 4.4% engagement rate and 1 million views on our creator's last video, we believe there is strong opportunity to create authentic content while showing your product during trips, building trust and purchase intent. Open to discuss a partnership?
entries.points: Cut the email down to 50 words by removing the sentence naming past YouTube sponsors, deleting all the audience description fluff, and pitching stable views and engagement rather than one video's stats—treat the first email like inviting someone to check out a store rather than trying to close the whole deal at once.
entries.rewrite: It seems like you are balancing targeting between frequent and beginner travelers, and that's a smart move. With strong engagement rate and strong, stable views, we believe there is strong opportunity to create authentic content while showing your product during trips. If you got this far, are you open to partnerships?

quote.quote: Look, we've noticed your recent partnership with this guy and this guy on YouTube. Why would you mention brand and influencer? Make no sense. It seems like you are balancing targeting between frequent and beginner travelers, and that's a smart move.

entries.situation: A student submits an initial outreach email to an outdoors influencer referencing their Mongolia trip and Toyota Priuses.
entries.student_email: Subject: [Name] sounds good? Hey [Name], Wow, found out from your Mongolia trip that it really is full of Toyota Priuses, learned something new. Given the outdoor content, brands like XYZ make sense for your channel. We find and introduce them to you and handle the boring stuff, so you could spend your time better elsewhere, like content. Does this sound good to you?
entries.points: Never start your personalization with 'Wow' and flip the phrasing so it reads naturally. Make the niche reference more specific than just 'outdoor content', focus the offer on the specific pain point of going back and forth with brands rather than 'spending time elsewhere', and consider a more direct CTA like 'Are you interested?'.
entries.rewrite: The Mongolia trip taught me about how popular Toyota Priuses are—learned something new. Given your content, brands like XYZ would make sense for your channel. We find and introduce them to you and handle the boring stuff so you don't need to spend all of your time going back and forth. Are you interested?

quote.quote: maybe it's better to say, you know, to focus on pain, pain only, be like, so you should, you don't need to spend all of your time going back and forth with influencers, stuff like that.

entries.situation: A student in the automotive niche submits an email with the subject line '40 grand into a K truck' and personalization summarizing what the creator did in the video.
entries.student_email: Subject: 40 grand into a K truck. You spent eight months and started the video by questioning whether it was worth it or not—most creators would have left that out. On a side note, we gather a list of influencers for brands such as Lectron and Russell Tools, and your build seems like a match for those..
entries.points: Turn the subject line into a curiosity-inducing question (e.g., '40 grand into a K truck - is it worth it?') so the creator opens the email to see what you mean. Avoid AI-sounding personalization that just narrates the creator's actions ('you spent eight months, you did this'), and do not end sentences with double periods ('..').
entries.rewrite: Subject: 40 grand into a K truck - is it worth it?

quote.quote: 40 grand into a K truck. I would say, is it worth it? You know, he has no idea what you're talking about, but once when he opens your email, you're like, yeah, okay, makes sense.

entries.situation: A student in the automotive niche submits a fifth email with the subject 'Oil pressure doesn't matter' and repeats the same 'We are gathering a list of influencers for brands such as...' offer.
entries.student_email: Subject: Oil pressure doesn't matter. Hey [Name], opening the video with 'oil pressure doesn't matter' is a great way to make... We are gathering a list of influencers for brands such as [Brand A] and [Brand B], and your channel seems like a good fit.
entries.points: Make the subject line more provocative or framed as a question (e.g., 'Did you just start a war?' or 'You made them angry') to spark curiosity. Also vary your offer across emails—test offers with specific brand names and offers without brand names to see what converts best.
entries.rewrite: Subject: Did you just start a war? / You made them angry

quote.quote: maybe you should say something about this, did you just started a word? Boom, there you go. Or you made them angry. You made them angry. What is this guy talking about?

entries.situation: A student submits long brand outreach emails in the tech/gaming setup niche claiming 'We represent [Creator]', referencing small moments from previous sponsored videos, and repeating the exact same offer paragraph across drafts.
entries.student_email: I noticed that [Brand] has sponsored content creators in the space, [Creator] in particular did a really good job at showcasing [product]. We represent [Creator], a YouTuber who is constantly posting aesthetic gaming vlogs and setup tours, averaging 70k views over the last three months, with a large US-based audience aged 18 to 35. We're reaching out on his behalf because he already featured products in his vlogs, and we think his content style would make him a very authentic and seamless fit to showcase your product to an aligned audience. Should I send over more details? We're happy to discuss further how we can make this work.
entries.points: Keep brand outreach emails under 6 sentences total and cut the offer length by 50%. Never say 'We represent [Creator]'—say 'We work with [Creator]'. Do not personalize to brands by referencing tiny moments inside a creator's video, because brand managers don't watch every video; make sure the personalization aligns with the offer. Replace vague fluff ('very authentic and seamless fit') with specific reasons why the creator benefits the brand, vary your offers across emails to avoid spam filters, and end immediately after the CTA question without adding extra closing fluff.
entries.rewrite: We work with [Creator], who averages 70k views with most of his audience aged 18 to 35 in the US, and [specific reason how the brand benefits]. Should I send over more details?

quote.quote: make this one as the most important part of your email, but make it, make it short, make it short, like 50% short, with large-based audience, with, if you want to say, with mostly of his audience age, 1835.

entries.situation: A student shares a draft of his cold outreach email to a brand in the meeting chat for the coach to critique.
entries.student_email: I appreciate the thoughtful execution ... Closely align with your brand. ... I'd be glad to share ... Looking forward to your response so I can share the details.
entries.points: Cut cringe flattery and keep the email very short and concise. Include specific details about your influencers so the email cannot be generically swapped to any niche. Replace weak closing lines like 'looking forward to your response' and 'if' clauses with a direct, low-friction CTA that makes it easy for the brand to reply.
entries.rewrite: I'd be happy to ... let me know this, I can do this, I can send this

quote.quote: Okay. I appreciate the thoughtful execution is a big cringe. Okay. But, uh, yeah, keep it, keep it more concise. Keep it very short. Right. Closely align with your brand. And you're not mentioning anything specific about. your influences

entries.situation: The second student's first follow-up email to MasterClass briefly highlighted audience overlap without bombarding them with extra numbers and asked them to check the first email.
entries.student_email: Circling back here — there's a clear overlap between MasterClass's audience and the viewers our creators bring in. Worth a quick look at their profiles? Talk soon
entries.points: A short, low-pressure first follow-up that points out the clear overlap between the brand's audience and the creators' viewers without dumping more analytics is effective.

quote.quote: So, no pressure, just, hey, check my first. Check my first email. Yeah, yeah, 100%.

entries.situation: A third student submitted a sequence to a wireless filmmaking gear brand's generic support inbox starting with subject 'You deserve more coverage', lecturing the brand on smartphone camera demand, naming two of their products in the offer, and asking them to forward the email to the marketing team.
entries.student_email:
Subject: You deserve more coverage

Hi there, With more people getting into content creation and smartphone cameras improving, the demand for wireless filmmaking gear is growing. For that reason, I believe that [X5-M] and [X6-S] deserve more coverage. We work with filmmaking and tech creators focused on mobile cameras who could be a great fit for the brand. Could you forward this to the marketing team? I'm sure they'll be interested.

Follow-up 1: Checking back in, in case my email didn't reach you. Let me know if you had a chance to pass it along to the marketing team.

Follow-up 2: Just following up in case you missed this. We're working with filmmakers across YouTube and Instagram whose audience could be in the market for your product. Could you point me to the right contact?
entries.points: Make cold emails frictionless and focused on positive outputs you can achieve for the brand rather than lecturing them on their own industry or repeating product names inside the offer. When emailing generic 'support@' or 'contact@' addresses (unlike 'sales@' or 'partnerships@'), skip the long script and simply ask who the right person is to speak with.
entries.rewrite: Hey, I have [brief value offer]. Are you the right person for this, or who should I reach out to?

quote.quote: I think this is not necessary, because if a brand is too small, I think one guy is doing a bunch of stuff. Yeah. And he's the CEO, he's marketing manager, he has finances, and he's everything.

entries.situation: A student pitches a minimalism YouTube creator (James) to a brand (reMarkable Paper Pro) referencing their past partnership with Ali Abdaal.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Minimalist creator open to partnership - [Creator Name]

Hi Helen, I saw your partnership with Ali Abdaal, and wanted to share a similar but more aligned creator. Our creator, James, the leading voice in minimalism who averages 180k views. Given the alignment, we are confident a YouTube integration showcasing the Paper Pro as a distraction-free tool for learning would convert well. Would you like me to send over his channel link? Kind regards, Ishaq, [Agency Name]
entries.points: Do not reveal the entire pitch and creator name in the subject line, avoid opening with 'I saw your partnership with...', do not use bold text, do not brag about view counts or mention your agency in the first email, and write a casual chatting-style email rather than a sales pitch.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: minimalist / small creator?

Hey, based on your previous collaboration with this guy, we had an idea that this creator would be good. His major audience is US. Should I send details? Let me know if you're interested in something like this.

quote.quote: And by the way, if you want to brag about views, first email is not placed for you. So don't do this. Be more, more, Insha Allah, be more casual with your emails and don't mention agency.

entries.situation: A student pitches a digital optimization creator (Jumbo) to a security/tech brand using the 'Creator x Brand' subject line.
entries.student_email:
Subject: [Creator] X [Brand]

Hi Salah, Jumbo is a highly aligned creator because his audience is obsessed with optimizing their digital environment. His viewers are looking for tools to secure their online presence... Should I send over his channel link for [Brand] to see his channel?
entries.points: Starting directly with why the creator is aligned is good, but push the creator's name slightly later in the sentence, avoid making salesy claims about what the creator's audience is 'obsessed with' or 'looking for', and keep the call-to-action short and direct.
entries.rewrite: One highly aligned, super niche-down creator is Jumbo... Should I send his details?

quote.quote: Obsessed with optimistic, I would say still too salesy. You know, we don't know this. So audience is a huge question mark. Trust me. Guys, don't do down that road. Try to avoid.

entries.situation: A student pitches a meal-prep creator to an AI calorie-tracking app employee using a playful, slang-heavy style and @username handles.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Planning 2026 - don't forget this

Hey [First name], Surprise, surprise. Your work with @[username] proves that chicken is fine just the way it is. We work with another guy that likes to keep things simple. Kush from @[username] is a meal prep creator with a 90% American audience. I think he can also use your app to break it down in his next recipe. Interested in his analytics? Regards, [Name]. I also reached out to Jack.
entries.points: The conversational concept is good, but tone down overly casual slang ('Surprise, surprise', 'another guy'), never use '@username' handles because they look like robotic automation (use the creator's actual name instead), say 'US audience' instead of 'American audience', and replace weak phrasing ('I think he can also use') with confident phrasing ('We think he would be a good fit').
entries.rewrite: Hey [First name], Your work with Jack proves that chicken is fine just the way it is. We work with another creator that likes to keep things simple. Kush is a meal prep creator with roughly 90% US audience. We think he would be a good fit for your app to break it down in his next recipe. Interested in his analytics? Let me know. Regards, [Name]. I also reached out to Jack.

quote.quote: My biggest takeaways from this one, my brother, would be too casual, it's too casual, too casual, so you're doing like too warm, this is still cold email, so be professional, doesn't have to be salesy

entries.situation: A student submitted a cold email to an outdoor/fishing creator (Jackman) with poetic AI-sounding personalization and asked if having unsponsored videos was intentional.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Something new to explore, Jackman

Hello,
The Wilderness Creek fishing caught my eye. Wading the shallow mountain streams is rare to find content like this. Most creators aren't touching content like that anymore. I work with content creators like yourself to score paid brand deals. I noticed your videos are not sponsored. Is that intentional?
entries.points: The subject line is good, but avoid poetic, AI-sounding personalization and never ask if unsponsored videos are 'intentional' because that invites the creator to say they don't want sponsors. Instead, state why their unique content made you reach out and pitch example brands that would fit.
entries.rewrite: I wish more creators do the same thing. This is actually why I'm reaching out. I work with content creators like yourself to score paid brand deals. I know that your videos are not sponsored, and I'm pretty sure brands like [Brand A] and [Brand B] and other similar brands would be a good fit for you. Let me know if you're interested.

quote.quote: I know that your videos are not sponsored, and then you can maybe go with, I'm pretty sure, brands like these and these and other similar brands would be a good fit for you. Let me know if you're interested.

entries.situation: A student read a cold outreach email to a Miami fishing creator with dramatic personalization ('That kind of footage pays') and two CTAs at the end.
entries.student_email: Chasing that triple-digit tarpon for over 30 minutes under the Miami night was definitely something I've never seen before. That kind of footage pays. We work with fishing creators to secure brand sponsorships, and I noticed your last few videos were not sponsored. We can assist with that. Are you open to working with brands? Let me know your thoughts one way or another.
entries.points: Tone down overly dramatic personalization so it sounds casual, keep the clear niche offer ('We work with fishing creators to secure brand sponsorships'), use a single direct CTA question ('Are you open to working with brands?'), and save 'Let me know your thoughts one way or another' for a follow-up.
entries.rewrite: We work with fishing creators to secure brand sponsorships, and I noticed your last few videos were not sponsored. We can assist with that. Are you open to working with brands?

quote.quote: And I noticed your last few videos were not sponsored. We can assist with that. Are you open to working with brands? This should be your CTA. Let me know your thoughts one way or another. This one, I would keep it for a follow-up.

entries.situation: A student's first follow-up to a fishing influencer opened with 'Hey, no pressure either way, that tarpon chase still has me thinking about it' before pitching similar brands.
entries.student_email: Hey, no pressure either way. That tarpon chase still has me thinking about it. Still happy to connect you with brands similar to [Brand A] and [Brand B] if you are open to it. Worth a chat?
entries.points: State clearly in the first sentence that you are following up in case they missed your previous email, and never claim you are still daydreaming about their video days later—a busy agency owner has no time for that.
entries.rewrite: In case you missed my email, I'm just following up. Still happy to connect you with brands similar to [Brand A] and [Brand B] if you are open to it. Worth a chat?

quote.quote: Chase still has me thinking about it. Nah, nah, nah, nah, Red flag, red flag, red flag. Bro, you fell in love with it. Don't say it, Souhanallah.

entries.situation: A student pasted YouTube transcripts into ChatGPT to generate four initial emails to productivity influencers, resulting in robotic summaries ('You compared the lotus flower growing through mud...') and nonsensical bridge lines ('editing four to five hours nightly... speaking of nice things').
entries.student_email:
Email 1:
Subject: Jack, it took that long
Hey, editing four to five hours nightly just to learn how to cut one five minutes video is wild dedication. Speaking of nice things, brands such as [Brand A] and [Brand B] would pair nicely with your content. Is this something you want to check?

Email 2:
Subject: Does it last that long?
Hi there, one notification can really be the reason someone goes down a two-hour doom scrolling. Speaking of nice, we have a few brands in mind that would work well with your content. Let me know if you're interested.

Email 3:
Subject: Are you ready?
Hey there, you compared the lotus flower growing through mud to how people only see the finished flower version of success. While we are on positive topics, [brands] would fit with your content. Want to discuss further?

Email 4:
Subject: Got something for you
You compare content to a video game map, with the audience at point A and you guiding them to point B. Speaking of which, sponsored content would be a fit.
entries.points: Stop feeding video transcripts into ChatGPT and parroting the creator's own words back to them. Watch one moment of the video, share a casual human reaction (e.g., joking you'll throw your phone away after hearing about doomscrolling), and anchor your bridge line logically to a word in your opener (like 'Speaking of dedication' or 'Speaking of five minutes').
entries.rewrite: Nice explanation about how checking one notification could lead to two hours doom scroll. I'm gonna throw my phone right now after I press send. Speaking of dedication, you can stop dedicating your time to finding brands—we have a few brands in mind that would work well with your content. Are you interested?

quote.quote: editing four to five hours nightly just to learn how to cut one five minute, one five minutes video is wild dedication, speaking of nice things, Where is the nice thing here? Habibi, is five hours at night learning how to is nice for you?

entries.situation: A student wrote a clever but overly long cold email and follow-up sequence to a history/education YouTuber, cramming both the initial pitch and follow-up reasoning into the first email and ending the final follow-up with 'email me when you want to get sponsored'.
entries.student_email:
Initial Email:
I assumed once when you said the S might stand for something else—Superman, OK, and Scheme S—it seems like Germans and British were competing in fancy names for their operations just as much as occupying the Netherlands. Which one do you think takes the cake? We too have a fancy operation going on where we are connecting YouTubers with EdTech platforms like [Brand A], [Brand B], and [Brand C]. Since history, language, and academics often overlap, we believe these brands would fit well for sponsor integration in your videos. Are you interested in exploring these partnerships with us? Let me know.

Follow-ups:
After your partnership with [Brand], it may be a good decision to branch into different sponsorship categories. Would you like to keep the momentum going by partnering with us? It's fine if language brands aren't your cup of tea because we deal with brands in other niches as well... It seems like content creation is keeping you too busy, which is exactly why partnering with us makes sense to reduce your workload. There's no cost to you... Email me when you want to get sponsored.
entries.points: The 'fancy operation' bridge and EdTech brand examples are good, but the initial email is too long for lazy readers. Cut the question at the end of the personalization and move the sentence explaining why history/language overlaps with EdTech into your first follow-up. In the final break-up follow-up, ask 'Should I circle back?' instead of telling them to email you when they want sponsors.

It seems like Germans and British were competing in fancy names for their operations just as much as occupying the Netherlands. We too have a fancy operation going on where we are connecting YouTubers with EdTech platforms like [Brand A], [Brand B], and [Brand C]. Are you interested in exploring these partnerships with us?

entries.situation: After getting no reply from an influencer's agency via email, a student (Omar) DMed the creator (Tim) directly on LinkedIn with a funny AI-generated meme of 100 clones of him on the Lovable logo, and the creator replied 'not sure I get it, haha'.
entries.student_email: Tim, I was bored and saw your latest video on YouTube about a weird future of user interaction. It made me think, who do you think would win? You as a Lovable ambassador, or hundreds of you? [Attached AI image of his face on the Lovable logo vs. 100 clones of him]
entries.points: The playful no-pitch LinkedIn icebreaker is great. Keep the conversation on LinkedIn and do not mention his agency unless he brings them up first; bridge from the joke ('100 of you would be difficult to feed...') into asking if he is open to brand partnerships. If he says yes, continue on LinkedIn or email; if he tells you to contact his agency, tell him you already emailed them without a reply and ask him to nudge them.
entries.rewrite: 100 of you would be difficult to feed! On another note, we have a couple of brands that could be a good fit—would you be open to some partnerships for your content?

quote.quote: If he mentioned agency, it has to go through them. Okay, just go, okay, I've reached out to them. For some reason, they are not answering. Your nudge would be super helpful. Would you mention something, you know?

entries.situation: A student submits their first cold outreach email to an automotive creator who flips Nissan 350Z/370Z cars.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Quick question

Hey [first name], I just watched your last video of flipping Nissan 350/370Z, and noticed that you have partnered with [Brand 1] and [Brand 2]. I wanted to ask if you are open to sponsorship with similar automotive brands. If so, please let me know.

Best,
[First name]
entries.points: Dedicate the entire first paragraph to genuine personalization and explain why the video stood out before pitching. Name specific brands instead of saying 'similar automotive brands', and remove 'please' from the CTA so you project high value rather than begging.
entries.rewrite: Watched your video flipping the 350Z — I'm still trying to sell my old Ford haha. Based on your content, we thought [Brand 1] and [Brand 2] would be a good fit for you. Let me know.

quote.quote: I wanted to ask if you're open to sponsorship with similar brands. Could be better. It's weight. I like to mention names of brands, you know. Based on your content, this and that. We thought these brands would be a good fit for you.

entries.situation: A student submits their second cold email to an automotive influencer working on a Toyota Tundra TRD Rock Warrior suspension job.
entries.student_email:
Subject: [First name], quick question

Your Tundra should be a true TRD Rock Warrior after you're done with the suspension job. Noticed you partnered with [Brand 1] and [Brand 2], checking to see if you're open to working with other brands for your upcoming videos. Want to discuss this further?
entries.points: Hyper-specific personalization that can only apply to that single creator is great and can even serve as the subject line. Smooth out the transition into the pitch ('checking to see' is slightly abrupt) and mention specific brand names, but keep the short, casual, non-fanboy tone and direct CTA.

quote.quote: this checking to see, this transition is a bit sloppy. If you... You're open to working with other brands for your upcoming videos. I want to discuss this further. CTA is nice. I like CTA, especially for influencers. I will still mention names.

entries.situation: A student in the tech/AI niche submits a long cold email to an Instagram creator who posted about Shopify's database query.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Hey [first name], check this

Hello [First name],

I came across your recent Instagram post discussing Shopify's database query, and I found it very informative. Your other posts on software and programming are also well explained.

I noticed your recent collaboration with BenQ for the ScreenBar. At [Agency Name], we specialize in connecting creators like you with software and AI brands that align perfectly with your audience and content format. We believe we could help you secure valuable partnerships in the tech space.

Please let me know if you're interested in exploring collaboration opportunities.

Best regards,
[Name]
Founder / Marketing Specialist, [Agency Name]
entries.points: The subject line ('Hey [first name], check this') is good, but cut the fanboy praise and two-variable fill-in-the-blank template style. Never say 'At our agency, we specialize in...' when starting out without case studies or brands, shorten the CTA to 'If so, let me know', and strip out titles like 'Founder' or 'Marketing Specialist', websites, and logos from your sign-off.
entries.rewrite:
Checking to see if you're open to working with other brands. If so, let me know.

Best,
[First name]

quote.quote: If you say specialize, that means you have, I don't know, 10 plus years of experience, right? So guys, avoid these fluffy words, right? Avoid it. It sounds salesy, it sounds unprofessional, and basically you are promising something that you don't have.

entries.situation: The tech/AI student submits a third cold outreach email using the same template structure, a wink emoji, and offering 'similar partnerships' after mentioning the creator's recent collaboration with Claude.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Check this data

Hey [first name], you combine humor, very informative and effortless. Your video on extracting data from a subreddit was very helpful... ;) I noticed your last post was a collaboration with Claude. I'm curious to know if you would be interested in similar partnerships. Do let me know, thanks.
entries.points: Stop reusing the exact same sentence structure across emails because Google flags repetitive templates as spam. Never use ellipses ('...') or wink emojis in professional outreach, and say 'some other brands' instead of 'similar partnerships' because creators who recently worked with a brand are usually under a 3-to-9-month exclusivity clause barring direct competitors.
entries.rewrite: I noticed your last post was a collaboration with Claude. I'm curious to know if you would be interested in working with some other brands.

quote.quote: maybe not mention similar, maybe more like some other brands would be better, because similar means if I work with NordVPN, and I didn't read your email a lot because, you know, it's fluffy, and you say similar, maybe you offer me something that ExpressVPN

entries.situation: A student in the mobile filming sub-niche submits an outreach email about Apple's Pro iPhone strategy asking if smartphone filmmaking is 'a niche you'd like to explore'.
entries.student_email:
Subject: How about Apple's strategy, Jeff?

Hi Jeff, you recently highlighted how Apple is leaning into content creators with their Pro iPhone lineup. Based on that and your content, I think you could be a good match with several smartphone filmmaking brands we are looking to connect with creators. Is this a niche you'd like to explore?
entries.points: Expand the personalization to 2–3 sentences by explaining the 'why' behind your observation. Change 'brands we are looking to connect with creators' to 'brands we are lining up creators for', and drop the CTA asking if they want to explore a niche—creators don't change their niche when sponsored by a brand from another category.
entries.rewrite: Based on that and your content, I think you could be a good match with several smartphone filmmaking brands we are lining up creators for.

quote.quote: When it comes to your niche, you build up your niche around your influencers. Brands could be from filmmaking, from tech, from AI, from cooking. Any other brand that is interested in working with your guys, that's important.

entries.situation: The mobile filming student submits a second outreach email saying 'Since we both care about Smartphone Cameras' and asking 'Is this something you'd like to make more videos about?'
entries.student_email:
Subject: Here's an idea

Hi [first name], I noticed a good part of your personal channel focuses on cameras and smartphone cameras. Okay, that's four videos, but the interest is clearly there. Since we both care about smartphone cameras, I think your content could fit well with several mobile filming brands we are looking to connect with creators. Is this something you'd like to make more videos about?
entries.points: Never claim shared personal passion ('Since we both care about smartphone cameras') in a first cold email because it sounds disingenuous and fanboyish; instead, anchor the transition on the creator's own demonstrated interest ('Since you showed interest in...'). Also tighten the CTA.
entries.rewrite: Since you showed interest in filmmaking brands, we have some brands we are planning to connect you with.

quote.quote: maybe we're more like, since you showed interest in filmmaking brands, guess what? We have some brands, we, I don't know, are planning to connect you because of this and that. So if you showed interest in this, use that, insha Allah, as your flow.

entries.situation: The mobile filming student submits their first follow-up email noting the creator hasn't uploaded for a month and must be preparing a video soon.
entries.student_email: Hey [first name], you haven't released a video for a month now, so I'm guessing you're preparing one soon. Just wanted to check if you had a chance to look over my first email.
entries.points: Observing a gap in the creator's upload schedule is a strong follow-up angle compared to generic 'bumping this email' lines. Make it even stronger by connecting their upcoming release directly to lining them up with brands.
entries.rewrite: Hey [first name], I'm following up because I assume your next video will come out in a couple of days, so it would be a good chance to line you up with some brands. Let me know.

quote.quote: I'm following up because I assume your video is coming, I don't know. It will come out in a couple of days, so it would be a good chance to line you up with some brands. Let me know.

entries.situation: The travel/outdoor student submits a second email to a creator building a sauna ('The sauna is starting to take shape with the walls, looking forward to seeing how it progresses') and mentions 'brands we are considering including [Brand 1] and [Brand 2]'.
entries.student_email:
Subject: How does this sound to you, James?

The sauna is starting to take shape with the walls, looking forward to seeing how it progresses. Given your recent content, we thought it might be a good time to connect about a potential collaboration. Brands we are considering include [Brand 1] and [Brand 2]. Are you open to chatting briefly?
Warm regards,
[First name]
entries.points: Saying 'brands we are considering including X and Y' is an honest, effective way to name-drop brands when you don't have them signed yet. However, expand the personalization to 2–3 sentences, add a lighthearted joke about the sauna instead of a generic 'looking forward to seeing how it progresses', build a smoother bridge to the pitch, and put the CTA on its own line.
entries.rewrite:
The sauna is starting to take shape with the walls — now you can cook yourself! Given your recent content, we thought it might be a good time to connect about a potential collaboration. Brands we are considering include [Brand 1] and [Brand 2].

Are you open to chatting briefly?

Warm regards,
[First name]

quote.quote: I think this is a good place to crack a joke, you know, because sauna could be, you know, good platform for making jokes, now you can cook yourself, you know, now you know when you're cooked or something like that

entries.situation: A student submits a cold email to an automotive brand pitching a creator running a 'penny to supercar' series, ending a full pitch with 'Are you the right person?'
entries.student_email:
Subject: Worth 60 seconds / Check this / [Name], thoughts

Hi [First Name],
Working across multiple brands at once means you're probably always on the lookout for placements worth bringing to your clients. [Creator] would be a good fit for [Brand], as he currently runs a penny to supercar series. [Influencer] has room to be part of the story consistently in front of [audience] rather than a one-off placement. Are you the right person?
entries.points: Proofread AI-assisted drafts so nonsensical phrases like 'working across multiple brands at once' do not slip through, and never combine a full salesy pitch with an 'Are you the right person?' routing question. Either send a brief routing inquiry or pitch the offer with a real call to action.
entries.rewrite: Hey, I'm looking for more brands to collab with influencers that we have in mind. Are you the right person that I should reach out to?

quote.quote: You cannot go with two of those. I have everything, here's analytics, here's everything you have to know, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, and then are you the right person for this? So your CTA, my brother, is not CTA.

entries.situation: A student with no closed brands or influencers sends a cold email to a travel/luxury creator referencing an $80,000 plastic valve maintenance bill and ends with 'Should I send more information?'
entries.student_email:
Subject: 80k for plastic

Hey [First Name],
The fact that a single valve made from plastic can cost over $80,000 in the [X] industry shows just how expensive owning your own [X] can be. At least your maintenance bill was a relatively good deal.

Speaking of good deals, we work with creators who have strong engagement rates. Since you fit that profile, we have a few brands in mind for you that would like to land deals. Should I send more information?
entries.points: The subject line '80k for plastic' is good, but trim the personalization so it is not overly wordy. After transitioning with 'Speaking of good deals', mention the brands you have in mind for the creator first rather than talking about working with other creators. Never ask 'Should I send more information?' when you have no closed brands or concrete information to send.

entries.situation: A travel influencer replies positively to a cold email asking which brands the student has in mind and what percentage cut the agency takes. The student answers both questions, immediately demands audience analytics in the same email, gets ghosted, and follows up wishing the creator a 'great Easter' with a smiley face.
entries.student_email:
Influencer reply: Clever cold email! Yes, I'm always open to working with additional brands. If you have some, please feel free to offer, and also let me know what percentage cut you take to coordinate the deal.

Student reply: Thanks for getting back to me. We are seeking 60 to 90s integrations with brands like [Brand A] and [Brand B]. Regarding rates, we align on your fee directly with you, while our cut is arranged separately with the brand. Before we proceed further, we would first need to see audience analytics to ensure this is a right fit. We are primarily interested in seeing audience age and country of viewership.

Student follow-up: Hi there, hope you had a great Easter :) Just following up on the last email. As mentioned previously, we'll be finalizing our list in the next few weeks. If this could be a fit, please let me know. Hope you had a great weekend.
entries.points: Explaining that you align on the creator's fee directly while arranging your agency cut separately with the brand is good, though keep the wording simple. However, never rush a cold creator by demanding audience analytics in that same reply—stick to one topic per email. Furthermore, never congratulate non-Muslim religious holidays like Easter, and re-engage the ghosting creator with a short check-in.

Next follow-up: Hey, I'm just checking one more time to see—are you in? Either way, let me know.

entries.situation: A student writes a cold email to a tech/productivity creator citing the exact title of his video ('My 2025 Dream Office Setup') and using the word 'sponsorship/sponsors' three times.
entries.student_email:
Hi [First Name],
Your 'My 2025 Dream Office Setup' video where multiple tools are shown in one place creates strong sponsorship opportunities for such content. I help line up relevant brands and handle coordination so you don't miss sponsorships in upcoming setup videos. Would you be open to additional sponsors in your videos?
entries.points: Never write out the exact full title of an influencer's video because nobody speaks like that in real life and it immediately sounds like AI—just refer to 'your last video' or 'your recent video'. Also remove links and stop repeating 'sponsorship/sponsors' throughout the personalization, offer, and CTA.
entries.rewrite: Hey [First Name], I checked your recent video—looked nice. We are looking for more influencers to pitch for brands like [Brand A] and [Brand B]. What do you think?

entries.situation: A student sends a cold email to a brand already active in influencer marketing with the subject 'John x [Brand] - Collab Opportunity', ChatGPT phrasing ('the way he explained... landed well'), a generic roster pitch without explaining why they fit, and 'Happy to send analytics' as the CTA.
entries.student_email:
Subject: John, [Brand] - Collab Opportunity

[Brand] sponsored [Creator X]'s last video, and the way he explained how it has all the tools to turn your dreams into reality landed well, since he even uses it to sell his candies.

We work with a roster of finance creators like [A] and [B] who receive 150k average views. [Brand] would align closely with their audience. Happy to send analytics.
Cheers, Hamoudi
entries.points: For brands already spending on influencer marketing, never put the brand name and 'Collab Opportunity' in the subject line—use curiosity hooks like 'John, check this' or 'Something for you, John'. Avoid ChatGPT clichés ('the way', 'landed well'), clearly explain why the creator's content aligns with the brand (or pitch one marquee creator plus a relevant sub-niche), and replace 'Happy to send analytics' with an action-oriented CTA.

entries.situation: A student submits a 4-email follow-up sequence to the same brand representative (John), pitching new creators in each follow-up, asking for a 5-7 minute call about a dedicated video in follow-up 3, and promising to circle back in Q3 in follow-up 4.
entries.student_email:
Follow-up 1: Hey John, just wanted to bump this. I believe there's a strong fit between creators like [A] and [Brand]'s audience. Open to explore a simple pilot? Cheers, Hamoudi

Follow-up 2: Hi John, circling back. Our finance creators like [B]...

Follow-up 3: Hey John, we have an upcoming campaign slot with [A] that could align well with [Brand]'s goals for a dedicated video collab. Would you be open to discuss for 5 to 7 minutes?

Follow-up 4: Wanted to check one last time. We are planning Q2 creator partnerships and [Brand] feels like a great fit. If now is not the right timing, I can always circle back in Q3.
entries.points: Never send four follow-ups to the same brand contact—cap it at two or three follow-ups (where the third is a closing break-up email asking what creator profile they want) before moving to a different contact at the company. Do not pitch a new creator in every follow-up or push expensive dedicated videos; follow-ups should simply remind them to check your initial email or mention a creator's upcoming video, and note that brands have 'customers', not an 'audience'. Asking 'Open to explore a simple pilot?' in Follow-up 1 is a good CTA.
entries.rewrite: Closing follow-up (Follow-up 3): I got it, you're not interested. Should I circle back later, or would you let me know what type of creators you're looking for?

quote.quote: So closing follow-up, what is closing follow-up? What is closing follow-up? I got it, you're not interested. Like, okay, I got it, I know, makes sense. Should I circle back or would you let me know what type of prayers you're looking for?

entries.situation: A brand founder/CEO named Claire replied asking for talent and fees; after sending his rates, the student waited six days and sent a very long Friday follow-up email apologizing that his earlier approach was 'slightly unorthodox.'
entries.student_email: Hey, Claire... That said, the approach I took with you was slightly unorthodox...
entries.points: Never send a wall-of-text follow-up or apologize for your pricing/approach, as founders will not read long emails and apologizing destroys confidence; instead, pitch founders briefly on taking their brand to the next level against competitors and ask for a morning or evening call.
entries.rewrite: Look, we understand, we know the ins and outs, we take consulting from other five, six figure agencies, and we know what works and what doesn't work when it comes to influencer marketing, we know how to take your brand from its current status to the next level and be competing with [competitors' names]. If this sounds good, how about we hop on a call this upcoming Friday, 10 a.m., 9 a.m.?

quote.quote: So for me to be like, oh, that said, the approach I took with you was slightly unorthodox, etc. It's like you saying, oh, I'm sorry for saying that the race were X, however, let's try and make it work.

entries.situation: A brand countered the student's $2,000 pitch for Creator 1 with $1,700, and countered Creator 2 with $1,200. The student replied with a counteroffer of $1,900 plus a $500 performance bonus at 100k views for Creator 1, and $1,500 plus a $500 performance bonus at 50k views for Creator 2, while praising their content alignment and audience engagement.
entries.student_email: Hello, hiya. After further review, we're willing to move forward with the following pricing for the two creators. The lowest we can offer is 1.9K, given the strong alignment of its content within the AI space and the relevance of its audience for the brand. Goal of driving conversions and try sign-offs. Additionally, we'd like to propose a performance bonus of $500 if the video reaches 100K views. We're proposing a counter offer of 1.5K along with the 500 if the video reaches 50K views similar to his other, his audience is highly engaged with tools, the streamlined workflow, making him a strong fit. We're looking forward to working together.
entries.points: Cut generic fluff about content alignment when the brand already knows the creator is a fit; keep concrete value like driving conversions and trial sign-ups, or back up engagement claims with exact percentages. Also, never attach a performance bonus to a tiny discount ($2,000 down to $1,900 + $500 bonus) that makes the total potential cost higher than your initial flat ask; only add a performance bonus when giving a substantial discount.
entries.rewrite: The lowest we can offer is 1.9K, given the relevance of this audience for the goal of driving conversions and trial-signups.

quote.quote: for example, the lowest you can offer is 1.9K, given the relevance of this audience for the goal of driving conversions and tri-signups. That's it. So I believe that the whole strong alignment of his content within the AI space, it's fluff.

entries.situation: After the first influencer raised his rates and the second influencer refused the brand's post-publication payment terms, the student emailed the brand saying the first creator confirmed his schedule was fully booked until May 8-12 and the second creator wasn't comfortable with the payment structure.
entries.student_email: Hello, apologists for the delay. I'm getting back to you to clarify your concern regarding, after checking in the internet about emperor availability, he confirmed that his posting schedule is fully booked. The earliest window he can offer is between May 8th and May 12th. Regarding We aligned with him that payment is issue when the video is live. He isn't comfortable with the structure, has decided not to move forward to the partnership this time, so we continue progressing with him.
entries.points: Do not refer to the creator in the third person ('he confirmed his schedule is fully booked', 'the earliest window he can offer') because it makes you sound like a powerless middleman and reminds the brand the creator gets deals without you; use 'we' instead ('we won't be able to accommodate', 'the earliest window we can offer'). Also, when a creator drops out over payment terms, avoid blaming the brand's payment structure and instead offer a replacement creator at a lower price as a make-good.
entries.rewrite: Apologies for the delay. To clarify your concern, unfortunately we won't be able to accommodate this integration for April due to too many bookings. However, the earliest window we can offer is between May 8th and May 12th. Unfortunately we won't be able to move forward with this influencer, so as a make-good, we found a replacement that can do it for a cheaper price instead.

entries.situation: A talent agency's head of talent quoted $20,000 for a fitness influencer, and the student read out the reply he sent asking if there was flexibility on the rate, which the agent ignored.

entries.points: Never ask an influencer or talent manager 'is there any flexibility?' when negotiating, because it surrenders the power dynamic and invites them to say no or ignore you. Instead, follow up with a concrete counteroffer rate and a firm, non-needy CTA.
entries.rewrite: This is the option, this is what we can do, if you want to move forward, let me know.
