entries.situation: A student reaching out to brands in the business niche used the subject line '[First name], is that you?' and wrote a single-paragraph cold email praising a past integration, claiming his creators bring in 'the same audience', and vaguely mentioning a creator with a 'majority US audience'.
entries.student_email:
Subject: [First name], is that you?
Your [something] integration with [Creator] was really well done. I always assumed forming an LLC was this complicated legal process. Turns out you can get it done in minutes without touching a lawyer. We work with other business creators who bring in the same audience. In particular, we have a creator in mind with a majority US audience that would be a great fit. Want me to share more details? Talk soon, [First name].
entries.points: Replace 'Is that you?' with loop-closing subject lines like 'Hey [Name], thoughts?' or 'Close the loop, [Name]'. Cut the generic opening compliment and start directly with the specific observation about the integration, separate personalization and the offer into distinct paragraphs, never say your creators bring in the 'same audience' (brands won't pay twice for the same eyeballs), and include concrete demographic numbers (e.g., 56% US audience, ages 34–52) or creator names to build trust.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Hey Jack, thoughts? / Close the loop, Jack
I always assumed forming an LLC was a complicated legal process—turns out you can get it done in minutes. That integration with [Creator] explained everything in detail.

We work with business creators, and we have a creator in mind with a 56% US audience (ages 34–52) that would be a great fit because [reason]. Want me to share more details?
Talk soon, [First name]

quote.quote: With brands, you know my couple of examples that I always give. Hey, first name, let's say, Hijak, thoughts, right? This one. This is an example from a book called Email Manifesto. Close the loop, for example. Close the loop, Jack.

entries.situation: A student's 3-step brand follow-up sequence pitched 'a clean overlap' between a past sponsor's audience and his creator's viewers in Follow-up 1, sent a one-liner ('Please do give me your thoughts') in Follow-up 2, and ended with 'Is right now not the best time for you... Regardless, let me know' in Follow-up 3.
entries.student_email:
Follow-up 1: Hi, there is a clean overlap between Vice Z's audience and the viewers our creator bring in. Want me to send over their profile?
Follow-up 2: Please do give me your thoughts.
Follow-up 3: Is right now not the best time for you? ... Regardless, let me know. Best regards.
entries.points: Never pitch 'audience overlap' to brands—highlight what the previous creator missed or what new eyeballs and outcomes your creator brings. Never send one-line 'Please do give me your thoughts' follow-ups as they are rude and trigger spam filters; write 2–3 sentences. Structure brand follow-ups in 3 stages: (1) soft reminder + outcome/creator detail, (2) a completely different angle/creator style (e.g., pitching an energetic creator if the first didn't hit), and (3) a professional closing asking what the issue was or if you should circle back next quarter, ending with 'Either way, let me know.'
entries.rewrite:
Follow-up 1: Hey, I'm just following up in case you missed my last email. Our creator [Name] can present your product in his style, which would generate [specific outcome]. Want me to send over their profile?
Follow-up 2: Okay, [Creator A] wasn't a good fit for you—what about [Creator B]? He has a completely different, more lively entertainment style. Let me know your thoughts.
Follow-up 3: I get it—it's not the right time, or these creators aren't what you're looking for. Could you tell me what the issue is so we can restructure our offer, or should I circle back next quarter? Either way, let me know.

quote.quote: Second follow-up is something different. Okay, something different. Couple of more creators, other sub-niche, something else. You basically, this is you trying to. To get them over. Like, okay, Mr. Beast wasn't a good fit for you. What about our show speed?

entries.situation: A student wrote a second travel influencer email with the subject line 'The magic was all in the silence', opening with 'Loved your video on this one! The captivating sound of nature when the engine turned off was unbelievable' and offering sponsorships 'from brands like X and Y'.
entries.student_email:
Subject: The magic was all in the silence
Loved your video on this one. The captivating sound of nature when the engine turned off was unbelievable. What is even more captivating is connecting you to brands that are a perfect fit for your content. We can help you secure sponsorships from brands like [Brand A] and [Brand B]. Please let us know if you are interested.
entries.points: Cut fanboy opening lines ('Loved your video on this one') and tone down overly emotional adjectives ('unreal' instead of 'unbelievable') because cold prospects don't know you. Also say 'brands that are similar to [X and Y]' rather than 'brands like [X and Y]' so you don't falsely imply you already represent those exact brands.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: The magic was all in the silence
The captivating sound of nature when the engine turned off was unreal. What is even more captivating is connecting you to brands that are a perfect fit for your content. We can help you secure sponsorships from brands that are similar to [Brand A] and [Brand B].

quote.quote: loved your video on this one, bro, don't sound like a fanboy. The captivating sound of nature when the engine turned off was unbelievable, you remove this, you start email with this, and just less excitement.

entries.situation: A student wrote a third travel influencer email with the subject line 'That was a piece of art', opening with 'Hi there, enjoyed watching your last video. The architecture at [Station] is stunning. I can see from your videos that you're more involved in hotel and flight reviews. If you're willing to explore more opportunities, please let us know.'
entries.student_email:
Subject: That was a piece of art
Hi there, enjoyed watching your last video. The architecture at [Station] is stunning. I can see from your videos that you're more involved in hotel and flight reviews. If you're willing to explore more opportunities, please let us know.
entries.points: Turn statement subject lines into questions ('Was that a piece of art?') to boost open rates, remove fanboy intros ('enjoyed watching your last video'), add one concrete detail explaining *why* the station's architecture was stunning, bridge directly from their hotel/flight reviews into your offer, and replace passive 'please let us know' CTAs with a direct yes/no question.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Was that a piece of art?
Hi there, the architecture at [Station] is stunning because of [specific detail]. Since you are more involved in hotel and flight reviews, we can help you get brands that perfectly fit your content. Would you like to work with these types of brands?

quote.quote: If you're willing to explore more opportunities, please let us know. No, no, no, no. With CTA here, you go strong, okay? Strong. How? You don't just say, let us know. You basically force them to do something.

entries.situation: A student wrote a fourth travel influencer email with the subject 'The tree should go' and personalization 'I enjoyed watching your last climbing video. The tree on your way up to the top of the tooth doesn't seem structurally secure at all', without a bridge line to the offer.
entries.student_email:
Subject: The tree should go
I enjoyed watching your last climbing video. The tree on your way up to the top of the tooth doesn't seem structurally secure at all. [Offer + long CTA sentence]
entries.points: Remove the fanboy opening line, simplify the observation ('That tree didn't seem secure on the top of the tooth'), and reuse a keyword from your personalization ('secure') as a bridge line into your offer ('Speaking of something that's secure, we can help you secure sponsorships...'). Keep the CTA short.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: The tree should go
That tree didn't seem secure on the top of the tooth. Speaking of something that's secure, we can help you secure some sponsorships from brands that would perfectly fit your content—brands like [Brand A] and [Brand B]. Are you interested?

quote.quote: I would use secure as my bridge word. Speaking of something that's secure, we can help you secure, again, why not, some sponsorships from brands that would perfectly fit your content. Brands like these and these. And then your CTA should be short.

entries.situation: A student wrote to a solo travel creator: 'Subject: They are now many years ahead. Hey Sammy, I liked your recent Japan vlog, captured Tokyo's technological advancements in a unique way. I help solo travel creators secure consistent brand partnerships so they can focus on... Open to exploring collaboration?'

Hey Sammy, I liked your recent Japan vlog, captured Tokyo's technological advancements in a unique way. I help solo travel creators secure consistent brand partnerships so they can focus on [creating content]. Open to exploring collaboration?
entries.points: Turn the subject line into a question ('Are they now many years ahead?'), specify *what* was unique about how they captured Tokyo instead of writing vague ChatGPT-style praise ('in a unique way'), use 'We help' instead of 'I help', and ask 'Would you like to hear more?' as the CTA.

Hey Sammy, [specific detail about how he captured Tokyo's tech]. We help solo travel creators secure consistent brand partnerships so they can focus on [creating content]. Would you like to hear more?

entries.situation: A student in the productivity/transformation niche wrote an influencer outreach email with the subject 'still staring' and a bridge from staring at a dot in the video to 'feast your eyes on this opportunity', naming three past sponsors and pitching complementary brands.
entries.student_email:
Subject: still staring
Hey [First name], you spent thousands of hours staring at a dot. Now, feast your eyes on this opportunity.
I noticed you're already partnered with brands like [Brand 1], [Brand 2], and [Brand 3].
There's room to bring in even more premium brands that fit your audience. Brands similar to [Brand A] and [Brand B] came to my mind. They complement the partnerships you're already doing.
Would you be open to exploring that?
entries.points: The hook and bridge line ('You spent thousands of hours staring at a dot. Now, feast your eyes on this opportunity.') are smooth and eye-catching. Only name 1–2 past sponsors instead of 3+, and merge the middle lines into one paragraph to reduce spacing/HTML.

entries.situation: A student wrote to a psychology creator referencing how the creator mentioned the cost of running his channel was getting too high, then pitched brands that 'fit naturally with the audience you've built'.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Is this how it ends?
I genuinely thought this was going to be your last video. You mentioned the cost of running the channel was getting too high. There are plenty of partnership opportunities that fit the psychology content you create. Brands like [Brand] came to my mind. They fit naturally with the audience you've built. entries.points: Hooking the creator with a pain point they mentioned in their video (high cost of running the channel) is an excellent way to pitch sponsorships. However, say the brands fit their 'content' rather than their 'audience'—otherwise, asking for their audience analytics later won't make sense if you claimed you already knew their audience.

entries.situation: A student wrote a slightly long initial email to a study creator that included personalization, an observation about current sponsors, and a second part naming similar study tool brands, and asked for feedback on CTAs like 'Would that interest you?' and 'Would you be open to exploring that?'.
entries.student_email:
Subject: curious number one student is no slouch
[Personalization]... when you only work with [Current Brands], there is still room for more tools that fit the serious student audience you're building. Brands similar to [Brand A] and [Brand B] came to my mind—they'd fit naturally with the study content you already created. Does this sound interesting?

Also keep initial CTAs short and easy to answer with yes/no ('Are you interested?'), saving longer phrasing like 'Would you be open to exploring that?' for later in the conversation.

entries.situation: A student wrote a cold email to a language-learning brand with a confusing subject line ('These are not the answers'), a long personalization sentence, and a vague offer ('creators have large reach to US viewers engaged in language learning, most of them are young adults who will be interested in acquiring math and coding skills').

entries.situation: A student reaches out to a tech/smart-home YouTuber referencing their '15 cool tech' video, stating they average 100k views as the offer, and asking 'Should I send more details?' as the CTA.

Hola [Name], Saw your 15 cool tech video. And the Black Voyage blue was a solid pick. The top tech series doesn't have to be difficult, we can bring the brands to you. You average 100k views, that's the profile they look for. Should I send more details?

Do not state the creator's average view count as your offer—an offer must state what value you provide (such as helping an unsponsored creator land relevant sponsors), not praise or verify their stats. Finally, replace 'Should I send more details?' with 'Are you interested?' because a beginner has no extra details to send.
entries.rewrite: Solid pick on the Black Voyage Blue because [reason]. Hey, I saw no sponsors on your recent videos—we can help bring you sponsors like [Brand X] and [Brand Y]. Are you interested?

quote.quote: If you saw a lot of guys start their email, I saw, I saw your, your video, blah, blah. You have to. Come up with something that's more unique, so in order to stand out, especially in this first line

entries.situation: A student writes a cold email to a smart-home YouTuber tying their video's 'no long-term headaches' rule to handling 'brand headaches', noting 'you are selective as we are', and ending by offering to send over 'the brief'.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Is it still a dumb home?
Hey [First Name], While you are busy turning a dumb home into a smart home, the first rule makes sense: no long-term headaches. You can also worry less if you let us handle the brand headaches. You have an average views [X], we connect smart home and tech brands, that's what they want. You are selective as we are. Should I send over the brief?
entries.points: Transitioning from the creator's video topic ('no long-term headaches') to handling 'brand headaches' and acknowledging that 'you are selective as we are' is strong pain/rejection recognition; build on it by promising to always double-check whether a brand is a good fit for them. However, remove any mention of sending a 'brief' in cold outreach to influencers, because you do not have a brand brief yet and real briefs are often confidential.
entries.rewrite: Since you're selective as we are, we will not get you brands that don't match your channel—we'll always double-check with you whether a brand is a good fit. Are you interested?

quote.quote: And you said like, you are selective as we are. We will not get you brands that are this and that. You know, we'll always maybe you can say, since you're selected. Alhamdulillah, we'll always, I don't know, double check with you

entries.situation: A student drafts a first cold email to a productivity creator referencing setting aside 30 minutes to switch off with family, then transitions with 'Speaking about productivity, I manage brand collaboration for creators in this space. I'm currently preparing for my Q3 sponsorship outreach to brands such as [X] and [Y].' with large spacing gaps between lines.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Remind me again
Hi [Name],

You said you set aside 30 minutes to switch off with family, I think it's a valuable reminder, as downtime has its place.

Speaking about productivity, I manage brand collaboration for creators in this space. I'm currently preparing for my Q3 sponsorship outreach to brands such as [Brand 1] and [Brand 2]. A potential sponsor could complement your [series]. What are your thoughts?
entries.points: Invert the first sentence to avoid starting with 'You said', ensure the transition matches the personalization (switching off with family is downtime, not productivity), do not claim you 'manage brand collaborations' when you have never done one, remove extra line breaks that make the email HTML-heavy, and say 'we are preparing for Q3 campaigns for brands such as X and Y' instead of 'my Q3 sponsorship outreach' so it doesn't sound like you haven't started reaching out yet.
entries.rewrite: As downtime has its place, 30 minutes to switch off with family is a really valuable reminder. We're currently preparing for Q3 campaigns for brands such as [Brand 1] and [Brand 2]. A potential sponsor could complement your [series]. What are your thoughts?

quote.quote: You have a lot of gaps, which makes your email, HTML heavy. Like, some email providers would think, obviously, AI and stuff, you have some pictures in it. So be careful. That's why I always say, like, don't have these gaps.

entries.situation: A student sends a long B2B cold outreach email to a HubSpot Marketing Manager with a multi-sentence summary of how a creator demonstrated an AEO tool across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, followed by a wordy pitch.
entries.student_email:
Subject: [Brand] partnership
Presentation of the new AEO tool felt like a natural part of the content. Liked how he integrated the tool to show his viewers how brands and products appear across AI search engines such as GPT, Gemini, Perplexity. What stood out was that AEO tool compares your brand/products to other competitors and what to do to improve. It's built to solve a problem the audience cares about. We work with a few creators whose audience share these interests and challenges. Therefore, there could be a fit for educational content that offers value to business founders and operators while incorporating some of it. Would this interest you? Let me know.
entries.points: Keep cold outreach emails to brands around 50 words max—short, easy to read, and designed only to tickle their curiosity—because B2B prospects and their AI filters skip long emails. Trim the personalization to two punchy sentences, and save the cut personalization material for follow-ups or split it across different employees at the same brand.
entries.rewrite: Presentation of the new AEO tool felt like a natural part of the content. It's built to solve a real problem the audience cares about. We work with a few creators whose audience share these interests. Would this interest you?

quote.quote: The rest of it, yeah, I can use for follow-up, I can use for something else. Maybe, you know, if you have long personalization, split it in half, use one for one worker, for one employee, another one for another employee.

entries.situation: A student sends a cold email to a travel YouTuber with the subject line 'Hey Ben road to 1 million' and body: 'Hey, I saw your last video on the sleeper train and the amount you paid was crazy, a flight to Glasgow would have been way cheaper. On the sleeper train, the amount you paid was crazy—a flight to Glasgow would have been way cheaper. We work with travel creators and connect them with travel brands. Are you currently exploring collaborations?

entries.situation: An influencer gave his rates and knew which brands the student planned to pitch, but refused to share his media kit or audience analytics ('my data is my own'). The student reads out the polite follow-up email he sent asking for just a screenshot of age and location breakdown, to which the influencer replied 'cool, let me know if anything interesting ever comes up.'
entries.student_email: The thing is, each brand targets specific age groups and region depending on their products. Having at least some audience info helps us match you with the right campaigns and save time on both ends. If you are open to sharing just the age and location breakdown, even a quick screenshot, it would really help. I appreciate your understanding.
entries.points: Giving a reason for needing audience data is good, but continuing to beg or offering to pitch him anyway without analytics is needy and disrespects your agency. Give the influencer a firm ultimatum: state flat out that the brands require audience analytics before you can pitch him to know if his audience is worth paying for, and if he will not provide them, part ways and move on.
entries.rewrite: Listen, I kind of need to know these things before pitching you to these brands. These brands are asking for it. They need it to know if they are willing to pay for your audience. If not, no problem. We'll part our ways. Thanks for answering my emails.

quote.quote: Honestly, if it was me, I wouldn't be needy here. Me saying, okay, I'll reach out and I'll let you know, it's kind of being needy here. I don't like that because it's disrespectful to my brand, my agency.

entries.situation: Student submits an initial cold email to a tech creator praising a glass-breaking sound effect and character transformation scene, claiming 'We manage brand sponsorship and finalizing our Q3 roster.'
entries.student_email:
Subject: Is it broken?
Hey! That glass break can sound and, and the character transformation scene are super smooth. Watching your workflow, brands like this and that would be a perfect, a perfect national fit. We manage brand sponsorship and finalizing our Q3 roster. For tech creators, let me know if you have slots available
entries.points: The subject line ('Is it broken?') and specific personalization are good, but remove bold formatting, soften 'would be a fit' to 'could be a fit', and delete the claim 'We manage brand sponsorships' because creators will immediately demand to know which brands and budgets you have.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Is it broken?
Hey! That glass breaking sound and the character transformation scene are super smooth. Watching your workflow, brands like this and that could be a fit. Let me know if you have any slots.

quote.quote: Watching your workflow, brands like this and that would be a perfect, a perfect national fit. This is good, but would be a fit. I would say, could be a fit.

entries.situation: Student submits an outreach email referencing a Muhammad Ali quote in the video, jumping abruptly to 'Here's the deal', pitching Codecademy, and ending with 'Are you ready to explore this opportunity?'

That quote from Muhammad Ali packed a punch. It's a solid reminder that belief can get you really far, even on tough days. Here's the deal. You keep sharing your journey, and we find brands that match your motivational vibes. We can connect you with names like Codecademy that want to inspire your audience. Are you ready to explore this opportunity?
entries.points: Cut opening personalization if it has no bridge line connecting it to the offer. Name brands that actively sponsor across niches (like Skillshare rather than Codecademy), and replace vague CTAs like 'Are you ready to explore this opportunity?' with a concrete next step.
entries.rewrite: You keep sharing your journey, and we find brands that match your motivational vibes.

entries.situation: Student submits an outreach email to a trading creator starting with generic praise about 'attention being your most valuable asset' before pitching TradeStation and Thinkorswim.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Was that formula for success?
That point about attention being your most valuable asset really resonates. It set the stage for a lesson that traders need to hear. You share valuable insights on trading that your audience craves. We can bring brands like TradeStation and Thinkorswim to sponsor your content. They want to teach students and traders to learn the best concepts. Are you interested in connecting with them?
entries.points: Remove the disconnected opening sentences and start directly with the line that ties into the offer ('You share valuable insights on trading...'). Focus most of your effort on the offer, and hedge specific brand names by adding 'brands similar to... and others'.
entries.rewrite: You share valuable insights on trading that your audience craves. We can bring brands similar to TradeStation and Thinkorswim and others to sponsor your content. They want to teach students and traders to learn the best concepts. Are you interested in connecting with them?

entries.situation: Student submits an email to a software engineering creator with two unrelated opening lines about 'reaching out for help' before stating 'You share valuable career advice that many aspiring software engineers need.'

entries.points: Cut the irrelevant opening lines and start directly with the personalization that supports your offer ('You share valuable career advice that many aspiring software engineers need'). Design your personalization around your offer first, then derive your subject line from it.

entries.situation: Student submits an email with a boring, AI-sounding opening line followed by a strong body ('You're all about authentic connection in your content. Let's fill the gaps with brands that align with your vibe... Are you open to it?').
entries.student_email:
Subject: Is it connecting well?
[Boring opening line] You're all about authentic connection in your content. Let's fill the gaps with brands that align with your vibe, like Things and Bombas. Your audience values genuine storytelling, and these brands are perfect. Are you open to it?
entries.points: Remove the boring first sentence because recipients see the first line in their inbox preview alongside your name and subject line; if it reads like ChatGPT, they won't open it. Starting directly with the second paragraph makes the email a 10 out of 10.

entries.situation: Student submits a long email to a DIY/gardening creator ('Jeff') with bolded brand names, claiming sponsorships will 'boost your audience trust and increase your authenticity', and signing off with 'let me know, brother.'
entries.student_email: Hey, Jeff. Came across your last video. It's rare to see people who still act for God's sake, and God is surely most appreciative. One little note, I noticed your videos are unsponsored by brands that fit your craft or style. Would you be interested in brand sponsorships with brands like [Brand 1], [Brand 2], and [Brand 3]? They align with your craft, boost your audience trust, and increase your authenticity. Your audience engagement and location also can be a plus. Let me know, brother. All the best.
entries.points: Shorten the email by cutting filler like 'Came across your last video', never call a cold prospect 'brother', do not bold text, and remove false fluff claiming brand deals 'boost audience trust'—viewers dislike ads, so only good content builds trust.
entries.rewrite: I noticed your videos are not sponsored by brands that fit your craft or style, so that's why I think brands like [Brand 1] and [Brand 2] would be good.

entries.situation: Student submits an email to a gardening creator ('Brian') using 'Speaking of missing out' as a bridge line, mentioning onboarding for Q4 in August, and including two CTAs ('would you be interested' and 'are the mentioned brands ones you would like to work with?').

entries.situation: Student submits an email to a gardening creator ('Jay') repeating 'My cucumbers appreciate' in the subject and opening, using the word 'growth/grow' three times, and writing 'I didn't see a sponsor in your last 12 videos.'

Never write 'I didn't see a sponsor in your last 12 videos' because counting their unsponsored videos sounds rude and mocking; soften it to say you didn't see a brand in a recent video so a sponsorship could be a nice addition.

entries.situation: Student submits an outreach email to a self-improvement creator referencing his motto 'Do the work', and explaining that 'we work with creators in the self-improvement space and help them land deals that actually fit their audience.'
entries.student_email: Three words since 2000: Do the work. Everyone is looking for a hack, but that is the hack, and there's nothing to it. We work with creators in the self-improvement space, and help them land deals that actually fit their audience. [Brands] are the kind of brands we would go after for your channel. Are you interested?
entries.points: Use the phrase from your personalization as a bridge line ('Speaking of the work, we can do the work for you'), and cut unnecessary explanations about how sponsorships work because creators already have partnership conversations daily.

entries.situation: Student submits an initial cold email to a tech brand praising their product launch like an excited customer and pitching a creator as if the student is the creator's exclusive manager ('we have a few slots open for the end of August. We reach audiences across the U.S. and the U.K.').
entries.student_email:
Subject: the new AI employee for developers
Great work on releasing the new product. We might have a few creators who would be a great fit for a campaign. [Creator] is a software developer, and we have a few slots open for the end of August. We reach audiences across the U.S. and the U.K. with a highly engaged audience of developers. Most importantly, the product aligns very naturally with their content and audience. Do you see a fit?
entries.points: Do not send a full sales pitch in your first cold email to a brand, avoid sounding like a gushing customer, and never write as if you exclusively manage the creator ('we have slots open', 'we reach') because the brand will ask about your management relationship and ghost you when they learn you aren't their exclusive manager.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: something new for developers
Collaboration with MrBeast was on point, a bit more energy would be a nice touch. Speaking of it, we have a very energetic influencer, [Name], and also a couple of them who could align with your products. Do you see a fit?

entries.situation: Student submits two detailed, sales-heavy first emails to brands ('Imagine an influencer filming one of his regular vlogs...' and 'We're working with a few creators ready to feature the new MacBook while the launch is still fresh...').

[Brand] has been moving fast, getting accessories out for the Mac mini in every color. Really impressive. We're working with a few creators ready to feature the new Mac mini while the launch is still fresh, ranging from reviews to home desk setups and developer vlogs, their audience spans the four biggest markets...

Save detailed, sales-heavy pitches for your second email after the brand replies; for the first email, test sending a short inquiry asking if they are the right person for partnerships.

entries.situation: Student submits a cold email to an automotive/car-build influencer referencing their new RAV4 build and pitching automotive brand sponsorships.

quote.quote: We're lining up creators for upcoming campaign. Easy. That's one. No pressure. You didn't say anything. You didn't promise anything. You're just asking. Just curious. So yeah, Allahumma barik, good email. I like it. Open to discuss this is CTA.

entries.situation: Student submits an email to a travel influencer with subject 'Gerson, where are you?', a long personal story about his niece snapping fingers at a waiter in Paris, and a weak offer ('I was thinking of few brands... let me know your thoughts').

entries.rewrite: Unlike me in Paris, you won't be embarrassed, because we have a couple of brands in mind that would suit your content. Let me know if you're interested.

entries.situation: An influencer replies saying they are not fans of the pitched brand and won't do a sponsorship with them; the student replies saying he is 'connected with agencies working directly with brands' and asks 'Are there any brands you use or feel comfortable featuring?'
entries.student_email:
Influencer reply: Hi, we are not big fans of this brand, so we will not look into having a sponsorship with them. Thank you for your understanding.

Student reply: No problem at all. Appreciate the direct feedback. I understand how important it is for your channel and the trust you build with your audience. You're selective about the sponsors you bring on, and I fully respect that. I'm connected with agencies working directly with brands across many niches, so if something aligns with your channel, I can help make it happen. Are there any brands you use or feel comfortable featuring?
entries.points: Briefly respect their selectivity, never mention other agencies to an influencer (represent your own agency), and never ask the influencer to come up with a list of brands for you—it is your job to bring specific brands to them and make the process frictionless.
entries.rewrite: You're selective about the sponsors you bring on, and I fully respect that.

quote.quote: Basically what he has to do, make the video of 90 seconds, sign the contract, send you an invoice, three, four steps. So that's how you have to make it. Now he has to give you a list of his top 10 brands.

entries.situation: Student submits an email to a travel creator about the history of the Raffles hotel, pitching specific hotel brands (Accor, Mandarin Oriental) alongside a generic category ('International Airline brands').

entries.situation: A student in the education/animation niche submits his first cold outreach email and follow-up to a software brand.
entries.student_email:
Email 1: Hey John, saw recent work with [Creator] showcased why influencers need your software to maximize their work across the social media jungle. It was brilliant and personal at the same time. If you are looking to expand into further markets, we work with several content creators in the educational and animation niche who have strong numbers in engagement, average views, and who are U.S.-based. Want me to share their media kits for collaboration?

Follow-up: Hey John, just a follow-up here. Regards.
entries.points: The personalization is decent, but the offer is weak and conditional ('If you are looking to expand into further markets'), which gives the brand an easy way to say no. Sell outcomes and proof (such as a viral video one of your creators made for another brand), make the CTA direct and confident ('Should I book slots for June?'), and never send an empty 'just a follow-up here' email—use the first follow-up as a gentle reminder that restates why your creators fit.
entries.rewrite:
Email 1 offer & CTA: We work with several content creators in the education and animation niches who have strong numbers in engagement, average views, and are U.S.-based. One of them helped [Brand] achieve their best numbers and views. Do you want the same outcome? Should I send more details or book slots for June?

Follow-up: In case you missed my last email, we have a couple of guys who would be a good fit because they do [X]. Want to see it? Looking forward to hearing from you.

entries.situation: The same education/animation student submits a second cold email and follow-up to a gaming brand mentioning anonymous creator view counts.

Email 2: Hey [Name], integration for your [Game] was clean, content specific, and to the point, showcasing the game and what users can expect. We have similar content creators in the niche of animation and the history of weapons with average views of [X] and [Y], and both are US-based. Are you happy to receive their media kits?

Follow-up: Hi [First Name], wanted to follow up on this quickly. Would you like me to send over their media kits for the two creators I mentioned? Both are US-based and I believe they could be a good fit for similar gaming integrations.

Replace awkward CTAs like 'Are you happy to receive their media kits?' with direct questions. Also, do not claim in your follow-up 'the two creators I mentioned' if you failed to name them in the first email—use the first follow-up to reveal their names and credentials.

entries.situation: A student in the soccer/goalkeeping niche submits his first brand outreach variation pitching a single goalkeeping coach creator.

entries.situation: A student who sent 250 emails with no positive replies submits his outreach email and follow-up to a fourth-generation family farm brand that does not currently run influencer marketing.
entries.student_email:
Subject: your story really motivate me

I watched [video] on website and really liked it, love how the fourth generation is still carrying on the legacy of this farm. Since you are expanding and demand is growing, I want to check if you're exploring creator-led collaboration. The creators I work with are in the food space and help drive strong awareness for brands like yours. Would you like me to share two relevant profiles?

Follow-up: Hey there, just wanted to follow up on my previous note. The creators I work with tend to perform well with story-driven content, which could be a strong fit for [Brand] as you continue to grow. Let me know if this sounds interesting.
entries.points: Drop the fanboy subject line ('your story really motivate me') and lead immediately with the fourth-generation farm legacy observation. When pitching brands that do not yet do influencer marketing, you must convince them with social proof of results achieved for other brands, invite them onto a call to educate them, and offer low-risk structures (CPM or commission-based deals) to get them started. In the follow-up, name a specific creator doing story-driven content rather than speaking vaguely.

entries.situation: A student in the sci-fi/Star Wars/Star Trek niche submits three influencer outreach emails and follow-ups using 'Dear [Name]', 'How is it going?', gushing fanboy compliments ('I was enjoying every single second'), and unrealistic brand suggestions (like Adobe Animate).
entries.student_email:
Email 1 — Subject: Ranking videos are cool
Dear [Name], How is it going? Saw your ranking videos with interest. I was enjoying every single second. They are original, creative, and funny. I noticed that you had one integration with an energy drink in your recent videos. Wouldn't it be great to have, for example, integration for cool games like Star Wars? Let's have a chat about the above and more opportunities.

Follow-up 1: Dear [Name], I was just checking if you had received my email. It will be great to hear back from you. Thanks. Kind regards.

Email 2 — Subject: Shadows of the Empire
Hi [Name] team, It was a pleasure to watch the Shadows of the Empire. The animation was top-notch and the storytelling was high quality as well. Would you be interested to do animations for Adobe Animate, or even the various lightsaber brands like Saber Forge or Ultra Sabers? Spend a maximum of 3 minutes watching a creator's video just to spot one quick hook, then transition directly into the monetization gap (e.g., noticing only one recent sponsor integration) and pitch realistic brands from a position of equal business status.
entries.rewrite: Hi [Name], [quick observation from first 3 minutes of video]. I've noticed you don't have a lot of integrations in your recent videos—let me help you, because we have these brands in mind for you.

entries.situation: A student sent a long, wide-paragraph email to a fitness influencer praising his physique and 1x4 workout split video, asking if he was open to exploring more brands, and signing off with 'Warmest'.

entries.situation: A student pitched a travel brand saying 'I like how [Creator] went from collecting firewood to walking us through all the features... I'm reaching out on behalf of travel creators who explore the world's most underreported places and whose audience are independently minded, globally curious people. What does an ideal creator partnership look like right now?'
entries.student_email: I like how [Creator] went from collecting firewood to walking us through all the [Product] features in his recent videos. I'm reaching out on behalf of travel creators who explore the world's most underreported places and whose audience are exactly the independently minded, globally curious people. What does an ideal creator partnership look for right now?
entries.points: Remove 'I like how' and state the observation directly, never say 'on behalf of creators' (which invites questions about whether you exclusively manage them; instead say 'we help brands get their products to the right audience'), cut poetic fluff ('underreported places', 'globally curious people') that doesn't show the brand what's in it for them, keep the email to 50–70 words, and replace the open-ended survey question with a strictly yes/no CTA.

We help brands get their products to the right audience—for you, these travel creators will work the best because their content is all about [Niche/Product Fit]. [Yes/No CTA]?

entries.situation: A student sent a cold email to a travel brand opening with 'I hope you are doing well', narrating how an older YouTube collaboration led him to their website, and asking if they were open to collaborating with another travel YouTuber.
entries.student_email: I hope you are doing well. I recently came across an older collaboration between you and [YouTuber], which led me to your website and amazing products. entries.points: Never say 'I hope you are doing well' in a cold email, don't narrate how you clicked onto their website, and if you reference an older sponsorship, use its age (e.g., 6 months ago) as a reason to refresh their marketing with new creators who can bring fresh eyes to a specific product via a short test pilot that can scale to 6 months—all in under 50 words.

We work with travel creators who can bring a fresh audience to [Specific Product]. Let's arrange a short test pilot collaboration—if everything goes well, we can go six months.

entries.points: Match the influencer's brief energy and cut 95% of the fluff. Do not lecture the creator on behalf of brands about audience geography and purchasing power, and do not timidly ask if there is flexibility—state your $3k budget allocation directly in two sentences.
entries.rewrite: Appreciate you sending the media kit over. Since we're looking at the higher US percentage, we can only allocate 3k. What is the deal breaker? Best.

quote.quote: Bro, match the energy. Hey, sounds interesting. Here's a link to my rates and then boom. Thanks for the response. We're mainly looking to build a wrong-time partnership with creators. No, no, no, Bring recurring brand opportunities. Fluff, fluff, fluff. No one cares.

entries.situation: After the influencer rejected the $3k counteroffer and insisted his integrated sponsorship rate was $15k, the student drafted a ChatGPT-style reply with em-dashes saying he understood the rate, offering $3k-$4k, and wishing the creator all the best with upcoming campaigns if not.
entries.student_email: Thanks for, I understand your rate... From campaigns we're running with, in the... current budget range, 3 to 4k video... happy to explore working together... if not, no worries at all, and all the best with your upcoming campaigns
entries.points: Never validate an overpriced rate by saying 'I understand your rate', eliminate ChatGPT phrasing and em-dashes, and stop sounding apologetic or like a needy fanboy wishing them all the best. Keep the reply neutral, firm, and concise by stating what you can allocate after internal discussion and offering to send the contract if it works.
entries.rewrite: thank you so much for sending the draft over you know hey after a lot of back and forth with the brand or after a lot internally back and forth internally this is what we're able to allocate if that works for I'm going to send you the contract

quote.quote: the responses are very chatGBT, and we don't do that, and you, bro, happy to explore working together, it's like, don't be, don't sound like a fanboy, if not, no worries at all, and all the best with your upcoming campaigns

entries.situation: A student reads out his proposed reply to an influencer who demanded a 15% commission split and full transparency on brand deals.
entries.student_email: hi, at the moment, you haven't looked at any numbers with yourself or brands yet, so until we get to there, let's work on a number before we work on percentages.
entries.points: Do not be vague or reveal to the influencer that you haven't looked at numbers with brands yet and still need to do outreach. Never explain your internal agency operations or profit margins to a creator; state directly that you agree on a flat price with him and handle brand profits separately.
entries.rewrite: hey, I understand where you're coming from, this is how we operate, boom, we agree on a price, we pay you the price, and the profits and everything, we handle this separately, and that's it. So, I don't if that works for you, I'm more than happy to, I don't know, to bring you a deal your own way, or a brand your own way, and if you like working with that, cool, we can make it work, and that's it.

quote.quote: Now, personally, I would, seriously, keeping it very vague, you know, you're not being like straight to the point, like, personally, would say, hey, I understand where you're coming from, this is how we operate

entries.situation: A student submits an entertainment-niche cold email to a brand with the subject line 'Let's collab', generic praise of a past collaboration, weak combined creator metrics, and a weak closing line after the CTA.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Let's collab

Hello [First Name],

Noticed your collab with [Creator]. That presentation was well made.

We are partnering with some science focused creators, including [Creator 1] and [Creator 2], that could shine a light on [Brand] to their audience, gathering 80+K views on average with 35% US audience.

Should I send over their demos? You'll know if it's a fit.
entries.points: Avoid generic subject lines like 'Let's collab' and personalize the subject line with the prospect's first name (e.g., 'Hey [Name], something for you' or 'your thoughts'). In the body, write 2-3 sentences of marketing-focused personalization (such as how a creator transitioned from content into pitching the product), avoid cringy poetic phrases like 'shine a light', wrap weak creator stats qualitatively ('stable views', 'strong engagement rate') instead of citing low numbers like 35% US audience, and end cleanly with 'Should I send more details?' without adding 'You'll know if it's a fit.'
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Hey [First Name], something for you / your thoughts

Hello [First Name],

I saw your collaboration with [Creator] and how smoothly he transitioned from his normal video to presenting your product.

We are partnering with science-focused creators, including [Creator 1] and [Creator 2], with stable views and a strong engagement rate.

Should I send more details?

quote.quote: I saw collaboration with this one. You don't have to mention Brent because you're emailing them as well. And you can see something about it, how he brought that, how he mentioned this, how transition from his normal video to presenting your product

entries.situation: In a health/fitness deal thread, after a brand replied with initial interest, the student sent a second email with a lengthy sales pitch explaining how the creator could integrate gut-friendly vegan supplements and mix of flavors.
entries.student_email:
Hey [Name],

I appreciate your reply. Just to give an overview, [Creator], one of our UK creators who shares content on [...], could easily be integrated into content as gut-friendly vegan supplements, especially with the mix of flavors and [...].

I've also attached a media kit for you to review.
entries.points: When a brand replies that they are interested, keep the second email short instead of overselling with a long paragraph—the more you type, the less they believe you. Send the creator's name with a YouTube channel hyperlink, a few key stats (subscribers, views, engagement rate), the attached media kit, and just two sentences on why their content and audience fit.
entries.rewrite:
Hey [Name],

Here is [Creator Name (hyperlinked to YouTube channel)] along with their stats (subs, views, engagement rate) and media kit.

We think he would be good for your brand because his content is all about [X] and his audience is all about [Y]. Let me know what you think.

quote.quote: What I usually do when they say, yes, we are interested, I usually send a name with hyperlink of their YouTube channel, you know, a couple of more stats like subs, views, engagement, rate those, and two, three, maybe two sentences.

entries.situation: The student sends another follow-up to a fourth employee ('Angela') at the same brand with long sentences, buzzwords ('align closely with mission and values'), no named creators or deliverables, and a weak closing ('Looking forward to your thoughts').
entries.student_email:
Hi Angela,

I wanted to follow up on my earlier note about exploring new influencer collaborations for [Brand]. Your recent partnership was a fantastic example of how well [Brand] resonates with an engaged audience. If you're open, I can share creator profiles and audience insights from the food and cooking niche that align closely with [Brand]'s mission and values.

Looking forward to your thoughts.
entries.points: Cut corporate buzzwords like 'mission and values' and vague closings like 'Looking forward to your thoughts'. When following up with another employee at a brand, state clearly which colleagues you previously emailed for context, name the specific creators and their strengths, list the deliverable formats available (short-form, integration, dedicated), and finish with a direct CTA.
entries.rewrite:
Hey Angela,

I'm following up—just to give you context, I sent an email to [Employee 1] and [Employee 2]. It's about [Creator 1] and [Creator 2] that we work with, and we think they would be a great fit for displaying your product because [specific creator strength]. We can do short-form content, an integration, or a dedicated video.

[Strong yes/no CTA]

quote.quote: for example, we can do it short form content, we can do integration, can do dedicated, and for them it's very clear, like, okay, this guy has been changed, first of all, second of all, this guy is offering something, and I can understand it

entries.situation: Student submits a cold email to a fitness/nutrition app brand referencing creatine testing from a recent campaign.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Hey [Name], thoughts

Hi [First Name],
Your recent campaign with [Creator] was on point! - Mentioning creatine testing made it easily relatable to anyone taking creatine.
Speaking of relatability, we work with creators like [Creator] who has a big US presence and posts vitamin related advice which made me feel he might be a good fit to share about your app.
Should I send the details?
entries.points: Avoid shallow, ChatGPT-style personalization ('was on point! - explanation') and weak transitions ('Speaking of relatability'). Describe the exact unscripted moment in the integration, transition via 'Speaking of testing' to propose low-pressure test campaigns, say 'we work with YouTube creators, including [Name]' instead of 'creators like [Name]', give an exact US audience percentage (e.g., 63%) rather than 'big US presence', and say 'supplements' rather than 'vitamin related advice'.
entries.rewrite: Speaking of testing, we have a couple of creators that we can run a couple of test campaigns and see how that goes... We work with YouTube creators, including [Creator], who has 63% US audience and his content is all about supplements, which made me feel he might be a good fit to share about your app. Should I send the details?

quote.quote: Personalization should be better. So if you talk about creatine, explain what he did. You know, he took, I don't know, five rounds, this and that. It was integrated seamlessly into the video. wasn't scripted.

entries.situation: Student submits a cold email to a brand's marketing team lead pitching a science and philosophy YouTube channel.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Targeting nerds

Hi Anne,
Tying your platform into [Previous Channel]'s narrative of finding order in chaos was an effective way to reach a science-focused audience.
The channel I'm recommending produces similar deep dive content in the philosophy and science space. His top audience is US-based and matches the intellectual demographic seen in your recent campaign.
Should I send over his channel stats for review?
entries.points: The subject line 'Targeting nerds' and the CTA are good, but the body relies on fluffy templates ('narrative of finding order in chaos') without explaining why the integration worked. Never pitch a creator as having 'similar content' and the same demographic as their previous sponsor, because brands don't want to pay a different creator for the exact same eyeballs; instead, highlight the creator's stats and unique content angle in one sentence.
entries.rewrite: His content is all about [specific angle], he averages [X] views with [Y]% engagement rate... Should I send over his channel stats for review?

quote.quote: You will basically wrap your offer around his content. What is he doing? So he has, let's say, good stats, right? Engager rate and stuff, maybe average views. Those are good. And then you're going to mention why him, why this guy.

entries.situation: Student submits his first tech brand email pitching a creator for a power bank sponsorship, formatted with large blank gaps between paragraphs.
entries.student_email:
Subject: [First Name], thoughts on the following

Hi [First Name],

Highlighting how quickly [Power Bank] charged itself and being enough to travel with by [Creator] video was a great move to make it stand out.

The next strong step could be putting it in the hands of someone who uses multiple devices and travels, making it the go-to power bank option.

On that note, we work with an influencer who does exactly that and has an average of 145k views per video. This power bank would fit his content well.

Let me know your thoughts.

Kind regards,
Muhammad
entries.points: Remove excessive line breaks because huge HTML gaps make a short email look bulky and can trigger spam filters. Avoid sounding like a hyped satisfied customer in the personalization, cut the fluffy transition ('The next strong step could be...'), go straight into the offer, and don't try to sell in the first email—just aim to get a reply with a simple yes/no CTA.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: [First Name], thoughts on this one

The way Jamie used the power bank and showed everything about it was [specific observation]. Speaking of [topic], we have a couple of guys that we work with [and why they fit the brand].

quote.quote: Also, the next step could be, no, no, no, no, no, no. Go straight to your offer. Speaking of this one, could be anything. We have a couple of guys that we work with, and say why they would be good for that brand.

entries.situation: Student submits a second tech brand email claiming a creator has a 'strong US-based audience (34.8%)' and focuses on narrow products.
entries.student_email:
Hi James,
A very smooth transition by [Creator] in your integration. He clearly outlined that there is more to [Product] than meets the eye beyond the standard.
On that note, we work with an influencer who primarily focuses on [Product] products. He also generates around 76K average views and strong US-based audience (34.8%) which may align with your interest.
Are you open to exploring this further?
entries.points: Cut cliché fluff ('more than meets the eye beyond the standard'), describe the creator's broader content niche rather than saying they only focus on one narrow product, and never call a 34.8% US audience 'strong' (strong is 60%+). When ~35% is their top country, say 'the majority of his audience is US' so you don't over-promise and get laughed at.
entries.rewrite: His content is all about [broader category], and the majority of his audience is US...

quote.quote: It's bad use of work. Like, you know, his content is all about this, and then we can squeeze a bunch of different things. But if you say, he only spoke about, he only is talking about power banks, it's not a good idea.

entries.situation: Student submits a third tech brand email (to a VPN/streaming service) praising their features as a 'genius move' and calling a 33.5% US audience 'strong'.
entries.student_email:
Highlighting ability to privately surf the internet, as well as giving customer access to watch movies and shows from around the world was a genius move in [Creator]'s video.
Notably, we work with an influencer who averages 155,000 views and has strong U.S. audience of 33.5%. Their videos are mainly focused on laptops.
entries.points: Stop sounding like a five-star customer review and don't call a sponsorship a 'genius move' because the campaign might have actually flopped; comment on how the creator executed the integration instead. Also, don't call a 33.5% US audience 'strong'—group US and Canada (if over 60%) as 'North America', or group US, UK, and Canada as 'English-speaking audience' or 'Western audience'.
entries.rewrite: The way he did that was [specific observation]... Notably, we work with an influencer who averages 155,000 views and has a strong North American / English-speaking audience...

quote.quote: Customer access to watching movies, shows around the world was, but what is your marketing aspect was this? Was a genius move in someone's video? What if this integration flopped or this collaboration? So don't say it was a good move.

entries.situation: Student submits a cold email to a granola brand ('Original salty sweet granola') opening with a comment on shopping discounts and repeating that food influencers would be a great fit.
entries.student_email:
Hey Dina,
Nothing beats discounts on products when shopping at Costco. The marketing campaign to promote Original Salty Sweet Granola with $3 off was strategic and doing the Purely morning routine giveaway was a good touch for impressions.
The campaign would be great with food cook influencers to promote the brand. We have a few food influencers that would be a natural fit for [Brand]: [Creator 1], [Creator 2]...
entries.points: Keep brand cold emails to 50–70 words total and personalization under 30–35 words so prospects don't stop reading. Cut satisfied-customer openings ('nothing beats discounts...'), don't lecture the brand that food influencers would fit their campaign, and instead name one or two creators and describe their specific video style.
entries.rewrite: We have [Creator 1] and [Creator 2], and their content style is all about [specific style], which would be a natural fit for [Brand].

quote.quote: We have this guy, this guy, this guy, maybe two, and their content is all about this, if it's too generic, it's all about food, not good enough, you know, you can talk about their style

entries.situation: Student submits a cold email to an organic oats brand praising their QR code farm-transparency feature and pitching food influencers who use 'healthy ingredients to make delicious food'.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Thoughts on transparency

The fact that consumers are able to scan a QR code to see where their own oats come from and to know if it's truly organic shows the company does care about transparency. Consumers are able to virtually meet and learn about the farmers and how they grow the oats.
I work with influencers in the food industry, [Creator 1] and [Creator 2]. These influencers would be a natural fit for [Brand], since they incorporate healthy ingredients to make delicious food.
entries.points: Shorten the personalization and tie it to how an influencer presented the QR code feature rather than sounding like a customer praising company transparency. Replace 'I work with' with 'We work with' to sound more professional, and give a specific angle for the creators instead of saying they 'incorporate healthy ingredients to make delicious food', which applies to every food creator.
entries.rewrite: [Creator] showed in a nice way how consumers can check where their oats come from and virtually meet the farmers. We work with [Creator 1] and [Creator 2]...

quote.quote: The fact that consumers are able to scan QR code, satisfy customers, to see where their own oats come from and to know if it's truly organic, shows the company does care about transparency. No, no, no, no. It's too long.

entries.situation: Student struggling with low reply rates submits a cold email to a keyboard/productivity brand referencing an Instagram Reel.
entries.student_email:
Hi [First Name],
I recently saw [Creator]'s reel building the [Brand] Series keyboard, and liked how he built the product step by step in a very natural way. It made the value clear without over-explaining.
Based on that, I thought your product could be a good fit for one of our creators. His audience engages with desk and setup-focused content, especially when we show everyday use. He also reaches a Gen Z lean...
Happy to chat if this sounds interesting.
entries.points: When struggling with reply rates, drastically shorten your email by cutting every unnecessary phrase. Drop the overused 'I recently saw' opening, trim the personalization so it isn't longer than the Reel itself, cut filler transitions ('Based on that...'), cut 'Gen Z lean', and remove 'Happy to chat if this sounds interesting'.
entries.rewrite: Building the [Brand] Series keyboard in [Creator]'s reel made the value clear without over-explaining. One of our creators' audience engages with desk and setup-focused content, especially when we show everyday use.

quote.quote: Guys, one tip for all of you. If you're struggling with the reply rate, just make your email short. Just make it short. So take this email, get rid of everything that you think it's not the best thing, it's not necessary

entries.situation: Student submits an automotive brand outreach email and follow-up referencing a creator who got 400k/40k views on a past integration for another brand.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Is this the best position?

Hi [Name],
Using [Creator] Auto's video to show why MOT checks matter when buying a car was a smart way to position [Brand].
We help brands expand this type of positioning working with automotive creators whose audiences are concentrated in the UK, US, and Australia. These creators have helped brands like [Other Brand] reach over 400k views, and could deliver similar results for [Brand].

Follow-up: Just a quick nudge on helping reaching more people.
entries.points: You can mention a creator's past sponsored video results even if your agency didn't run that deal, and remove corny ad-like lines ('We help brands expand this type of positioning'). However, be careful about promising 'similar results' with high view numbers because it sets expectations and prompts brands to demand a view guarantee. Also, make sure your creators' audience geography matches the brand's target market, and keep follow-ups as a simple reminder on your previous email rather than pitching 'helping reach more people'.
entries.rewrite: The way he grabbed his phone and checked that car in [Creator] Auto's video was a nice move... Follow-up: Just a quick nudge on my previous email.

quote.quote: Maybe, maybe you can be more creative and just say, you know, the way he grabbed his phone, saw that car was, I don't know, this and that was a nice move.

entries.situation: Student submits an overly flattering cold email to a cookware brand ('The innovation of pushing boundaries') listing three influencers and their follower count (1.3 million).
entries.student_email:
Subject: The innovation of pushing boundaries

Hey Tim,
[Brand] is less of a cookware company and more of a tech innovator redefining the kitchen—pushing boundaries with [Product 1], [Product 2], and [Product 3]. It's no surprise they caught the eye of Bon Appetit and Food & Wine.
Since [Brand] prioritizes kitchen innovation, partnering with influencers like [Creator 1], [Creator 2], and [Creator 3] with 6%+ engagement and a following of over 1.3 million home cooks is a natural fit for showcasing [Brand] cookware.
Should I send more details? Let me know.
entries.points: Eliminate over-the-top fanboy fluff praising the brand's products; instead, reference a sponsored video segment, a marketing promotion on their website (such as a 20% discount, which counts as a marketing angle rather than customer praise), or a LinkedIn update. Pitch one or two creators rather than a menu of three, use one CTA, and always pitch average views rather than follower count because follower numbers mean nothing to brands.
entries.rewrite: Hey Tim, just checked your website—the 20% discount is a nice move... [Pitch 1-2 creators with average views instead of followers and a single CTA].

quote.quote: Just talk about segment, bro. Just talk about, if you're afraid to talk about segment, go to their website. Hey, just check your website. 20% discount is a nice move. It is. That's it.

entries.situation: An influencer's talent agency replied to a new student's cold email asking 'what brands are you aligned with?', and the student reads his draft reply that speaks vaguely about targeting aligned brands without naming any specific companies.
entries.student_email: we're targeting brands that align, that value this influencer's audience. I'd be happy to share more about our approach and our partnership development.
entries.points: Do not reply with vague statements without naming brands; indirectly sidestep whether you are currently partnered with them by naming specific target brands (X, Y, and Z) you plan to reach out to, followed by the rest of your message. If they press on whether you already have connections with those brands, be honest that you do not yet, but explain that you have three or four other creators on board and are pitching those brands for sponsorships next month.
entries.rewrite: Brands we're thinking about, or the brands we're going to reach out to are X, Y, and Z. We're targeting brands that value this influencer's audience, and I'd be happy to share more about our approach and our partnership development.

quote.quote: Just say, yeah, brands we're thinking about, or the brands we're going to reach out to are X, Y, and Z. And then you can have the rest of your email to kind of bake it in.

entries.situation: A travel creator asked for a full campaign overview, expected deliverables, and pricing structure, and the student replied proposing one sponsored Instagram Reel and asking for their media kit.
entries.student_email: Thanks for getting back to me. The initial collaboration would be one sponsored Instagram. For pricing, we usually work with either a fixed fee or a CPM-based fee, depending on the creator's profile and the brand's requirements. Feel free to send over to your media kit and review whether your profile matches, what we're looking for.
entries.points: Stating a concrete deliverable ('The initial collaboration would be one sponsored Instagram Reel') and saying you will review whether their profile matches what you are looking for is great positioning. However, cut 'and the brand's requirements' because it invites questions about a brand you don't have, and replace passive phrasing ('Feel free to send over your media kit') with a direct question.
entries.rewrite: Thanks for getting back to me. The initial collaboration would be one sponsored Instagram Reel. For pricing, we usually work with either a fixed fee or a CPM-based fee, depending on the creator's profile. For me to review whether your profile matches what we're looking for, could you share your media kit?

quote.quote: He's like initial collaboration would be one sponsored Instagram. He doesn't have anything, but that's what he wants. He's not saying the brand wants this, or we have this. No, he's an initial collaboration would be this. Boom, makes it real instantly

entries.situation: A creator replied that they are open to hearing more, and the student responded by stating target audience geographies and requesting analytics.
entries.student_email: Thank you for answering back. We're mainly looking for U.S.-U.K. audiences. Could you share and send your analytics?
entries.points: Stating a concrete target demographic such as 'We're mainly looking for U.S.-U.K. audiences' before asking for analytics makes the opportunity feel real and keeps the conversation moving forward without fluff.

quote.quote: Thank you for answering back. We're mainly looking for U.S.-U.K. audiences. Could you share and send your analytics? That's good. Yeah, that's a good email to see, unlike we are mainly looking for U.S.-U.K. audiences. This is good.

entries.situation: A student (Aleem) shares a negotiation thread with a brand where he quoted 2,250 euros, the brand countered around 1,500-1,800 euros, and he closed by asking for a brief and contract if the timeline made sense.
entries.student_email: Thanks for reaching out, I will attach the audience to the channel as requested. The last video trip to someone could work for a segment. The rate is 250 euros... 150, okay, 1500. For test integration, I go, I'm locked up, I'm sure the more we didn't be great. So integration should be first 3 minutes 60 seconds... if you share a quick break, I set a timeline to get the video out fast... if the timeline makes sense, feel free to send contracts, so we can start
entries.points: The power dynamics and closing ask for the brief and contract are strong, but before accepting the brand's 1,800 counteroffer, push back once more with a firm minimum (such as 2,000) since you can always fall back to 1,800 if they refuse.

quote.quote: for example, if I was him, like I would say 2.2, and they would counter with 8.8, 1.8, I would say, okay, 2, 2 is like the bare minimum, 4, 2, 1, 2, this would be my negotiation

entries.situation: A brand lowballs the student at £1,200 and £1,400 total for two integrations per creator. The student counters firmly with a single-integration rate ($2,700), a two-video bundle ($5,000), the CPM breakdown, and an option to do a single video at their original offer.
entries.student_email: The price of both, I just told them straight up, it goes very low. Said usually the price is $2,700 for single integration. We can look at doing a combo. ... $5,000 ... two integrations, the CPM that we're working at ... I can get a single integration around the price that they originally offered
entries.points: When a brand lowballs, reply concisely without fluff, state politely that their offer is too low, explain the CPM, and give structured options (such as a bundle discount or a single integration at their initial budget).

quote.quote: With the counter, he's letting me know, this is very low. So, like, you're saying it in a polite way, but you're like, listen, you're low-boarding me, right? But he's saying it in, like, polite, professional way, right?

entries.situation: The brand counters at £3,750 mentioning a long-term partnership, and the student replies with a one-liner matching their energy, ignoring the long-term partnership fluff, countering at £4,500, and stating 'if not, we'll have to pass.'
entries.student_email: 3,750 is still too low. I could squeeze it in for 4,500. ... if not, we'll have to pass.
entries.points: Match the brand's brevity, completely ignore their 'long-term partnership' fluff without addressing it, don't overly thank them for raising their offer, and project non-neediness by being willing to say you'll pass if the rate isn't met.

quote.quote: Like, you see the long-term payment thing? He didn't even bring it up. He doesn't care about that, because he knows that's fluff. Don't address it, right? Don't be like, yeah, we can squeeze this in, and we're all looking for a long-term partnership.

entries.situation: The brand agrees to move forward only if a £20 CPM target (112,500 view guarantee) is added to the contract. The student counters by dropping both the price (from £4,500 to £4,000) and the view guarantee (to 75k).
entries.student_email: I think it's too high, the view guarantee. So, we can lock in 4,000 for each creator with a 75k view guarantee.
entries.points: When a brand introduces a view guarantee (which removes their risk), do not lower your price at the same time. Frame the view guarantee as something you don't usually do and a special favor for the long-term partnership, while holding firm on your £4,500 price (or increasing it).
entries.rewrite: Look, we don't usually do view guarantees, however, because we want to have a long-term partnership with you, we'll do it, however, the price will need to stay at 4.5k.

quote.quote: Look, we don't usually do. But because we want to have a long-term partnership with you, we'll do it, however, the price will need to, like, 4.5k, but, so I think, instead of negotiating a price there, you should have just negotiated with VG

entries.situation: After an influencer replies with their rate, the student replies briefly referencing specific past collab videos to confirm the integration style and asking for their analytics or media kit.
entries.student_email: just get better of an idea, because I just wanted to know from his videos, better idea you've played collabs, is it like this ones ... I'm confident we could find a match, if you can, can you just send me analytics or a media kit
entries.points: Keep replies to influencers simple, conversational, and on-topic without over-explaining that you are an influencer marketing agency, how you connect brands, or how you take commissions.

quote.quote: Influs do need to know that you are Influs of marketing agency, and you do this, and you do this, and this is how take commissions. They don't need to know that. It's very simple. Just keep it on topic

entries.situation: After the influencer mentions using the brand's product, the student sends over the Q2 campaign brief and asks which flavors the influencer uses most so he can get them added for free.
entries.student_email: working on Q2 for a campaign, and just seeing who's interested in partnerships. I'm guessing you'll be open to a long-term partnership with the brand. Once I have them, I'll send them out, I'll give you a little breakdown ... what flavors do you use the most, and I can see if I can add it to the free.
entries.points: Ask brands to include extra free products or favorite flavors for influencers or their managers; it costs you nothing out of pocket and builds massive goodwill and long-term relationships.

quote.quote: And I spoke to the brand, I said, look, you know, student integration, and could you send an extra product to his manager, who really likes it, and they were like, of course we'll do it, but for me, that built up, like, the relationship really good with that guy

entries.situation: When the influencer pushes back that the 112.5k view guarantee is too high for a first collab, the student replies that they can lower the view guarantee if pricing is adjusted slightly, and suggests placing the integrations on a specific high-performing video series on the creator's channel.
entries.student_email: We can work a lower, work out a lower guarantee if it makes them more comfortable, that's not an issue. The pricing would just need to be adjusted slightly. As a first-time collab is just something we need to be slightly flexible on. Look at your channel, you hit him well above the view guarantee on [certain series of videos] ... what's the timeframe on the videos
entries.points: Show the influencer you know their channel and want to help them succeed by suggesting specific high-performing video series where they can easily hit the view guarantee.

entries.situation: After waiting four days to reply to a creator who sent analytics and quoted 24k (South African Rand), the student tries to warm him up with heavy compliments on his pastry filling recipe and work ethic, points out that 25% of his audience is in South Africa, promises room to revisit and increase rates once brand KPIs are met, and timidly asks if there is flexibility to start at 11k-12k or if that is outside his range.
entries.student_email: I never heard of creamed before, maybe a different version for pastry fillings. It's unique and looks delicious. Definitely saving the recipe. I took time to go through your contact and analytics. It's clear how much time and effort you put into your work. one thing I did notice is that about a quarter of your audience is in South Africa, which is unlikely to be the target for the campaigns we're currently planning. Of course, In the long run, or in the long term, once a relationship is built with the brand, and they see the KPI, they see KPIs being met, there will be room to revisit and increase rates In terms of campaign budgets, while you mentioned, 24k? Is there any flexibility to start at? 11k? 12k? Would that be outside your range?
entries.points: Cut the excessive flattery ('glazing')—which makes creators inflate their prices and wastes their time—and never promise future rate increases you cannot guarantee. Instead of asking timid, double questions, state the maximum budget you can allocate based on the US audience percentage and close with a firm next step to send the contract and creative brief.
entries.rewrite: Hey, since we're looking for higher US percentage, the highest we can allocate is 11k or 10k, if that works for you, let me know, and I'll send you over the contract, I'll send you over the creative brief.

entries.situation: The student writes to the creator claiming to have a few kitchen brands in mind that would align with his content and asks to see his audience analytics 'if you don't mind sharing,' while other students suggest saying 'please share with us' or 'share your media kit.'
entries.student_email: we have a few kitchen brands in mind That we think would align well with your content We'd just like to know you, to know about your audience first, if you don't mind sharing.
entries.points: Do not mention hypothetical kitchen brands unnecessarily, and strike a balanced tone when requesting audience analytics: avoid weak, apologetic phrasing like 'if you don't mind sharing' or 'please,' as well as barked commands like 'give me your media kit.' Clearly state that to move forward you need audience analytics—specifically the top five countries and age groups—since some creators do not know what a media kit is.

entries.situation: A student reaches out to a large AI/tech creator with a subject line about Claude owing $490, offering to approach two specific brands on their behalf, and follows up by explaining their plan to contact those brands.

entries.situation: A student submits a cold email to a tech brand asking whether the subject line or body is bad.
