entries.situation: Gaming outreach student sent an email with the subject line 'Teaming up', referencing a teaming strategy in Showdown, bridging with 'Here's something else we could probably team on', and saying 'I'm reaching out to gaming influencers to help them collaborate with brands like [X and Y]. I think you would be a prime prospect now that you've been uploading again recently.'
entries.student_email:
Subject: Teaming up
That teaming strategy in Showdown is always a highlight for me, unless I'm on the receiving end. Here's something else we could probably team on. I'm reaching out to gaming influencers to help them collaborate with brands like [Brand A] and [Brand B]. I think you would be a prime prospect now that you've been uploading again recently.
entries.points: Good personalization and bridge line, but make the subject line more curiosity-driven around the keyword 'strategy' (e.g., 'Is that strategy even working?'), say 'brands including X and Y' instead of 'like X and Y', and soften 'prime prospect' to 'since you are uploading recently, you could be a fit.'

I'm reaching out to gaming influencers to help them collaborate with brands including [Brand A] and [Brand B]. Since you are uploading recently, you could be a fit.

entries.situation: A student (Mustafa) sends a first cold email to a history and geopolitics YouTuber referencing his latest video on Dancing Bacha Boys and noting his last sponsorship was a month ago.
entries.student_email: Hello [Name], really like the latest video about Dancing Bacha Boys... never hired, never included, never partnered with. I have noticed that your last partnership was about a month ago with [Brand], so I'm wondering if you are currently open to brand/collaborations? Best, Mustafa
entries.points: Do not over-explain basic industry terms by writing 'brand partnerships/collaborations'—just say 'partnership'. Avoid starting with a vague, overused compliment like 'I really like the latest video'; mention a specific detail from the video instead. Finally, strengthen the offer by stating you can bring them brands in their space ('brands like X and Y') without promising those exact brands.
entries.rewrite: We can bring you brands in this space, brands like [Brand A] and [Brand B]. We can help you with catchy brands XYZ.

quote.quote: To be honest, since the offer is the most important part, you should continue. We can bring you brands in this space, something, something, you know, brands like this and these.

entries.situation: A beginner student pitches a documentary/history creator by stating 'I admire the level of research' and introducing his named agency ('I run OK11, a marketing agency specialized in long-form documentary and research-based content').
entries.student_email: Just went through some of your recent videos, like the American Experiment with Stock Crashes. I admire the level of research and detail you put into your content. I run OK11, a marketing agency specialized in long-form documentary and research-based content. I think your channel stands out and would meet the criteria we look for in our partners.
entries.points: Replace fanboy phrasing like 'I admire' with an objective compliment ('The level of research you put into that last video was outstanding'). Do not mention your agency name if you have no social proof, and do not position yourself as an established agency with brands if you are a beginner—the influencer will immediately ask which brands you work with. Instead, frame your offer around providing a service that gets them sponsorships at their desired rate.
entries.rewrite: The level of research you put into that last video was outstanding.

quote.quote: obviously not for free, but I can get you rent, I mean, it is for free, like, you don't have to pay me nothing, you get the price you're looking for, so, insha Allah, wrap your offer around it

entries.points: Avoid needy phrasing like 'I would be happy to add you.' Stay in control and maintain high status by framing it around whether they meet your criteria.
entries.rewrite: I would be interested if you would fit the criteria—I'm sure you will fit the criteria, so let's talk about it.

entries.situation: A student writes a long opening paragraph summarizing the historical plot of the creator's video about King Richard before pitching a roster for historical long-form creators.

entries.situation: A student sends an initial email and follow-up to a racket sports creator with the subject line 'Quick thoughts on your content', tells him 'I'd love to see more doubles-focused tutorials', ends with 'Please let me know', and follows up mentioning his 'fitness-oriented audience'.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Quick thoughts on your content
Hi, the recent content has really caught my eye. I particularly like how you keep the instructional videos concise and practical. I'd love to see more doubles-focused tutorials... Apart from those, you seem to have room for additional relevant sponsorships. Would you be open to... Please let me know. Cheers.

Follow-up: I'm writing to you in case you missed my last email. Pickleball and hydration brands are actually looking for creators like yourself with a fitness-oriented audience. Let me know your thoughts.
entries.points: Avoid the subject line 'Quick thoughts on your content' because ego-driven creators may assume you are criticizing their videos and skip the email. Cut fanboy requests like 'I'd love to see more doubles-focused tutorials', and replace passive CTAs ('Please let me know') with direct questions ('Are you interested? What do you think about it?'). The follow-up line ('Pickleball and hydration brands are actually looking for creators like yourself with a fitness-oriented audience') is much better because it focuses on the creator's audience.
entries.rewrite: Are you interested? Are you in? What do you think about it?

quote.quote: Okay, quick thoughts on your content. This is tricky. Why? Because it might sound like an idea, like I have an idea for your content. Your content is crap, let me help you. They are full of ego, and they will skip your email.

entries.situation: A student emails a brand with the subject line 'Who thought of that angle?', complimenting how a past creator video used research-backed information to address consumer objections, and pitches a sports creator who uses public challenges.

entries.situation: A beginner student sends his first-ever cold emails to tech and productivity influencers, praising their 'incredible view' or being amazed by a Bluetooth phone keyboard, and claiming 'We are currently lining up influencers with brands like Opera and monday.com'.
entries.student_email:
Email 1 Subject: More on your horizon
Your workspace setup really caught my eye, particularly the incredible view of the water and city skyline. Something else that could be on the horizon for you is more brand partnerships. We are currently lining up influencers with brands [like Opera] and others in the tech and productivity space, and we think you might be a good fit. Is this something you're open to?

Email 2 Subject: Never seen that before
Hi, using a physical keyboard to type on your phone, that's certainly something new to us. On a related note, we noticed that a few of your recent videos were not sponsored, and we were curious if you were open to more brand partnerships. We are currently lining up creators with tech brands... Is this something you'd be open to?

Email 3 Subject: The next step
Hey, moving to New York to start a new chapter is a big step, and it looks like you've engineered that transition pretty well. Basically, we are no software engineers, but one thing we can engineer is opportunities... lining up creators with brands in the tech and productivity space such as monday.com, and we think you could be a good fit. Would you be interested?
entries.points: Tone down fanboy adjectives ('caught my eye', 'incredible view') and never act amazed by ordinary things like pairing a Bluetooth keyboard with a phone—use light humor or a clever bridge instead (like the engineering transition in Email 3). Most importantly, do not claim 'we are currently lining up influencers with brands [like Opera or monday.com]' when you have not even started brand outreach yet, as it misleads creators into thinking you already have those deals in hand.
entries.rewrite: In a world of AI, you're linking your keyboard with your phone—how lazy you are!

quote.quote: Hey, moving to New York to start a new chapter is a big step. And it looks like you've engineered that transition pretty well. Basically, we are no software engineers, but one thing we can engineer is opportunities. Okay, nice.

entries.situation: A student sends short, templated one-liner emails to DIY influencers using the subject line 'Partnership Request' or 'Quick question', skipping the offer or claiming 'I work with brands in the DIY space', followed by a bulky agency signature.
entries.student_email:
Email 1 Subject: Partnership request
Saw your latest bathroom transformation for Danny and Kristen. Doing that completely for free for your neighbors says a lot about you. Would you be open to future partnerships?

Email 2 Subject: Partnership Request
Hey, just watched your Home Depot video, the classic metric versus imperial struggle had me laughing when you couldn't read the tape measure at all. I've noticed you worked with brands like Snickers Workwear before. Would you be open to working with more?

Email 3 Subject: Partnership Request
Came across your channel, I love the concept of turning simple builds into actual income. I work with brands in the DIY space and think there could be a fit. Would you be open to partnerships?
entries.points: Never use 'Partnership Request' as a subject line for influencers—it is overused and implies you already have a brand sponsorship in hand. Do not jump from complimenting a bathroom renovation straight to 'Would you be open to future partnerships?' without an offer explaining what you do, and do not falsely claim 'I work with brands in the DIY space' if you do not work with any yet. When you find a funny specific moment (like struggling to read a metric vs. imperial tape measure), use it for both your subject line ('Can you read it?') and a humorous opening line.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Can you read it?
How many football fields, how many hot dogs, how many parrots is that?

entries.situation: A student emails a Marketing Manager at Recraft with the subject line 'Integration idea for V4.1', praising a past creator's dedicated video and pitching a single creator ('Eric') by stating he has '2.4 million impressions over the last 28 days' and that 'he is highly interested in AI'.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Integration idea for V4.1
[Creator's] dedicated video was great at showcasing how to maintain brand visibility consistently across different assets using Recraft's tools. Speaking of visibility, we work with several creators whose audience would be an excellent fit for a similar dedicated video or integration demonstrating [Product]. For example, one of our creators, Eric, has 2.4 million impressions over the last 28 days. His audience is primarily age 25-35, and he is highly interested in AI, productivity, and business systems. Would you be interested in working with our creators?
entries.points: The personalization and transition ('Speaking of visibility...') are solid, and the subject line can be softened to 'This might help you with V4.1'. However, citing '2.4 million impressions over the last 28 days' is meaningless because the brand cannot tell which platform (YouTube long-form, Shorts, IG, TikTok) or how many videos generated those impressions—if sharing analytics, use specific metrics like average views, engagement rate, and top countries, and mention multiple creators. Also describe what the creator's audience is interested in (not what the creator personally likes), and use a more direct CTA like 'Should I send details?' or 'Want to chat about it?'
entries.rewrite:
Subject: This might help you with V4.1
CTA: Should I send details? Let me know what you think. / What do you think about it? Want to chat about it?

quote.quote: would you be interested in working with our peers, I will still go with something stronger, okay, something like, should I send details, let me know what you think, or maybe, what do you think, think, about it?

entries.situation: A student reads out his cold outreach template to a UK-only men's health brand (low testosterone testing) that previously sponsored a football entertainment creator.
entries.student_email: Hey [Name], I've been really impressed with how your brand is raising awareness around low testosterone in men. The campaign with [Influencer] was a great example. His honest breakdown in the simple testing process made it easy to connect with. Are you open to collaborating with more influencers in the same niche, targeting a UK male audience? I see a strong opportunity to grow the message and drive sales. Would you be open to me sending over more details and ideas?
entries.points: The opening compliment referencing their previous influencer campaign is good, but the email is too long and asks 'Would you be open...' twice. Don't ask if they want to target a UK male audience when their product only serves UK men; instead, use the foot-in-the-door method to pitch a specific creator with strong UK male demographics, ask one clear closing question, and offer to jump on a call to show you are serious.
entries.rewrite: We have this guy, has a strong male UK audience, and I believe this guy would do very well because of X, Y, Z. Would you be open to discuss further details on how to collaborate together, or we can jump on a call and discuss further details?

quote.quote: On the email, obviously, you're asking them would you be open twice, right? Would you be open to working with people in the similar niche? Would you be open for me to send? more details right

entries.situation: A student submits a cold email to an outdoor/hiking brand with the subject line 'Check this out' and body copy claiming their creator can 'uplift your presence and drive conversions' with a 'solid 3.7% engagement-to-view ratio.'
entries.student_email:
Subject: Check this out

Came across your partnership with [Creator] on YouTube, wondering if you're interested in reaching more people in the outdoor community. One of our outdoor influencers is able to uplift your presence and drive conversions through 60 to 90 seconds video integrations. With 60% of his audience based in the USA and a solid 3.7% engagement-to-view ratio, we are confident in the impact his content delivers.
entries.points: Personalize the subject line with their name ('Hey [Name], check this out'), cut 'on YouTube' when referencing their collaboration, and don't put a CTA question in the opening line. Never praise a brand's physical product—praise the marketing execution of their past creator integration. Keep language at a 3rd-to-4th-grade reading level instead of promising conversions ('uplift your presence and drive conversions'), don't call a 3.7% engagement rate 'solid' (5% is solid, 10%+ is legendary), and clearly explain what content your unknown creator makes and why it fits the brand.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Hey [First Name], check this out

Came across your collaboration with [Creator]—the way he highlighted [aspect] was a good touch. One of our outdoor influencers makes content on [topic] with 60% of his audience based in the USA, so we are confident he would be a good fit. Let me know what you think—should I send more details?

entries.situation: A student submits a ~200-word cold email to an online education brand with the subject line 'Productivity creators for [Brand] - [Agency Name]' pitching detailed class integration concepts for two creators.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Productivity creators for [Brand] - [Agency Name]

Hope you're having a great week so far. I was impressed by the partnership with [Creator] in June. His content on minimalism and simple living was a great fit for [Brand]. This reminded me of two creators we work with who could build on the success by targeting two key high intent audiences.
[Creator 1]: His content focuses on productivity for creative writers, analytical readers, and hobbies for aspiring polymaths. He is a natural fit for showcasing [Brand] courses on writing, art, and entertainment. In particular, a relevant class would be the art of storytelling.
[Creator 2]: Teaches his audience how to learn efficiently (meta-learning). A partnership where he positions [Brand] as the ultimate platform to apply his study techniques to attract dedicated lifelong learners like himself. The relevant class would be Neil deGrasse Tyson's class on...
We believe both creators have high potential in showcasing... Would you be interested in learning more on either of these creators, including their audience analytics and rates? Let me know what you think.
entries.points: Remove your agency name from the subject line and body—brands only care about the offer, not who your agency is. Keep cold emails to 50–70 words (3 sentences for opening, 5–7 sentences max for offer, 1 sentence for CTA) at a 4th-grade reading level so a busy brand manager can skim it in 5 seconds. Cut fluff like 'Hope you're having a great week so far,' don't say 'I was impressed' (which kills power dynamics), don't say 'This reminded me of two creators,' and save specific video/integration ideas for after they reply.
entries.rewrite:
Subject: Productivity creators for [Brand]

I saw your partnership with [Creator]—his content on minimalism and simple living was a good showcase for [Brand]. We work with a couple of creators, including [Creator 1] and [Creator 2], with [X] audience and [Y] average views, whose content is all about [topic], and we are confident they would be a good fit. Should I send more details?

quote.quote: I would say three sentences, okay? Three sentences here are good enough. Explaining everything. In offer part, which is this offer part, you can go five, maybe seven, if you like to write. CTA should be just one sentence.

entries.situation: The talent agent declined CPM/VG terms on the first creator and pitched two other creators; the student replied that the other two could possibly work if the agent sends their demographics first.
entries.student_email: Thanks for letting you know in advance, the other two could possibly work, but you have to learn more about them. Could you please send over their demographics?
entries.points: Use conditional, high-status language ('the other two could possibly work, but...') so the agent has to comply and send demographics before you commit.

quote.quote: The other two could possibly work, you know, hey. They could work, but, but, like, you need to answer our question, big man, like, we got, you know, we got the offer, now you need to comply, maybe they're good, but first send us this,

entries.situation: While negotiating rates with the talent agent, the student held firm on their offer but offered a higher rate if the creator included a view guarantee (VG).
entries.student_email: If you're happy to include the VG, we could offer a higher rate.
entries.points: Holding firm on your base offer while offering a higher rate only if the creator includes a view guarantee (VG) is an effective negotiation play.

quote.quote: If you're happy to include the VG, we could offer a higher rate. Okay, this is good. Whoa, whoa, whoa, whoa. What was this? Okay, this is good.

entries.situation: The talent agent threatened to block access to all their creators unless the student agreed to their rate on Name 5, and insulted the student ('not impressed... give yourself a chance to redeem yourself'). The student caved, accepted the 1k rate citing 'median views' and engagement rate, and thanked the agent for their honesty.
entries.student_email: hi, given median views... of 40k, and no peer response service, or case studies, we wouldn't normally work with rates of 1 for 1k, however, because of this engagement rate, and the fact you can see a long-term partnership with yourself and your agency, we would accept your offer. ... I appreciate your honesty and look forward to working with you in the future.
entries.points: Never use 'median views' (use average views), never cave using flimsy excuses you already knew before negotiating, and never thank an agent who insults you or tells you to 'redeem yourself.' You hold the money and the leverage. If you agree to include the creator only to get access to another creator on their roster, state that directly and demand professional communication moving forward while showing readiness to walk away.
entries.rewrite: Given Name 5 average views of 40k and no previous sponsor or case studies, we wouldn't normally work with rates of 1k. However, since Name 4 is a very good fit, we are willing to include him in our campaign. However, moving forward, if you want to kick off this long-term partnership with this brand, and have more opportunities, we would have to keep it more professional. If you want to move forward, let me know. If not, no worries.

quote.quote: However, moving forward, if you want to kick off this long-term partnership with this brand, and have more opportunities, we would have to keep it more professional. If you want to move forward, let me know. If not, no worries.

entries.situation: A YouTuber with 1.2M subscribers whose views have dropped from 1M to an average of 60k across erratic topics (military history, philosophy, comedy, poems) admits his channel earnings have fallen from $4k-$5.5k/month to barely $3k. The student replies with three lines of excessive praise and offers $1,000 for an initial test integration, ending with 'let me know what you think,' after which the creator asks for a performance-based per-view deal.
entries.student_email: Thank you for sharing that. ... appreciate the context, and I can see the value in your longer military focus ... however, for now, with safe initial testing regression, that number would realistically make work for a K ... with a plan to get your long-term sponsorship ... let me know what you think
entries.points: Subscriber count means nothing when a creator's views have collapsed and their content topics are erratic. When a declining creator admits they are struggling, you hold all the leverage: do not cross into 'fan territory' with multi-line flattery, do not offer as high as $1,000, and do not ask 'let me know what you think.' Be polite, brief, and firm by stating the exact budget you can allocate ($400–$500 for the first test video, with room to increase later if it performs well).
entries.rewrite: Hey, bro, thanks for sharing that. For the first one, we can allocate you 400, 500 USD, I don't know, okay? If that does well, maybe we can, you know, talk about, you know, higher rates in the future. Let me know if that works for you, and I'll get back to you once I have more details.

quote.quote: he's going, 1.2 million subs, how his golden eyes are gone, golden day, sorry, eyes, and he was hitting a million, now he's averaging 60k, I wouldn't work with this guy in the first place, and his subs mean nothing, nothing, literally nothing

entries.situation: Student submits a cold email to a tech YouTuber reviewing a MacBook.

entries.points: Avoid generic praise ('Nice quality review overall'), overused course lines ('Your last couple of videos were not sponsored. Did you stop doing them?'), and talking directly about missing monetization as a stranger. Instead, offer to handle brand outreach for them and use a direct CTA.

entries.situation: Student submits two more cold emails (about drawer organizers and the S26 Ultra camera) with repetitive short follow-ups.
entries.student_email:
Email 1:
Drawer organizers look game-changing. You make them seem like a must-have.
Speaking of game-changing, I simply want to check if you'd be interested in a couple of brands, and if we have them in mind, am I aligned with your upcoming content. Should we discuss this further?
Follow-up: Brands in the space moving quickly this month, and your name is still on the list.

Email 2:
Downgrading the S26 Ultra camera seems strange. Let's hope it doesn't make that big of a deal.
Talking about deals, we are drafting a new influencer sponsorship campaign. We are planning to work with tech brands that align with your audience.
Follow-up: Reach out again to make sure that last email slipped through cracks.
entries.points: Avoid fanboy personalization without substance, fix broken English with Grammarly, and make the offer concrete by naming specific brands or asking if you should send a list of brands rather than repeating 'brands in the space are moving quickly this month and your name is still on the list'.
entries.rewrite: Talking about deals, we are drafting a new influencer sponsorship campaign for brands like [Brand 1], [Brand 2], and [Brand 3]. Are you in?

quote.quote: Drawer organizers look game-changing. You make them seem like a must-have. You're missing on why. Must-have. Okay, don't just stop on fanboy talk. Come on, give me something.

entries.situation: A student sends a compressed, single-paragraph email to an entertainment/travel brand saying they 'recently checked' a 'recent YouTube video', represent 'a few influencers who would like to speak to their audience about this product', and asking 'Would you be against me sending over some profiles for you to check out?'
entries.student_email: Hello team, I recently checked [recent YouTube video] and noticed that the feature, and loved how easy it looked to carry around, and actually used, felt super practical. We represent a few influencers who would like to speak to their audience about this product. Would you be against me sending over some profiles for you to check out?
entries.points: Break the email into separate paragraphs using line breaks so it isn't a compressed wall of text, and avoid repeating 'recently' and 'recent' or acting like you stumbled on their video by accident. Be specific instead of saying 'a few influencers', drop claims that influencers are passionate about speaking to their audience about the product, replace defensive CTA phrasing like 'Would you be against' with 'Would you be open', and offer specific 'analytics' or 'YouTube channels' instead of vague 'profiles'.
entries.rewrite: I saw your last video... Would you be open to me sending over some analytics / YouTube channels for you to check?

quote.quote: Would you be against? So we are not fighting, We are not fighting with them. You know, would you be against? Would you be ready to fight with me? No, just see. Just see. Would you be open? Open is good enough.

entries.situation: A student emails a fitness brand's Director of Marketing starting every paragraph with 'I', flexing that he is a fitness enthusiast who travels a lot and needs to download their app, vaguely pitching a YouTuber with a 'really engaged audience' filming a series, mentioning he already emailed others at the company, signing as 'Founder and Manager' with a linked website, and sending a one-line follow-up.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Influencer Partnerships?

I recently came across a video from [Influencer] that featured [Brand]. And I must say, as a fitness enthusiast who travels a lot, I need to download it.

I represent [Influencer], a YouTuber with a really engaged audience. He is currently filming a high production travel and training series, and so I believe he would be great at talking about your app.

I have reached out to [Name] and others, but wanted to contact you directly given your role as a Director of Marketing.

If you're interested, I'd like to explore this further.

Best regards,
[Name]
Founder and Manager
[Website Link]

Follow-up: Just wanted to see if you read my last email :)
entries.points: Stop starting every paragraph with 'I'—focus on the brand and their uplift, and don't act like a customer or flex personal hobbies. Include concrete engagement numbers (if strong) and specific details about where and what the creator is filming. Don't tell a director you already emailed 'others' at the company, as they'll assume someone else will handle it. Use a stronger CTA, drop 'Founder' from your signature, write your website as plain text rather than a hyperlink, and write longer, specific follow-ups so they don't get flagged as spam.
entries.rewrite: I'm just following up to see if you're interested or if partnerships with this type of influencers is something that you're looking for

quote.quote: Yeah, bro, you're not customer. You're an agency for selling influencers. Don't be, I need to download it. I mean, if you can, just don't say it. Just don't say it, you know. Okay, you need to download it and don't flex about yourself.

entries.situation: A student reaches out to men's lifestyle, fashion, and health brands with initial emails and follow-ups, getting zero replies.

entries.situation: A student submits their first brand outreach email in the automotive and engineering niche and asks what to improve besides length.
entries.student_email:
Subject: Idea for the next build

I noticed [Brand] works with creators like [Creator] in the automotive and engineering space. I am currently working with another creator in that space whose content lines up naturally with what you are already doing. Change the influencer-style subject line ('Idea for the next build') to a B2B subject line, make the personalization about a specific past sponsorship, name the creator and the exact vehicle/product they would build a custom prototype for, and use 'Do you need more details?' as the CTA.

He could design a custom part for his SUV build using your [specific product] in his video. Do you need more details?

entries.situation: A student submits five brand outreach emails in the grappling/BJJ/MMA niche that personalize from a marketing agency angle and cite metrics like '74% watched beyond 30 seconds', '3% engagement rate', and '34%' audience share.
entries.student_email:
Email 1:
Subject: They might work for you
Targeting the mental load pain point was a good way to make [Product] relevant. A live unpredictable public sparring challenge keeps the audience watching to see what happens next while [Creator]'s introduction video makes his transition from grappling onto games... Which style would better fit?

Email 2:
Subject: This might be useful
Mental load of getting back into routines after summer and framing [Product] as a solution was clever. 74% of viewers watched beyond 30 seconds of this video, making it a perfect place to integrate your pre-roll, and last month other brands leveraged this.

Email 3:
Subject: Next influencer idea
Hi, B-rolls of the London trip were a good way to build customer trust. Kabeer's Muay Thai trips averaged 3% engagement rate, making them a strong format for putting [Brand] in front of an engaged audience. Will this feature in the next video?
entries.points: The marketing-lens personalizations (like praising London trip B-rolls for building customer trust) and the subject line 'Jack, this might work' are good, while 'Next influencer idea' is too pitchy. However, the offers delay naming the creator like a guessing game and brag about weak numbers (watching past 30 seconds is not retention, 3% engagement on a small channel is weak compared to 5–7%+, and 34% audience share is low). Put the creator's name first and state clearly why they can outperform.

[Creator A], who did [B-rolls of the London trip to build customer trust], was good. We have [Creator B], who can do even better—here is why: [strong specific reason/5-7%+ engagement]. Should I send more details?

entries.situation: A student submits four initial brand outreach emails and one follow-up in the gaming PC/tech niche (which got one next-day reply).
entries.student_email:
Email 1:
Subject: Why not be seen in this manner, Jack?
Mentioning the material on your PC case that made it look different was a good touch in the collaboration with [Creator A]. Speaking of different, [Creator B] can show how your PC case provides a different style from the ones he used previously for custom builds.

Email 2:
Subject: Why not gain the high ground, Jack?
Mentioning how you are lowering the price of your laptop in this collaboration made you stand out from your competitors. Another way to stand out is by positioning your laptops as the most powerful portable device when [Creator B] reviews another. Would you be interested?

Follow-up:
Hey, wanted to bring this to your attention. We also recommend working with [Creator C] since he got a PC. He can show his audience how the lower [feature] gives his PC a new look.

Email 3:
Subject: Isn't that a missed opportunity?
Mentioning the product with standard warranty was a nice way to incentivize the audience of [Creator A]. You can incentivize [Creator B]'s audience by showing how your thermal paste lowers CPU temperature when he covers CPU development.
entries.points: Rated 7/10: the marketing-expert personalizations (noting how a past collaboration highlighted a lower laptop price, extended warranty, or PC case material) and focusing on end results rather than product features are strong. However, the rhetorical-question subject lines ('Why not be seen in this manner, Jack?', 'Isn't that a missed opportunity?') are for influencers rather than B2B, Sentence 1 should lead with the collaboration name first, and the offer should emphasize *why* the pitched creator is the right match rather than telling the brand what to do.
entries.rewrite: In the collaboration with Mr. Luce, mentioning the material on your PC case that made it look different was a good touch. Speaking of a good touch, [Creator B] would be a great fit because [reason why his custom builds/audience match], and he can show how your PC case provides a different style from the ones he used previously.

quote.quote: Mentioning the material on your PC case that may look different was a good touch in the collaboration with this guy. Flip it. In the collaboration. With Mr. Luce. Mentioning material on your PC case that may look different was a good touch.

entries.situation: A student reads out the follow-up email he sent to a brand contact (Nikita) one week after sending over a list of influencers.
entries.student_email: hello, Nikita. hope this finds you well. Just wanted to follow up and see if you had the chance to see my last email in the review, the list of influencers. Feel free to reach out for any further questions. Best regards, Soufiane.
entries.points: Never send a generic 'just checking in on my last email' follow-up because it annoys the prospect and adds zero value. In the first follow-up, add value by pitching a concrete upcoming video from your influencer and offering the brand first right of refusal; in later follow-ups, let them know you will assume they are not interested and approach a competitor.
entries.rewrite: look, we've got this video, we're looking for a sponsor, um, and we thought of you first before going ahead to someone else. Right? So do let us know if you're interested.
